The Duchess of Sussex has said she is “deeply distressed” over accusations involving child sexual abuse images against her estranged father, Thomas Markle Sr, and revealed she was made aware of “disturbing allegations” against him in 2018 by the Metropolitan police.
Meghan issued a statement after the Sun newspaper published claims that her half-brother Thomas Markle Jr alleged he had found a stash of images belonging to their father at his former home in the Philippines.
In an interview with the Daily Mail, Markle Sr denied possessing child sexual abuse images, calling the accusations “sick lies”.
It is understood that authorities in the UK had previously told Meghan that allegations made about her father in a 2018 letter sent to Scotland Yard, and subsequently shared with her by the police, were being investigated.
Meghan was informed by the Met of the “troubling and disturbing” allegations in the summer shortly after her wedding, it is believed.
In a statement through her spokesperson, Meghan said: “I am deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed.
“In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.
“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them.
“I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.
“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”
The 2018 letter was understood to have been shared with Meghan by the royalty and specialist protection unit within the Met police.
Markle Sr has been estranged from the duchess since he failed to attend her wedding to Prince Harry on health grounds, and has never met his grandchildren, Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five.
The Sun reported that Markle Jr told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr was living until he returned to the US in May after having a stroke.
Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the Sun reported.
Meghan’s father has vehemently denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail that the accusations were “sick lies”.
He told the newspaper the computers had not been in his possession since he left Rosarito, Mexico, with his son in January 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”.
Speaking from a rehabilitation centre in Florida, where he is learning to walk with a prosthetic limb after his left leg was amputated because of a blood clot, he told the Mail: “I’m shocked, I’m hurt and I’m very upset that my son is making these accusations against me. I could never do what I’m being accused of. It’s the worst thing anyone could accuse me of.
“This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”

- Roblox The Hollow runs for nine nights, with a new game and a monster every day.
- The event features daily quests, haunted mazes, and exclusive rewards.
- Players can complete maze puzzles and quests to unlock UGC items and badges.
After the success of last year’s The Hunt, Roblox is back again with another spooky Halloween event called The Hollow. This time, you are at a haunted plaza, and your goal is to clear every floor by solving puzzles and collecting exclusive rewards. This guide will tell you how to solve every puzzle quest in Roblox The Hollow event through a detailed walkthrough so you can earn every badge and unlock every UGC reward.
Getting Started with Roblox The Hollow
The Hollow is a similar event to Roblox The Hunt. Once you launch the Roblox experience, you will spawn in a destroyed floating city. In front, you will see the Bloxhilda’s Plaza; this is where you will access most of the activities. Here you can:
- Access the shop to buy items to explore the plaza and customize your avatar.
- Teleport to different games and complete their objectives to collect rewards.
- Enter the theater and watch streams with other players.
- Access the elevator to unlock relics.
Note: To buy things from the shop, you will need cash, which you get by completing the quests.
Day 1: All Quests and Maze Puzzle Solution
Floor 1 Maze Puzzle and Rewards
The Floor 1 maze drops you in a large lobby that looks endless, especially because you get chased by the Seek entity from Doors. You need to find all the missing pieces of the puzzle before you can get the relic. Follow these steps to complete it:
- Enter The Hollow event hub and follow the highlighted path to the elevator.
- Take the elevator to the first floor.
- Explore the maze and collect all five missing puzzle pieces.
- Find the Relic Room and place all the pieces into the puzzle.
- Rearrange the pieces to connect the starting point to the endpoint. Both ends should light up when the puzzle is correct.
- Open the door, collect the relic, and return to the elevator without getting caught.
Completing this puzzle will give you Lord Umberhallow BLOXikin UGC that you can equip on your shoulder and an exclusive badge.
How to Complete the Doors Candy Vault
Day 1 begins with the Doors, one of the most popular survival/escape experiences on Roblox. This quest requires you to open a Candy Vault and collect candies along the way and escape the estate before the timer runs out. You can play with your friends. Follow these steps to complete this quest:
- Enter the Doors experience from The Hollow hub.
- Explore the mansion and search drawers for candy and keys.
- Once the vault opens, the timer starts ticking, and you only get 20 minutes to make your way through the floors while avoiding the entities.
- Run downstairs and eat all the candies you find along the way.
- Put the ones you don’t want into the cauldron, as some candies might take some of your HP.
- Reach the bottom floor and exit the vault to finish the challenge.
Note: Keep an eye on Abe as you explore. He can sneak up behind your group, so one player should watch him while the others move through the floors.
Completing this challenge will give you the Sweet Deceit badge and unlock the All Seeking Antlers UGC.
Stay tuned on this page, bookmark it, and revisit on day 2 for more puzzle solutions and the full Roblox The Hollow walkthrough guide for every quest.
What is Roblox The Hollow event?
The Hollow is a Roblox Halloween event where you can complete daily challenges and solve maze puzzles to earn exclusive rewards.
How many days does The Hollow Event Last?
The event will last nine nights, with a new monster and maze challenge each day.
How do I claim The Hollow rewards?
To claim the rewards, you need to complete the challenge and return to the Hollow hub. This is where you can interact with the displayed reward and unlock it.

UPDATED FRIDAY PM: Right now, Warner Bros/DC’s R-rated Clayface is puffing its chest with a $9.5 million Friday (including previews) and an estimated $23M-$25M opening weekend at 3,458 theaters. If that comes to be it’s a solid start in the vicinity of other mid-October genre movies like Smile ($22.6M opening) and last year’s Black Phone 2 ($27.2M).
But it still remains to be seen what type of blood transfusion audiences give Nathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes this weekend as the A24 documentary You Can See Everything is coming on strong with a $5.8M Friday, up 5% from a week ago, and what’s looking to be an awesome $19M+ second weekend after its wide expansion from 855 locations to 2,655.
That will get the 10 -day total for the doc to $44.6M. Some rivals think a $20M+ second weekend remains a possibility. But at a $19M second frame, You Can See Everything is up 22% from its opening. Obsession was +39% in its second weekend (though that was during a Memorial Day weekend).
Watch on Deadline
At this point in time, Clayface is keeping himself together for a No. 1 finish atop the domestic charts after great audience scores (93% on RT) and solid reviews (75%).
RelishMix says, “Convo runs positive for Clayface with a felling that James Gunn has finally cracked the code on how to make a villain movie, without Batman holding its hand. Fans see the trailer like a masterclass in restraint, ‘the zero-dialogue approach and letting dread do the talking is working.’ There’s affection bubbling up for Batman: The Animated Series with comments pitching Mr. Freeze, Scarecrow and Poison Ivy follow-ups. Viewers are also spinning Clayface against Spider-Man villain universe, ‘This as the blueprint nobody asked Sony to copy but should have.’ plus, ‘No Dialogue, only horror sounds, and some eerie song playing in the background, THIS is what a horror teaser should be like.'”
Fathom’s theatrical release of Laika’s stop-motion Wildwood is also coming in where it was expected: at $11M+ in third place after a $4.2M Friday (including previews). That’s much better than the Portland, OR studio’s previous movie, 2019’s The Missing Link ($5.9M), which United Artists/Annapurna handled at the time. Travis Knight’s previous Laika movie, Kubo and the Two Strings, released by Focus Features, opened to $12.6M in 2016 and legged out to $48M domestic.
Paramount/Legendary’s Street Fighter is fourth at 3,575 theaters with a second Friday of $2.7M and a three-day of $9.5M, -79%, for a 10-day cume of $47.8M.
In No. 5 is Black Bear’s $2.5M domestic acquisition of period sex comedy Wicker, with a first Friday (plus previews) of $2.4M and a 3-day of $6M+ at 1,471 locations. This is a great start for Black Bear and an upscale female movie. Audience score on RT is excellent at 94% on par with critical score of 93%.
Outside the top 5 is Sony/Spyglass/TSG’s Klara and the Sun from Taika Waititi and starring Jenna Ortega and Amy Adams. The movie isn’t looking good at a $300,000 Friday at 880 locations for what’s looking like a 3-day of $900K. Critics refuse to be emotionally moved with 55 reviews at 23% Rotten.
UPDATED FRIDAY AM after Thursday PM exclusive: Warner Bros/DC’s Clayface came in exactly where we spotted it: at $3.5M in previews. We understand the fanboys who showed up last night enjoyed it too with 4 1/2 stars on PostTrak and a 94% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes.
Meanwhile, A24’s You Can See Everything ends its first week with $25.6M, compared to Street Fighter‘s $38.3M.
The three-hour Nathan Fielder-Lance Oppenheim documentary bested Street Fighter and was the No. 1 movie on Monday ($2.5M), Wednesday ($2.6M) and Thursday ($2.2M). Tuesday was strong with $2.6M.
Black Bear’s Sundance pickup Wicker is off to a solid specialty start with $620K in previews, and that’s with 92% reviews and 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes. Pic is booked at 1,471 locations. Previews are above Conclave ($491K, $6.6M opening) and not far from The Social Reckoning ($617K previews, $5M opening), and similar to The Roses, another Olivia Colman movie ($606K, $6.2M opening).
Taika Waititi’s feature take of Klara and the Sun is in limited release this weekend in under 1,000 locations. Previews were shiny with $85K at 782 sites from showtimes that began at 4 p.m.
Here are this week’s grosses:
- Street Fighter (Par) 3,575 theaters, Wk $38.3M/Wk 1
- You Can See Everything (A24) 855 theaters, Wk $25.6M/Wk 1
- Other Mommy (Uni) 3,370 theaters, Wk $11.1M (-70%), Total $47.6M/Wk 2
- Whalefall (Dis) 3,065 theaters, Wk $10.8M/Wk 1
- Sense and Sensibility (Focus) 2,545 theaters, Wk $10.2M/Wk 1
PREVIOUSLY, Thursday PM EXCLUSIVE: Peter Safran and James Gunn’s DC entry into lower-budget genre movies, Clayface, is off to a solid start in previews Thursday night with an estimated $3.5 million, if not more.
Domestic weekend forecasts are between $20M-$25M, which if that occurs would deliver the newly combined Paramount-Warner Bros its second back-to-back No. 1 opener at the box office after last weekend’s Street Fighter ($31M).
Previews started at 2 p.m. today for the James Watkins-directed Clayface, which though based on the Batman villain is a stand-alone story about babyfaced Hollywood actor Matt Hagen (Tom Rhys Harries), who in reaching for the stars falls short, kisses the wrong girl at the party, and — oops — there goes his face. The screenplay by Mike Flanagan in December 2024 got Gunn and Safran excited, and it was off to the races to make this movie, which is coming in at a net production cost of $44M before P&A, shot in the UK.
In regards to preview comps, Clayface‘s money is higher than the R-rated Sony/Marvel movie Kraven the Hunter ($2M previews, $11M dismal opening), and not far from the pre-Covid PG-13 DC spinoff Birds of Prey ($4M previews, $33M opening). Next to horror films, Clayface‘s cash is similar to Blumhouse Atomic Monster’s Other Mommy ($3.6M previews, $27.8M opening) and ahead of 2022’s Smile ($2M previews, $22.6M opening).
The hope is that the DC movie isn’t frontloaded tonight, as all eyes are on the potential hold of A24 documentary You Can See Everything following its great midweek business and fantastic $15.6M opening last weekend. The documentary co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim about Theranos architect Elizabeth Holmes expands to 2,600 locations Friday after bowing in 855 sites.
Clayface glides into the weekend with a 76% certified fresh Rotten Tomatoes critics score, which is higher than The Flash (63%), Supergirl (52% Rotten), Joker Folie à Deux (31%), Shazam: Fury of the Gods (49%), James Wan’s Aquaman and the Lost Kingdom (33%) and almost as good as Birds of Prey (79% certified fresh).
Note this isn’t the first time in DC movie history that it has ventured into low- to midsized-budget fare. In the early aughts there was DC/Vertigo’s The Losers, in 2010, which cost $25M before P&A and opened to $9.4M and finaled at $23.5M domestic. There was also the Josh Brolin-Megan Fox 2010 fantasy western Jonah Hex, which bombed with a $5.3M opening, $10.5M stateside final next to its $47M production cost. And there was the Wachowskis’ R-rated 2005 feature take of the DC Vertigo title V for Vendetta, which yielded a No. 1 $25.6M North American opening off a $50M production cost. Its final domestic take was $70.5M, and $134.7M global.
We’re hearing that previews for the Fathom release of Laika’s stop-motion animated title Wildwood is around $1M. The hope is that the Travis Knight-directed movie can break double-digits in its opening. The 100% certified fresh critical score and 98% with audiences on RT will certainly help.
We’ll have more preview grosses in Friday AM.

Why Rwanda's deal for F1 race remains controversial
- Published
Formula 1 will return to Africa for the first time in a generation after Rwanda agreed a 10-year contract to stage a race, with the sport's governing body (FIA) keen to create a "lasting legacy".
The event - to be called the African Grand Prix - will be held on a new, purpose-built circuit in Bugesera, 25 miles south of the capital Kigali, with the first edition in the "early 2030s".
For Rwandan President Paul Kagame, the ambition is to "pave the way" for other F1 races on the continent.
However, the announcement has drawn criticism from some quarters amid allegations of sportswashing and questions around the East African country's human rights record.
Why is this big news?
Africa has not hosted an F1 race since 1993, and the clamour to return to the continent has been growing in recent years - with seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton among those leading the calls.
Morocco was the first African nation to host a Grand Prix in 1958 and 23 races were then held in South Africa between 1962 and 1993.
President Kagame said it was "an honour and privilege" for Rwanda to be chosen for its return.
"This partnership is long overdue but it is a success and a milestone for the entire continent - especially for African fans," he added.
South Africa had been keen to secure its own F1 race, and sports minister Gayton McKenzie remains bullish about his country's hopes of emulating Rwanda.
"They have worked on it longer than SA and deserve it," he posted on X.
"Remember though that one country, Italy, has had two [F1 races] a year, and some react like a continent of [54] countries can only get one. SA will get F1, even before 2030."
- Rwanda to host F1's first race in Africa since 1993 
  - Published1 day ago
- A 'landmark' moment - why has Rwanda been chosen to host F1? 
  - Published1 day ago
What is still to be decided?
The year of the first African Grand Prix in the 2030s, and its timing in the calendar, are yet to be announced.
F1 is likely to want to avoid holding the race in Rwanda's main rainy season of March to May, while there is a shorter, less disruptive, rainy season from October to November.
The sport is committed to keeping the season at no more than 24 races.
Former F1 driver Alex Wurz will be involved in the design of the circuit, which is due to use the undulating Rwandan landscape to produce a track with a natural flow and elevation changes of nearly 200m to challenge drivers.
Could the race boost African participation?
Jody Sheckter remains the only African to win the F1 Drivers' Championship, triumphing in 1979 with Ferrari.
"It's so expensive to get in," the South African told Newsday on the BBC World Service when discussing whether or not the race in Rwanda could open the door to more drivers from the continent.
"I built my own cars at the beginning. You can't do that anymore."
Africans hoping for a career in motorsport have previously had to chase their dream overseas, according to fellow driver Axcil Jefferies, who has previously competed in Formula 2.
But the Zimbabwean believes that could now change.
"F1 coming to Africa will highlight to everyone what a big industry motorsport is," he said.
"All the elements will inspire the youth, whether that's to come in as an engineer, as a mechanic, as drivers, as team coordinators."
South African presenter Kriya Gangiah, who hosts SuperSport's F1 Extra Africa Trackside podcast, is also hopeful of a boost in the number of female fans and drivers in Africa.
"The more you see something and the more that is present in your world, the more you take interest in it," she said.
"Being in paddocks in South Africa, you're seeing the amount of women that are making it into the sport and are actually doing really well. A lot of the girls are giving the guys a proper run for their money."
Why is the deal controversial?
Allegations of sportswashing - hosting sporting events to improve a country's international reputation - have long been levelled against Rwanda.
Securing an F1 race is part of the country's wider strategy to increase tourism, international investment, services and entertainment.
The country has hosted the Basketball Africa League finals in all but one year since 2021 and staged cycling's World Road Championships last year, the first time the event had been held in Africa.
Visit Rwanda has either sponsored or had partnerships with Arsenal, Bayern Munich and Paris St-Germain, although its sleeve sponsorship of the Gunners ended this year after drawing criticism from supporter groups.
However, the tourism brand then became the front-of-shirt sponsor of fellow Premier League club Aston Villa.
Meanwhile, Rwanda's central African neighbour, the Democratic Republic of Congo, has filed a case against the country at the International Court of Justice, accusing it of breaching multiple international treaties covering genocide prevention, racial discrimination, women's rights and torture.
Human Rights Watch previously said that "the space for freedom of expression" and "political autonomy" is shrinking in the country.
"Rwanda is buying into the world's biggest sports to polish its image and deflect from its appalling human rights record," said Amnesty International UK's head of campaigns Felix Jakens.
"A 10-year Grand Prix 'presented by Visit Rwanda' is a sportswashing prize for the Rwandan authorities."
The Rwandan government has dismissed such accusations, with chief tourism officer Irene Murerwa calling them "a distraction' from the "amazing and outstanding achievements the country has made" when previously challenged by BBC Sport Africa.
"The benefits trickle down to every Rwandan," she said in December 2024. "Hosting F1 would be another step in our journey to becoming a world-class destination."
What has F1 said?
F1 is not blind to issues around sportswashing, with several countries on the calendar accused of utilising the strategy - not least Saudi Arabia.
F1's own charter commits it to "respecting internationally recognised human rights in its operations globally" and emphasises the importance of understanding and monitoring potential human rights impacts and engaging with stakeholders.
A statement in the context of the Rwandan announcement said: "We have the opportunity to inspire and bring the passion of F1 to 100 million people across Africa and sport can be a positive force for good."
However, it has still drawn criticism from human rights organisations, with Amnesty International's Jakens believing the organisation's words "ring hollow".
"It should use its influence with the Rwandan authorities to push for change, rather than lend its brand to a PR exercise," he said.
When asked about the sportswashing accusations levelled against Rwanda when it was bidding to host a race, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem told BBC Sport Africa: "When people cannot get what they want, they always blame it on sportswashing.
"I honestly don't care about what they say."

India began its FIFA Under-15 World Cup campaign with a 4-2 win over Laos in Azerbaijan on Saturday.
Bibiano Fernandes’ Blue Colts made a bright start on Saturday morning and created two chances in the opening four minutes. A powerful left-footed effort from inside the box by Deepak Singh Arambam was pushed away by the Laos goalkeeper Anousith Souksavanh in the third minute, before Macdonnish was denied by the advancing custodian a minute later.
India took the lead in the seventh minute after brilliant footwork from Deepak, who worked his way into the small box before cutting the ball back for Macdonnish to tap home.
The pressure continued to pay off, with India doubling its advantage in the 11th minute. A Laos clearance was blocked by Deepak, and the ball fell to R Lalremruatfela, who took a touch before slamming home with his left boot.
ALSO READ | Vincent Kompany collapses during training
Laos responded almost immediately, pulling a goal back in the 12th minute through Anavin Xayyasone, whose long-range effort left India goalkeeper Jenit Ningthoujam rooted to the spot.
The tempo dropped following the early flurry of goals, with neither side creating a clear-cut opportunity before the five-minute half-time break.
India threatened again after the restart, with a header from Macdonnish drifting inches wide following a corner in the 21st minute. Laos, however, drew level three minutes later when Souksavanh Siliseng struck first time from outside the box, finding the bottom corner.
The equaliser prompted India to raise its intensity, with much of the play taking place in the Laos half.
The Blue Colts regained the lead in the 31st minute, with R Lalremruatfela collecting a pass from Soumojit Sarkar before firing left-footed into the far corner from outside the box to make it 3-2.
India extended its advantage in the 33rd minute when Sarkar struck from just inside the halfway line, sending the ball over the goalkeeper and into the net.
The Blue Colts managed the remainder of the match well to preserve their two-goal advantage and secure all three points.
India will next face Cameroon and Grenada on Sunday.

An experimental vaccine offers new hope to patients with melanoma, one of the most aggressive forms of skin cancer. The pharmaceutical companies Merck and Moderna released the results of a Phase 3 clinical trial that evaluated the efficacy of a personalized mRNA-based vaccine that, when combined with immunotherapy, reduced the risk of disease recurrence or death by 42 percent compared to treatment with the immunotherapy drug alone.
Georgina Long, medical director of the Australian Melanoma Institute and the study’s principal investigator, said in a statement that these results are “transformative” and “have the potential to make a foundational shift in how we treat patients with earlier-stage melanoma.”
The trial, known as INTerpath-001, included 1,137 people with high-risk melanoma who had undergone surgery to completely remove their tumors. The participants were divided into two groups. Those in the first group received only Pembrolizumab, a drug that helps the immune system detect and fight cancer cells, while those in the second group were treated with the same drug in combination with the mRNA vaccine, called Intismeran Autogene.
After monitoring the participants for an average of 24.6 months, the researchers determined that addition of the vaccine reduced the risk of cancer recurrence or death by 42 percent compared to Pembrolizumab alone.
The results also showed that the experimental treatment reduced the risk of the disease spreading to other parts of the body by 38 percent. At the end of the follow-up period, 82.2 percent of patients who received both treatments remained recurrence-free, compared with 70 percent of those who received Pembrolizumab alone.
“The results of the INTerpath-001 study represent a major breakthrough in the treatment of melanoma and, in particular, in the development of personalized medicine,” Eva Muñoz Couselo—who leads a melanoma research group at the Vall d’Hebron Institute of Oncology, in Barcelona and who was not involved in the study—told SMC Spain. “For the first time, a Phase III trial has demonstrated that an individualized therapeutic vaccine, designed on the basis of the molecular characteristics of each patient’s tumor, can significantly improve the outcomes of conventional immunotherapy.”
The laboratories explained that the vaccine was developed from a tumor sample taken from each patient, which was used to identify specific mutations that would create distinct proteins the immune system could learn to recognize in order to attack cancer cells. The scientists selected up to three of these molecular signatures per patient.
During the trial, some participants experienced mild side effects such as fever, fatigue, and pain at the injection site. These side effects were seen in earlier trials as well, and the Phase 3 findings demonstrate similar safety when the vaccine is used in the combination with Pembrolizumab.
“These results reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer,” Stéphane Bancel, CEO of Moderna, said in a statement.
The pharmaceutical companies emphasized that the vaccine is not designed to prevent melanoma but rather to reduce the risk of recurrence and death following prior medical treatment. They also noted that the therapy remains under investigation to validate its efficacy and obtain approval from health authorities before widespread use.
Most people diagnosed with melanoma have a high chance of survival, especially if detected early, but as one of the most common cancers, melanoma kills over 50,000 people globally each year. In theory, similar vaccines could be developed for other kinds of tumors in the future. Earlier this year, another trial demonstrated that personalized mRNA vaccines can greatly improve survival among patients with pancreatic cancer, one of the deadliest kinds of tumor.
“This is the major breakthrough, because conceptually it would make it possible to treat not only melanoma but also other tumors in which the immune system can be reactivated,” Marisol Soengas—a leading melanoma researcher at Spain’s National Cancer Research Center also not involved in the trial—told SMC Spain.
That doesn’t mean a cure for cancer is right around the corner. “The challenge is to ensure that this personalization can be scaled up to a large number of patients and that the cost is affordable for health care systems,” Soengas said. “It is logistically complex. It is literally a bespoke vaccine.”

Minneapolis withdrawal was 'surrender', Trump's ex-border patrol chief tells BBC
- Published
The former US border patrol chief who became the public face of the highly controversial deportation drive in Minneapolis earlier this year has defended the operation, describing the withdrawal of agents from the city as a "surrender" by the Trump administration.
In an interview with the BBC, Greg Bovino also said he was "not responding" to a lawsuit filed by the family of a woman shot dead during the operation. He appeared to dismiss the legal action, praising the officers deployed to Minneapolis and saying "people do lawsuits all the time".
Bovino, 56, was removed from his role shortly after the fatal shootings of US citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti in January.
The two shootings, which were captured on video, triggered a bipartisan backlash and widespread protests. Trump then said he was "going to de-escalate a little bit" and withdrew hundreds of immigration agents from the city.
Earlier this month, Good's family filed two civil lawsuits against the Trump administration over her killing, alleging wrongful death and a conspiracy to interfere with the civil rights of protesters.
One of the lawsuits names several top officials, including Bovino and Jonathan Ross, the agent who shot Good, "for their respective individual roles in the operation that led to Renee's death". It alleges that the government's operation in Minneapolis created "an unprecedented environment for state-sponsored violence".
Asked about Bovino's remarks, the family's lawyers said he was "spewing propaganda" and could not be "judge, jury, and executioner". They added: "Our legal team looks forward to the depositions of Mr Bovino and all of the defendants in this matter".
A White House spokeswoman previously called the lawsuits "baseless".
Speaking in Detroit where he was campaigning for tougher immigration enforcement, Bovino said the administration "threw the towel in" and called for more deportations, which he said were now at a "virtual standstill".
He added that he regretted "not going harder in Minnesota and arresting even more illegal aliens".
Bovino said his agents in Minneapolis were the "real victims" of what he called "the most violence that any law enforcement mission ever in the history of the United States has been up against".
Challenged by the BBC over how immigration agents handled both shooting incidents, Bovino rejected suggestions that video evidence undermined his claim that Good and Pretti had intended to harm the agents.
"The evidence is that violence was perpetrated against agents of the US government, and this is a society of laws and people need to follow the law. If not, there are consequences," he said.
Trump initially blamed Good's own actions for her death, saying just hours after she was killed that she "violently, willfully and viciously ran over the ICE officer". Weeks later, he called her death a "tragedy" and said agents were sometimes "going to make a mistake".
The withdrawal from Minnesota, which saw some 700 immigration agents leave the state, also saw Bovino removed from his post. The operation was taken over by the White House 'border tsar' Tom Homan.
When asked why he was removed, Bovino told the BBC: "You'd have to ask the administration. I still haven't gotten the final word on that."
Kristi Noem, who was Homeland Security Secretary at the time of the operation, was fired by Trump in March.
Bovino has since retired from the US border patrol. He has become known for his hardline stance on immigration, often going further in his statements than Trump's own officials and claiming without evidence that 100 million people are illegally in the US and should be deported.
He has called for "total spectrum immigration enforcement" with support from the US military involving "cruise ships packed to the gills, cars, planes, trains, automobiles, all headed out of the United States packed with illegal aliens".

When asked about Bovino's comments about Minneapolis, a White House spokesperson said "the president has delivered the largest reduction in illegal immigration in modern history".
"He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," they said.
Bovino has also floated "exploring" a presidential run in 2028. "If politicians aren't going to step up and do their job then you might see something happen," he told the BBC when asked about his intentions.
Bovino recently addressed a far-right rally by activists in Michigan who are calling for authorities to deport Abdul El-Sayed, a US citizen and Democratic candidate running in the state's tightly fought race for a Senate seat.
American-born Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the Senate if he wins the seat against Republican Mike Rogers.

Despite seven years of Android folding phones, Apple's iPhone Duo launch has spurred developers to create quirky, weird, and fun apps that experiment with the folding design (leaving Android owners feeling like second-class citizens yet again).
I've reviewed almost every folding phone in the past decade, and my inbox has never seen this many app pitches from indie developers wanting to show off their app for Apple's first foldable.
Some of these apps aren't necessarily new but use the phone's hinge to offer fresh experiences. You'll also find a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on apps that make best use of the larger screens on the App Store. From a game that has you closing the phone to grill a piece of toast to a clever way to memorize flash cards, here are nine unique apps to try on your new Apple handset.
Battlefleet Duo
Board games will have a field day on the iPhone Duo, and Battlefleet Duo is the best example. On the larger 7.6-inch screen, you get a sprawling canvas, but in tabletop mode, you can view your ships on the bottom screen and the enemy's fleet above. That's especially great if you have a friend with the iPhone Duo, as you can play local multiplayer and sit across from each other just like you would with the old-school Battleships. You can play two free battles every day, or unlock unlimited battles with a one-time $5 purchase—no ads or subscription.
Flipcorder: Retro Camcorder
Reminiscing about the long-lost days of the pre-smartphone era? Flipcorder offers simple pleasure, turning your iPhone Duo into a camcorder, so you can make new memories that feel like the old days. Open the app, and the outer display will show a “closed lens”—open the Duo to “take the cap off,” then start recording. The user interface is retro, and video clips have a filter to emulate VHS (it has a MiniDV filter too). I really like that you can view your “tapes” and everything is cataloged by day, so you can see 30 minutes of footage in one stitched-together clip.
As you’re recording, the person on the other end can see a preview of the video on the outer display—that kind of dual-display experience is only available to camera apps, so if you were hoping to read a book and have the outer display appear as the book cover, that's sadly not possible at the moment.
RectoVerso: Flashcards
Flashcard apps are a dime a dozen, but nothing quite captures the physical experience of flipping around a flashcard like RectoVerso. This $13 app lets you import your own text—your classroom notes or even a PDF—and uses Apple Intelligence to automatically create flashcards on the subject matter. Alternatively, you can import decks from Anki, another popular flashcard app, or write your own. The magic is when you're actually studying. Don't know the answer? Slightly open the iPhone Duo, and the answer will gradually appear—fully open, and you get the full answer. That way you can bang your hand on the desk and say, “Ah, I totally knew that.”
PianoFold
Who doesn't love a rhythm game? Pop your iPhone Duo into a 90-degree angle and let the blocks in PianoFold reach the middle crease—that's when you tap the corresponding column. You need to time your taps perfectly, unless you enjoy listening to Bach get butchered in real time. There are 40 levels across eight chapters, and the game rates your performance (out of three stars) at the end of each song. You can retry as many times as you'd like. The first two chapters are free, though you can also play one song for free every day. For full access, you'll have to pony up $5. There are no ads and no subscription.
Toastie
When I showed my wife Toastie, she remarked that it might be the first time she ever wanted an iPhone (she uses a Pixel). That's high praise! This delightful $3 app asks you to construct a sandwich on the iPhone Duo's inner screen. Each recipe has specific instructions you have to follow, and when you're done, you'll need to close the iPhone for a few seconds—however many the recipe says—to “grill” your sandwich. Open the phone back up, and it's ready to serve! That is, if you haven't burned it. There are only 10 recipes, so you'll probably get through this quickly. But hey, at least you can say you've used the world's most expensive toaster.
Portal
Want to focus? Or relax? Portal lets you play relaxing soundscapes—listen to a volcano's bubbling lava or waves crashing on a beach—but you can also see these sights on the Duo's 7.6-inch canvas, in tabletop mode, or on the outer screen in tent mode. It's very relaxing and an excellent companion for travelers who rely on a sound machine to fall asleep. You can also follow calming breath exercises, or set focus timers to get stuff done. The app boasts more than 100 vistas, from Iceland's black beaches to enchanting UK woodlands. The app is free, though you can only access three portals refreshed monthly. Full access costs $3 a month, $30 per year, or $100 for a lifetime membership.
If you like the idea of Portal, you might want to check out Fold Focus, though it's designed to help you get work done rather than relax. Close the Duo to focus on a task, and the pixel animation on the outer display will start building a city. Open your phone before the timer ends and everything will come crashing down.
FirstSeed Planner
Want to try a new calendar app? Maybe your current one isn't optimized for the Duo (ahem, Google Calendar). Try FirstSeed Planner. The developer has fully enabled Duo support, letting you view the calendar on one screen and a daily planner on the other. It supports drag-and-drop actions between the two halves of the screen, and I also love the space at the bottom for writing notes for the day. And when Apple enables stylus support on the Duo later this year, you can handwrite in FirstSeed, making your Duo feel more like a paper planner. It's free, but the Pro version costs $3.49 per month, $30 per year, or $90 for lifetime access. The paid versions unlock features like automatic backups and weather forecasts.
Delta Emulator
If you’re big on retro gaming, you’ve probably heard of Delta. The popular emulator just rolled out its biggest update yet, headlined by support for the folding iPhone Duo. Prop the Duo at a 90-degree angle, and custom skins transform the device into a classic clamshell like the Nintendo DS—complete with automatic sleep mode when you close it. Just remember: It’s strictly an emulator, so you’ll still need to source your own ROMs responsibly.
Tiny Computers
Bring your favorite PCs and Macs back to life with Tiny Computers. This $4 app houses a library of 10 computers, from the Commodore 64 to the iMac G3. Fold the Duo into tabletop mode to bring the museum of machines to life—a vintage screen up top and a functional, clickable keyboard below. The operating systems are interactive, so you can run retro paint apps, secret terminal commands, or kill time with classic desktop games like Solitaire.

4 dead, more casualties feared after blast at firecracker factory in Bihar's Siwan
The blast ripped through a house in Bihar's Siwan from where a licensed firecracker unit was being run.
Four people have been killed and more casualties are feared after an explosion ripped through a house in Alampur village in Bihar's Siwan district on Friday evening. Preliminary investigation revealed that a licensed firecracker manufacturing unit was running in the house where the blast took place.
The explosion was so intense that the debris from the next part of the building fell onto the road. Siwan district magistrate Vijay Prakash Meena and Superintendent of Police (SP) Bharat Soni are at the spot.
"We have managed to recover some mangled bodies of those killed as their body parts are all disintegrated. As of now, we cannot say the number of casualties but two to three bodies have been located. We are identifying the bodies which are totally dismembered," Meena said.
Locals claimed that the firecracker manufacturing unit destroyed in the explosion was running in the house of a man named Mohammad Amiruddin Mian who said to be a noted firecracker trader.
Police said that many members were present in the house when firecrackers exploded. Subsequently, flames engulfed other firecrackers stored in the premises, setting off a chain of explosions. For about two hours, the sound of explosions kept ringing out intermittently.
A local named Junaid Rizvi told a media channel that body parts of some of those killed in the blast were thrown in the air. " It was a horrible sight. Parts of bodies of those kileld in the blast were strewn all over," Rizvi claimed.

Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority'
- Published
Fifa president Gianni Infantino insists he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football, as he laughed off questions about whether he had considered resigning over the World Cup sell-off debacle.
In a rare interview, he struck a defiant tone to BBC Sport about his own position in the wake of the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and said it was not always easy to bring different points of view "under one roof".
"There is nothing bad in disagreeing," he said. "We see it every day in so many countries in the world. It's OK to disagree. It's OK to have different points of view, but then we need to be able to move on."
Two months ago, Infantino was facing mounting calls to stand down as president of the organisation he has led since 2016.
The heads of European football's governing body Uefa, the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, which runs the game in North and Central America, signed a letter accusing the Fifa president of breaking trust "through deception".
Last week Uefa demanded that Fifa release all key documents relating to FFE by 2 November, with Uefa general secretary Theodore Theodoridis saying that the organisation had failed to address "a number of fundamental questions".
Under FFE, which Infantino scrapped within days, a portion of the commercial rights of football's world governing body would have been sold to a private investment firm.
Since the delivery of the letter, Infantino has been travelling the world, appearing in Morocco, the Dominican Republic, Cape Verde, and Japan, managing to shore up support to the point where his re-election as president for a fourth term next year now looks inevitable.
He has also proposed to increase the amount of money handed out for football development across the world by $3.4bn (£2.6bn).
Fifa has done some things 'maybe less good'
During the interview he reflected on having been "fully endorsed" by the Asian Football Confederation - following a U-turn by its president Sheikh Salman - and having the backing of "all African countries".
But only last week, he apologised to the Fifa Council over the "communication and consultation" regarding FFE.
He was told by Council members in that meeting that he was not "fit to be Fifa president" if he did not give them the documents they have asked for, including the rationale for FFE.
Yet, when pressed on when he would be providing the requested papers, he did not give a clear answer, saying they had to follow a "legal process" and that they were "working on it".
"We'll answer of course all the questions that are asked as far as the process allows, as far as we can," he said.
Speaking from the first Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, he said he and the Fifa administration were doing "as best we can" but admitted they have done "some things which are maybe less good".
He also said that they need to have dialogue "more often" with Uefa, in an effort to repair their strained relationship.
Asked by the BBC if he was fit to be Fifa president, and whether he had considered standing down, he laughed, before saying: "Well you know I was elected by 211 member associations from all over the world.
"I think what is important is that in an organisation like Fifa, there can be different views, different points of view.
"But if we are serious about democracy, about the democratic process, about believing that everyone has the same vote and the same voice all over the world, that football belongs to everyone, if we are serious about that, then we need, to respect as well the views of the vast, vast majority.
"I'm just coming back off Tokyo where the Asian Football Confederation has fully endorsed me. I was in Cape Verde where all [Confederation of] African [Football] countries have endorsed me. I'm speaking to all associations everywhere in the world."
He continued: "There are different points of view it's not always easy to bring them all under one roof but we need to respect and I do respect all opinions all views and then it will be up to the Fifa member associations to decide who they want as a president and how they want Fifa to be run."
The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November - although none have yet filed and he could stand unopposed.

England among teams at U15 World Cup
Infantino arrived in Baku on Friday for the Fifa Under-15 World Cup and Festival, which is being held in Azerbaijan and features teams from 189 member associations.
England, Spain, France, Argentina and Brazil are all taking part. Russia have also sent a team, marking the country's first appearance in a Fifa-sanctioned tournament since the world governing body, and Uefa, suspended Russian teams from international competitions in February 2022 following the invasion of Ukraine.
This tournament is only for boys, with next year's tournament being girls only, and then from 2028 Fifa's plan is to have boys and girls competing in the tournament annually.
Matches are played in an 8v8 format, on smaller pitches and with 20-minute halves.
"It's just beautiful to bring the world together at such a young age to create something like this," Infantino said.
"When some of these boys participate in a World Cup 10 years, 20 years from now, they will all remember that their first World Cup was here."

A year after India-Azerbaijan ties soured over the latter's support for Pakistan during Operation Sindoor, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar’s visit to Baku, the capital city whose name is likely traced to the Sanskrit word Bagavan meaning “God” or “City of God”, signals a fresh diplomatic push to repair relations. Jaishankar’s visit comes as New Delhi and Baku seek to revive bilateral engagement after a period of diplomatic friction triggered by the India-Pakistan conflict in May 2025. Jaishankar, who arrived in Azerbaijan on Friday for a one-day visit, held talks with Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov, describing them as “very productive” and saying the discussions had helped establish a path towards improving bilateral relations. “Our talks dwelt on further expanding our bilateral relations. We spoke about economic cooperation, including in trade, investment and energy, which are central to our bilateral ties. Given our complementary economies, we believe that there is very good scope for further enhancement of our bilateral trade and investment,” Jaishankar said. The two sides also agreed to coordinate more closely on the International North-South Transport Corridor (INSTC), a connectivity initiative that could give India greater access to markets across Eurasia. Situated on the Caspian Sea, Baku has historically been a crossroads of trade and cultural exchanges between Asia and Europe “We are both invested in the International North-South Transport Corridor. That’s very important for us. We agreed today that we will coordinate more closely in that regard,” Jaishankar added. The visit, the first by an Indian foreign minister to Azerbaijan in eight years, comes amid efforts to overcome the diplomatic fallout from Operation Sindoor. Azerbaijan’s support for Pakistan following India’s military strikes strained relations, while India’s growing defence partnership with Armenia has been another source of bilateral unease. Trade and investment could provide a practical foundation for rebuilding relations. According to the Indian Embassy in Baku, bilateral trade reached $401 million in 2025, with Indian exports accounting for $226 million and imports from Azerbaijan standing at $175 million, largely comprising crude oil. India also has significant energy interests in Azerbaijan. ONGC Videsh Ltd (OVL) has invested more than $1.2 billion in acquiring stakes in the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli (ACG) oil and gas fields and the associated Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan (BTC) pipeline. In November 2024, OVL acquired an additional 0.615% participating interest in the ACG oil and gas field from Norway’s Equinor for $60 million, alongside a 0.737% stake in the BTC pipeline. The acquisition raised OVL’s interests to 2.925% in ACG and 3.097% in the pipeline. Jaishankar said the two countries had agreed to deepen cooperation in oil and energy and expand engagement into other sectors. Connectivity is another potential area for closer cooperation. Delhi and Mumbai have direct air links with Baku, although IndiGo suspended its seven weekly Delhi-Baku flights in January 2026 amid the conflict involving Iran, the US and Israel. Azerbaijan Airlines continues to operate direct services between India and Azerbaijan. The two countries have also discussed increasing flight frequencies, while Air India announced a codeshare partnership with Azerbaijan Airlines in August 2026. Better air connectivity could support tourism, business travel and wider people-to-people exchanges. Tourism, however, illustrates both the potential and the vulnerability of these ties. Indian arrivals in Azerbaijan rose from 4,853 in 2014 to 243,589 in 2024, before declining to approximately 166,944 in 2025, according to figures published by the Indian Embassy in Baku. The decline followed a citizen-led boycott of Azerbaijan by Indian tourists after Baku backed Pakistan during Operation Sindoor. Jaishankar also thanked Azerbaijan for assisting Indian nationals, particularly students evacuated from Iran during the conflict earlier this year. He acknowledged the care extended to Indian students in Azerbaijan and suggested expanding participation by Azerbaijani professionals in India’s Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) programme. The renewed engagement builds on Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s brief meeting with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek in September 2026. According to the Indian Embassy in Baku, it was the first in-person interaction between the leaders of the two countries. The Ministry of External Affairs said terrorism, security issues and common threats were among the subjects discussed during Jaishankar’s visit. MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal said the two countries recognised the need to cooperate to advance peace, prosperity and security for their citizens and address shared challenges. Bayramov also welcomed Jaishankar’s visit, saying it provided an opportunity to exchange views on the current state and future prospects of Azerbaijan-India relations. For New Delhi and Baku, the immediate challenge is to translate this diplomatic opening into tangible cooperation without allowing their respective strategic partnerships to derail progress. Trade, energy, tourism and the INSTC offer avenues for rebuilding ties. Jaishankar’s visit may have reopened the door to engagement. Whether that translates into a meaningful reset will depend on what follows. Quentin Tarantino surprised audiences on Friday night at AFI Fest when he shared the first 17 minutes of “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”
Tarantino made a special appearance at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood, following a screening of “Once Upon a Time … In Hollywood.” Following the Q&A moderated by Rotten Tomatoes’ Jacqueline Coley, the filmmaker said, “Well, I could talk a little bit about ‘The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth’ or I could show you the first 17 minutes.”
Directed by David Fincher, who was also in attendance, the film sees the return of Cliff Booth played by Brad Pitt. The film picks up in 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The logline reads: “Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.”
Popular on Variety
He’s curious when he gets a call from talent agent Karen Crosby (Elizabeth Debicki), on behalf of her client, TV megastar Charlie Peters (Scott Caan) — a man known for doing his own stunts. And he’s further entertained and intrigued when he meets other characters in Charlie’s world, from his knowing wife Toni (Carla Gugino) to pro football champion turned screen star Roderick “Hot Rod” Harrison (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Then there are the Verdusco brothers (Matt Groove and JB Tadena), mysterious gangsters causing mayhem across the city. What was once a fairytale is now a crime story — a cocktail of violence, ambition and desire that could only happen in LA.
Tarantino, who wrote the screenplay, shared his decision to revisit Cliff Booth. He said, “I tend to not remember good reviews of mine in quotes; I remember the bad reviews in quotes, but I don’t really remember good reviews of mine in quotes. But one quote that I do remember somebody writing about ‘Once Upon a Time in Hollywood’ was, ‘This seems like the first world Quentin Tarantino has ever created that he would like to live in’ and there is that aspect; I loved the Cliff Booth character,” Tarantino said. “I loved the way that Brad played him, and there was this aspect of him as sort of like a paperback hero. I could see like a series of paperbacks with Cliff Booth getting involved with this adventure or that adventure or something like that.”
While further plot details can’t be spoiled, the opening sequence has Tarantino’s distinguished style of writing and visually, the Hollywood of 1977 is, in true Fincher style, gritty and dark.
The Netflix film also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Peter Weller and is set to premiere in Imax theaters on Nov. 25, before hitting the streamer Dec. 23.
The evening kicked off with Tarantino introducing the film and shared that had not seen the film at that theater.
In the Q&A, Tarantino shared how he had spoken with Burt Reynolds about playing the George Spahn character. Tarantino recalled, “He said yes and we became friendly, but he passed away before we could make the film. But we did get to rehearse with him and do the script reading with him, so actually, the last performance Burt Reynolds ever gave was as George Spahn in the script reading.”
The character would be played by Bruce Dern.
He also talked about his upcoming play “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which stars Sacha Baron Cohen and is set to premiere in London’s West End next year. “I’m not going to talk a whole lot about that, but our previews are in February. In November we’ll start rehearsals.” He went on to say, “I’m just a writer and that’s just kind of what I do. I’m always writing.”

Going into the summer transfer window as Premier League champions, hope sprang eternal for Arsenal.
An opportunity to capitalise, encouraged by a sense at Emirates Stadium that their competitors were in transition because of managerial instability.
If ever there was a moment to strike in recruitment, this was it.
The plans were ambitious: a shortlist with more than 20 players on it. They were targets at Real Madrid and Atletico Madrid, even at Chelsea and Tottenham.
But as the window shut on Tuesday night, you could not escape the sense of unfulfillment - certainly from a section of supporters.
Arsenal's close season was one characterised by some unquestionable successes, but also riddled by difficulties and frustration.
Ahead of their home match against Chelsea on Sunday, BBC Sport details Arsenal's transfer window and whether manager Mikel Arteta, sporting director Andrea Berta and, perhaps most pertinently, owners Kroenke Sports Entertainment can deem their summer operation a success.
Why it became Guimaraes and not Anderson, Tonali or Scott
Bruno Guimaraes's £75m capture from Newcastle United was Arsenal's most eye-catching signing.
Heading into the summer, Arsenal were keeping abreast of Guimaraes' situation at Newcastle, although others were considered a higher priority.
For instance, their interest in Elliot Anderson was widely reported, but it was clear the England international was joining Manchester City.
Guimaraes' former Newcastle team-mate Sandro Tonali and Bournemouth's Alex Scott were also among the midfielders explored before a move for the South American accelerated.
At the ages of 26 and 23 respectively, Tonali and Scott are younger than Guimaraes, who turns 29 in November.
But numerous factors, including availability and price - Tonali joined Spurs for a minimum £92m - made their signings difficult.
Aston Villa's Amadou Onana was also among the options considered, but the Belgium international suffered a serious knee injury at the World Cup.
By mid-June Guimaraes, who had universal backing inside the Emirates, emerged as the club's primary focus.
Berta knew the player's camp well and Guimaraes was admired by Arteta, who had made it clear he wanted proven talent to take his starting XI - rather than the wider squad - to greater heights.
Berta used his strong relationship with Guimaraes' representatives to facilitate Arsenal's move, hence why Newcastle maintained they had had no direct contact from the London club until days before his move was completed.
It is not uncommon for Berta to lean on intermediaries to conduct negotiations, although the approach has had varying degrees of success.
For instance, Arsenal actively sought moves for Leicester City teenagers Jeremy Monga and Louis Page over the summer.
But sources insist that the lack of club-to-club discussions meant both players ultimately did not join Arsenal, with Monga eventually signing for Manchester City when he appeared to be on the verge of moving to the Emirates.
That said, Berta's success in pivoting the club towards a deal for Guimaraes when it became clear other targets were not viable was well received behind the scenes at Arsenal.
Konsa was first-choice defensive option
The signing of Ezri Konsa was equally complex. Konsa was viewed internally as Arteta's first-choice defensive option.
Arteta wanted players used to the rigours of Premier League football - hence the moves for Guimaraes, Konsa and the failed efforts to land Morgan Rogers from Aston Villa.
Konsa's ability to play at right-back was also viewed as a major benefit. Arsenal considered signing an orthodox right-back, with Ivan Fresneda among the options, but Konsa's versatility was a key factor.
But Berta appeared reluctant to meet Villa's valuation. A week before the Konsa deal was confirmed, Arsenal made a £40m offer, which was duly rejected.
Sources claim the deal was eventually sealed by the ownership at both clubs, and the transfer was agreed at £51m, with £4m in add-ons.
In the event of not reaching an agreement for Konsa, it is understood Tottenham duo Cristian Romero and Micky van der Ven were identified as targets – but Arsenal's north London rivals would not consider selling to them.
Como centre-back Jacobo Ramon is a player the club will continue to monitor, but clauses attached to his current contract make the deal difficult.
Tarik Muharemovic, who joined Leeds United, was another considered.
In attack, Christos Tzolis' impact since arriving from Club Brugge in a deal worth about £35m means the Greece international has been heralded as one of the discoveries of the summer.
It is understood the potential deal for the former Norwich winger was initially raised by an intermediary close to a senior member of the coaching staff during the close season.
Berta's number two, Maurizio Micheli, watched Tzolis play for his country against Sweden in June and was suitably impressed.
So far, the 24-year-old looks a positive addition to Arteta's squad.
Arsenal, who also made Piero Hincapie's loan deal permanent and signed Illan Meslier on a free transfer, are happy with the signings they have made.
The captures of Guimaraes and Konsa, who will both be 30 by the end of next season, have raised eyebrows given the combined £126m fee, amid concerns over how the pair's longevity may impact the natural evolution of the squad.
Yet it is undeniable that Guimares and Konsa add elite quality and experience to Arsenal ranks, and ultimately the club feel they paid the going rate to get those deals over the line.
Arsenal miss out on marque attacker
While the club delivered proven talent for Arteta in defence and midfield, Berta's remit of adding an elite attacker ended in disappointment.
Rogers was the club's primary target heading into the window, and the early indications were positive amid a strongly held view internally that the forward wanted to join.
At the start of the summer, it was Arsenal's understanding that Villa valued Rogers at £100m. Arsenal valued Rogers at £80m.
Berta, however, was confident of negotiating the price down to a level he and the club believed could get the deal done.
In the meantime, however, Berta explored alternatives - Bradley Barcola, Kenan Yildiz, Yan Diomande and Nico Paz were admired.
Anthony Gordon was a long-term target, but he had agreed before the World Cup to join Barcelona.
Yildiz and Paz will continue to be realistic targets moving forward. Eli Junior Kroupi is another the club will watch once he returns from injury for Bournemouth.
Anderson's move from Forest to City for £116m, however, altered the complexion of Villa's outlook on Rogers' future.
Villa increased their valuation to £120m and ultimately Chelsea ended up signing the attacker for £117m.
Arsenal, it is understood, were given the opportunity to match Chelsea's offer but refused, believing their £80m valuation was fair - but it does beg the question of whether Rogers would be a Gunners player now if Berta had acted sooner.
Ultimately, the failure to land Rogers arrived as the first of a series of blows to Berta in his efforts to deliver a top-class left-sided attacker for the team.
Arsenal genuinely believed they had a realistic chance of signing Vinicius Jr before he decided to sign a new contract at Real Madrid.
Berta and Arteta were all in on the Brazil icon. The club were prepared finance the deal too.
While the transfer would likely have cost a British record fee and been one of the most lucrative remuneration packages in Premier League history, the benefit to Arteta's team and the Brazil superstar's commercial value meant Arsenal were absolutely prepared to complete the deal.
Yet well-placed sources expressed to BBC Sport over the summer that Vinicius did not want to leave Real, while others feared Arsenal were being used to strengthen the attacker's efforts to secure a more lucrative contract at the Bernabeu.
Those concerns came to fruition as Vinicius signed a new long-term contract in Spain in another Arsenal disappointment.
There were similar reservations about Arsenal's well-documented pursuit of Julian Alvarez.
The Atletico Madrid forward showed very little indication that he was willing to join Arsenal; his preference to join Barcelona was one of the worst-kept secrets of the window.
But Atletico's point-blank refusal to sell to Barcelona was deemed reason enough by Berta and Arteta to persist with their interest in the hope of Alvarez changing his mind until the closing days of the window.
Alvarez, however, preferred to stay at Atletico, even though his relationship with the club is at an all-time low.
Did Arsenal waste their time with Vinicius and Alvarez? The answer varies depending on who you speak to.
When it became clear Alvarez was unlikely, Berta explored his options.
Intriguingly, Arsenal have admired Chelsea striker Joao Pedro, who was deemed not for sale over the summer, although there were concerns over how he would fit into Arteta's system.
It is claimed Berta relies significantly on his vast network of agent connections rather than acting on the club's existing scouting information when analysing the market.
For example, last summer, when all the scouting information pointed towards a move for Benjamin Sesko, Berta's arrival meant the club pivoted to Viktor Gyokeres, who is currently second-choice striker.
This summer the club's late dalliance with Lyon winger Malick Fofana provided a further example of Berta leaning on his agency connections after management agency Roc Nation offered Arsenal an opportunity to sign the Belgium international.
Berta's relationship with Roc Nation was particularly prevalent this summer given Arsenal's pursuit of Vinicius and the sale of Gabriel Martinelli, who are both clients of the agency.
It remains to be seen how much of an impact Arsenal's failure to sign a recognised top-level attacker impacts their season, particularly in light of Martinelli and Leandro Trossard's departures.
Arsenal will move towards player trading model
Arsenal headed into the window with a clear remit of ensuring the club become more sustainable and adept at trading.
Part of that directive is to ensure the club remain compliant with domestic and European financial regulations.
Depending on who you talk to, the size of the potential deals for Vinicius or Alvarez would have raised doubts over Arsenal's ability to stay within the regulations.
Nevertheless, ensuring they maximised the benefits of player trading will become an increasing part of Arsenal's financial operation in the future.
There was already evidence of that through the sale of Martinelli, whose £60m exit to Al-Hilal was the club's record departure. Arsenal have also secured a sell-on clause in the deal.
The exits of Martinelli, Trossard, Gabriel Jesus, Christian Norgaard, Jakub Kiwior, Fabio Vieira and Karl Hein secured the club in the region of £114m.
Through intermediaries, a possible exit for Myles Lewis-Skelly was explored, with a fee of about £80m believed to have been mooted for the midfielder.
Manchester United, who were attracted to Lewis-Skelly's ability to play at left-back, were interested but ultimately deemed his valuation too high.
Of course, it is Berta's job to have a firm grasp on the level of interest in the club's players and their market value but, nevertheless, the thought of Lewis-Skelly's departure resulted in huge uproar from supporters.
As BBC Sport revealed last month, the Gunners resisted any temptation to sell Ethan Nwaneri on a permanent deal, the academy graduate landing a season-long loan deal to Borussia Dortmund that includes a January recall option if required.
The minimum £15m fee secured in Trossard's deal to Besiktas is also viewed as a good deal inside the Emirates given the Belgian turns 32 in December.
Having spent nearly £450m in 12 months, Berta's work in the market has helped the club deliver their first league title in 22 years.
Yet, despite the money splashed, there remain clear issues in the squad - certainly in attack.
The summer window has left many supporters feeling questioning Berta's body of work at Arsenal.
And with the average age of the squad increasing following the captures of Konsa and Guimaraes, can the current options build a dynasty of success before the club need to spend heavily again on regenerating the team?

The Marineland belugas keep dying. Was it a mistake to move them?
So far, 6 out of 30 whales transferred out of closed Ontario theme park have died
A few months after a mass relocation effort that stretched across the Atlantic Ocean, six whales have died out of the 30 that were transferred from the now-shuttered Marineland theme park in Niagara Falls, Ont.
The most recent death, a beluga named Cyprus, was announced on Sunday by SeaWorld San Diego — one of five facilities in the U.S. and Spain that took in the marine mammals after Marineland said it could no longer care for them.
The deaths have raised questions about the impact of the transfers on their health and well-being and whether they were fit to travel, and rehashed concerns about the conditions they were living in during the years they spent at Marineland.
But was there ever a better option for the last captive whales and dolphins in Canada?
Advocacy groups such as Animal Justice have pointed to the federal and provincial governments, as well as Marineland, saying they failed to properly plan for the animals' futures. Experts have said they're worried these deaths are just the beginning. Meanwhile, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans maintains the transfers were the best possible rescue plan.
Cyprus, a beluga whale who was rescued from Marineland in Niagara Falls in August, is shown in an undated photo published to social media by SeaWorld San Diego. SeaWorld announced the whale's death on Oct. 18. (SeaWorld San Diego/Facebook)
"This was, I would say, almost kind of a Hail Mary effort in terms of trying to make sure that we could provide a better life for these whales," Dr. Doug Whiteside, the head veterinarian at the Calgary Zoo and a member of the Canadian Veterinary Medical Association's animal welfare committee, told CBC News.
They were already under chronic stress from the conditions they faced at Marineland, Whiteside said. Transferring them caused additional stress, even though international regulations were followed and they went to high-calibre institutions to receive full-time care, he said.
"Is it a risk? Absolutely ... any sort of acute stress may push them over the edge," he said.
While we can't underestimate the stress of the transfers on the whales, that doesn't mean it's not in their best interests to try to give them a better life, said Angela Fernandez, director of the Animal Law Program at the University of Toronto's law faculty.
"People knew that there were stronger and weaker individuals in the mix, just like there would be among a group of 30 human retirees," Fernandez told CBC News.
"You would not evacuate an old-age home and take only the strong individuals if there is capacity to take everyone."
What happened to Marineland?
Marineland, once Canada's most popular amusement park, has been the subject of controversy for years, with animal rights activists and others vehemently opposed to its practices.
A federal law passed in 2019 that bans keeping whales, dolphins and porpoises for breeding or entertainment in Canada shuttered its business model. Then it never recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic's tourism slump.
In 2024, the park was put up for sale and began relocating many of its animals. But in 2025, the federal government blocked Marineland's request to export the remaining belugas to an aquarium in China. Marineland responded by asking for emergency funding from Ottawa, warning that it might otherwise have no choice but to euthanize them.
Releasing them into the wild would lead to certain death for the mammals raised in captivity, marine experts noted. And there was no appropriate seaside sanctuary for them in North America. A proposed sanctuary in Nova Scotia was still years away from being developed.
In May, the Department of Fisheries and Oceans endorsed a rescue plan to split up all remaining whales between Oceanogràfic València in Spain and four U.S. locations: Georgia Aquarium in Atlanta, Shedd Aquarium in Chicago and two SeaWorld facilities in San Diego and San Antonio, Texas.
By the end of August, the last whale had been shipped out.
This situation was entirely avoidable, said Camille Labchuk, executive director of Animal Justice, based in Toronto. The animal law advocacy group had pushed for a proactive plan to move the whales to a seaside sanctuary for years, she said, adding there was still time to plan a responsible transition after the 2019 legislation passed.
"It was obvious to everyone that Marineland would one day close, because the public no longer wants to see miserable whales swim in circles in tiny tanks," Labchuk said.
"A seaside sanctuary was always going to be a challenging undertaking ... but these challenges don't excuse the failure to plan for a better option."
Concerns about fitness to travel
Since their transfer, four whales have died at Chicago's Shedd Aquarium, one whale and a dolphin have died at Oceanogràfic València and another whale has died at SeaWorld San Diego — representing one-fifth of the rescued whales.
The first, Peekachu, died on Aug. 25, about two weeks after arriving in Chicago. Rain was next on Sept. 2, followed by Osiris on Sept. 21, both of them also at Shedd. Necropsies for Peekachu and Rain, and preliminary results for Osiris, identified long-standing intestinal and liver issues that began before their rescue, the aquarium wrote in a blog post.
Jelly Bean died on Sept. 17 at Oceanogràfic València, and then Echo, a dolphin, died at the same facility on Sept. 23. They had been experiencing a list of health complications and organ abnormalities that may have developed prior to the transfer, the aquarium said in a news release.
- Animal Justice urges investigation into Marineland beluga death in Chicago, wants relocation efforts halted
- Marineland belugas that died in Chicago had chronic inflammatory disease, preliminary necropsy findings show
On Oct. 9, Shedd announced the death of Caspian two days earlier, noting it had been concerned about her health for weeks. The aquarium hasn't yet released her necropsy results. Cyprus, the sixth ill-fated beluga, died last weekend. SeaWorld San Diego said an ultrasound determined the animal's intestinal tract did not appear to be functioning normally.
There wasn't much transparency around the condition of the whales and dolphins before they were transferred due to their private ownership, U of T's Fernandez said. "After years and decades in captivity, it would be surprising if they didn’t all have significant health problems."
The deaths raise questions about whether the animals were fit to travel and whether every possible precaution was taken, Labchuk said, adding that the public deserves transparency.
'Heartbreaking,' says former trainer
Kristy Burgess, who worked as a trainer at Marineland from 2022 to 2025, called the deaths "heartbreaking."
Burgess has previously spoken out about the conditions at Marineland, noting that the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and that the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls.
She now says she wishes there had been more opportunity for independent experts to contribute to the decision-making, as well as greater transparency around the planning, risks and ongoing health of the animals.
"Change has to come with a realistic, carefully considered plan for the animals themselves," Burgess said.
Former Marineland trainer Kristy Burgess says the beluga pools were in desperate need of repair and the whales were eating paint peeling off the walls. (Submitted by Kristy Burgess)
Whiteside, the Calgary Zoo's head veterinarian, said his understanding of the situation is that there simply wasn't a better option.
The belugas were in a "horrible situation" crowded into crumbling pools at Marineland, he said.
At least a transfer gave them a chance for a better life, he said, even if some didn't survive.
The experience is a sad example of what can happen when institutions like Marineland aren't held to account, Whiteside said.
By not being held to account, Marineland allowed the animals to get to a state where they were chronically stressed, crowded in pools and eating paint, he said.
"Right from the get-go, this sets you up for potential failure."
'Their best chance of survival'
Before the animals' transport began, federal Fisheries Minister Joanne Thompson said she had taken reasonable steps to ensure their safety, including individual health assessments for each animal.
In a statement to CBC News on Wednesday, Thompson said she was still confident in the rescue plan, noting that the transfer was "a significant and complex undertaking."
"Marineland was no longer able to care for these animals. I remain confident that this rescue plan gives these belugas their best chance of survival and that they are being cared for by experienced professionals who are deeply committed to their welfare," she said.
The experts and advocates who spoke to CBC News say their concern now is for the fate of the remaining Marineland whales.
"It's almost a certainty that more belugas and dolphins will die," Labchuk of Animal Justice said.
But Fernandez said "that means 24 are safe, at least for now."
CBC News has reached out to Marineland for comment but has not received a response.
Beluga whales swim in a tank at Marineland in Niagara Falls on June 9, 2023. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)
