Violent clashes erupted in Paris on Saturday as police fired tear gas and used water cannons to disperse protesters during a nationwide march. Over 400,000 gathered to demonstrate against school underfunding and the rising cost of living, with unrest also reported in several other French cities.
According to France's interior ministry, nearly 1,000 were arrested with the numbers being likely to rise.
The procession brought thousands onto the streets and intensified pressure on French President 
Emmanuel Macron
's government.
Visuals from the streets of France showed the immense gathering of thousands of protestors holding banners in their hand to express their stance against the rising cost of living.
However, what began as a peaceful procession through the French capital turned violent when thousands of demonstrators reached Porte de Vincennes, on the city's southeastern outskirts. Visuals from the scene showed thick clouds of tear gas filling the streets as mask-clad protesters threw cobblestones and other projectiles at security forces.
Police deployed armoured water cannons to push back groups of demonstrators in crowded areas. Separate footage showed shopfronts being looted and windows smashed, raising concerns after widespread rioting damaged more than 3,000 businesses across France the previous week.
The Paris prosecutor's office confirmed 64 arrests linked to Saturday's protest. Forty people, including six minors, were held in custody, primarily on suspicion of weapons offences or intending to commit violence and damage property.
Unrest spreads across France as 70,000 officers deployed
Clashes were also reported in Lyon, Clermont-Ferrand, Strasbourg and Marseille, where police fired tear gas. Water cannons were used to disperse crowds in Nantes and Nice.
The French interior ministry estimated that 410,000 people took part in the demonstrations nationwide, including 110,000 in Paris. The CGT trade union, however, put the national turnout at nearly 800,000.
France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez deployed 70,000 police officers and security personnel across France, supported by armoured vehicles and helicopters. The security operation followed the previous week's unrest, when authorities acknowledged that police had lost control of several city centres.
Security was tightened around major landmarks in Paris, including the Arc de Triomphe. The Louvre and Orsay museums, along with the Art Basel fair, also closed for the weekend as authorities sought to protect prominent venues from further violence.
Students, teachers demand better education facilities
The demonstrations began last month after complaints about staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris. The movement has since expanded, drawing students, teachers and trade unions into a wider campaign against deteriorating public education and mounting financial pressures.
Government figures show that public middle and high schools lost 15.4 million teaching hours during the 2024-25 school year because staff absences went unreplaced. As a result, 7.5% of scheduled class time was not delivered.
Students are demanding 250,000 additional higher education places, changes to the Parcoursup university admissions system, a freeze on rents in public student accommodation and a monthly increase of 200 euros in grants.
Economic concerns have added to the discontent. Energy prices rose 21.3% year-on-year in September, while overall inflation reached 3.1%, putting further pressure on households already struggling with the cost of living.
Protesters voice anger over inequality and lack of opportunities
The march brought together people from different generations and professions, many of whom said they feared the long-term consequences of inadequate public services and rising economic inequality.
Camille Chesnier, 27, who has an engineering degree and a master's degree but remains unemployed, described the difficulties faced by young people trying to find work and secure housing.
"There are enormous numbers of people in the same situation as me but who aren't privileged and who find themselves living on the streets and in squats and, frankly, it's very tough."
Bénédicte Pittion, a 46-year-old teacher who marched alongside her 16-year-old daughter, Garance, said the young demonstrators had not received an adequate response from the authorities.
"The young people who have been demonstrating have not been heard, and as a parent and as a teacher, I stand with them."
Garance said she felt "really scared" after the violence during previous weekend protests. However, she argued that staying home would allow the government to claim victory.
Soumaya Abed, 58, a veteran nurse wearing a red CGT union vest, criticised the decision to push the march towards the outskirts of Paris.
"They are using what happened last week as an excuse to quiet protesters. But it won't stop the movement. It won't stop students from demanding better conditions in schools."
Louis Ledoux-Xatard, another Paris protester, said growing economic inequality had left him concerned about the country's future.
"Looking at countries like the United States, we don't want to end up like them, where part of the population has everything and the others have nothing. I never imagined that I'd be taking to the streets so much before my thirties."
Macron faces mounting pressure as protesters reject concessions
The protests pose a fresh challenge to Macron, whose approval ratings have fallen to their lowest levels since he took office in 2017. The unrest comes in the closing months of his term, as discontent over public services and living costs continues to grow.
Macron met student representatives on Friday and promised changes to university admissions. However, protest organisers rejected the offer as insufficient, signalling that the government's response has done little to ease tensions.
The movement has also drawn comparisons with the yellow vest protests, which began in 2018 over fuel taxes and expanded into a broader revolt against the cost of living and perceived economic inequality.
The yellow vest movement has called for another national day of action on October 31 to defend the right to demonstrate, suggesting that the latest clashes may be part of a wider period of unrest rather than an isolated outburst.

Ukraine says Starlink is back to normal after disruptions
Ukraine said Saturday that the Starlink satellite system and the military's Starshield were back to high operating speeds after more than a week of disruptions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X that the restoration began overnight.
"The most important thing today is that Starlink and Starshield operations have been restored to the speeds we had before the restrictions," Zelenskyy said. "The speeds are now where they need to be."
The Starlink network has been critical for Ukraine in its defense to Russia's full-scale war.
Ukraine uses Starlink for drone operations, logistics such as delivering food and water to soldiers, and frontline communications. Zelenskyy said the satellite service also helps defend Ukraine from Iranian-made Shahed drones used by Russia.
Trump Administration and Musk deny blame
The U.S. and Ukraine had been at odds over who to blame for the more than week-long disruptions to Elon Musk's SpaceX operated satellite technology.
Zelenskyy told NBC's Meet the Press Sunday that Ukrainian officials believed the U.S. government was behind the disruptions and restrictions to Starlink and Starshield. He said SpaceX put the restrictions in response to a "message from [the] American government."
In an Oct. 14 post on X, Musk stated that Starshield is owned and controlled by the U.S. government.
"Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS," he said.
The Trump Administration has denied interfering with Ukraine's Starshield access.
Speaking to reporters Friday, President Trump declined to answer a question regarding who ordered the restrictions.
"I wouldn't tell you if I did know," Trump said.
Trump also defended Musk, dismissing concerns that the SpaceX CEO played a role in the limitations.
"Elon will never do anything wrong," Trump said. "I know him very well. He's a fair person."
Ukraine's Defense Ministry said Saturday its monitoring systems were officially recording the restoration of Starlink and Starshield operating speed. It said connectivity remained stable at speeds of more than 250 mph.
The restrictions had capped the speed at about 100 mph. This hindered Ukraine's ability to intercept drones and disrupted missions.
Ukraine Defense Minister Yevhen Khmara said the restoration is the result of "direct dialogue" by Zelenskyy.
"This result is important, above all, for our front line, for service members, for drone operations, logistics, and communications," Khamara said.
In his post about the restoration, Zelenskyy thanked "all Americans" including members of Congress, the State Department and President Trump.
The restoration comes as there is a renewed push for peace talks led by the U.S. Russia has agreed to a trilateral meeting with Ukraine and the U.S. next month.
Russia and Ukraine also agreed to a localized ceasefire in the Russian occupied city of Oleshky in southern Ukraine. The White House said the ceasefire was brokered by First Lady Melania Trump, with an agreement for humanitarian aid and civilian evacuation as there is a growing food crisis in the city.
But Ukraine and Russia still continue to trade attacks elsewhere.
Ukraine attacked a chemical plant in the Russian city of Tolyatti on Saturday. A Russian drone struck a residential building in Kyiv's Obolon District Saturday causing a fire.

The internet’s mad scramble on Wednesday to patch a pair of critical vulnerabilities in PHP, a widely used web scripting language, was already too late to stop every attack, newly released details reveal.
Wednesday’s release of fixes for two critical vulnerabilities in PHP caused administrators and security staff to race to identify and patch vulnerable websites and apps, while attackers inevitably reverse engineered the fixes to learn how to exploit the flaws. Some governments and other groups even proactively took key websites down in anticipation of the release, so they wouldn't be targeted before they could apply the patches.
But in addition to detecting such active exploitation on Wednesday, research published Wednesday evening by Amazon Web Services indicates that at least one actor had started attempting to exploit the bugs—known collectively as PHP2Shell—on October 17, four days before Wednesday's public revelations.
AWS analysts spotted the October 17 exploitation on Wednesday while looking back at activity on one of their so-called honeypots, or intentionally vulnerable web servers or other digital lures that help researchers study attack methods and trends. The attempt came from an IP address that AWS says is linked to a “commercial anonymization network,” in other words a proxy network or VPN.
“While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” CJ Moses, AWS's chief information security officer, wrote in the research post.
Proof-of-concept exploits for PHP2Shell began emerging publicly on Wednesday, with some seeming to appear hours before the public disclosure at 10 am ET. In the hours leading up to the disclosure, AWS researchers say their honeypots were hit with multiple exploitation attempts anonymized using various providers and seemingly with various attack goals, likely indicating multiple different actors. “Technical analysis is ongoing, and it’s unclear if any of these attempts would have succeeded in real-world systems,” Moses wrote. He added that “PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild.”
The PHP Foundation did not immediately respond to WIRED's request for comment.
Though it is unclear how the exploitation on October 17 happened or where it came from, AWS emphasizes that the findings underscore how coordinated vulnerability disclosure must evolve and speed up given global access to AI tools that can accelerate vulnerability analysis and allow less technically proficient actors to quickly develop new exploits.
“The time from patch to working exploit is shrinking for structural reasons,” Moses wrote. “In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed.”

Voters in Canada’s Alberta have overwhelmingly rejected a proposal to begin a process toward independence, the national broadcaster CBC has projected, delivering a victory for prime minister Mark Carney and supporters of Canadian unity.
With more than 1 million votes counted early Tuesday, about 76% supported remaining in Canada, compared with 23% who backed beginning a process that could lead to separation. About a third of ballots had been counted.
Even though the vote was not explicitly about independence – a point that frustrated separatists – the ballot question nonetheless exposed divisions in Alberta’s politics and raised questions about the durability of national unity.
Delays at roughly 100 of the 1,400 at polling stations across the province pushed results back by more than two hours – but shortly after polls closed on Monday evening, the results suggested a decisive win for those looking to remain in Canada.
The separation question – whether to remain in Canada or begin a legal process that could lead to a second vote – was one of 10 put to Albertans on Monday. The others covered issues including immigration, healthcare, education and the province’s constitutional powers. Elections Alberta said the remaining results could take days to count.
In the days leading up to the vote, provincial leaders and federal politicians crisscrossed the province to make the case for a unified country.
Prime minister Carney, who grew up in Edmonton, warned against a vote from residents of the oil-rich province simply looking to “send a message” to the federal government.
“A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of deep uncertainty and lost opportunities for Albertans and Canadians,” he told an energetic crowd last week.
The Conservative leader, Pierre Poilievre, whose parliamentary seat is in the province, told a crowd of supporters that Albertans were not “quitters”.
“To those people who are thinking about taking out their frustration on the current government by voting for separation in the referendum, I say this: Canada is more than a government,” he said. “It is a people, a flag, a land, a history and a promise.”
Data from Elections Alberta indicated roughly 43% of eligible voters – or 1.3 million Albertans – had already cast ballots before Monday’s vote through advance voting and mail-in ballots. That figure pointed to a potentially higher turnout than the province’s last referendum in 2021.
The Alberta premier, Danielle Smith, has said publicly that she will vote to remain in Canada, but that she will not require elected members of her party to do the same.
Her tenure as leader of the United Conservative party is due in large part to separatists within the party who ousted her predecessor, Jason Kenney. In recent months, Smith has tried to placate both the separatists and federalists in the party, in a province where a majority is not interested in secession.
The referendum has also become a political liability for Smith’s party, which has seen popular support tumble in recent months, including the loss of a one-time conservative stronghold during a byelection.
Still, members of the separatist movement told the Guardian they would continue their push for independence.
In an interview before the results, the Calgary mayor, Jeromy Farkas, a staunch opponent of the independence movement, told the Guardian the city’s “best future is here, as a Canadian city” amid fears that uncertainty could lead to capital flight.
“I am Canadian because I’m Canadian, not in a transactional way and regardless of the flavour of prime minister,” said Farkas.
“And I’m going to continue to make the case for how our future is strongest together because no result will permanently put this to bed,” he added, “The separatist movement sees this as a long-term project.”

New Delhi, Oct 24: The Centre has directed states and Union Territories to strictly enforce a ban on the reuse of single-use medical devices and disposable surgical items in public and private healthcare facilities, citing infection risks and instances of patients being charged the full cost of reused equipment.
In a letter dated October 16, the Directorate General of Health Services (DGHS) said it had come to its notice that certain private and corporate hospitals were sterilising and reusing devices meant for one-time use, particularly in critical specialities such as cardiology, nephrology, oncology, cardiothoracic and vascular surgery, and neurosurgery.
"It has been observed that such devices and disposable surgical items, after being used for one procedure, are being subjected to sterilisation and subsequently reused, despite being designated for single use only," the letter said.
The DGHS said the practice raised concerns relating to patient safety, infection prevention and control, regulatory compliance and healthcare expenditure.
It also flagged instances in which patients were allegedly charged the full cost of these devices despite their reuse, or the cost was reimbursed by the concerned government authorities.
Devices reportedly being reused include cardiac catheters, guidewires, balloon and ablation catheters, introducer sheaths, dialysis equipment such as dialysers and blood tubing, surgical staplers, laparoscopic trocars and orthopaedic drill bits. Syringes and needles have also been identified among items being reused, according to the Association of Indian Medical Device Industry (AiMeD).
Even after sterilisation, devices designed for one-time use may not be safe for reuse, as inadequate reprocessing or deterioration can compromise their performance and leave biological material behind, the directorate said.
The practice could expose patients to cross-infections, device malfunction, reduced performance and other procedure-related complications, the DGHS warned. These infections may include hepatitis B and C, HIV and bacterial infections.
The directorate said the practice could violate provisions of the Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940, the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, and applicable infection prevention and biomedical waste management requirements.
"It has accordingly been decided that the reuse of single-use medical devices and disposable surgical items shall be strictly prohibited in all healthcare organisations, including both public and private healthcare facilities, under the administrative jurisdiction of the Government of India, states and Union Territories," the letter said.
The DGHS has asked chief secretaries, state health department officials, directors of health services, the Drug Controller General of India (DCGI) and state and UT drug controllers to ensure strict vigilance and effective enforcement.
Authorities have been asked to inspect and monitor healthcare establishments, ensure compliance with the directive and take appropriate action in cases of violations.
"All single-use devices/disposable surgical items should be utilised strictly in accordance with the instructions and recommendations of the Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM)," the letter said.
The letter also referred to a Central Government Health Scheme (CGHS) office memorandum issued in December 2016 concerning the reuse of such devices in hospitals empanelled under the scheme.

Dr. Sajjan Singh Yadav, an Indian Administrative Service (IAS) officer from the 1995 batch, on Saturday (October 24, 2026) was transferred as Chief Secretary (CS) to Jammu and Kashmir, at a time when the significant number of files approved by the elected government stand for clearance in the CS office for the Lieutenant Governor’s nod.
An order of the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) said, “With the approval of the Competent Authority, Dr. Sajjan Singh Yadav, IAS (AGMUT:1995) is hereby transferred from Delhi to J&K and posted as Chief Secretary, J&K with effect from November 01 2026 or from the date of joining, whichever is later”.
The Centre picked an officer from the Arunachal Pradesh-Goa-Mizoram and Union Territories AGMUT) cadre despite senior officers in J&K queued up as probables for the SC post, which include IAS officers Shaleen Kabra, Ashwani Kumar Sharma and Dheeraj Gupta.
Mr. Yadav, a resident of Haryana, has a doctorate in Public Health from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine and a Master’s in Public Policy from the University of Minnesota. He brings in multi-sectoral experience as he served as Mission Director, National Nutrition Mission (POSHAN Abhiyan); Director, National Rural Health Mission; and Commissioner of Food & Civil Supplies, Trade and Taxes, and Excise in Delhi. This year, Mr. Yadav also served as Delhi Additional Chief Secretary and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of the Delhi Jal Board.
His entry into J&K comes at a time when the Chief Minister’s office and the Lieutenant Governor’s office remain at loggerheads over a series of issues, especially their spheres of work. The ruling National Conference has repeatedly accused the L-G office of not approving the Cabinet-approved files on regularisation of daily wagers, rationalisation of reservation and finalisation of Transaction of Business Rules, which remain undecided even after two years of completion of the Omar Abdullah government on October 16. The L-G office and the CM office also failed to reach a consensus over the names of the Advocate General and the Public Service Commission head.
Current J&K Chief Secretary Atal Dulloo, who is retiring later this month, is not leaving on a positive note. J&K CM Abdullah named him on record in the assembly as one who opposed the government’s resolution on Statehood in the Assembly recently. Opposition Peoples Democratic Party (PDP) legislator Waheed-ur-Rehman Parra also moved a Motion of Privilege against Mr. Dullo and Law Secretary Anchal Sethi, stating that the power of an elected Legislature to initiate, deliberate upon, amend and adopt resolutions is a core parliamentary function.
The Opposition PDP said officers were entitled to provide administrative or legal advice to the Government within the scope of their duties “but such advice cannot be permitted to become an instrument for questioning, constraining or intruding upon the legislative privileges and authority of this House”.

Meanwhile, ruling NC legislator Tanvir Sadiq termed Mr. Dulloo “a son of the soil” and asked him to clear the regularisation file and send it to the Chief Minister. “Daily wagers and casual workers await regularisation. Mr. Dulloo is here till November 31. He is the son of soil. If he wants something to be done for posterity and his own people, he should return the regularisation file. This will allow us to meet the demand made to people of J&K. History will judge you (Mr. Dulloo) for your contribution to your own people,” said Mr. Sadiq.

Oil spill washes up on UAE beaches after tanker strike
- Published
An oil spill from a tanker attacked near the Strait of Hormuz is spreading along the United Arab Emirates (UAE) coastline, forcing the closure of some beaches and coastal areas.
Satellite images from Monday show the beginnings of the oil spill from a ship matching the location and dimensions of Gem No.2, which was damaged between 9 and 10 October during a record surge of vessel strikes by Iran.
The slick of oil had spread more than 35km (22 miles) from the tanker by Wednesday, the satellite imagery showed.
UAE authorities said on Thursday that the incident is affecting beaches near the northern city of Umm Al Quwain and verified video from Friday shows the oil washing ashore, colouring the water black.
The UAE's Ministry of Climate Change and Environment said on Thursday that it "immediately began containment" in order to "limit environmental impacts".
Prof Steve Widdicombe, director of Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre in the UAE, told BBC Verify it was "inevitable that there will be an impact", but researchers caution it is too soon to assess extent of the damage.
Initially a much smaller oil leak could be seen emerging from the ship on 19 October.
But the slick appears to have rapidly spread over two days, according to radar satellite imagery reviewed by BBC Verify and intelligence firm MAIAR.
Oil spills can cause immediate deaths of marine animals and other organisms, for example by physically trapping turtles, smothering the feathers of seabirds or damaging the gills of fish.
They can also cause longer-lasting damage, Prof Widdicombe said, if species remain exposed to toxic compounds from the oil which could impact their ability to reproduce.
Researchers have cautioned the environmental impact at this stage is very uncertain, as it depends on factors including the volume and type of oil spilled, how quickly it evaporates or breaks down and the effectiveness of the clean-up operation.
But the spill does extend towards Siniyah and Khor Al Beidah islands, a globally recognised Key Biodiversity Area containing habitats like corals, seagrasses and saltmarshes, as well as species including green turtles and the critically endangered Halavi guitarfish.
The proximity of the spill to this area is the "most concerning environmental angle", according to Eoghan Darbyshire, a scientist at the Conflict and Environment Observatory.
Tanker hit 14 days ago
BBC Verify analysis of the dimensions and location of the ship indicate they match a crude oil tanker called Gem No.2.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard reported the Panama-flagged tanker was "struck by an unknown projectile" on 9 October, just north of the town of Al Jazeera Al Hamra, causing a fire on board that was later extinguished.
Verified footage first posted on social media on 10 October showed the crew running across the deck and putting on lifejackets as a large cloud of black smoke rose over the ship.
Iranian state media shared footage of a ship matching Gem No.2 which appeared to show the vessel on fire with burning oil spilling into the sea.
The ship had been attempting to exit the Strait of Hormuz via an "unauthorized and dangerous route", according to state media.
All 22 Indian crew members were rescued, the Indian consulate in Dubai said on 11 October.
Gem No.2 is one of a record number of ships that reported being attacked in and around the Strait of Hormuz at the start of October.
Security experts told BBC Verify this was part of an Iranian effort to assert greater control over the strait, in response to the US military successfully escorting more vessels through the vital shipping lane.
Tankers and other commercial vessels have come under attack from both Iranian and US forces in and around the Strait of Hormuz amid the conflict between the two countries.
Another major oil slick washed up on the shores of Iran's Qeshm Island in August, which experts said threatened wildlife, protected ecosystems and fishing communities.

It looks like the long-rumored touchscreen MacBook might actually get announced next week, and after using the Lenovo Yoga 9n for our testing of Nvidia’s RTX Spark platform, it got me thinking: this is a lot of what I want from a touchscreen MacBook.
I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
Not that I believe for a second that Apple will actually make a 2-in-1 convertible.
I hope Apple’s touchscreen MacBook takes some lessons from this Lenovo laptop
Not that I believe for a second that Apple will actually make a 2-in-1 convertible.
Like the Apple silicon in modern MacBook Pros, RTX Spark is an Arm-based processor with a beefy integrated GPU and lots of unified memory. And the Yoga is the most fun RTX Spark laptop so far because it’s a 16-inch 2-in-1 convertible with a stylus. Its Nvidia-powered compatriots also have touchscreens, like most Windows laptops, but they’re conventional clamshell designs.
The Lenovo Yoga does all your typical 2-in-1 stuff: it can be used as a clamshell laptop, and it can fold its hinge all the way back for tent mode and tablet modes. As a tablet, you can use it in either landscape or portrait orientation, and getting the keyboard out of the way is great for watching movies, playing games with a controller, or integrating your laptop into a multi-monitor desk setup with keyboard and mouse.
The Yoga 9n’s included stylus works for note-taking and drawing on its excellent OLED display, but you can also use it on the haptic trackpad for a Wacom-like experience, without blocking the screen with your hand. And the stylus is magnetic, allowing it to attach to the Yoga’s lid — either on its own, or while housed in its case. I particularly enjoy using the Yoga’s stylus for photo retouching in Lightroom Classic or Photoshop. I haven’t used a stylus for that kind of work in ages, since I gave up my old Wacom, but having one that works on either the screen or the trackpad is incredibly convenient
I expect a touchscreen MacBook Pro would have Apple Pencil support. And like on the Lenovo, it would go a long way to get me back to using a stylus for retouching. But I hope that also like the Lenovo, it works on the trackpad too — the more options, the better. And if a touch-enabled MacBook supports the Apple Pencil (which it should), I’m also hoping it attaches to the laptop, both for convenience and for wireless charging, as on the iPad Pro. Lenovo’s stylus relies on USB-C charging, which is fine, but not as convenient as always having it charged and ready to go while attached to your laptop.
I don’t expect Apple to make a standard convertible laptop after all this time. Simply joining Windows manufacturers in making a 2-in-1 or swapping the MacBook Pro’s Mini LED for a touchscreen OLED and calling it a day doesn’t seem very Apple. I’m hoping for something special, like Apple’s own take on the Microsoft Surface Laptop Studio — a clever idea that brought the touchscreen forward instead of flipping it backwards — or something totally fresh. And there are hints in macOS 27 that Apple is updating to Golden Gate to make touch functions feel more natural than just poking and prodding at things designed for a mouse cursor. As fun as I find 2-in-1 Windows laptops and Chromebooks, using those desktop operating systems with a finger or a stylus can get clunky.
My hopes are high for Apple to wow us, because this MacBook Pro with touch is sure to be expensive. And Apple’s recent design decisions aren’t faultless. The HomeView’s lack of apps is perplexing. The iPhone Duo is a little messy. Current MacBooks are so great, it’s easy to forget the butterfly keyboard fiasco wasn’t all that long ago. After all this time of holding out on adding a touchscreen to the MacBook, Apple has to make it worth it.

As reported by Music Business Worldwide, Spotify appears to be stepping up enforcement of existing policies regarding Family and Duo subscription plans by requiring users to scan a QR code in person on the plan manager’s device in order to maintain access to it. Those who fail to scan the address verification QR code within seven days will see their account demoted to the free tier and be barred from joining any other Duo or Family plan for 12 months.
Spotify’s support documentation verifies the policy after users on Reddit began posting reports of receiving the QR prompt. The enforcement stems from Spotify’s requirement that family plan members reside at the same address—a seemingly reasonable policy in concept. But what if you have a child away in college, a spouse who works on the road, or any number of other circumstances that might see families separated by physical distance? The policy could extend beyond friend groups looking to save a buck, affecting actual families who thought they were using the program as intended.
Goldman Sachs analysts, in their October 15 Music in the Air: 10 Years On report, made available by HITS Daily Double, estimate that “a meaningful share of family plan users are not actual household members, but rather friends sharing a plan to reduce costs.” The report goes on to add, “We see additional monetization upside from tightening household verification on multi-user plans. Most family plans require members to reside at the same address, but enforcement has been minimal in practice.”

Why are doctors paid less for procedures on women?
A little-known system determines what surgeries are worth. It almost always values men more highly.
In the moody alcoves of a lobby bar in Chicago in 2021 over French 75s, Dr. Louise King, a gynecologic surgeon, and Katie L. Watson, a bioethics professor, found themselves in conversation about a topic that had long frustrated them both: Female surgeons are consistently underpaid compared to male surgeons, even after accounting for specialty, rank, age, and other factors.
What troubled them even more was how the pay gap compounded in King’s own field. Surgeons who perform procedures that are specifically for women, like gynecological surgeries, are paid less for their services than surgeons who perform comparable surgeries for the male anatomy. Gynecologic surgeons are also predominantly women. Over the course of the conversation, Watson termed this situation “double discrimination,” a phrase that captures the overlapping dilemma of lower pay for surgeries in a specialty that is overwhelmingly female and also serves a primarily female patient population.
Key takeaways
- Doctors are paid less for gynecologic surgeries than for similar surgeries on men. That pay gap has barely improved in the last 20 years.
- The value of each procedure is largely set by a committee of doctors that relies on self-reported, and sometimes inaccurate, surveys in which doctors report the skill and time their own procedures require.
- When doctors are paid less to treat women’s health concerns, hospitals allocate fewer resources to those services, leading to worse outcomes for women
- Experts say the gap can be closed by reconsidering how gynecologic surgeries are valued and removing sex-specific billing codes.
That term, which has since entered the medical literature, stuck because the problem it describes has been well documented for decades. In 1997, a group of gynecologic surgeons published a paper in the journal Gynecologic Oncology with a title that gets straight to it — “Is Adam worth more than Eve?” Dr. Barbara A. Goff, now chair of Obstetrics and Gynecology at University of Washington Medicine, and colleagues found that doctors are paid around 44 percent more for performing male-specific procedures than analogous female-specific ones.
In the three decades since, the problem hasn’t been fixed. To the contrary, it has been effectively institutionalized, built into the systems and codes that determine how surgeons bill for procedures of all kinds. Today, gynecologic or female-specific procedures are in large part still reimbursed at lower rates than male-specific procedures even when they take similar time and skill.
Those disparities have consequences that extend beyond the compensation of individual doctors. When gynecological procedures don’t bring in as much money to hospitals, those same hospitals are disincentivised to offer women’s health services. That can lead to worse care for women and, crucially, fewer training opportunities for the surgeons who do that work.
But this historically persistent inequality is not a foregone conclusion.
How healthcare services are billed changes all the time as procedures get reevaluated, new ones get added, and medical societies and experts push for revisions. In fact, one of the biggest changes in how maternity care is billed and reimbursed is set to take effect early next year, splitting up services for prenatal care, delivery, postpartum care, and more. While this is a long-overdue fix for obstetrics, gynecologic surgery — which covers most of a woman’s life outside of childbearing years — continues to be left out of the conversation.
And although real change will require concerted efforts, King and Watson — and other advocates who have spent years documenting this disparity — have a fairly clear sense of how to start fixing it.
How surgical procedures are valued
The work of deciding how much a medical procedure is worth starts well above the head of any given doctor, medical practice, or hospital. In the United States, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, a federal agency that administers healthcare and health insurance policies, sets rates for different procedures based on a metric called relative value units (RVUs). An RVU is supposed to take into account how long a procedure takes, the skill it requires, and the intensity of work it demands. Both Medicare and private insurers consider these figures when they’re settling on reimbursement levels. If a procedure has a higher RVU, it is valued more highly, and makes more money.
In a recent study, cheekily titled “Price and Prejudice,” researchers from the Mount Sinai Health System found that out of 55 pairs of sex-specific procedures that they evaluated in 2023, 75 percent had lower RVUs for procedures on female patients. On average, RVUs for male-specific procedures were 30 percent higher, and when those procedures were performed in a hospital or surgical center, surgeons were paid around 26 percent more.
For example, doctors will often perform biopsies — taking a small sample of tissues, cells, or fluids — on both male and female genitalia to diagnose problems. In 2023, researchers found that Medicare’s standard national rate for reimbursing surgeons was $121.32 for a penile biopsy but only $65.74 for a vaginal biopsy.
Loading interactive graphic…
King, the director of reproductive bioethics at Harvard Medical School Center for Bioethics and a contributor on the study, believes that when the RVU system was created back in the 1990s, gynecological services were largely ignored, leaving the specialty undervalued from the start. While Medicare and Medicaid Services have undertaken some efforts to make RVUs more equitable across specialties over the years, that undervaluation has persisted.
That problem may come down to how those values are determined in the first place — and who determines them. RVUs are set by a committee of doctors convened by the American Medical Association (AMA), with most of the seats allocated to members of major medical societies. The committee surveys different doctors on the time and skill required for procedures in their specialties. Based on these responses, the committee recommends values for each service to the federal government, which has historically accepted nearly 90 percent of them.
While the data quality of the underlying surveys has improved over the years, it is still not very high, said Dr. Miriam Laugesen, a tenured associate professor of health policy and management at Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health. Because the committee’s process isn’t transparent, it is often unclear what evidence its valuations rest on. This leads to distortions of all kinds, she said.
”It’s not a government process; It’s not a federal advisory committee,” Laugesen said. “It’s just a committee that was put together by the [AMA]. It’s pretty unusual in terms of how policy is made.”
In particular, King said that the surveys have a very low response rate from some specialties and are only sent to a small subset of doctors. She has never received a committee survey in the 17 years that she has practiced.
The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) has a core seat on the committee that determines RVUs. But most ACOG members are general OB-GYNs, who split their time between obstetrics and gynecology and typically operate relatively rarely. The surgeons who perform the bulk of gynecologic operations are subspecialists – gynecologic oncologists, urogynecologists, and minimally invasive gynecologic surgeons — who complete an additional fellowship after residency. They mainly belong to their own societies and don’t have a seat at the table when RVUs are being determined.
”From a purely cynical or economic standpoint, [ACOG] has no reason to advance billing for gynecology. It doesn’t represent a large portion of the practices of their members,” said King, adding that ACOG has been heroic in its efforts to obtain reimbursement equity for its own members. (One unintended possible result of that advocacy is that pushing for a smaller pay gap for services related to pregnancy has in turn sent the message that women’s bodies are literally worth less, and are less deserving of care when they’re not engaged in the god-given duty of reproduction.)
The result is that doctors in specialties like OB-GYN who operate infrequently are answering the surveys about complicated surgical procedures that gynecologic surgeons perform more frequently. King said that her surgical schedule aligned more closely with those of general surgeons. For example, she operates two to three times a week whereas, according to her, an average OB-GYN will likely operate once a month.
“So they’re not the right people to be answering these surveys. They [the survey committee and ACOG] don’t target the surveys to people who operate a lot,” she said.
Part of the problem with using surveys to determine a key foundation of medical reimbursements is that the data is self-reported by doctors. This is especially relevant when more objective avenues may be available. One of those avenues is the American College of Surgeons’ National Surgical Quality Improvement Program, which is an initiative that collects and manages key surgical data to track quality and improvement in surgical fields, including the actual time spent performing surgical procedures, making it a more definitive measure than self-reported surveys.
Dr. Shitanshu Uppal, a gynecologic oncologist and division chief for gynecology oncology services at the University of Michigan, and his colleagues analyzed 901,917 surgeries using both the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program as well as the self-reported surveys used to determine RVUs. They found that median RVUs per hour vary widely between specialties. Gynecology had the third-lowest median RVUs per hour of all the specialties studied. In effect, that means that gynecological surgeons are paid less for every hour that they work.
The researchers also found that compared to the operating times logged for real surgeries in the Surgical Quality Improvement Program, surgeons in certain specialties tended to report longer procedure times in the self-reported surveys sent out by the RVUs committee. Specialties that reported longer operating times were more likely to be awarded higher RVUs, leading to greater hourly rates of reimbursement.
According to Uppal’s analysis, urologists — a profession most often associated with procedures on men because their work routinely concerns the prostate and the testicles — reported times that exceeded the baseline data by a median of 20 minutes. By contrast, estimates from gynecologists only exceeded the actual time by a median of five minutes, meaning that urologists tended to overestimate their time spent in surgery by four times as many minutes. Generally, urologists earn much more than general OB-GYNs, who in turn earn more than other subspecialties like gynecologic surgery. Despite having access to reliable electronic records of operating time, Uppal and his colleagues note, the AMA committee still continues to use self-reported operating times, which influences their RVU recommendations, ultimately cementing disparities in female-specific procedures.
“The system that they have now developed over time,” King said, “now creates discrimination because of its complexity.” She added that this is how systemic discrimination is perpetuated, even if systems or rules appear seemingly neutral.
How low reimbursement rates make women’s lives worse
The US healthcare system has never been especially good at putting its money where its mouth is when it comes to women’s health. Experts have been sounding the alarm on sex-based disparities in medical billing for a long time — long enough that governing authorities like the committee responsible for RVUs and ACOG have had time to respond to the concerns.
Over the years, the gap between male-specific procedure reimbursements and female-specific reimbursements has decreased slightly. But researchers of the Price and Prejudice study showed that between 2003 and 2023, there were no statistically significant improvements to the pay disparities. Comparing a smaller set of procedures across 1997, 2015, and 2023, they found that the gap had narrowed only minimally.
One common justification that ACOG provides for the pay gap is that obstetrics and gynecologic services see a higher-than-average share of patients on Medicaid, which pays doctors less than other insurers. King agreed this is a real factor, but it doesn’t explain why Medicare itself values procedures on women lower in the first place. And as her account of double discrimination makes clear, undervaluing gynecology ultimately affects women everywhere for the worse.
“I have patients who are waiting for surgery with me for a year at a time. I mean, that’s crazy.”
— Dr. Louise King
Lower reimbursements in gynecologic surgery disproportionately affect female surgeons because they represent a majority of this specialty. It’s not just the surgeons’ salaries that are affected. Hospitals and facilities work on a revenue-based model — if gynecologic surgeries are not bringing in enough money, institutions tend to allocate fewer resources to those procedures. That, in turn, can limit access to operating rooms, surgical staff, and operating times.
“I have patients who are waiting for surgery with me for a year at a time. I mean, that’s crazy,” King said. As a minimally invasive gynecologic surgeon, she surgically treats women with endometriosis, fibroids, cysts, or other such conditions.
It also affects the training that gynecologic surgeons receive. When there aren’t enough resources to operate regularly, opportunities to train residents are rarer than they should be. The result is that low reimbursement rates have contributed to a workforce of low-volume gynecologic surgeons who are sometimes not as well-trained as other surgeons who operate frequently.
The relationship between volume of surgeries performed and patient outcomes is well-documented in other fields. Research shows that surgeons who operate infrequently have worse outcomes, including more complications before, after, and during surgeries, compared to surgeons who operate regularly.
Low-volume gynecologic surgeons — who perform a particular procedure less than 12 times a year — have significantly higher rates of causing bowel and urinary tract injuries in their patients. Especially in benign gynecological surgery (procedures not related to cancer), having surgeons who operate frequently also increases the number of minimally invasive procedures performed, which is related to better patient outcomes.
Payment reform is an uphill battle, but not a lost cause
It takes multiple years and pressure from different entities to update or add new RVUs for procedures — but crucially, it is not impossible. The first few steps to creating a sustainable system might look like submitting gynecology-related procedure codes for reevaluation to the AMA committee or prompting a congressional report on the matter.
For example, for years there has only been one billing code for endometriosis, regardless of the complexity of surgery or technique used. This disincentivizes surgeons from taking on complicated surgical cases of endometriosis because of the low reimbursement rate. Reevaluating that rate or diversifying the various surgical approaches that different cases require would help affected women get the care they deserve.
Medicare’s payment system also has what’s called a budget neutrality rule, which dictates that significantly increased payments for any given procedure must be offset by cuts elsewhere. The AMA itself believes that reforming this rule would make it easier to work toward reimbursement equity for female-specific procedures.
Experts have suggested creating gynecology-specific conversion factors to bring parity to a system that naturally undervalues these procedures, while others think that eliminating sex-specific billing codes whenever possible is the right move. For example, the code for genitalia biopsies is different for men and women. This means that those procedures can be reimbursed differently even though they are essentially similar. Adopting one sex-neutral code for any genitalia biopsies would avoid this. While the reform required for this would be substantial, researchers believe that it would narrow the billing gap significantly.
Authorities often justify lower RVUs for female-specific procedures by pointing to training: Gynecologists spend fewer years learning to operate than urologists and other higher-paid surgical specialists, according to King.
Historically, surgeons who operated on the female pelvis trained in ways that were more closely aligned with general surgeons than OB-GYNs. When obstetrics and gynecology merged into one specialty in the 1900s, the training for gynecologic surgery was truncated.
“General OB-GYNs will train for four years and of that four years about 18 months is devoted to surgical training in gynecology,” said King, contrasting the new training period to those of general surgeons, which is in years.
She believes that training periods should be increased for gynecologic surgeons. That change would secure better reimbursement for the speciality, while also producing better trained surgeons who would be more attuned to advances in minimally invasive surgery that will ultimately improve the outcomes for their female patients. In some cases, the experience gained during a two-year fellowship in gynecologic surgery was equivalent to 19 years in practice.
In their initial work on double discrimination, Watson and King argued that failing to implement solutions for parity is tantamount to saying that female patients deserve less well-trained surgeons than male patients.
As with most women’s health issues, it is unclear if this systemic disparity in medical reimbursement is the result of conscious misogyny or a by-product of ignorance. But that question of origins matters little when its consequences have been enshrined in medical policy, with lasting consequences for the practice of medicine more generally. We have allowed this wage gap to persist, even as many have sounded the alarm for decades. It is long past time to heed their warnings.
October 7, 2026, 5:50 pm ET: This story was originally published on October 2 and has been updated to include the sourcing on the RVU gap resulting from training for gynecologic surgery.

A complaint I hear a lot from my millennial peers is that our parents didn’t teach us enough about money. I can say that personal finance wasn’t dinner table conversation in my house, and even as I went off to college and started fending for myself, it was almost a taboo subject. When it came to money, people either had it or they didn’t, and you definitely didn’t talk about it.
Should you let a chatbot manage your money?
ChatGPT can give decent financial advice — to the people who need it the least.
Maybe this is why the average American isn’t exactly fluent in personal finance, and the situation is getting worse. Americans can only answer about 50 percent of basic questions about borrowing, savings, and risk on a financial literacy survey, according to a 2026 study by TIAA, a retirement services company. About a third of those surveyed said they have a hard time making ends meet and are debt-constrained. These figures have remained relatively unchanged for nearly a decade, but dropped to their lowest level in this year’s study.
It makes sense: It’s hard to learn about money when it’s not taught in schools, and it’s such an intensely private topic. It’s also hard to make good financial decisions when you’re one of the growing number of American households struggling to pay bills, repay debts, and save for the future — and feeling very stressed about it.
In a perfect world, each of us could sit down with a financial adviser to get help — but most of us can’t afford that. Instead, average Americans tend to find personal finance tips on TikTok, in Reddit threads, by watching Suze Orman on YouTube or How to Get Rich on Netflix, or by Googling their questions.
Now we have AI tools, too.
With access to an internet’s worth of information and financial advice, ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI chatbots can answer any question you ask. They can help you put together a basic budget or, armed with your bank statements and the details of your student loans and your retirement accounts, tailor solutions to your specific situation. Or, at least, that’s the promise.
Key takeaways
- More people are turning to AI for financial advice: One in five Americans have used AI to help manage their money, and some experts think chatbots could be better than the status quo.
- AI works best if you know what questions to ask: Those with basic financial literacy will be able to make the most of these tools, while those without it — who might need help the most — could be led astray.
- Better advice comes with greater risks: Sharing your financial information with a chatbot helps personalize its recommendations. This raises privacy concerns, so you might want to delete your data when you’re done.
- Think of AI as a financially savvy friend: Chatbots can answer money questions you might be embarrassed to ask someone else and use that context to help build your budget.
AI could create a more utopian, more equitable future, where reliable, hyper-personalized advice is just a prompt or two away for people who can’t afford to meet with an expert in real life. But machines are built by people, and there’s good reason to be concerned that these machines will simply replicate the biases and disparities built into our current system.
Here’s what experts say about how to make the most of these tools — and how to think about all of the inherent risks of uploading a lot of personal financial information to a chatbot or, worse, giving an AI agent the keys to your bank account.
The steep rise, risks, and rewards of AI financial advisers
Nearly 20 percent of Americans have used AI tools like ChatGPT for financial advice, and close to 25 percent for Gen Z adults and millennials have tried it, according to an August Gallup poll. These numbers could tick up too: In October, OpenAI started rolling out a dedicated personal finance tool to its ChatGPT Free and Go users in the United States, which effectively means anyone can try it. ChatGPT Finances lets you securely connect your bank account to the tool using a platform called Plaid, and then you can basically have a conversation with the chatbot about your real-time finances down to the penny. It’s like an AI-powered Mint (RIP) that you can talk to directly.
Regardless of where you encounter a chatbot or how much data you give it, experts say these tools could genuinely help improve financial literacy. You can talk to them about money problems you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family, or ask questions and receive actionable, personalized information. There are real upsides to using AI this way.
Taha Choukhmane, an associate professor of finance at the MIT Sloan School of Management, has been studying outcomes when people turn to chatbots for financial advice. In general, these AI tools give pretty good advice, and that advice gets better as people become more practiced in asking the right question, according to research he published earlier this year.
“We were actually quite surprised that relative to the status quo, the average American would be better off if they were to follow the advice,” Choukhmane told me. But he added a caveat: “Just following the advice without understanding the advice puts you at risk of not fully understanding the risk.”
But you shouldn’t trust everything a chatbot tells you and should verify everything before making any decisions.
Chatbot advice has some significant limitations. First, it’s not impartial. The finance industry has a vested interest in steering you toward certain ways of managing your money, and that typically means selling you products, like loans. If you’ve ever searched for personal finance tips on Google, you’ve probably noticed that a lot of the top results come from banks and other financial institutions. This is by design, according to John Campbell, an economics professor at Harvard. But because AI is aggregating all of that advice, the specific influences and possible bias is less obvious.
“AI is very promising for providing low-cost financial advice in plain English that will arguably be better than what many people would be able to do on their own,” said Campbell, who’s also the co-author of Fixed: Why Personal Finance Is Broken and How to Make It Work for Everyone. “One caveat is that chatbot advice is quite likely — unless a model has been carefully trained — to reflect the average of whatever’s being posted on the internet, and that may or may not be first-rate advice.”
An example Campbell gives is the question of when to start taking Social Security benefits. While you’re eligible at age 62, many economists agree that you should delay your benefits, which, based on the way the government calculates your monthly payouts, will allow you to enjoy much higher benefits later in life. But paid financial advisers can recommend starting as early as possible, since waiting longer reduces the amount of money that needs to be managed, which reduces the adviser’s fees. That means there’s a lot of conflicting advice online, much of it supplied by the finance industry. And that’s the information used to train AI models.
“The advice is much more mixed,” Campbell said. “And so if a chatbot is learning from that, it may not actually give the best advice.”
It can be hard to recognize bad advice anywhere in life, but especially when you’re talking to a machine that’s programmed to please you. A chatbot could encourage you to consider a balance transfer, to lean in on credit card rewards, or to refinance your mortgage — all decisions with upsides and downsides for you, but definite upsides for banks — without you realizing how much of its training data comes from the finance industry selling these products. What’s worse is that if you do end up taking bad advice, it might be years before you realize it. You won’t know that you refinanced a mortgage at a bad time until a better time comes along.
That leads me to the other major issue with using chatbots for money advice: People who lack financial literacy are the most likely to fall for bad advice, because they simply don’t recognize it as such. They also tend to be less wealthy, which means they can’t afford big mistakes.
One way to mitigate risk, oddly enough, is to give the AI chatbot more personal information. The more details about your situation it has to consider, the more it can offer personalized advice. More context also means better advice, according to Choukhmane.
“There’s a trade-off there,” Choukhmane said. “There’s real risk around privacy, and so I think everyone needs to find their level of control.”
Don’t assume your data is safe
Any time you’re talking to a chatbot, you’re putting a lot of trust in tech companies to take care of the personal details you’re sharing. Sending sensitive financial data is an especially risky proposition. While tech companies, including OpenAI, promise to keep your data secure, there’s already a long list of breaches, leaks, and privacy violations that serve as cautionary tales.
It’s also impossible to know what tech companies might do with your data in the future. Most of them will use it to train their models, unless you tell them not to. Some of them will use the data to serve you personalized ads.
Then there’s the risk of bad actors getting into your ChatGPT, Claude, or Gemini account. If you’ve been using a chatbot for financial advice and uploading your bank statements, a hacker could gain access to a stunning amount of information that could enable them to do all kinds of terrible things to your life.
“They could steal your identity and open accounts and then quickly bankrupt a person,” said Delicia Reynolds Hand, a senior director at Consumer Reports. “It’s not even so much the primary underlying accounts that could be at risk, it’s more just access to this information.”
The steady march of AI progress is making this situation even more complicated. The previous era of chatbots offering financial advice is quickly bleeding into a new phase of AI agents logging into bank accounts on users’ behalf. If you’re using a tool like Claude Cowork or even an AI assistant like Muse, you can give an agent the login credentials to your bank account, and because the agent is operating its own computer, it can actually make transfers, apply for loans, or really do anything in your account. This is reportedly driving major banks wild, since they don’t know which logins are coming from humans and which are agents. And because we know that AI agents are unpredictable, it’s hard to know how that access might go wrong.
Beyond data security and privacy, you should also be aware of the simple fact that nobody’s really at fault if you end up losing money using these tools. Chatbots are not regulated in the way that human financial advisers, who have a fiduciary duty to act in your best interest, are.
“If I get bad tax advice from H&R Block or a tax adviser, there are a clear set of rules and guardrails in place to manage what I can expect in that relationship and where the service they use has liability and where that liability ends,” Hand said. “Currently, that’s not the case for these tools.”
Trust but verify — and then delete your data
In the final years of the Cold War, Ronald Reagan popularized an old Russian proverb: Trust, but verify. The phrase is somewhat nonsensical, since trusting someone implies that you don’t need to verify what they’re saying, and verifying what’s said implies you didn’t trust them in the first place. But if you are willing to shoulder a bit of risk, consider approaching AI this way, especially when your life savings are on the line. I’d also suggest adding a coda to the phrase: And then delete your data.
Chatbots are not stand-ins for licensed financial advisers, he said, and you shouldn’t let them make decisions for you.
The great paradox with tools like ChatGPT and Claude is that they’re very good at generating truthy text. It sounds authoritative and looks correct — and usually is. Except when it isn’t. AI is famously unpredictable and prone to hallucinations. You can ask the same question twice and get two different answers. That doesn’t mean these tools are useless. It just means you have to approach them with caution. You have to interrogate these chatbots, challenge whatever advice they give you, and then crosscheck that with other, more reputable, sources.
“If you’ve never used these tools, I would not encourage you to just change all your financial plans based on your first conversation,” Choukhmane said. “You want to be quite careful. Start using these tools, start understanding, ask a lot of follow-up questions.”
When it comes to mitigating risk, consider giving ballpark figures for your income or spending when you’re talking to a chatbot about your finances. Uploading financial documents, even if they’re redacted, is inevitably filling a tech company’s vault with your sensitive information without necessarily knowing what will happen to it next. You should also dig into your privacy and security settings to make sure you’ve turned on multi-factor authentication and that your personal data is not being used to train AI models and gets deleted after 30 days.
Ethan Bloch, the product lead for ChatGPT for Financial Services, made a similar set of recommendations when I talked to him recently. Chatbots are not stand-ins for licensed financial advisers, he said, and you shouldn’t let them make decisions for you. They’re designed to inform and help you think through complex topics.
“You should liken it to just talking to a friend who has some very informed opinions about finance,” Bloch told me. “But if you’re actually making some large financial decision — your portfolio or retirement — you still need to seek out the help.”
Regardless of how experienced you are with chatbots or how much data you’re prepared to hand over, remember what Campbell, the Harvard professor, said. If your financial literacy isn’t great, AI chatbots can be trouble. And if you’re like most Americans, you could probably stand to learn a little bit more about things like mortgages and interest rates.
Yes, Chatbots can be a good way to brush up on financial literacy. You can ask them the money questions you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family. But you can also learn about money the old-fashioned way: Reading books and websites written by reputable, independent sources. The Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. has a portal of financial education resources, including games and quizzes. Khan Academy has a course that covers everything from credit scores to college savings. There’s a personal finance subreddit that I joined years ago and read almost daily. There are budgeting apps, like YNAB which has its own huge Reddit presence.
Whatever you do to learn more about personal finance, simply doing something is progress. Talking about personal finance isn’t the taboo it once was in the US, and it’s even a required course in the vast majority of American high schools now. And while AI won’t magically solve your money problems, it can help get you started. Just be careful. Your livelihood could be on the line.

Since the news about Christina Applegate’s multiple sclerosis misdiagnosis was released, texts from friends in disbelief have been popping up on my phone. “How could this happen?” they asked. “I wonder what else it could be?” they questioned. Because it took so long to receive my multiple sclerosis diagnosis, they assume that I might be wondering if I, too, could be misdiagnosed. “I’m not surprised,” I responded each time someone reached out. “MS can be difficult to diagnose.”
“She came into my room and said, ‘Congratulations — you don’t have MS,’” Applegate shared on a recent episode of her podcast, “MeSsy.” While the doctor thought this was positive news, Applegate told her listeners that she was not happy at all. “You don’t get misdiagnosed, and all of the sudden I’m better,” she said. I felt her disappointment as if it were my own — because not long ago, it was.
I’ll never forget when my neurologist said the words, “I think what we’re dealing with here is MS.” It was 2017. He’d mentioned the possibility at previous appointments, and I’d already been living with debilitating weakness, pain, and fatigue for 13 years, so I wasn’t completely shocked. But I was scared, and also relieved.
On that day, those two letters — MS — were so much more than a couple of symbols from the alphabet. They held the weight of 13 years of repeated lab work and office visits. They carried the anger of being told I was exaggerating and the hopelessness of feeling as though there was no solution to the weakness preventing me from walking. They provided the validation I deserved for waking up every day for 13 years and choosing to keep searching despite being told I may never receive an answer. Those letters were definitively spoken after all other possibilities had been ruled out. But what happens when every other possible disease isn’t considered first? Perhaps a misdiagnosis.
Across the country, news programs are interviewing doctors to understand how such a critical mistake can be made — and asking what else could be causing her debilitating symptoms. But Applegate is not alone. While data appear to be limited, recent publications from specialized MS centers suggest that around 30% of those originally referred for MS were eventually diagnosed with another disease.
There is no one test to confirm MS. It doesn’t yet have a measurable numerical value like high blood pressure or elevated cholesterol does. The McDonald Criteria for diagnosing MS were recently revised to prevent misdiagnoses from occurring. They didn’t provide clarity in my case even as I begged for an answer.
Other diseases that cause similar symptoms and findings include lupus, Lyme disease, fibromyalgia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and less common conditions like neuromyelitis optica and MOG antibody disease. During my diagnostic journey, I was tested for these conditions and other, much rarer — and only newly discovered — antibodies that cause diseases of the nervous system. And researchers continue to discover novel antibodies that cause similar neurological autoimmune diseases, so some people diagnosed with MS today could potentially learn they have a disease that falls outside of the MS umbrella in the future.
Ongoing research is focusing on finding measurable MS biomarkers that would make diagnosis much clearer. Ultimately, if symptoms continue to worsen on treatment, as they did for Applegate, a new medication or diagnosis should be considered.
While some autoimmune conditions — like Sjögren’s, Hashimoto’s thyroiditis, and rheumatoid arthritis — have antibodies that can be measured in the blood and used to confirm diagnosis, MS does not yet have a known antibody. Diagnosis relies solely on symptoms, MRI, and spinal tap findings. But other conditions can present with similar findings and symptoms. Essentially, MS is a diagnosis of exclusion.
For years, I was misdiagnosed with fibromyalgia, but I always felt there was more going on. My MRI findings were nonspecific, meaning they could stem from other causes, and they were initially blamed on migraines. But ultimately, my spinal tap showed oligoclonal bands (proteins found in the spinal fluid) and white blood cells, confirming an autoimmune, inflammatory neurological diagnosis. By that point — more than a decade after my symptoms began — other diseases that mimic MS had been ruled out, but only because I was forced to inquire about them after doctors had wrongly written off MS early in my diagnostic search. Perhaps the one — and only — perk of a delayed diagnosis is an eventual definitive one.
Michael Levy, a neuroimmunologist at Massachusetts General Hospital, told Boston 25 News it was likely Applegate’s age (diagnosed in her 40s rather than mid-20s) and her lack of response to treatment that prompted doctors to reconsider. But as I texted with friends about her setback, I found myself questioning that reasoning. “Without presenting a new diagnosis, I don’t understand how they can rule out MS,” I contested. If they’d pinpointed a new diagnosis via a measurable marker, one that better explained her symptoms, that would make more sense. But without another clear answer, and already having met the criteria for an MS diagnosis initially, I wasn’t sure how they could discount it completely.
I was yearning for more information: What did her MRI show? Was a spinal tap performed? Did she, too, have oligoclonal bands? What medication had she been taking as her symptoms progressed? Did she try another? Internally, I returned to my darkest days as I struggled to stand while doctors failed to help. From one once-undiagnosed patient to another, I wanted to ease her despair of learning she’s once again facing a disease with no name.
In my case, so much was ruled out, there was nothing left but MS. And my MS treatment has drastically changed my life, restoring strength and allowing me to return to many activities I was unable to do while undiagnosed and untreated.
Applegate feels as though her reason for pushing onward has been taken from her. “It’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down. It’s this weird feeling of like I became this, you and I, the poster children for MS. All that I did, everything that I was doing, I had a f—ing reason as to why my day sucked every day. And now I don’t have a reason,” she said on her podcast.
But Applegate is no longer solely impacting the MS community. Through her honesty, she’s also helping those who may soon realize they don’t have MS and every person struggling to find a diagnosis. I hope she realizes that her reason has not been erased — it has multiplied.
Lindsay Karp is a freelance writer and essayist with clips in the Washington Post, Boston Globe, Time, USA Today, and other outlets.

Since five members of the American Diabetes Association were ejected from its scientific session in New Orleans on June 5, the professional organization has released two explanations, one apology, one summary of its review of the events, and one notice of further review. Members have protested through petitions and an 1,100-member boycott. The flagship journal has stopped accepting manuscripts and grant reviews, fundraisers, and educational activities have ceased.
On Friday, the ADA posted a news release about the long-awaited review, three days after it disclosed without explanation the departure of Rita Kalyani, its chief medical and scientific officer.
The post offers background for the evictions, citing a “written threat that there would be protest and disruption,” but also backs off from previous explanations, noting that the “ADA’s code of conduct didn’t explicitly state that distributing materials inside the convention center was prohibited.”
