New Delhi, Oct 24: Union Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology and Earth Sciences, and Minister of State in the Prime Minister’s Office, Personnel, Public Grievances and Pensions, Department of Atomic Energy and Department of Space, Dr. Jitendra Singh today inaugurated the world's first- of -its-kind 'Air Pollution Analysis' facility for Delhi NCR. Known as 'Integrated Atmospheric Chemistry and Aerosol Toxicity Analysis Laboratory ' (AATAL), it is also equipped to identify real-time sources of air pollution.
Describing it as a first-of-its-kind integrated facility in the world, the Minister said Delhi-NCR had been chosen in view of the serious public concern over air pollution. He said the facility would take air-quality assessment beyond simply reporting pollution levels to identifying the composition of pollutants, their sources, their relative contributions and their potential health implications, while providing real-time information and advance forecasts to support timely action.
The inauguration took place at IITM’s Delhi Branch in the presence of Dr. T. Srinivasa Kumar, Secretary, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Dr. A. Suryachandra Rao, Director, IITM and DG IMD Dr Mahapatra. The facility has been established under 'Mission Mausam' announced by PM Sh Narendra Modi to strengthen scientific understanding of atmospheric pollution and provide actionable evidence for air-quality management in Delhi-NCR. The laboratory brings together advanced atmospheric measurement instruments, detailed chemical analysis, pollution-source identification and decision-support capabilities within an integrated framework.
Addressing the gathering, Dr. Jitendra Singh said India had made substantial progress over the past 10–12 years in air-quality forecasting and analysis. He said the new facility represented a significant step forward because it would help establish not only how much pollution is present in the atmosphere, but also what it consists of and where it originates.
“Earlier, the discussion would largely revolve around whether the pollution level was 100 or 200. This facility will help us understand the composition of pollution as well as the contribution of different sources. This is important for addressing the concerns of the people of Delhi and ensuring that action is based on scientific evidence,” the Minister said.
AATAL will help scientists distinguish between different sources of air pollution, including vehicular emissions, industrial activity, biomass and crop-residue burning, construction and road dust, and pollutants transported from surrounding regions. By estimating the relative contribution of these sources, the facility will help authorities understand which activities are driving poor air quality at a particular time and where interventions may be most effective.
Explaining the significance of real-time source apportionment, Dr. Jitendra Singh cited an instance, while talking to the reporters, the screen showed that at that precise moment, transport was contributing approximately 25 per cent of Delhi air pollution, with the overall pollution level recorded at around 180. He said such information could help move the response to air pollution from general assessments to more targeted interventions based on the actual sources contributing to the problem.
The laboratory is equipped with advanced instruments for analysing the chemical composition of atmospheric gases and aerosols, including fine particulate matter (PM2.5), metals, toxic elements and other components. Its capabilities will help scientists investigate how pollutants interact and transform in the atmosphere and how different components contribute to the overall pollution burden.
Dr. Jitendra Singh said the facility would provide information on the smaller constituents of air pollution, including metallic elements and other potentially harmful components. He explained that pollutants can differ in their health implications, making it important to understand not only their concentration but also their composition and potential toxicity.
The resulting scientific evidence can help health authorities better understand the potential risks associated with different types of particulate pollution. It can also support closer coordination between scientific institutions, health agencies and environmental authorities in assessing the implications of air pollution for public health.
The laboratory is integrated with IITM’s AIRWISE, Air Quality Warning and Integrated Decision Support System for Emissions, which combines air-quality forecasts, observations and source-apportionment information to support pollution management.
The project team explained that AIRWISE provides air-quality forecasts at a spatial resolution of 400 metres for the next 72 hours, enabling the system to assess how pollution may vary across different pockets of Delhi. It can also help identify the sources expected to contribute to deteriorating air quality in specific locations. Dr. Jitendra Singh said the integrated capability would provide real-time information as well as forecasts for the next four days, helping authorities prepare for changing pollution conditions.
Dr. Sachin Ghude, Project Director, MAQWS, said the integrated facility would strengthen air-quality management in Delhi-NCR by providing early warnings and detailed information on the sources contributing to pollution, including stubble burning, vehicular emissions, construction and road dust. He said the information would help the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) and other implementing agencies identify the major sources of pollution, plan targeted interventions and assess their effectiveness.
He added that the associated air-quality forecasting system provides forecasts at a 400-metre resolution for the next 72 hours, enabling pollution levels and their likely sources to be assessed for individual pockets of Delhi. Describing the forecasting capability as a major technological advance, Dr. Ghude said India had developed a high-resolution system comparable with global forecasting systems, with the potential to extend similar capabilities to other cities.
Emphasising the importance of coordination among government agencies, Dr. Jitendra Singh said air pollution could not be addressed by a single department working in isolation. He described the initiative as an example of the whole-of-government approach advocated by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, bringing together scientific institutions, environmental authorities, pollution-control agencies and disaster-management stakeholders.
The Minister said coordinated engagement among the Ministry of Earth Sciences, the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change, pollution-control authorities and disaster-management agencies would be important for translating scientific information into effective action.
For the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) and other implementing agencies, the facility will provide measurement-based evidence to identify the sources responsible for deteriorating air quality, prioritise sectors and locations for intervention, and support coordinated measures across Delhi-NCR. When combined with AIRWISE forecasts, this information can strengthen decisions relating to preventive measures and responses under the Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP).
The inauguration of AATAL marks an important step towards connecting advanced atmospheric science with public policy and on-ground action. By bringing real-time measurements, chemical characterisation, source apportionment and forecasting together, the facility will help authorities move towards a more precise understanding of air pollution and a more coordinated response to the challenge facing Delhi-NCR.

You’re reading our ESMO in 30 Seconds newsletter. Sign up here to get updates from the major European cancer conference in your inbox.
Hello again from Madrid, where we can tell you it’s Day 2 of the European Society for Medical Oncology’s annual meeting, but definitely not what day of the week it is. Perhaps some of the other nearly 40,000 people here can relate?
Enjoy today’s newsletter; we’ll be back with one more edition wrapping up the conference Monday afternoon. And on Thursday, join us for The STAT Recap, where we’ll catch you up on all the ESMO news you need to know, and answer your questions live.
In the meantime, we’re at [email protected] and [email protected].
Inside Moderna and Merck’s ‘presidential’ presentation
Adam Feuerstein/STAT
No surprise, the arena-sized room was packed with ESMO attendees eager to see Georgina Long of the Melanoma Institute Australia present the intismeran INTerpath-001 study results. The unfortunate data leak on Thursday made her talk less dramatic, but at the end, she received extended applause and a limited standing ovation.
Long summarized the intismeran results — a 42% reduction in the risk of disease recurrence and a 38% reduction in the risk of distant metastasis-free survival — as a “new benchmark for adjuvant treatment of melanoma.”
“More critically,” she added, “it establishes intismeran as a landmark advance in personalized cancer medicine.”
The full trial data will be published next month in the New England Journal of Medicine, Long also noted.
Inge Marie Svane of the University of Copenhagen, the discussant following the data presentation, was positive if not overly enthusiastic about the trial, describing the results as “compelling” and adding that they “mark a crucial moment for personalized cancer vaccines.”
But Svane also pointed to a number of outstanding questions, including whether there would be a survival benefit with intismeran, and what exactly was driving the vaccine’s benefit — was it the specific targeting of the neoantigens, or was it the general immune boost that studies have suggested mRNA vaccines provide?
She also took no position on the best way to treat the approximately 40% of higher risk melanoma patients enrolled in the study — a key debate with commercial implications. If intismeran is approved, it will compete against neoadjuvant immunotherapy, or treating patients before surgery. Svane laid out pros and cons of each approach, leaving the question of which will benefit patients more unanswered.
On mistrust and mRNA
The vast majority of the discussion about Merck and Moderna’s cancer vaccine centered on the quality of the data and the further application of individualized cancer therapies. But Toni Choueiri, of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, raised an important point during an address in a special session all about mRNA vaccines.
Mistrust and misinformation, Choueiri said, “is a key challenge to adopting anything that is mRNA.”
It seems that many people who hold unfounded doubts about mRNA vaccines for infectious diseases separate the technology’s potential in cancer — no more so than the people running the U.S. health department. While the federal government is throwing its weight behind cancer vaccines, it’s also drastically cut funding for mRNA vaccine research for pathogens.
But Choueiri said the pandemic highlighted how widely and quickly myths can spread, citing 2022 survey data that indicated 15% of people falsely believed that the mRNA Covid-19 shots could alter human DNA.
The concern is that such misguided fears could have ripple effects to anything called a vaccine, particularly if it’s made with mRNA. Choueiri noted that some people have moved away from using “vaccine” when describing products like the Merck-Moderna treatment, instead calling it a personalized neoantigen therapy.
Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel, speaking to STAT a couple of hours before the intismeran presentation, believes showing the benefits of an mRNA-based therapy in cancer — a disease that has affected a broad swath of Americans — will go a long way towards shifting perceptions of people who might have viewed mRNA in a negative way.
“I think the cancer treatment is going to help a lot,” Bancel said. “People will realize what we already know, that mRNA is a molecule that’s already in your body.”
An expanded use for Amgen’s Imdelltra in small cell lung cancer
The combination of Amgen’s Imdelltra plus Astrazeneca’s Imfinzi used as a maintenance regimen improved overall survival in patients with extensive-stage small cell lung cancer — a successful outcome that is expected to expand the commercial opportunity for Imdelltra in small cell lung cancer.
The presentation also drew a standing ovation from some in the room.
In the DeLLphi-305 study, the median overall survival for patients treated with Imdelltra and Imfinzi was just over 21 months compared to just under 13 months for patients receiving Imfinzi alone. Statistically, the doublet regimen reduced the risk of death by 58% compared to Imfinzi.
Cytokine release syndrome, a type of immune side effect, was reported by nearly half of the participants in the doublet arm, but the cases were mostly mild to moderate.
The 563 patients enrolled in the study had extensive-stage small cell lung cancer that had not yet progressed following first-line immunotherapy. The study was published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.
The results appear to set a new survival benchmark for maintenance therapy in small cell lung cancer. A previous study that combined Jazz Pharma’s Zepzelca with Roche’s Tecentriq reduced the risk of death by 27% compared to Tecentriq alone.
“The separation of the curves that we’re seeing here is not the kind of thing that we typically see in small cell lung cancer,” Jacob Sands of Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, who presented the data, told reporters. “These are extraordinary hazard ratios.”
Stephen Liu, a Georgetown University oncologist who was the study’s discussant, echoed that point.
If patients are eligible for the treatment approach, Liu said, “I can’t think of a subset where I would not want to offer this regimen.”
Astrazeneca’s bladder cancer push falls short
The neoadjuvant, or presurgical, use of Astrazeneca’s drug Imfinzi in patients with muscle-invasive bladder cancer reduced the risk of death by 42% compared to surgery alone. The risk of disease progression or death was reduced by 49% compared to surgery alone.
The positive results, however, don’t quite match the current standard of care.
Astrazeneca’s Phase 3 VOLGA study treated advanced bladder cancer patients with Imfinzi plus Pfizer’s Padcev before surgery, followed by Imfinzi after surgery, and compared their outcomes to patients who only underwent bladder surgery.
The study was published simultaneously in the New England Journal of Medicine.
At two years of follow up, 63% and 45% of the patients in the Imfinzi-Padcev and surgery only arms, respectively, were alive without tumor progression. Overall survival at the same time point favored the Imfinzi-Padcev group over surgery alone, with 78% and 69% of patients alive, respectively.
The VOLGA outcomes fell short of the current standard of care for the neoadjuvant treatment of muscle-invasive bladder cancer. Merck’s Keytruda plus Padcev reduced the risk of death by 50% and the risk of tumor progression by 60% compared to surgery alone.

Arunachal Pradesh: Dam protesters burn NHPC office, vandalise MLAs' houses in Pasighat
The Pasighat office of NHPC, several government offices, one police station and seven to eight police vehicles were allegedly set on fire.
Hundreds of protesters opposing the proposed 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) allegedly set several government offices and police vehicles on fire at Pasighat in Arunachal Pradesh's East Siang District on Friday evening, officials confirmed on Saturday.
According to officials, the Pasighat office of National Hydroelectric Power Corporation (NHPC), several government offices, one police station and seven to eight police vehicles were allegedly set on fire and damaged by hundreds of protesters claiming to represent Gen Z.
The houses of ruling Bharatiya Janata Party state president Kaling Moyong and MLAs Oni Panyang and Ninong Ering were damaged, and some property was taken away by the protesters, officials said.
"There was a 12-hour bandh on Friday from 5 am till 5 pm by some people opposed to the project. It went off peacefully in Pasighat, but after 5 pm some protesters calling themselves Gen Z insisted on continuing the bandh and blocked the highway. This caused inconvenience to people and halted traffic. The local magistrate and security forces tried to persuade them for two hours to disperse," said Jayanti Pertin, deputy commissioner of East Siang.
"There were several hundred of the protesters. But when they didn't disperse, the magistrate ordered the firing of tear gas shells. There was no baton charge. After that, the protesters got unruly and started pelting stones, which caused hurt to some policemen and officials," she added.
Pertin informed that the protesters then started targeting the NHPC office, Pasighat police station and seven police vehicles, which were burnt down. Some of them damaged the houses of the BJP state president and the two MLAS.
"Eight protesters who sustained minor injuries were later given first aid treatment at the local hospital. The situation remained tense until around 4 am on Saturday. Now it is under control," she stated, adding that no one has been arrested till Saturday noon in connection with the violence.
Arunachal Pradesh chief minister Pema Khandu condemned the violence and urged protesters to talk.
"I strongly condemn such violent protests and urge everyone who has concerns regarding the SUMP project to come and sit for talks instead of resorting to such means. Protesting is a democratic right, but should be done within limits and without causing harm or damage to anyone or properties," Khandu said.
4 women injured in tear gas shelling
Friday evening's incident follows injuries sustained by four women anti-dam protesters earlier that morning after police reportedly fired tear gas shells to disperse protesters at Dite-Dime near Geku.
The incident occurred at the 65 Bridge in Dite-Dime, where a large number of people had gathered in support of the shutdown when tensions escalated around 7 am after a group of protesters allegedly attempted to breach barricades and attack security personnel.
Friday's shutdown disrupted normal life across Siang and Upper Siang districts and parts of East Siang, with shops and business establishments remaining closed and residents largely staying indoors.
The bandh was jointly called by Adi Bane Kebang United (ABK), SUMP Affected Area Youth Association (SAAYA), Siang Indigenous Farmers’ Forum Youth Wing (SIFFYW) and Adi Galo Welfare Society.
The organisations are demanding the release of 10 arrested activists within 24 hours, the reinstatement of suspended gaon buras, the withdrawal of all pre-feasibility report (PFR) activities in dam-affected areas, and the removal of paramilitary and Central forces deployed in the region.
The project
The state government sees the 11,200-MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP) as a strategic safeguard against China's massive hydropower development on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet, but those who call the river's banks home in Arunachal Pradesh fear displacement, ecological destruction, and the loss of ancestral land.
The Yarlung Tsangpo flows into Arunachal Pradesh as the Siang, before joining other tributaries to form the Brahmaputra in Assam and eventually entering Bangladesh.
Officials have expressed concerns about the possible consequences of upstream water regulation, including changes in river flows, potential diversions, and sudden water releases. The Arunachal Pradesh government argues that SUMP could help moderate such fluctuations by creating substantial downstream water storage.
At the heart of the controversy is the government's proposed Pre-Feasibility Report (PFR), a preliminary technical exercise intended to determine whether the massive dam can be built and where it could be located. The government maintains that the PFR is not an approval for construction but only a scientific assessment of the project's technical and geological viability.
For the Siang Indigenous Farmers' Forum (SIFF), which is leading the resistance, however, the survey represents the first step towards a project that could fundamentally alter the region's geography, ecology and indigenous way of life. Protesters have demanded an immediate halt to survey activities, withdrawal of security forces from affected areas and meaningful consultations with local communities.

Repoll recommended at 3 booths in Agra Teachers MLC seat after SP candidate alleges irregularities; threatens conversion
Polling in 11 MLC constituencies (five graduate and six teachers constituencies of the Legislative Council) was held on Friday.
A re-poll has been recommended at three booths in the Agra Teachers' MLC (Legislative Council) constituency following complaints of irregularities.
Polling in 11 MLC constituencies (five graduate and six teachers constituencies of the Legislative Council) was held on Friday. A total of 152 candidates were in the fray in the 11 constituencies.
Returning Officer has recommended a re-poll at booth no. 20 in Kheragarh tehsil, booth no. 21 in Kshetra Panchayat Saiya, and booth no. 26 in Kshetra Panchayat Fatehabad. UP Chief Electoral Officer Navdeep Rinwa has forwarded the proposal to the Election Commission of India.
Deep Dive
The recommendation came after Samajwadi Party candidate Aakash Agarwal alleged large-scale irregularities and intimidation of his supporters during Friday's polling.
There is a direct contest between the BJP and the SP in all constituencies. The polling was held between 8 am and 4 pm. Voting was held in 72 districts of UP. A total of 1,481,310 voters were registered to exercise their franchise at 2,697 polling booths in the state. The counting of votes will take place on October 27, and the results will be declared on the same day.
SP candidate's allegations
Aakash Agarwal met Divisional Commissioner Nagendra Pratap and later broke down before the media.
“Do I have no right to contest the election? I am being targeted to such an extent that police might plant drugs or arms on me and put me behind bars alleging I am a Pakistani,” he said, a video of which is viral on social media. Hindustan Times could not independently verify the video.
“This is all being done to favour those who claim to be protectors of Sanatan, and thus I do not intend to remain in such Sanatan. I will go to Eidgah in Lucknow next month and will convert to Islam,” he added as seen in the video.
Agra Police Commissioner Deepak Kumar visited booths in Saiya and Fatehabad after the complaints.
“On receiving complaints, I visited certain booths. SP leaders were assured of free and fair polling. Directions of the Election Commission are being complied with,” Kumar said.

Food regulator FSSAI has asked food business operators (FBOs) to transport perishable items under controlled-temperature conditions across the supply chain to safeguard public health.
In a social media post on Sunday (October 18, 2026), FSSAI said it has issued an advisory on “handling, storage, and transportation of perishable foods like khoa, paneer, meat, and fish under controlled temperature conditions throughout the supply chain”.
The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has also asked State food safety officers to maintain strict vigilance and take action if rules are not followed.
FBOs must ensure strict adherence to hygiene and temperature standards, it added.
FSSAI mentioned that it has specified hygienic and sanitary requirements for FBOs under Schedule 4 of the Food Safety and Standards (Licensing and Registration of Food Businesses) Regulations, 2011.
"It has been brought to the notice of FSSAI that perishable food commodities such as khoa, paneer, meat, fish, etc., are at times not handled, stored or transported under appropriate temperature conditions," the advisory noted.
Because of their perishable nature, these food items are highly susceptible to microbial growth and spoilage if not maintained under appropriate temperature conditions.
As per the conditions laid out under licenses, FBOs are required to maintain the prescribed temperature throughout the supply chain, from procurement/sourcing to delivery to the end consumer.
"Subjecting these food products to temperature abuse may adversely affect public health and constitute non-compliance with the hygiene and sanitary requirements," the advisory said.
The regulator has asked FBOs to transport only in clean, covered, and hygienic vehicles or conveyances suitable for food transportation.
FBOs have also been told to use only food-grade packaging and suitable secondary packaging materials.
"Protect the product from dust, moisture, pests, physical damage and cross- contamination during storage, loading, unloading and transportation," FSSAI told FBOs.
Further, FBOs have been told to maintain appropriate records and traceability of consignments.
The regulator has also advised the commissioners of food safety at the state level, Indian Railways and Regional Directors of FSSAI to direct the concerned licensing authorities and food safety officers to maintain strict vigilance during inspections and transportation checks to ensure compliance with the law.
In case of non-compliance, they can initiate appropriate action, including seizure and destruction of the food items.

While security cameras are ostensibly for, well, security, they can also be super handy for making sure your kids came home at the right time, checking up on your pets when you’re away, and investigating that weird sound in the middle of the night without having to get out of your toasty bed.
I’ve tested so very, very many security cameras, and there are a few reasons I think you should snap up this particular Eufy Security Wall Light Cam S4 deal at $80 off. I’m also going to highlight a couple of other Eufy options currently on sale.
The Eufy Wall Light Cam S4 looks and acts as a modern, motion-activated wall light, perfect for illuminating a driveway, porch, or back gate, which is where I have mine (no more stubbed toes when I take out the trash at night). Eufy has also packed in a 4K camera that you can swivel to get the right angle, offering a wide, crisp view of your chosen spot. It records locally, with 32 GB of storage built-in, and it's subscription free, including the on-device AI detection, which can accurately distinguish between people, vehicles, and pets. Installation is quick and easy, and it connects directly to your Wi-Fi. You’ll just need a decent signal at your chosen spot.
To sweeten the deal, there’s a solar panel to keep the battery topped off. It sits neatly on top, but you can detach it for better placement to catch the sun’s rays. Despite being in a busy spot, mine has stayed charged for the last couple of months, though I suspect that may change as we head into winter.
What I like best about this security camera is the wall light functionality. You can set the brightness and color temperature (I like a warm light). You can also schedule it to only trigger between specific hours or set it to be activated from sunset to sunrise based on your location. I also love that it doesn’t scream outdoor security camera; you only notice it if you look closely.
Some downsides: the frame rate is just 15 fps, so fast-moving subjects can appear blurry, particularly in the dark (though the light helps with that). Some folks will also need to top off the battery off on occasion, so you’ll want to keep it somewhere within reach. I also feel it’s overpriced at the original $250, but at $170 ($80 off), that's less of an issue.
If you need an indoor camera, the Eufy S350 is also on sale right now at $100 ($40 off), and it’s a wonderfully versatile, feature-packed, dual-lens camera. It even has automatic tracking, making it ideal for checking in on your cat or dog throughout the day. It regularly dips down to this price, so you might want to wait for Black Friday, when I predict it will drop another $20.
The EufyCam C35 2-Cam Kit at $130 ($70 off) is also worth considering right now. These cameras work inside or out with an easy magnetic mount and come with a handy HomeBase Mini for local recording and onboard AI that includes facial recognition. This is a common discount, but it's still a great deal for a two-camera kit with hub.

Using Google’s products and services has always been fundamentally precarious—doing so gives the world’s largest advertising company a lot of juicy personal data. Google has long said it won’t use the sensitive data from products like Gmail, Drive, and Photos for ad personalization, but a change to the company’s privacy policy appears to dismantle that firewall.
On October 16, Google issued an update to its privacy policy, spotted by Android Authority. The ad personalization section used to include a clear limit on data from certain apps. “We don’t show you personalized ads based on your content from Drive, Gmail, or Photos,” the document said. Now, Google has updated it with the following language.
This equivocation opens the door to using data from apps like Gmail and Photos in ads when it’s shared with other Google services, and it just so happens Google has a mechanism for doing that, with Personal Intelligence. The company released Personal Intelligence in early 2026, allowing users to hand data from multiple apps to Google AI products. The idea is that the added context from your existing data will lead to better AI answers, but it’s also proving to be a privacy minefield.
Personal Intelligence connects your data to the Gemini app but also to features like AI Mode search. While the Gemini app does not currently have ads, you may see sponsored content in AI search tools. Google’s changes to the privacy policy appear to acknowledge that data shared with AI search via Personal Intelligence could, therefore, contribute to ad personalization.
According to Google, this clarification still doesn’t mean ads are “based directly” on your personal data. Here’s the company’s full statement:
“Connecting your apps is entirely opt-in. Ads will continue to be relevant to things like your query, the context of the response and your interests. Ads will not be based directly on your Gmail inbox or Photos library, and as always, sensitive information will not be used to tailor ads.”
Google’s statement is essentially a roundabout way of confirming that Workspace and Photos data may inform ads. If you interact with AI Mode while Personal Intelligence is enabled, there’s a chance that summaries and insights from your data will inform the answers you get. Because that same data is used for ad targeting, it’s accurate to say that your personal data is an element of ad targeting in AI search. The privacy policy now makes that clear.

The story so far:
France reported the first known human infection with Shamonda virus on October 22, 2026. The patient, who was severely immunocompromised and receiving treatment for a serious illness at the Hospices Civils de Lyon, died in early October. Investigations are underway to determine whether the virus caused or contributed to the death, and how the patient acquired the infection.
French authorities suspect that the patient was infected by the bite of a Culicoides midge in eastern France, where the virus had been circulating among animals during spring and summer. The specific insect responsible has not been identified. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), the virus has been detected in farm animals in Austria, Belgium, France, Germany, Ireland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, the Netherlands, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland, as well as Jersey.
French authorities say that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge of the virus. The World Health Organization (WHO) has also said that wider spread is unlikely based on the information currently available. However, investigations into the human case are continuing.
What is Shamonda virus?
Shamonda virus is a vector-borne virus belonging to the genus Orthobunyavirus in the family Peribunyaviridae. It is part of the Simbu group of viruses, which also includes Schmallenberg virus and Akabane virus.
The virus was first isolated from cattle in Nigeria in the mid-1960s and has since been reported sporadically in cattle in parts of Africa and Japan. Before the recent case in France, it was considered an animal pathogen that did not infect humans.
Cattle are considered its main animal hosts, although infections have also been detected in sheep, goats, horses and alpacas. In livestock, infection can cause fever, diarrhoea, lethargy, loss of appetite and reduced milk production. In pregnant animals, it has been associated with abortions and congenital abnormalities in offspring.
Neurological signs have also been reported in horses infected with the virus in Europe. The extent to which the variants circulating in Europe differ in their effects on animal health remains under investigation.
How does it spread?
The virus is understood to spread primarily through the bites of infected Culicoides midges, tiny blood-feeding insects. The precise midge species responsible for transmitting the European variants has not yet been established.
According to the World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH), there is currently no evidence of horizontal transmission, or spread between animals through direct contact or other routes. Vertical transmission, from a pregnant animal to its offspring, has been reported.
Two genetically distinct variants, designated Shamonda virus Europe 1 (SHAV-EU1) and Shamonda virus Europe 2 (SHAV-EU2), have been identified in Europe in 2026. Research indicates that they may have been introduced separately. Their geographical distribution, effects on livestock and long-term significance remain under investigation.
Why is it in the news?
The detection in a human has raised questions about whether Shamonda virus can cause disease beyond its known animal hosts. French authorities have reported that the brain complications observed in the patient before death were considered very likely to be linked to the infection. However, investigations are continuing to establish whether the virus caused or contributed to the death.
The patient was severely immunocompromised and had an underlying serious illness. It is not yet known whether similar complications would occur in people with different health conditions or whether people without immune suppression could develop symptomatic infection.
The case highlights the importance of the One Health approach, which recognises the links between human, animal and environmental health. Monitoring infections in livestock, investigating unusual human infections and sharing laboratory findings can help identify emerging health risks.
The virus is also affecting livestock production. A study of nine French dairy herds found a 15%–75% decline in bulk milk production during clinical episodes associated with infection. Affected cattle also showed symptoms such as diarrhoea, reduced activity and, less consistently, fever. The findings are from a small number of farms and do not establish the typical impact across all affected herds.
How prevalent is it?
The prevalence of Shamonda virus in humans is unknown. The French case is the first documented human infection, but it does not establish when the virus first began infecting people or whether other infections have gone undetected. There is insufficient data to estimate the number of human infections worldwide.
In animals, the virus has been identified in parts of Africa and Japan. Its detection in European livestock in 2026 has expanded its known geographical distribution. By October 22, the ECDC had reported detections in farm animals across 12 European countries and Jersey.
These reports indicate the geographical spread of detections, not the proportion of animals infected. Differences in veterinary surveillance, laboratory testing and reporting make it difficult to compare the burden between countries.
There are no verified figures establishing the prevalence of Shamonda virus in India so far. However, the absence of reported detections does not establish that the virus is absent from the country.
The virus is not subject to routine official surveillance or control measures under the European Union’s Animal Health Law. This may limit the completeness of information on its distribution and prevalence in livestock.
How is it diagnosed and treated?
In animals, the symptoms of Shamonda virus infection can resemble those of other livestock diseases. Laboratory testing is therefore needed to confirm infection. Molecular tests, including polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assays, can detect the virus’s genetic material, while genetic sequencing can help distinguish between variants.
Evidence on the clinical presentation and management of human infection remains limited. There is currently no established, Shamonda-specific treatment protocol for human infection. Further investigation is needed to determine how the virus affects humans and what clinical management may be appropriate.
According to WOAH, there are no commercially available vaccines against Shamonda virus. No established vaccine is available for preventing human infection.
What is the public health risk?
French authorities have said that no public health risk to the general population has been identified based on current knowledge. The WHO has assessed wider spread as unlikely on the available evidence. These assessments reflect what is currently known and may change as further information becomes available.
Key questions include how the patient acquired the infection, whether the virus contributed to the death, whether other human infections have occurred and whether the virus can spread between people. There is currently no evidence of sustained human-to-human transmission.
Surveillance of livestock, laboratory investigations and coordination between animal and human health authorities will be important in answering these questions.
For now, the available evidence supports continued monitoring and investigation. The first human case is significant because the virus was previously considered unable to infect humans, but it does not establish that Shamonda virus is spreading widely among people or that a human outbreak is under way.

Nigeria has confirmed an Ebola case in its capital, Abuja, after a woman who arrived from Uganda tested positive for the virus, the health ministry said.
The woman began showing symptoms on 7 October and was admitted to a hospital in Abuja four days later, where she was later diagnosed with Ebola. It is unclear when she arrived in Nigeria, Africa’s most populous country.
The health minister, Muhammad Pate, said authorities had begun tracing 44 people identified as contacts of the patient. “We are doing everything possible to contain this case by tracing all the contacts the individual may have had,” he said.
Uganda’s ministry of health said the patient had only transited through Uganda and that she is a Nigerian woman who had been on a business trip to Congo’s eastern region. The Nigerian authorities have not disclosed her nationality.
“Travel through Uganda does not establish that infection occurred here. The location of exposure remains under investigation,” the ministry said in a statement. The ministry insisted Uganda has “no confirmed active Ebola cases”.
Nigeria is the latest country to report an Ebola case as the outbreak spreads across the region. Kenya confirmed its first case earlier this month and has since recorded nine infections. Uganda had previously reported Ebola cases, but it later declared itself free of the virus.
Dr Jean Kaseya, the director general of the Africa Centers for Disease Control, said on X that “we are facing an extremely serious threat,” with a fatality rate of nearly 50% of cases.
“This Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak has already become the most geographically extensive in history, affecting several countries spread across three regions of Africa,” he said.
The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control said two weeks ago it was stepping up surveillance following the detection of Ebola in Kenya and strengthening the country’s preparedness for a potential outbreak.
“These efforts have focused on early detection, isolation and referral, laboratory diagnosis, infection prevention and control, contact tracing, risk communication and protection of health care workers,” the agency said.
Nigeria established an Ebola taskforce in June after the outbreak in Congo in mid-May.
The spread of Ebola beyond Congo has heightened fears among health authorities about the rapid transmission of the rare Bundibugyo virus, which has infected more than 9,500 people and killed more than 4,600 people.
The latest Ebola outbreak is the fastest-spreading on record and is on track to exceed the deadliest on record, the 11,000 people killed in West Africa’s regional outbreak between 2014 and 2016, WHO has said.

Drinking water supplies dwindle in Yemeni city besieged by Houthi rebels
Drinking water has been scarce for over a decade in Taiz, but the problem has reached crisis levels in recent weeks as Iran-backed Houthi rebels besiege Yemen's third-largest city in their escalating conflict with government forces.
The needs of Taiz's more than 1 million residents are now barely being met, humanitarian groups say, as access to wells is limited, desalination plants run low on fuel and water delivery trucks are largely prevented from entering the city.
Families are rationing every drop. Before Taiz came under siege, Hadil al-Shahid and her two young children used about 10 liters (about 2.6 gallons) of bottled water per day for drinking and cooking; now they are making the same amount last about four days.
"We stopped drinking coffee and tea, which we used to drink daily," al-Shahid said in a phone interview.
Families like al-Shahid's are paying as much as 75% more for bottled water than just a few weeks ago, and some have begun to buy water on credit.
The siege of Taiz — a strategic gateway to southern Yemen — isn't only constricting water supplies. Shortages of groceries have sent food prices soaring. Fuel is also in short supply, making it difficult to maintain basic services such as hospitals and sanitation, which compounds the public health risks.
Amnesty International has called on the Houthis to immediately open roads into the city, saying Taiz is being pushed to "the brink of a severe humanitarian disaster."
Houthis strangle Taiz, cut off residents' access to wells
Yemen descended into civil war in 2014, when the Houthis seized much of the country's north, including the capital of Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government into exile. Taiz has been a focal point of fighting ever since.
War-related damage to Taiz's aging water infrastructure magnified the pressures of population growth and frequent droughts that led to shrinking supplies of groundwater. Residents began paying for water delivered by trucks, a mostly reliable alternative — until recently.
By August, Yemen had become a widening front in the Iran war. The Houthis ramped up their advance on Taiz last month, after a lightning-fast capture of the port city of Mokha, an area about 130 kilometers (80 miles) away that is vital to controlling shipping through the Red Sea.
As Houthi forces took control of more land and roads surrounding Taiz, residents' access to nearby wells was cut off and deliveries of water from outside the city declined.
The truckers that have managed to ferry water into Taiz have in some cases tripled their rates to make the perilous journey.
As Taiz's fuel supplies dwindle, its water utility is struggling to maintain limited operations and desalination plants are running well below capacity.
The city is also enduring shortages of fuel and food
Since August, Taiz province, which includes the city and surrounding areas, has taken in roughly half of those displaced from other parts of Yemen because of the fighting — an estimated 124,000 people, according to the United Nations' migration experts. That is only compounding the pressure on Taiz's limited supply of water and other necessities.
Some displaced families are now living in makeshift shelters or tents and surviving on one meal a day, said Jens Laerke, a spokesperson for a division of the United Nations that focuses on emergency aid.
Fuel for cooking and transportation has also become scarce — and more expensive. The price of cooking gas has more than quadrupled, according to Hani Bafaqih, a water, sanitation and hygiene expert at the aid organization CARE in Yemen. To get by, some families are cooking over fires made by burning wood, charcoal or cardboard.
These fuel shortages have made it harder for community kitchens to provide free hot meals to families and have also forced waste-collection services to shut down.
"The shortages feed into each other. Without fuel, water pumps, hospital generators and solid-waste collection stop. With less clean water and waste piling up, the risk of disease, including cholera, rises," Laerke said. The health risks are exacerbated by thirsty families tapping into unprotected wells that could be contaminated with waterborne diseases, he said.
Food prices are also soaring. Flour and rice are about 50% more expensive than they were over the summer, according to aid groups, and fruits and vegetables are hard to find.
Ahmed Abdel Gaber is living with nine other family members in the ruins of another building after being displaced from their home by the fighting. He used to earn money hauling construction material, but that income is no longer steady and his family is barely scraping by.
"We heavily rely on assistance and donations from people to get food," he said in a phone interview.
Al-Shahid, a hair salon owner, said her income also dried up a few weeks ago. The salon was forced to close as former customers began to prioritize their spending on food and water. Her 10-year-old daughter and 5-year-old son now eat mostly rice, bread and cheese, she said.
Why Taiz matters to the Houthis
While the Yemeni government still controls the center of Taiz, the siege is making it difficult to deliver supplies to its forces there. In the hills surrounding Taiz, the government forces are trying to repel the Houthis but face stiff resistance, especially east of the city.
Gaining control of Taiz city is vital to the Houthis if they seek to advance south toward Aden and Lahj, analysts say, but that won't be easy.
"Any Houthi attempt to seize parts of the city, let alone take it entirely, would likely require a prolonged and costly battle, with significant casualties among Houthi fighters," said Ahmed Nagi, a senior analyst at the International Crisis Group.
Three Houthi officials said the rebel group controls roughly 80% of the countryside surrounding Taiz and several key neighborhoods inside the city. The Associated Press couldn't independently verify the claims by these officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they weren't allowed to brief the media, but Yemen's foreign minister, Afrah al-Zouba, has acknowledged the rebel group's tightening grip on the city.
The Houthis' fight for control of the city is made significantly more difficult because of its large civilian population, the officials said.
Earlier this week, missiles fired by the Houthis struck a residential area in Taiz, killing two teenage girls and renewing attention on the dangers faced by civilians.
Abdel Gaber said he can hear loud explosions every day from fighting that is happening roughly 5 kilometers (3 miles) away. The family isn't returning to their home in a mountain village out of concern for their safety.
Leaving Taiz is not an option for al-Shahid because the costs of travel and renting a home in another province are prohibitive.
"Staying in our home is inevitable — whether it be a matter of life or death," al-Shahid said.

Streaming giant Netflix recorded its highest-ever quarterly paid net subscriber additions in India in the September quarter of 2026, crediting a strong local content slate and its first transaction-based loyalty bundle with Flipkart. Revenue in India grew about 18% YoY on a foreign exchange-neutral basis, which excludes the impact of currency movements, Netflix said in its quarterly shareholder letter. Viewing hours rose 24% YoY, while viewing hours per member increased by a low-to-mid single-digit percentage. Netflix did not disclose the number of paid net additions in India or how many came through the Flipkart partnership. During its Q3 earnings call, co-CEO Greg Peters pointed to India as an example of how locally produced titles were translating into higher engagement, membership growth, and revenue. Local Content Drives Engagement Lock Upp, Netflix’s first daily reality series, recorded more viewing hours in India than any other title on the platform, measured over its first 91 days. The scripted series Musafir Cafe recorded 9 Mn views, while Operation Safed Sagar clocked 11 Mn views. The India performance formed part of broader growth across Asia-Pacific, Latin America, and Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Peters said local titles in these regions were driving engagement and business growth. He also said Netflix’s subscriber retention remained healthy across regions. Globally and in the US, churn – the rate at which subscribers leave the service – improved YoY in Q3 and was lower than the company had forecast. Globally, Netflix reported revenue of $12.87 Bn in Q3 2026, up 12% YoY. Operating income rose 37% to $4.46 Bn, while its operating margin expanded to 34.6% from 28.2% a year earlier. For 2026, Netflix expects revenue of $51.1 Bn, representing 13% YoY growth. Neumann said membership growth, pricing, and advertising were expected to support strong revenue growth in 2027, although the company had yet to issue formal guidance for the year. Netflix also plans to introduce its advertising-supported subscription tier in 15 additional countries in 2027, with the first launches scheduled for March.

From Chelsea reject to Watkins 'upgrade' - Jackson makes fast Villa start
- Published
Nicolas Jackson's double to defeat Manchester City on Saturday capped an excellent start to the striker's spell at Aston Villa.
Signed from Chelsea as a direct replacement for Ollie Watkins - Villa's main source of goals for the previous six seasons - it was imperative the 25-year-old Senegal international hit the ground running in claret and blue.
Jackson has done just that, scoring seven goals in his first 11 appearances for Villa - six in the last six - and helping his new side to a 100% start in the Champions League and spearheading their recovery after a slow start to the Premier League campaign.
"The players, the manager, the team - everything is incredible," Jackson told BBC Match of the Day.
"I'm very happy that I'm here and hopefully we can do amazing things together."
Improved form at Villa Park
Jackson spent two full seasons at Chelsea after joining in 2023 and had a year on loan at German giants Bayern Munich before moving to Villa in the summer for a deal worth up to £65m.
There is a much smaller sample size from his time at Villa Park compared with his spell at Stamford Bridge, but on several metrics, he is showing signs of improvement.
Jackson scored 24 goals in 65 Premier League appearances for Chelsea, netting every 210 minutes on average, with a shot conversion rate of 15%.
That compares with four in seven games for Villa, averaging a goal every 138 minutes with a shot conversion rate of 21%.
One of the criticisms of Jackson at Chelsea was he had lots of chances and did not convert as many of them as he should.
In his early weeks at Villa, he is outperforming his expected goals tally by exactly two.
Both of their shots on target against City came from Jackson's right foot - and both ended up in the net.
'He looks like a really good piece of business' - Keown
England international Watkins scored 91 Premier League goals in 221 league appearances for Villa before moving to Saudi Arabia club Al-Hilal in August.
He was a consistent scorer, never failing to reach double figures for Premier League goals during each of his six seasons with the club.
The respective statistics of Jackson and Watkins from last season suggest Jackson is more involved in general play than the England forward, while also being involved in more chances.
If Jackson's current run of form continues, his fee may prove to be a bargain.
Former Villa and England defender Martin Keown told BBC Sport: "I've liked him all season. I think he's key to Villa's success.
"I think he's an upgrade on Ollie Watkins, I really do.
"Ollie was magnificent for them, but this guy is more of a predator [in and around the penalty area]. Pace will always trouble top defenders and he's got it in abundance.
"I think having worked with the manager before at Villarreal, he's sort of fast-tracking his quick development.
"He looks like a really good piece of business right now."
'So many players improve and thrive' under Emery
Saturday's win was achieved on the fourth anniversary of Emery's appointment as Villa boss.
Under the Spaniard, they have become fixtures in the upper echelons of the Premier League, regulars in European competition and ended a 30-year wait for a major trophy by winning the Europa League.
Results are one thing, but there are also numerous examples of players who have been rejuvenated or scaled new heights in their careers under Emery's management at Villa Park.
Former Scotland defender Rachel Corsie, who had a spell playing in the Women's Super League for Aston Villa late in her career, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "Emery is quite unique. A lot of coaches will focus on the tactical detail, but he's so intense with it.
"I remember from when I was here that his car is always at the training ground. I know people will say that's a natural thing and the life of a manager, but I would say it's an incredible amount of time.
"He loves to get the detail right. He never gets tired of trying to better people individually and that takes an incredible amount of work. So many players come here, improve and thrive."
Jackson has prior experience of playing under Emery, having been coached by him at Villarreal, where he spent three years before Chelsea signed him for £35m.
Emery told BBC Match of the Day: "I knew him at Villarreal and he started playing the level he is now. I know his capacity to exploit his qualities and I know, as well, his humility.
"The mentality is coming through - how focused he is in life and professional career."
Speaking to TNT Sports, Jackson added: "It's not easy [to settle at a new club] but easier because of the coach and the players.
"It's an incredible dressing room with an incredible manager. I'm very happy to be here and hopefully I will score many goals."

Fear of Trump challenging mail-in ballots appears to be flooding early voting sites
More than 22 million Americans have already voted. Did Trump’s threats to voting by mail backfire?

Early voting turnout for this year’s midterm elections is shredding records across the country.
The surge comes as mail-in ballot returns are plummeting compared to previous midterm election years, a likely reaction to Donald Trump’s threats to voting by mail and his attempts to take control of the nation’s elections, according to voting rights groups and election experts.
As of Friday morning, more than 22 million Americans have already cast their ballots with less than two weeks before Election Day, according to the Election Lab at the University of Florida, the leading authority for independent voting data. More than 45 percent of all ballots cast thus far came from Democratic voters.
But several states with close races that could determine the balance of power in Congress are reporting sharp declines in the number of mailed ballots compared to the same period in the 2022 midterms — even as they report record-breaking turnout.
In Ohio, mail-in ballot requests this year declined by roughly 28 percent even as early in-person voting increased by nearly 200 percent. In Georgia, more than 69,000 mail ballots were accepted by election officials as of Thursday, marking a more than 50 percent decline from the same period in 2022, while in-person turnout continues to break records.
“We continue to break records each day of early voting,” Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said this week. “This is evidence that Georgians trust our election process.”
Raffensperger, a Republican, was at the center of the president’s failed attempts to overturn election results in the state in 2020, opening a sprawling investigation into Trump’s efforts to reverse his election loss, which he has attributed to baseless allegations of widespread fraud.
The president has waged a years-long crusade against mail-in voting, a process he has labeled “inherently corrupt,” a form of “cheating” and “sad” and “crazy.”
“ELECTIONS CAN NEVER BE HONEST WITH MAIL IN BALLOTS/VOTING,” Trump wrote in August, just weeks before the Supreme Court rejected his attempt to restrict mail voting before midterm elections.
Trump’s plan would have required states to use a standardized envelope design and submit lists of eligible voters through an online portal. The U.S. Postal Service would then be allowed to refuse delivery of mail-in ballots from any state that failed to comply with these rules.
The ruling delivered a major blow to Trump’s attempts to centralize control of the nation’s elections, which would have given the nation’s postal agency expansive authority to decide who gets to vote in an unprecedented shakeup of election administration.
He also failed to convince Republicans in Congress to pass legislation to overhaul election administration and has not ruled out the possibility of emergency actions to restrict ballot access before Election Day.
Elections officials and voting rights groups have warned that the president’s threats and contradictory statements — he’s still encouraging Republicans to vote by mail, sensing major losses in November — have not only confused voters about the rules but have also cast doubt about the security of their ballots.
An NBC News poll this summer also showed that fewer than one-quarter of Democratic voters said they planned to vote by mail this year, amounting to a double-digit drop from 2024, when 34 percent of Democrats said they were planning to cast their ballots by mail for that year’s presidential election.
But election officials are reporting a significant spike in early voting turnout as a sign of voter enthusiasm, particularly in states with tight races for the House and Senate.
In Texas, early voting is up 74 percent compared with 2022, according to state election officials. In Kansas, early voting turnout has more than doubled. Maine and North Carolina are also seeing increases of more than 30 percent compared to the same period in 2022.
Michael McDonald, a political science professor at the University of Florida, found that while requests for mail ballots are down, voters are returning them fast.
“The punchline is that if Donald Trump’s attacks on mail balloting shifted some Democrats to voting in-person or casting ballots earlier, he probably did Democrats a favor since rejected mail ballots are the most frequent way voters disenfranchise themselves,” he wrote.
Still, even without the fallout from the president’s failed attempts to rewrite the rules for mail-in ballots, cost-cutting measures across USPS that have forced mail sorting facilities and post offices to consolidate could be leading to significant delays — particularly for rural voters.
For example, in 11 predominately rural counties in eastern Washington, nearly 2,000 ballots have arrived later, compared to about 600 in 2022, according to an investigation from ProPublica.
Those delays could endanger the validity of voters’ ballots and potentially lead to rejections without enough time for voters to correct any errors.
Democratic members of Congress are also pressing social media companies for details on how they plan to stop election misinformation from spreading on their platforms.
In letters to Google, Meta, TikTok and X this week, Rep. Jamie Raskin, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, warned that any posts “suggesting that a lawfully cast mail-in ballot will not be counted — even if made by senior Republican officials — are not a matter of opinion.”
“They are false statements that clearly fall within your own prohibitions and standards,” he wrote Friday.
“We plan to exercise vigilant oversight of your platform and other social media companies to ensure that propaganda and fabrications indeed do not work to prevent Americans on your platform from participating in our democratic process,” he added.

Manipur SoO pact with Kuki groups not extended, says Konthoujam amid crackdown after 3 Meitei killed
Manipur home minister says the Suspension of Operations pact with Kuki militant groups has not been extended as security forces intensify a crackdown after three Meitei youths were killed.
Manipur home minister Govindas Konthoujam on Friday said the Suspension of Operations (SoO) pact with Kuki militant groups had not been extended, as security forces stepped up a crackdown following the killing of three Meitei youths in Imphal East earlier this week.
He said 18 cadres found at a designated Kuki militant camp in Kangpokpi district were being investigated, with 17 set to be formally arrested on Friday as their identities and affiliations were established.
The Suspension of Operations pact was first signed on August 22, 2008, between the governments of India and Manipur and Kuki militant groups representing 25 outfits under two umbrella organisations: the Kuki National Organisation (KNO), which comprises 17 outfits, and the United People’s Front (UPF), which comprises eight outfits. The pact aimed to cease hostilities, with the militant groups agreeing to completely stop any form of violence.
The cadres of these groups are housed at 14 designated camps.

The latest SoO pact was renewed during President’s Rule in Manipur on September 4, 2025, for a period of one year, despite demands from people across the state, particularly members of the Meitei community, for the pact to be abrogated.
Search operations were underway to arrest all those involved in the killing of three Meitei youths in Imphal East four days ago.
“There is no SoO agreement in existence in the state and therefore the question of violation of SoO ground rules does not arise. Eighteen cadres were found inside Sinai camp (a Kuki militant designated camp in Kangpokpi district) during security operation recently. Among them one was identified as a cadre of Kuki National Front (KNF) (a Kuki militants outfit under the two umbrella group) while the identities and affiliations of the remaining 17 cadres are yet to be established. All the 17 will be formally arrested on Friday,” said Konthoujam.
Around 9 am on Monday, militants opened fire on 16 firewood collectors — all belonging to the Meitei community — at Khongban Sunurok village in Imphal East district. Three people were killed and three others were injured.
Police said the deceased were identified as Lairenlakpam Inaobi, 57, and Arubam Ronin, 35, both from Nongshum village, and Keshtrimayum Sushil, 32, from Uyumpok village. Both villages are in the Meitei-dominated Imphal East district, bordering the Kuki-dominated Kangpokpi district.
Security forces subsequently apprehended three individuals, two of whom allegedly admitted to involvement in the assault, police had said.
Interrogation of the three suspects was underway, Konthoujam said, adding that one was suspected to be a cadre of the KNF (N). Police suspect their involvement in the killings, but further details are expected to emerge from the ongoing investigation.
“The operation will continue in connection with the recent killing of the three youths. The government will not turn back from its operation. We cannot disclose much at this stage,” he said.
This is the first incident of conflict between Meiteis and Kukis since July 13, when armed Kuki groups attacked Meitei residents in Bishnupur’s Torbung Bangla. In the last few months, at least 50 people have died in the northeastern state, the majority in clashes between Nagas and Kukis.
He added that any new recruitment by groups previously covered under the SoO arrangement during the period without an extension would be treated as illegal and would invite stringent legal action.
The ethnic clashes in Manipur first began between the Meitei and Kuki communities before involving almost every community. The state’s Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities have shut each other out from the areas they dominate since the ethnic clashes began in May 2023, leaving at least 260 people dead and displacing 60,000.
The Meiteis, mostly Hindu, live largely in the Imphal Valley. The Kukis, predominantly Christian, reside in the hills. The state government has maintained that there are no buffer zones dividing communities in the state, but it has identified certain sensitive areas.
The Naga-Kuki tensions intensified following two ambushes on May 13 that left four people, including three church leaders, dead. In the aftermath of the ambushes, 48 people were taken hostage, triggering protests, shutdowns and a blockade along all three national highways in the state.
A new government was formed in February, nearly a year after the imposition of President’s Rule. It includes representatives from all three major communities as part of an attempt to maintain ethnic balance.

73 goals from dropping deep - we ask Kane to break down how he did it
- Published
As Harry Kane's career has progressed, the 33-year-old has taken an increasingly complete role, popping up to collect the ball as deep as his own box.
Many wonder why a talisman tasked with scoring doesn't spend more time closer to goal, but last season the England and Bayern Munich striker scored 73 goals - the highest tally of his career - while playing deeper than he ever has done.
When I mention this paradox, a grin spreads across his face.
"Until you really understand football and understand what we've been talking about, it's so easy to say 'stay high, you're going to score' but it doesn't work like that," Kane says.
I sat down to speak to Kane about the finer details of his game, shedding light on his unique role.
Watching Kane train, his professionalism is palpable. England's record goalscorer is one of the first out on the pitch. The younger players indulge in playful kick-ups as he watches, engaged in conversation with a member of staff.
From a distance, that makes it easy to confuse him with a coach but, given his role on the pitch, it is a fitting mistake.
Kane's style of play reflects who he is as a person, with those who know him saying he is well-rounded and humble on and off the pitch.
The season is in its infancy but Kane isn't basking in the success of the past 12 months. With only five days of pre-season training under his belt, the England captain completed 90 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 win over Borussia Dortmund to lift the German Super Cup.
As demanding as his roaming role is, he has taken the physical demands of it in his stride. Across the past six seasons, STATSports - a sports technology company Kane has invested in - found his distance covered, high-speed running and accelerations were up 8%, 22% and 42% respectively.
And given how the tactical landscape has changed over that time, it is particularly impressive Kane has been able to not only keep up, but stay ahead.
"Over the last five or six years, man-to-man pressure has become bigger," Kane says.
"European football is physical and top teams are trying to win the ball back high, trusting their defenders and midfielders to defend man for man to win their battles."
Given that change, the best teams have recruited physical athletes and brilliant dribblers who can beat their man when the game becomes a series of one-against-ones.
Kane, not known for his dribbling - and by his own admission "not the fastest", has thrived on his own terms.
Against Dortmund, there was a specific moment Kane dropped deep, looking to arrive in space unmarked. Recognising the danger, two players converged on the Englishman.
Kane's dribbling is cerebral. His speed of thought provides him solutions to problems others would attempt to solve with their feet alone.
After getting low and using his strength to shrug centre-back Waldemar Anton off him, Kane rose, slightly adjusting his body to the right. These micro-adjustments are a hallmark of his game and through them he is able to shift an entire team's momentum.
Fooled by this feint, Daniel Svensson and Jobe Bellingham found themselves wrong-footed as Kane snapped the ball back the other way, opening up the entire pitch from within Bayern's half.
1 of 4
Earlier this year, Bayern boss Vincent Kompany shed light on Kane's unique role, explaining it as being 50% coached and 50% Kane deciding what to do.
"I think it's partly instinct, using my football brain and getting the feeling on the pitch," says Kane. "If, for example, I want to drop and see if the centre-back really wants to commit, he might commit into midfield, but is he going to commit if I drop all the way to my box?
"After the first five or 10 minutes you really get an understanding of how the opposition are going to play, which dictates how I play."
There is a shared understanding at Bayern of an approach that allows team-mates to make sense of rotations that, to the naked eye, appear random.
Kane, who is given more freedom than most, is at the centre of it.
"I feel like my position now is as one of two 10s, and you work together," he says. "You can double up on one side to overload, which causes the opposition centre-backs a problem of who to mark.
"If they want to mark both, they've got to go man-to-man and then that leaves space for our wingers or full-backs to run into.
"It's posing all these questions to the opposition but, personally, I love having someone close to me who I can link with."
Kane built his reputation playing as a lone number nine, so it is interesting to hear him identify instead as a number 10 - in a front two.
"When you're the number nine on your own you can get marked by two centre-backs and you struggle to get touches on the ball," he says. "You're relying on everyone else to find you with the ball."
Showing Kane two clips from last season, I ask him to talk through what was going through his head.
"The thing with our formation is, as long as there's someone in each position, it doesn't really matter who it is. Lucho [Luis Diaz] in this clip is playing as one of those 10s.
"I've come off to try and create a bit of space and Lucho's gone through the centre."
Distracted by Kane's dropping-deep movement, one of the opposition midfielders is pulled towards him. This creates space, allowing Joshua Kimmich to punch the ball through to Diaz.
"I think it's Serge [Gnabry] making the run in behind which takes the defenders back, which allows me and Lucho that space in between. Lucho lays it off and whenever I'm in that position, around 20-25 yards out, I'm always looking if I can get my shot off."
It is one of many examples of Kane initially dropping deep before scoring.
"By playing deep when the play develops, I end up coming into a number 10 spot when everyone's dropped," he says. "I can get shots off from the edge of the box, which is a big strength of mine, or I'm running off the back of players where no-one's picking me up - because the midfielder finds it hard to [track]."
1 of 3
The second clip is from Bayern's Champions League tie against Club Brugge.
Usually Kane is marked by an opposition centre-back, but the Belgian club give that responsibility to their holding midfielder - something he recognises and exploits.
Lennart Karl scores without Kane touching the ball, but the striker's involvement is undeniable.
"These are the little runs, again, not everyone sees," Kane explains. "With Jamal Musiala and Lenny, they're so good at receiving the ball and dribbling so there'll be times where I will actually stay higher and let those guys get on the ball a bit deeper, and I'll try and make runs in behind.
"Without changing my game too much, I try and complement the players around me.
"I know Lenny is so good in those pockets and when he gets there, I'm more thinking of running in behind because, one, he can play me in and I can go through on goal, or two, he can dribble with the ball and do exactly what happened here.
"As soon as Lenny gets in that pocket I make the run and not always to get the ball, sometimes it is just to drag the defender away.
"Now he's one-against-one with a centre-back in the middle of the pitch and that's dangerous for any centre-back."
1 of 3
With the Ballon d'Or announcement on the horizon, Kane's name is in the conversation, primarily for the sheer volume of goals he has scored. What is easier to miss in that debate is the rest of his game.
Kane plays for the team in each phase of the game across the entirety of the pitch, while at the same time producing extraordinary individual numbers that match the likes of Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Erling Haaland.
He has described himself as playing in the role of a number 10, nine and six at times.
In a football world of specific and heavily drilled tactical roles, that is quite the achievement.

Fire breaks out at Hitler's mountain retreat in Germany, suspect arrested
In short:
A fire has torn through a retreat built for Adolf Hitler in Germany's Bavarian Alps known as the Eagle's Nest.
Around 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator's remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence.
What's next?
German police have a suspect in custody, with local media reporting that investigators suspect the fire was the result of arson.
German police say they have detained a suspect following a fire at Adolf Hitler's mountain retreat, known as the Eagle's Nest, in the state of Bavaria.
Around 200 firefighters were deployed to tackle the blaze at the Nazi dictator's remote and difficult-to-access Kehlsteinhaus residence, on the peak above Obersalzberg in southern Germany.
Firefighters saw flames rising high into the air as they approached the scene, only to find the building "completely ablaze", police said.
"A suspicious person was taken into temporary custody," they said in a later statement, adding that nobody was injured in the blaze.
Police spokeswoman Lisa Maier said firefighters struggled to tackle the fire due to its location at an altitude of 1,834 metres.
The building was only accessible with "heavy breathing apparatus", she said.
Authorities were alerted to the fire on Friday evening, when a smoke detector triggered a fire alarm at around 9:50pm local time, police said.
No reason for the fire was given, but German media reported that the investigators suspected it was the result of arson.
As snow fell on the Alpine peak, the Eagle's Nest was still engulfed in flames in the early hours of Saturday, a weather camera showed.
The fire appeared to have been doused by Saturday morning, although smoke continued to rise from the smouldering building.
Monument to Hitler
Officers blocked access to the road leading to the retreat.
The firefighters found no-one inside the building.
Ms Maier said the investigation was still ongoing, with police planning a media conference later over the weekend.
German tabloid Bild reported that the authorities arrested a motorcyclist they came across on their way to the scene.
Built between 1937 and 1938, the Eagle's Nest forms part of the toxic legacy of Hitler's Third Reich, which was responsible for the deaths of millions of Jews along with Roma, LGBTQ people and communists in the Holocaust.
It was designed to serve as a monument to Hitler's rule, though the dictator himself only occasionally visited the complex, due to his fear of heights.
Built of stone and granite, the residence offers an exceptional view of the picturesque Bavarian Alpine landscape.
It survived World War II undamaged and later gained notoriety through its use as a shooting location in many post-war Hollywood films.
Since 1952, it has hosted both an exhibition recounting the house's Nazi history and a restaurant.
The website says the Eagle's Nest "stands for the insanity of the regime and the world on the Obersalzberg, where plans for war and mass murder were formed".
Hitler visited the Eagle's Nest 14 times from 1938 until the end of World War II in1945.
He used the mountaintop teahouse strictly as a showpiece to welcome select foreign dignitaries, including French ambassador André François-Poncet, rather than host them at his official residences or at a military command centre.

A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining “userland” access that he says “lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO.”
The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called “tethered” hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.
Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI’s Codex to poke at SmileBasic’s language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After “substantial effort for ~2 weeks,” that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory.
From there, Hajhamid writes that he started poking around for access to the Switch 2’s internal sysmodules, looking for ones that could provide more privileged access to the console’s core functions. Eventually, he found a buffer overflow in the console’s FileSystem services module that exposed a cached data pointer, granting arbitrary read and write privileges. From there, Hajhamid writes that he could execute “privileged filesystem actions” and eventually achieve native code execution through a faked filesystem process.
Hajhamid, who goes by Pepsipu online, showed off a host of new modded characters in Mario Kart World as a proof of concept for the exploit. Others are similarly showing off simple demos and in-progress developer tools running on exploited hardware.

France president Emmanuel Macron has called the shootings in the Paris suburbs which killed one person and wounded at least five others, including a 12-year-old girl, as “a racist terror attack”.
