Perspective: The next James Bond
Perspective: The next James Bond
This weekend, perhaps even as we speak, auditions are being held in London to cast the next Bond.
James Bond. Double-oh—well, you know.
Deadline reports that at least three actors will be screen tested: Jack Lowden, Josh O' Connor, and Callum Turner, who are all fine, experienced British actors and...how do I say this? Hunks.
The Bond selected by Amazon MGM Studios will succeed Daniel Craig, who has owned the role since Casino Royale in 2006, following a parade of other fine, hunky British actors stretching way back to Sean Connery, who starred in Dr. No in 1962.
The literary Bond — a name poached from Dr. James Bond, an American ornithologist who wrote the field guide, Birds of the West Indies, when author Ian Fleming was living in Jamaica — was a Cold War creation. Fleming wrote Casino Royale in 1953, when Great Britain was feeling diminished. Brits had won World War II, with pluck and skill, but were losing their empire. British agents (Guy Burgess, Kim Philby) kept slipping out to Moscow with official secrets before British intelligence could discover they were spies.
It was all damaging to Britain, and embarrassing. But then James Bond strode into the pages of popular culture, dapper and deft. The Soviets and their allies might have sophisticated weaponry and boundless barbarity. But did they drink their martinis shaken, or stirred?
The great espionage novels of Graham Greene and John LeCarre depicted spycraft as a grimy, compromising business. But Fleming's 007, and the onscreen Bonds who played out those stories, dispatched danger in exotic locales, and without rumpling the pleats on their dinner jackets.
Of course ogres and adversaries can shift shapes over decades. I find myself more curious about what forces will next threaten the world when James Bond, whoever plays him, returns to film. So many devices can now listen to, watch, and track our lives second by second, and feed us information they hope will steer our opinions. It may make you think of a line in Dr. No, where Bond tells the scientist who believes he can control the world with his inventions, "Our asylums are full of people who think they're Napoleon. Or God."

Srinagar, Oct 24: At last 34 Kashmiri pilgrims who travelled to Saudi Arabia to perform Umrah remain stranded after the cancellation of their return flights, with dwindling financial resources making it increasingly difficult for them to meet daily expenses.
The pilgrims were scheduled to return to Kashmir on October 13 but could not board their flights amid prevailing security concerns, as per news agency JKNS.
The stranded pilgrims have appealed to the Jammu and Kashmir Government for urgent intervention to facilitate their safe and early return home.
The prolonged stay has left the group under financial strain, with several pilgrims reportedly struggling to afford accommodation, food and medicines. They said their available funds were running low, leaving them uncertain about how to manage their expenses until their return.
According to an updated flight cancellation schedule shared by the Indian Embassy in Riyadh, IndiGo flights to and from Riyadh will remain cancelled until October 31, 2026, while services connecting Jeddah, Dammam and Madinah will remain cancelled until October 27.
While some passengers have managed to return through indirect routes and connecting flights, the stranded pilgrims said the high cost of these alternatives was beyond the means of many members of the group.
They have urged Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha and Chief Minister Omar Abdullah to intervene and coordinate with the Ministry of External Affairs and the airlines concerned to ensure their safe and early return to Jammu and Kashmir.
The pilgrims said the prolonged uncertainty had compounded their financial difficulties and caused considerable mental distress, urging the authorities to take immediate steps to resolve the issue.

This week, Snopes received emails and searches from readers asking if U.S. President Donald Trump's administration chopped down 430 trees last weekend at East Potomac Park in Washington, D.C., the same site where Trump planned to renovate the East Potomac Golf Links property.
Earlier this year, the Trump administration revealed visual plans to overhaul the property into a championship-style golf course. Then, Trump announced on Truth Social that work on the golf course would begin in September. The DC Preservation League filed a lawsuit challenging the project, with District Court Judge Ana Reyes presiding over the case.
One reader asked us via email, "Did the Trump administration order removal of 430 trees from the East Potomac Golf Links?" People shared the claim on Bluesky (archived), Facebook (archived), Threads (archived) and other social media platforms.
In sum, the claim that the Trump administration cut down and planned the removal of 430 trees from the same park where planned golf course renovations will take place is true. 
A memorandum opinion that Reyes authored on Tuesday, in which she granted an emergency motion for a temporary restraining order in the DC Preservation League's case against the Interior Department, confirmed the tree cutting was taking place. That order blocked the Trump administration from continuing the work for two weeks, through Oct. 26.
Reyes' opinion, arriving one day after an emergency hearing on Monday, specifically mentioned the suddenness of crews cutting down 430 "healthy, non-invasive" trees, with the government only notifying the court minutes prior to close of business on a holiday weekend. She also noted the Trump administration argued the removals aligned with recommendations in a 2019 National Park Service report, leading Reyes to write she was "skeptical" of the timing. More about that report appears later in this article.
Snopes' email correspondence with the Interior Department, in which a department spokesperson appeared to indirectly acknowledge that crews cut down hundreds of trees with no reasonable notice to the court, also appears later in this article. We emailed the park service, an agency the Interior Department oversees, and the White House, as well as the DC Preservation League to ask for additional documentation and a statement, and will update this article if we receive further information.
430 trees cut down with very little notice
Reyes' opinion, handed down on Tuesday, laid out the timeline of events:
- Tree-cutting plans began internally within the Interior Department at least early last week.
- The government provided unreasonable notice to the court (at 4:55 p.m. last Friday) of its plans to remove "up to 529 trees" to restore the golf course's "historic links-style character."
- Tree-cutting work began 15 hours later at 8 a.m. on Saturday.
- An emergency hearing occurred the following Monday — on Columbus Day, a federal holiday.
During the Monday hearing, Reyes reportedly said she was "furious" that the government told the court they knew of the tree-cutting plans at least days earlier than they notified the court. In May, she told the government she wanted to receive notice if crews planned to remove more than 10 trees, the Associated Press reported.
An NBC4 Washington journalist reported, "In all of my years of covering court proceedings, I have never seen a judge so angry," adding Reyes was "raising her voice" at government attorneys.
Reyes wrote in the opinion:
The Government then did precisely what Plaintiffs feared. Sometime between the September 3 hearing and October 2, plans moved from removing only hazardous, dead, dying, or invasive trees to removing hundreds of healthy, non-invasive trees. And then it removed them without providing meaningful notice to Plaintiffs or the Court.
Reyes wrote that Trump administration lawyers said the Interior Department "ordered, considered and approved" a plan for the park service to oversee the cutting down of hundreds of trees, as well as that the government said it knew of no reason for any urgency to complete the work. She said the administration acknowledged in court that crews cut down 430 nonhazardous trees, adding that "about 300 additional trees are on the literal chopping block" but weren't yet fallen thanks to a "rain delay." (A tally of well over 700 targeted trees exceeded the "up to 529 trees" part of the notice Reyes said the government provided.)
Journalists live-posting from Reyes' courtroom on Monday documented the administration's mention of chopping down 430 nonhazardous trees and planning to cut 299 more — out of the park's roughly 3,800 total trees.
We emailed Riverbend Tree Service in Virginia, a company with crews that appeared in a local news video report, to ask if its workers were present and when they first learned of the job, among other questions, and will update this story should we receive details.
Interior Department response, 2019 plans
In an email to Snopes, an Interior Department spokesperson chided Reyes for her involvement with the case and didn't directly respond to our request to confirm the department ordered and approved the removal of hundreds of trees with very little notice. The email appeared to only indirectly confirm the tree-removal work.
The department spokesperson described the current state of the golf course as "riddled with garbage and choked by overgrown trees" and that "the work carries out a plan, seven years in the making, to address tree overgrowth" at the park.
Reyes wrote that the government claimed the tree-cutting work, referenced as a Tree Management Plan (TMP), applied to a Cultural Landscape Report the park service authored during Trump's first term in 2019, and had "nothing to do with" Trump's golf course plans. She continued, "The Court is skeptical," and wrote:
The Government claims that the TMP implements a 2019 Cultural Landscape Report and has nothing to do with the Washington National Plan. It is a coincidence, the Government seems to suggest, that DOI cut down hundreds of trees at the Course weeks after the President asked DOI to cut down trees at the Course, and not, say, any other time in the last seven years.
That 2019 report credited golf course architect Walter J. Travis with designing "the original links-style, eighteen-hole course" in 1917 and emphasized retaining the character and history of the property. One part of the report said the early design of East Potomac Park Golf Course (EPPGC) originally largely lacked trees:
Links–style courses typically have very few trees and shrubs. Too many trees would interfere with the characteristic views and ever–present wind.
At EPPGC there were some trees originally, but overwhelmingly the property was treeless allowing for views across the golf course and to the surrounding water. Many trees have grown up within the course due to lack of maintenance, creation of dumping areas, and aggressive planting without regard to the history or function of the golf course. Trees and understory will have to be managed in order for EPPGC to return to its links character.
The Interior Department's email response to Snopes featured three attached images allegedly showing glimpses of a large garbage problem at the park. We followed up to ask if the images showed debris from Trump's White House East Wing demolition, seeing as crews reportedly began dumping debris from the construction site of Trump's ballroom project on the golf course last October. A department spokesperson denied it with a one-word answer: "No."
For further reading, we previously reported about a similar rumor alleging Trump ordered the removal of cherry trees from the same park, the site of the nation's first cherry blossom planting. Reyes' opinion didn't mention anything about the removal of cherry trees.

An Indian expatriate who won 100 million dirham (approximately ₹240 crore) in The UAE Lottery has spoken about how the windfall has changed his life a year after the win. Anilkumar Bolla, a 29-year-old technology professional based in Abu Dhabi, won the jackpot in October 2025. Since then, he has purchased properties in India and the UAE, bought cars for himself and his brother, gifted gold jewellery to his mother and acquired farmland for his father. Reflecting on the past year, Bolla, who hails from Telangana, said the biggest change has been the opportunity to spend more time with his family. Bolla won what was described as the largest lottery prize ever awarded in the UAE when he secured the 100 million dirham jackpot in October 2025. Speaking about the year since his win, he said spending time with his family had become a priority. “The most important thing is that I am spending quality time with my family,” he was quoted as saying by Khaleej Times. Describing the experience as “transformative”, he added: “Winning the lottery reshaped my life and my ambitions as well.” The money has also enabled him to enjoy material comforts. Over the past year, Bolla has purchased an iPhone 17 Air and four to five high-end watches. However, he said helping his family has been among the most meaningful outcomes of his lottery win. One of his early purchases was gold jewellery for his mother. “It was her dream to have a few ornaments, so I brought it all together and gifted it to her,” he said, according to Gulf News. The gift brought tears to her eyes. Bolla comes from a farming family in Telangana. Although he has purchased properties in India and the UAE since winning the jackpot, his family continues to live in the same house they occupied before his ₹240 crore lottery win. Bolla describes the house as his father's dream home. He has, however, gifted his father farmland where he can pursue his interest in organic farming. "My happiness is always linked to my family," he said. "Whatever I've done for them, those things are really special to me, and those are the things that make me the happiest, more than what I do for myself." A year after his win, Bolla says the excitement he initially felt about travelling has faded. During the past 12 months, he has travelled to several destinations and enjoyed new experiences with his family. Bali, Thailand and Amsterdam were among the places he visited. "Somehow, the excitement has faded away, but I'm really grateful for the opportunities I'm getting and the things I'm doing," he said. With many of his wishes fulfilled, Bolla has begun exploring potential business ideas and long-term financial planning. His investments include property near the airport in Abu Dhabi and at Dubai Marina. Asked what advice he would offer other lottery winners, the Indian techie said: “Welcome to the millionaires’ club. AMC Theatres CEO Adam Aron has issued an open letter to New York City residents reiterating the company’s desire to continue operating its longstanding Kips Bay 15 multiplex in the Manhattan neighborhood of that name, but concedes the decision is not AMC’s to make.
Neighbors of the Kips Bay-Murray Hill section of Manhattan along Second Avenue near the East River have been vocal about the planned closure of the multiplex that’s been a central commercial hub since 1999 (AMC took over the venue in 2006). The property on which the multiplex sits was privately purchased last year by NYU Langone, one of New York’s major health care systems.
AMC announced in August that the purchase would likely mean the closure of the multiplex by the end of this year, prompting an outcry and protests from residents and other businesses in the area.
Watch on Deadline
Following “direct engagement” from Manhattan Borough President Brad Hoylman-Sigal, AMC’s Aron issued the open letter concurring with Hoylman-Sigal that the neighborhood needs such amenities as a movie theater, supermarket and housing.
Writes Aron, “Since news first broke that our popular AMC Kips Bay 15-screen movie theatre located at 570 Second Avenue in Manhattan will soon be forced against our will to close its doors, I’ve been struck by the extraordinary support that this AMC theatre has received from within the local surrounding community.”

Early 1900s India was a place where your gender determined what you could be in life. That nation could not stomach the thought of, trivial as it was, common as it is today, a woman pursuing the sciences. This antediluvian thought though, this kind of restriction was only the cause of a temporary disruption Mary Poonen Lukose’s path to glory.
It is inescapable irony that India’s first woman Surgeon General Mary Poonen Lukose was not allowed to study science. Born in Ayamanam (incidentally, Arundathi Roy’s backdrop in the God of Small Things) in Kottayam in 1886, Mary was so bright, she topped the matriculation exam. Nevermind how bright she was, her gender was a disqualifier as Maharaja College in Tiruvananthapuram declined her admission to the sciences. Only a temporary detour, Mary went on to get a degree in history, becoming the first woman from Travancore to graduate from Madras University in 1909.
However, her family could afford to send her to London to pursue medicine, and she was the first Indian woman to graduate in Medicine from the University of London, according to an article published by Cambridge University Press (CUP) as part of a compendium of Modern Asian Studies. She earned an MBBS from the University of London in 1915, trained in obstetrics and gynaecology, and studied paediatrics at Great Ormond Street Hospital.
Reports of her life, rendered through an autobiographical account, Trailblazer, released in 2020, record Mary as working hard in Dublin at the Rotunda Hospital, coping with the increasing work load created by the outbreak of World War 1 in 1914. When her mentor and guide, her father passed away in 1916, Mary was shattered; she had to take a call on whether she would continue in England or come back home to serve her people. She, of course, decided to come home and blazed a path of glory, only long forgotten. She returned to Travancore in 1916 as its first woman doctor.
The CUP article further quotes from an autobiographical note penned by Mary herself: “In her autobiographical essay, Mary Poonen Lukose reflects on her decision to become a doctor. She traces it to her early experiences helping out in hospitals where her father worked as a doctor, and to his example and influence on her. ‘As I grew up, he made it a point to instill into me the spirit of service to humanity.’
The article further notes that the style of her 1916 job application, her requests for references, and the correspondence surrounding it suggest that she was aware of the fact that her qualifications were exceptional for an Indian woman of her time.
Mary Poonen Lukose went on to build the scaffolding of modern public health in Travancore, one that can be attributed to the many advances that Kerala has achieved today in health care indicators. Her work helped lay the ground for what we now celebrate as the “Kerala model” of health—fronting strong primary care, institutional childbirth, public health outreach, and unusually good social indicators. Acknowledging her contributions, in the 2018 budget speech, the finance minister of the State said, on record, in the House: ‘Dr. Mary Poonen Lukose is one of the most talented people in the development of Kerala’s health system.’
At the Women and Children Hospital in Thycaud, Mary worked as an obstetrician and superintendent, initiating daughters of local birth attendants into training midwifery, an attempt to subsume traditional midwifery into scientific deliveries and maternal care. Some historic references to her indicate she performed Travancore’s first Caesarean section before 1920, reportedly sometimes working only by the light of a hurricane-lamp light.
As Surgeon General from 1938, she was responsible for 32 government hospitals, 40 dispensaries, and 20 private institutions. In colonial era India, this could be notched up as a mega achievement for a woman, not only in health care, but also an administrator. Mary also founded a tuberculosis sanatorium in Nagercoil, and established the X-Ray and Radium Institute in Tiruvananthapuram.
It was not only for the issue of providing women adequate health facilities that she lent her voice, but was equally vociferous on women’s political rights. She herself, in 1922, was nominated to Travancore’s legislative council, becoming the State’s first woman legislator.
But Mary was a multi-splendored person, capable of achievements across sectors. As the nuns sing in the Sound of Music of Maria the reluctant nun: How do you catch a cloud and pin it down? Mary co-founded the Tiruvananthapuram branch of the Young Women’s Christian Association and served as its president for 50 years. She was also a member of two professional bodies, the Indian Medical Association and the Federation of Obstetric and Gynaecological Societies of India.
Many honours came her way, including the Vaidyaśāstrakuśala by the Maharaja of Travancore in 1935, and the Padma Śhri in 1975, just a year before her death at the age of 90.
Mary is part of a legacy of tall women in Indian health care that helped sculpt systems that are propping the nation up today, including Muthulakshmi Reddy, Kadambini Ganguly, and Anandi Joshi. They are the forebearers who chipped away at the glass ceilings that prevented them from rising, and cleared the ladder for women who came after them, though history has not given them their due space.
But it is now time for reparation, it is time to say their name loud. Say her name: Say Mary Poonen Lukose, so every one can hear, and celebrate.

Trump administration sues to block certification of upcoming Alaska election
- Published
The Trump administration wants to block the certification of the Senate election in Alaska if Republican Senator Dan Sullivan loses, arguing that another candidate with the same name may confuse voters.
The justice department said in a federal lawsuit filed on Thursday that the inclusion of another Dan Sullivan on the ballot could lead some to mistakenly cast their votes for the wrong candidate.
Polls suggest the race between Senator Sullivan and Democrat Mary Peltola is tight, with Peltola holding a narrow lead in the final days before the 3 November vote.
The US government wants the judge to bar the state from certifying the results if Senator Sullivan loses by a margin less than the other Sullivan.
"I'm the one that said do it," US President Donald Trump told reporters when asked for his thoughts on the lawsuit after he landed in Florida for a campaign rally on Friday.
Trump has referred to the second Sullivan's candidacy as a "scam" and said his administration was looking at "powerful legal options" to end it. The retired teacher previously denied his candidacy had an ulterior motive.
Previous efforts to remove that Sullivan, a retired teacher, from the ballot have already been rejected by the Alaska Supreme Court.
For the 3 November midterm election, the senator will be listed on the ballot as the Republican incumbent.
Alaska's ranked-choice voting system means that voters could select both Sullivans if they are unsure at the ballot box.
In court documents, the justice department said Alaska "will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its elections" if it includes "any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J Sullivan".
The second Sullivan, who was also a US Forest Service worker, was reportedly once a member of the Alaska Independence Party before registering as a Republican earlier this year.
In the filing, Associate Attorney General Stanley E Woodward Jr asserted that the sole purpose of his candidacy was to benefit Peltola's campaign by reducing the number of votes for the senator.
"Given the substantial likelihood that the inclusion of Dan J Sullivan will confuse or mislead voters looking to cast a vote for Senator Sullivan and thus distort the will of Alaskan voters, there is a substantial likelihood that a certification of the election will reflect an electoral process that lacked integrity," Woodward argued.
Dan J Sullivan has repeatedly denied those claims, telling the local Petersburg Pilot newspaper earlier this year that he "wouldn't even know who to speak to" in Peltola's campaign.
He said separately to Courthouse News that it was his "sincere hope that people know who and what they are voting for but, ultimately, choice is good and voters' intent will be as varied as the candidates who are running".
In the event Peltola wins, and the margin of loss suggests possible confusion, the lawsuit calls for certification to be delayed pending an investigation into whether voters were mixed up on the names as well as any "necessary and appropriate" steps to determine what would have happened had the second Sullivan been kept off the ballot.
Neither candidate has so far commented on the lawsuit.
The Senate race in Alaska - which Trump won by 14 percentage points in 2024 - is among the most closely watched in the upcoming midterm elections.
The president's approval ratings in the state have been badly hit by voter disapproval of rising prices and the war in Iran.

India, Azerbaijan explore stronger trade and energy ties as Jaishankar meets Aliyev in Baku
S Jaishankar’s first visit to Azerbaijan in eight years focuses on expanding India-Azerbaijan ties in trade, energy, investment, tourism and connectivity.
India and Azerbaijan on Friday explored ways to expand cooperation in trade, investment, energy and connectivity as external affairs minister S Jaishankar met President Ilham Aliyev and foreign minister Jeyhun Bayramov in Baku to take forward a reset in bilateral ties that have been fractious in recent years.
This was the first visit by an Indian foreign minister to Azerbaijan in eight years, against the backdrop of a thaw in bilateral relations, which have been impacted in the past by Azerbaijan’s close ties with Pakistan. During the four-day conflict with Pakistan in May 2025, India was angered when Azerbaijan’s foreign ministry issued a statement condemning the military attacks on Pakistan.
At his meeting with Aliyev, Jaishankar conveyed the greetings of President Droupadi Murmu and Prime Minister Narendra Modi and discussed the strengthening of bilateral ties. “Appreciate his positive sentiments for this shared endeavour,” Jaishankar said on social media.
Jaishankar said his “productive discussions” with Bayramov had “charted a pathway forward for our relationship”. The two sides agreed to deepen political consultations, exchange visits, enhance economic activities, build connectivity and foster people-to-people ties.
The two foreign ministers also discussed regional and global developments, including the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia and the shared threat of terrorism, and Jaishankar said the two sides had a “common interest in promoting peace, progress and prosperity”.
Bayramov said he emphasised the “importance of continued dialogue and exploring opportunities for cooperation in areas of mutual interest”.
Jaishankar’s visit was a follow-up to a meeting between Modi and Aliyev on the margins of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit in Kyrgyzstan in September and the first bilateral foreign office consultations in almost four years in April. People familiar with the matter said that the visit was part of efforts to reset the overall relationship.
At a media interaction with Bayramov, Jaishankar said that his discussions with the Azerbaijan President focused on ongoing cooperation, including “what we could be doing more, what we could be doing differently”. Bayramov added that the discussions would help elevate ties to a higher level.
Despite the presence of more than 1,000 Indian firms in Azerbaijan and ONGC Videsh Ltd’s investment of $1.2 billion in the Azeri-Chirag-Gunashli oil and gas fields and the associated Baku-Tbilisi-Ceyhan pipeline, two-way trade languished at around $600 million in the first half of 2026. Both ministers spoke about expanding economic cooperation**,** and Bayramov highlighted the potential for collaboration in energy, pharmaceuticals, digital services and mining.
Connectivity, including additional flights, also figured in discussions**,** as Azerbaijan has become a popular destination for Indians, receiving 166,944 tourists from the country in 2025. India was the fourth-largest source of tourists, after Russia, Türkiye and Iran.
Jaishankar noted that both sides had agreed to coordinate more closely on the International North-South Transport Corridor, and said, “Air connectivity is also something that we value. There are daily flights, but obviously to deepen the relations we have to think about how to grow that further.”
He also thanked the Azerbaijan government for helping in the evacuation of Indian nationals from Iran after the start of the West Asia conflict earlier this year.
The peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia also figured in the discussions, and Jaishankar said India welcomed the peace agreement reached by the two countries in August 2025 and hoped it would lead to a durable peace. “India has a very clear position that disputes should be settled through dialogue and diplomacy, and in that context, our discussions covered West Asia, Europe, Eurasia,” he said. “We have a common interest in promoting peace, progress and prosperity. And threats like terrorism, conflict and instability are our common enemies.”

Peacock series Crystal Lake doesn’t feel like a Friday the 13th movie when you first press play, even though it’s set up to be a prequel to the original film. (This review includes spoilers of the original Friday the 13th movie but avoids major Crystal Lake spoilers.)
Instead, Crystal Lake strives to build a drama that’s half homage, half uncharted territory, while giving a long-awaited backstory to Pamela Voorhees. The original villain in the first film, Pam Voorhees, shocked audiences in 1980 by popping up out of nowhere in the midst of a brutal camp counselor killing spree, then confronting the final girl with a Norman Bates-like delivery of the movie’s chilling tagline, “Kill her, mommy,” using the voice of her drowned son, Jason.
Although the hockey-masked killer, Jason Voorhees, became the horror icon at the center of the franchise, his mom, Pam, continued to fascinate fans, who knew very little about her. Beheaded in the first film after just 13 minutes onscreen, her spirit would occasionally appear in later films, but the original actor, Betsy Palmer, who portrayed Pam refused to return, largely because the character has no depth.
Ars dug into news archives and found interviews where Palmer explained that the later films did nothing to expand the character, offering only “stupid” lines. There was no reason for the actor—who at the height of her fame dated James Dean and was often typecast as the sweet-faced girl-next-door—to stoop to stepping back into Pam’s shoes. She famously only agreed to do the first movie because her Mercedes broke down on the Connecticut Turnpike and she needed a new car. She worked 10 days to capture her scenes, got paid $10,000, bought a new car, and expected nobody to remember her performance.
“I read that script and thought ‘What a piece of junk,’” Palmer said in 2005.
Palmer often criticized the later movies for bringing back Jason’s mom but giving her nothing to do. So, while some die-hard Friday the 13th fans may find Crystal Lake slow and foreign in the first few episodes, it’s worth sticking around for the first stab at fulfilling Palmer’s dream of Pam being more than just a helicopter mom of a vengeful boy living at the bottom of a cursed lake.

Xbox’s first chief operating officer (COO) is leaving after the new role was created just a few months ago. Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today, according to an internal Xbox memo seen by The Verge. Chiang has been at Microsoft for 21 years, serving as the head of Minecraft before being promoted to Xbox chief operating officer in July.
Xbox’s first chief operating officer is out after just a few months
Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft after 21 years.
Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft after 21 years.
Xbox CEO Asha Sharma announced Chiang’s departure in a surprisingly short memo today. “Helen Chiang is leaving Microsoft today. I’m grateful for her years of service and wish her well,” said Sharma. As Chiang is departing today, her immediate responsibilities are being split up between other Xbox leaders for now, and Sharma notes that “We’ll share more on COO leadership as plans are finalized.”
That sounds like the COO position isn’t going away after just a few months, but it’s not clear why Chiang is departing after such a short stint in the role. At the time of Chiang’s promotion, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma described the new chief operating officer role as a first for Xbox, “with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services.” The role was created as part of Xbox’s big “reset.”
Chiang reported directly to Sharma, and was promoted to “bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”
Chiang departs amid rumors that Xbox is preparing more layoffs this month, in November, and January. The sudden and short memo from Sharma, coupled with Chiang’s responsibilities being assigned to other Xbox leaders, makes it seem like this wasn’t a resignation.
I asked Microsoft to comment on Chiang’s departure, and the company refused to discuss the circumstances of her exit. “We don’t discuss individual personnel matters,” says Kari Perez, Xbox vice president of communications. “We’re grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

What to know about the Melania Trump-brokered ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky
A Russian-occupied city in southern Ukraine is set to get a brief pause in the war so aid can get in and residents can get out
A small city in southern Ukraine, cut off for months by fighting, is set to get a brief pause in the 4 1/2-year-old war so that aid can get in and residents can get out.
U.S. first lady Melania Trump brokered the localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine around Oleshky, a Russian-occupied city she said is “on the brink of disaster.”
Ukrainian, Russian and U.S. negotiators reached the deal Friday. Officials on all sides have confirmed it, but many details have not been released.
Oleshky is located in Ukraine's partially occupied Kherson region. It sits on the Dnipro River, which separates Ukrainian forces from the city’s Russian occupiers. Moscow’s forces captured it on the first day of the full-scale invasion in February 2022. Its buildings were shelled and burned.
In June 2023, floodwaters swamped the city after the Kakhovka Dam collapsed in an explosion that an Associated Press investigation found was likely caused by the Russian military. Hundreds of residents were killed.
Once home to about 24,000 people, the city has had scarce food and medical supplies for months. There is no electricity, heat or running water. Roads out of town are mined and lined with burned-out cars, and drones buzz overhead. With another harsh winter approaching, those still there face death from hunger or disease.
Ukraine has repeatedly appealed for a local ceasefire to organize evacuations. As the occupying power, Russia is obligated under international law to make sure civilians under its control have what they need to survive.
The deal sets out three stages: a ceasefire, then delivery of humanitarian aid, then evacuation of civilians who want to leave Oleshky, according to Dmytro Lubinets, Ukraine’s human rights ombudsman and its chief negotiator in the talks.
Before any aid moves, mines will be cleared on the routes into the city, Lubinets said.
Russia’s human rights ombudswoman, Yana Lantratova, who took part in the negotiations, said firstly they plan to establish what residents need and then deliver food, medicine, hygiene products and other essentials. She said anyone who wants to leave the combat zone will be guaranteed safe passage.
Lubinets told the AP that the ceasefire will begin Tuesday, two days before the humanitarian mission starts, and will last several days.
Russia’s chief of the general staff, Gen. Valery Gerasimov, said Russian forces “will cease fire on the Kherson axis” from 4 a.m. Tuesday Moscow time, which is late Monday in the United States. He said Russian forces would also carry out “engineering reconnaissance” and ensure the “humanitarian convoy” can move safely into the city.
Ukraine's General Staff said the ceasefire will begin at 3 a.m. Tuesday Kyiv time, since Ukraine moves its clocks back an hour on Sunday while Russia does not.
Lubinets said the pause would apply across the Kherson region and neighboring areas essential to the operation.
Lubinets gave no details on how the ceasefire or the aid mission would be monitored or carried out, citing the sensitivity of the negotiations. He declined to say whether Melania Trump would travel to Ukraine.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said people who want to leave Oleshky will be able to. He would not say whether they would be taken to Russian- or Ukrainian-held territory. Asked how long the evacuation would last, he said only that it would most likely take several days.
“The operation will be carried out gradually and is extremely challenging to implement,” Lubinets said.
The first lady began talks on Oleshky after she heard about the situation at one of her events during the U.N. General Assembly session in September, the White House said. She and a representative then worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to set the terms. She had already been working with officials from both countries on a separate matter.
“When Melania Trump learned about the situation in Oleshky, the negotiation process began under her coordination,” Lubinets said. He said the sides spent several weeks discussing ideas and developing “new approaches, mechanisms and tools” to help civilians there survive.
Helping children in conflict zones has become one of her signature issues during her husband’s second term. She hosted a U.N. Security Council meeting on the issue earlier this year. Last year she wrote to Russian President Vladimir Putin about efforts to reunite families with children she described as “displaced by the war.” Her senior adviser, Marc Beckman, says she has helped reunite nearly three dozen children.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has lobbied various world leaders for help reuniting children he says were taken by Russia after the invasion began in 2022. The International Criminal Court in 2023 issued an arrest warrant for Putin for war crimes, accusing him of personal responsibility for the abductions of children from Ukraine.
The development comes as tensions have increased to new highs between the Trump administration and Ukraine’s government. Kyiv has faced restrictions on the satellite internet system it relies on to knock down Russian attacks, with President Donald Trump and other top U.S. officials sending mixed messages about who was responsible for throttling the Elon Musk-made Starshield system.
Trump also recently waived new Russia sanctions, reached an agreement with Russia to import diesel fuel and pushed Zelenskyy to make a deal to end the war. In renewed efforts to revive the peace process, Trump envoy Steve Witkoff traveled to Norway this week for talks with Zelenskyy before meeting Putin in St. Petersburg, Russia.
Zelenskyy did not mention the ceasefire in Oleshky during a remote appearance at the Hudson Institute, a Washington think tank, on Friday. He did note that American Patriot missile interceptors were still on hold.
He also spoke of the importance of the United States to renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war, including a possible joint meeting with Trump and Putin.

My Oura Ring now feels like a keepsake from a former self. I picked it out with the company’s sizing kit, but within a month, it no longer fit the same way. Since January, I have shed over 40kg of fat. The ring, once snug, now slips and spins, holding on with costly accuracy to the shape I used to be. I knew I’d need new clothes as my body changed, but I barely considered the fate of my health tracker.
There’s a quiet satisfaction in letting a beautiful watch claim your wrist. A smart ring grants that luxury, quietly gathering the data we now expect from ourselves. It never lights up a dinner table or interrupts with a sleep report until you ask for it. The appeal is clear: you can care about your health without announcing it to the world.
For Indian buyers, however, the introduction came with an awkward timetable. Oura Ring 4 went on sale here on March 18, 2026, starting at ₹28,900, with membership priced at ₹599 a month. On May 28, Oura announced Ring 5 globally, with shipping from June 4. The new ring in the shop was suddenly the previous ring in the range. After waiting for an official Indian launch, it was difficult to feel especially courted by the sequence.
On the move
Then comes the reality of daily life. If you eat with your hands, the ring joins you at lunch, its polished surface flirting with unruly masala. Cooking means kneading dough; cleaning up means plunging into a sink of dishes. You can take the ring off, but then you need a safe spot for it. For something prized for its low-maintenance charm, it still demands attention at unexpected moments.
Oura’s instructions acknowledge some of this domestic life. You can clean its titanium rings with mild soap and water, then dry them thoroughly. Showering is permitted. The company advises considering removal when handling hard cookware or lifting weights, where friction can scratch the finish. Wearing it directly beside another ring can scratch either piece.
Jewellery brings its own negotiations. Delhi-based certified fitness professional Aarja Bedi, who is engaged, has begun wearing her smart ring on the corresponding finger of her right hand. She likes the idea of a titanium band alongside traditional pieces, but is less sure about the comfort of wearing them together. “You don’t want to be figuring out finger real estate the week before a big occasion,” she says. Oura recommends the index finger, with the middle or ring finger also suitable. The wedding band need not surrender its place to the sleep score.
The data debate
Chennai-based fitness coach Raj Ganpath, author of Simple, Not Easy, stopped wearing an Oura he had bought from the United States. The fit troubled him; changing sizes from India was inconvenient, and the morning readings didn’t consistently match the morning he thought he was having. His Garmin has stayed. He chooses information relevant to his training, including its VO₂ max estimate of aerobic fitness, without feeling obliged to attend to everything it produces. “You need to know what data is important for you and what you need to track,” he says.
Raj describes someone waking quite happily, reading an unfavourable sleep report, and beginning to feel tired. The number has acquired the authority to revise the experience. Mumbai-based Ritesh Shaiwal, athlete and director of Easyhuman, wants clients to pay attention to sleep scores and heart rate variability, the variation in timing between heartbeats, without waiting for permission from a gadget to feel motivated. “It is ok to use it, but don’t get dependent,” he says. There is a difference between being interested in your sleep and having it marked every morning.
Those subtleties could be introduced more warmly at the sales counter. During my visits to over a dozen stores in Delhi and Mumbai, I noticed it was a challenging to find staff who could confidently explain Oura. Instead, conversations often shifted towards Gabit. While this was my experience, not a national audit, but with Gabit available at Croma and Ultrahuman already in Indian retail, Oura might need to ensure that its reputation alone isn’t the only thing guiding demonstrations. When someone is buying for the first time, they really benefit from having someone who can clearly explain what happens after opening the box and why the monthly payments continue.
The software provides part of the answer. GLP-1 Insights was launched for English-speaking users in India starting June 4, including on Ring 4. Users can log medication doses, record side effects, and track weight alongside sleep or recovery data. Between medical visits, days can blur: when did the tiredness start? How did last week go? Having a record could make discussions with healthcare providers more effective. This update matters beyond simply adding a new app feature.
A record still requires interpretation. A readiness score cannot establish that a medication caused a change, and a weight entry cannot tell you how much of the loss is fat. Oura says the feature does not recommend dosage changes or replace a clinician. It can help someone arrive at an appointment with a better account of what happened, without supplying the medical conclusion.
One size doesn’t fit all
On June 23, Oura announced a collaboration with LillyDirect, Eli Lilly’s US healthcare platform, offering eligible customers a complimentary Oura sizing kit. That detail really matters. The company is there to help people find their perfect ring size, especially for treatments that might change it. The kit starts by answering that question early on. But what about the answer later on? Not everyone taking medication to lose weight will need a smaller ring, but the possibility doesn’t require much imagination. Oura is inviting these customers to wear its product through the process. A paid plan with a defined size-change benefit would let them buy with confidence about what follows. Eli has no reason to organise an exchange of my ring. The company selling it as a companion to my changing body has every reason to consider one.
Oura’s published warranty says replacement rings come in the original size. Its sizing guidance directs people with a poor fit to support, leaving room for an individual solution, but I could not find a published Indian benefit guaranteeing a replacement after weight loss. Retail exchanges follow the retailer’s policy, which might cover situations like selecting the wrong size at checkout. In my case, I was confident that I chose the right size from the start.
Ultrahuman has provided clearer details. Its two-year UltrahumanX plan, available to eligible users, allows a Ring AIR wearer to request a smaller replacement after losing weight, according to its terms. Only one ring replacement is permitted for the reasons listed, whether due to weight change or fit adjustment. While the limit matters, it’s equally important to understand the offer thoroughly before you put the ring on your finger.
I would gladly pay Oura for a size-replacement plan in India. I am invested enough in its insights to want to keep wearing it, especially with the new GLP-1 features. There is still lunch to get through, the question of where I left it before doing the dishes, and a steadily loosening fit. Mine may soon need to be a different size. I would like that to be a conversation about continuing to wear it, rather than buying it all over again.
So, should you consider getting one? If you’re looking for a subtle health companion that offers useful insights without another screen demanding your attention, Oura is definitely worth thinking about. Its GLP-1 features provide even those starting treatment with another reason to consider it, though I would suggest keeping an eye on the potential size change. Many users won’t experience the same issues I do. They’ll simply wear the ring, go about their day, and discover helpful information whenever they open the app. Despite my own concerns, I still believe Oura is a great choice. I just hope the company makes it easier to keep the ring fitting perfectly as I get smaller.

U.S. President Donald Trump is poised to lift tariffs on some Canadian products as Republicans in border states lobby for relief from trade actions that have put them in a shaky political position ahead of November's midterms.
Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins said on Friday that the Trump administration will scrap tariffs on some paper and plastic products, refrigeration and packaging equipment, agricultural machinery and seaweed and algae products, among others, after she relayed how damaging these levies have been for consumers and businesses in her state.
Trump hit these products with a 50 per cent tariff in August, apparently retaliating for Canada's countermeasures on some U.S. goods that were imposed after the president first launched his trade war last year.
Collins said these Canadian products are "essential" to some Maine businesses and farms and cannot be easily replaced with any U.S. alternatives.
She said, for example, Maine's blueberry growers rely on Canadian-made specialized harvesting boxes that work with existing processing equipment. Plus, a U.S. supplier of cardboard totes widely used in the agricultural sector recently stopped making that particular product, "leaving producers with no choice but to turn to Canada," she said.
"I will continue working directly with administration officials to seek additional relief and encourage a broader trade agreement with Canada, our neighbour, ally and largest trading partner," Collins said in a social media statement announcing the changes.
U.S. Sen. Susan Collins campaigns in Fryeburg, Maine, earlier this month. Collins, a Republican, is in a tight race with Democrat Troy Jackson. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)
Collins, a 30-year veteran of the U.S. upper house, is in a pitched battle for re-election in Maine as she tries to hold off a Democratic challenger, Troy Jackson, who has made Trump's trade war with Canada a centrepiece of his campaign.
A moderate Republican who has sparred with Trump in the past, Collins had earlier pressured the administration to drop U.S. tariffs on products like road salt given her wintry state depends on Canadian supplies to keep the roads clear.
Another border state Republican Senate candidate, Michigan's Mike Rogers, has publicly called for an end to the trade war with Canada, saying the tariffs have raised prices at a time when inflation is already high.
Polls show Trump's trade war with Canada is deeply unpopular among American voters in both major parties.
- Lawsuit challenging Trump's tariffs against Canada filed in U.S. Court of International Trade
- Podcast How Canada and tariffs are factoring into U.S. midterm elections
The tariff climbdown comes on the same day Trump claimed that Canada "very much wants to make a deal" with the U.S. to restore trade peace.
"Canada now is very much prepared to make a deal," Trump told reporters Friday, while falsely claiming Canada been making "$90 billion a year" from the U.S. every year.
That's an apparent reference to the U.S. trade deficit in goods with Canada, which Trump's own U.S. Trade Representative pegs at $48.3 billion US — much of it driven by U.S. refineries buying large volumes of Alberta oil at a discount to world prices. The U.S. consistently runs a trade surplus in services with Canada.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, meanwhile, said during a bilateral visit to Turkey Friday that Canada is open to a mutually beneficial deal with the U.S. that protect Canadian interests — but the government is in no rush.
"We could sign it this afternoon if the U.S. were there. If it has to be months from now or longer than that, or another administration, before a proper deal comes into place, we will do that," he said.

The Indian startup ecosystem continued to mature in FY26, with 22 new-age tech companies making their public market debut as against 13 in FY25. At the same time, a growing number of startups turned profitable or moved closer to profitability after years of cost rationalisation to adjust to the new funding realities. Despite a tough Q4 for many startups due to geopolitical uncertainties, Indian startups are expected to improve their top and bottom line numbers in FY26. Of the 106 startups in the tracker, 66, or about 62.3%, reported profits in FY26. However, the profitability picture remained uneven. Together, these 66 startups generated a net profit of ₹14,546.9 Cr, while the remaining 40 posted a cumulative loss of ₹31,797.2 Cr, underscoring that sustainable profitability remains a work in progress for a section of the ecosystem. Even so, the scale of India’s startup ecosystem continued to expand. The 106 companies generated ₹4.89 Lakh Cr in operating revenue in FY26, a sharp 33.17% increase from ₹3.67 Lakh Cr in FY25. Zion Suzuki: Good in the air, decent distribution and made three important stops to deny Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Josko Gvardiol with a brilliant, fingertip save. 7

Will a macaque eat a grape sitting on a pile of poo? A study on germaphobia
In the very early days of COVID-19, millions who'd rarely thought twice about germ avoidance became germophobes.
Some folks wiped down groceries before stuffing them into the refrigerator. Others let mail quarantine outside for days lest it harbor stray viruses. With the hindsight that SARS-CoV-2 spread primarily through the air, these sorts of precautions seem extreme. But in the moment, they were perhaps reasonable ways of avoiding an unknown pathogen.
Around this same time, a different virus hit a macaque sanctuary in Texas. New research suggests the monkeys responded in similar ways as humans did to COVID-19 — by being extra germophobic.
Humans are far from the only animals to avoid possible sources of disease. Scientists have found that critters as diverse as monkeys and nematodes (aka roundworms) can sense and steer clear of feces, for instance, which can harbor harmful bacteria.
"Something that has been less studied is the question of how flexible this avoidance is," says Stephan Kaufhold, a cognitive scientist at UC San Diego. He wanted to see if experiencing an outbreak could make individual monkeys even more wary of picking up pathogens.
The outbreak in the Texas sanctuary, home to over 100 macaques, offered Kaufhold and his colleagues an opportunity to put that question to the test.
Grape expectations
In 2020, macaques in an enclosure at the sanctuary started getting sick with an HIV-like virus called SRV.
Once a monkey gets infected through bodily fluids, the disease "can take a rapid progression, where about three to four weeks after you initially get infected, you might die," says Kaufhold. Many monkeys died, while others developed chronic immunodeficiency.
Sanctuary staff quickly started separating monkeys quickly, ultimately creating two groups — those who'd experienced the virus, either by getting sick themselves or witnessing others get sick, and those who hadn't experienced the outbreak.
To see if those different histories made the monkeys more germophobic, the researchers presented individuals with two tasty treats — grapes.
"They get a fantastic diet at the sanctuary, but not grapes every day, so grapes were definitely a treat," says Kaufhold.
One red grape was presented on a non-descript, clean-looking piece of wood. The other was on top of macaque poop, encased in epoxy. "Basically not to make the animals eat off actual feces," says Kaufhold. "It did look quite gross, feces with a glossy wet look. Definitely worked also in triggering disgust in humans."
From 2022 to 2024, the researchers presented monkeys with this choice in nearly 200 trials. Among monkeys who didn't experience the outbreak, 79% ate the poop-plated grape. But only 47% of the outbreak veterans ate it, researchers report in the journal Royal Society Open Science.
Essentially, those who'd been oblivious to the outbreak were more likely to throw caution to the wind and eat the poop-plated grape than those who'd lived through it.
"I was surprised," says Kaufhold. "I think it's pretty clear evidence that something is going on." Kaufhold thinks that something might be a heightened sensitivity to disgust.
"If you think about disgust, the evolutionary origins most likely are to try to protect the body from contamination because there are pathogens and parasites that we ideally would want to avoid," he says. Becoming more easily disgusted after a devastating outbreak could pay off if it means avoiding infection, of whatever cause.
Of course, scientists can't know whether macaques are actually experiencing disgust. "But the possibility that things like disgust are influencing the behavior of other species, and especially species like primates, it's definitely a possibility worth considering," says Andrew MacIntosh, a biologist at the Wilder Institute who wasn't involved in the study but has done similar experiments with macaques.
"It seems plausible that past exposure to outbreaks could make individuals more cautious or risk averse," he says, but he thinks more evidence is needed to show that. For example, the experiment was carried out several years after the outbreak, enough time for other factors to influence these behaviors, he says.
MacIntosh also points out that the fecal avoidance experiment bears little connection to how the initial outbreak spread, through bodily fluids transmitted through scratches or bites. "The mode of transmission of that virus has really nothing to do with fecal contamination," he says.
Kaufhold doesn't think that's a problem.
"We're not claiming that macaques had any sort of understanding of the mechanism of viruses, it just seems to be an increased caution," he says. People didn't initially know how SARS-CoV-2 spread either, he says, but many went to great lengths to avoid infection. Those impulses may have been shaped not by paranoia, but by evolution, as a way of staving off sickness in an uncertain world.

In the world of hi-fi, there’s “high end,” and then there’s Goldmund. Since 1978, the Swiss manufacturer has produced exquisitely designed, astonishingly high-performance and staggeringly expensive audio equipment. As it nears half a century of proudly uncompromised engineering, its determination to position its products as credible alternatives to jewellery, art, or other pricey indulgences for the superrich shows no sign of abating—quite the opposite.
I was recently invited to Goldmund's headquarters in Geneva, Switzerland, to experience the new Mimesis Statement, the company’s flagship analog preamplifier. Goldmund's HQ, incidentally, features the sort of high ceilings, generous use of concrete and glass, and fanatical tidiness that puts me in mind of a Bond villain who's decided to devote their time to audio gratification rather than global tyranny.
In a traditional stereo chain, a preamplifier takes the low-level signals from your source gear, handles volume and input selection, and feeds that clean signal to a power amp to drive your speakers. Most people use an integrated amplifier, one that combines pre-amplification and power amplification in the same box.
Those who want to take things to the next level often separate pre-amplification and power amplification into two boxes—to keep the precious audio signal away from any electrical activity that might compromise its integrity. Goldmund, naturally, is convinced that a preamplifier alone needs to occupy three separate boxes.
The first box, the one with the buttons, dials, and display, houses the pre-amplification electronics. It’s where your source equipment—turntable, network streamer, whatever you fancy—connects using the generous selection of balanced and unbalanced inputs. The other two boxes are external power supplies serving the left and right channels of your stereo signal.
Goldmund reckons this radical separation, along with painstaking internal architecture featuring complete symmetry, voltage regulation stages, and optimized heat dissipation, guarantees signal integrity and utterly consistent operating conditions in all circumstances.
It’s apparently not enough to make a preamplifier with such a low total harmonic distortion figure (0.0002 percent) that it’s extremely difficult to measure in the first place. No, it has to be housed in three chassis with mirrored-glass displays, metal-coated controls, and Goldmund’s signature slender gold-line design flourish to confirm its identity.
In the US, the Goldmund Mimesis Statement analog preamplifier costs $240,000. No, I didn't accidentally add a few zeros. We’re already into “fairly fancy European sports car” territory here, but a preamplifier by itself doesn’t constitute an audio system. For the Mimesis Statement to do its thing, it needs a music input signal, which it will output to a power amplifier. From there, it goes to a pair of speakers.
Thankfully, Goldmund offers plenty of options. During my listen to the Mimesis Statement, it is connected to the company’s Eidos network streamer (yours for $27,000) at one end and a pair of Thelos 9800 power amplifiers (nearly 800 pounds per amplifier, 1,560 watts per channel, an imposing aesthetic, and $500,000 each) at the other. The amplified signal then moves to a pair of Theia Passive four-way floor-standing loudspeakers ($215,000 for two). That’s a total system price of $1,482,000—not so much “sports car” as “very nice apartment, probably with a balcony.” And I haven’t even added in the price of cables.
What does all that money buy you? Well, it most certainly buys a distinctive industrial design language, attention to detail and precision where fit and finish is concerned that’s beyond OCD, hand-soldered circuit boards, military-grade alloys crafted using established Swiss watchmaking techniques, and the sort of overall physical presence that’s more commonly associated with the stuff they build at NASA.
But can a stereo system possibly be worth $1.5 million? The answer has to be “no.” I’ve been a part of the audio equipment appraisal process for over two decades, and I know full well that the law of diminishing returns kicks in long before you’ve spent six figures, let alone seven. But Goldmund isn’t selling you a hi-fi any more than Rolex is selling you a wristwatch—it’s selling you an unmistakable symbol of status, wealth, and success. It’s selling you exclusivity. It’s selling you what it sincerely believes is the pinnacle of artisanal engineering.
And it’s also selling you a serving of detailed, tremendously insightful, and eloquently communicative sound. I am not a prospective Goldmund customer, but if I had the disposable income, I really think I might be.

Duelling petitions highlight rift over paroled murderer at McGill law school
New letter argues university failed to make sure students are safe
Students at McGill University's law faculty remain divided over the presence of a convicted murderer in the classroom, with a new counter-petition outlining why some students feel unsafe and don't want him in their presence.
The anonymous open letter, dated Oct. 19 and put forward by a group of students, accuses the university of failing in its duty to protect female students.
It outlines concerns about Jeffrey George Ewert, who was convicted of second-degree murder and attempted murder for attacks against two women in B.C. in 1984.
The authors argue that attempting to rehabilitate a convicted murderer without adequate safety frameworks goes against the university's core values and breaches its duty of care to the student body.
"McGill’s failure to do so unduly and disproportionately harms the young women of our community," the document reads.
The students want the university to form a committee that would include both students and experts on the rehabilitation of violent offenders in order to develop guidelines for next steps.
"Any decision to resume Ewert's in-person studies must be made only after the committee has developed this framework," the letter goes on to say.
The authors say they chose to withhold their names because signing the document raises safety concerns for them.
Earlier petition calls for Ewert's return to university
Ewert is serving a life sentence and was granted day parole in 2025.
He sexually assaulted and killed one woman and, less than six weeks later, beat and choked a 15-year-old so severely that she was paralyzed and disabled for life, according to a summary of his case in his parole board file.
While various clinical assessments ranked Ewert’s risk of reoffending as moderate to high, official parole documents say with close supervision at a halfway house and clinical follow-up, that risk “seems to fall more into the moderate risk category.” He has not been on campus since early October.
The letter follows an earlier petition arguing Ewert should be allowed to return to university.
That document argues the exclusion undermines Ewert's access to education and rehabilitation as an Indigenous man and a survivor of the Sixties Scoop.
Annica Dickens, one of the authors of the petition and a third-year law student, said she was troubled that Ewert was removed from campus without being given the chance to address the concerns first.
"People cannot meaningfully rebuild their lives if their opportunities can be withdrawn so readily," said Dickens in an email.
Meanwhile, a second letter supporting Ewert, addressed to the university's leadership, has been signed by hundreds of academics, students and citizens.
It reiterates many of the concerns raised by Dickens and asks that the university restore Ewert's full access to the Faculty of Law and "review how decisions concerning Indigenous, racialized and formerly incarcerated students are made."
Security of students 'paramount,' McGill says
McGill University did not provide an update on Ewert's status, or answer questions about allegations raised in the counter-petition.
A spokesperson told CBC News that the "safety and security of our students is paramount. Full stop."
Citing privacy laws, the university declined to comment on the specific case, but said "McGill would act quickly and decisively should concerning information be brought forward about a student’s background or behaviour on campus."
The controversy has sparked debate within the broader legal community in Canada.
In an op-ed in the Montreal Gazette, one lawyer wrote there is a "bitter irony in asking women entering a profession that demands confidence, advocacy and strength to share their education with a man whose own file describes a need to dominate and control women."
Lisa Kerr, an associate professor and director of the Criminal Law Group at Queen's University, cautioned that "we should be very hesitant about any measures that could result in the exclusion of people with criminal records from accessing education.
"Canada's incarcerated population is in desperate need of education and job training," she wrote in an email to CBC.
"We want people with criminal records and experiences of incarceration to access education and gain the skills for successful reintegration."
Lisa Kerr is an associate professor and director of the Criminal Law Group at Queen's University. (Queen's University)
CBC Montreal contacted other law faculties in the province, including Université de Sherbrooke, Université Laval, Université du Québec à Montréal and Université de Montréal, to ask what measures they have in place to manage or mitigate risks when admitting students with past violent criminal convictions.
All four universities said they are not permitted to ask applicants about their criminal history.
“This violates the Charter of Rights and Freedoms,” said Geneviève O’Meara, a spokesperson at Université de Montréal.
Simon La Terreur, a spokesperson at Université Laval, said the university does not intend "to take the place of the competent authorities in assessing the risk a person may pose for the purposes of parole, but the safety of our university community remains a priority nonetheless."

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected
- Published
A Kenyan businessman was able to spend time in one of the regions worst-affected by Ebola, then travel to two more countries before his illness was identified.
The 40-year-old - who was only diagnosed with the deadly infectious disease after arriving seriously ill at a Nairobi hospital - became Kenya's first confirmed case. He died two days later on 5 October.
That his infection went undetected at multiple health facilities in the Democratic Republic of Congo and two airport health screenings in Uganda and Kenya has raised serious questions about these nations' biosecurity during a significant outbreak.
More than 4,000 people have died from Ebola in DR Congo this year, in what is the second most deadly known outbreak to date.
Africa CDC, the continent's leading public health agency, has now reconstructed the Kenyan patient's movements across nearly six weeks, revealing several missed opportunities to detect his infection and potentially preventing dozens of people from coming into contact with the deadly virus.
DR Congo
The account, presented by the agency's emergency director, Dr Wessam Mankoula, provides the clearest picture yet of how the businessman travelled thousands of kilometres while growing increasingly unwell.
The man, whose identity has not been made public, had lived in DR Congo for seven years and had travelled across three of its provinces on business.
Exactly when or where he contracted Ebola remains unclear - but it was present in all three provinces he went through by early October, according to the World Health Organization (WHO).
The man had spent much of late August and early September in the province of Bas-Uélé, visiting towns including Buta, Aketi and Likati.
The WHO confirmed an Ebola case in Buta in August, prior to his visit, though there is no evidence he contracted the virus there.
His symptoms first emerged around 15 September. He was given antibiotics and sent home.
Two days later, he was admitted to the Tongo Etandi Health Centre in Bondo, where he remained until 19 September.
Despite suffering from fever and a rash, he was diagnosed with a skin infection.
Without an Ebola test being taken at any point during his travels, it is hard to say exactly when he contracted the virus. Those symptoms are consistent with the early stages of the disease, but also other infections common to the region, such as malaria.
On 20 September, he flew to Kisangani, a city with a population of about 1.5 million people on the Congo River, where he spent more than 10 days seeking medical care.
We do not know which hospitals or clinics treated him there, nor what medications they gave him. Kisangani is the capital of Tshopo province which has only recorded 51 Ebola cases.
- What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult? 
  - Published15 September
Uganda
However, on 1 October, more than two weeks after first becoming ill, the businessman boarded another domestic flight to Beni, before continuing his journey to Kasindi, a busy border town.
Both Beni and Kasindi are in North Kivu, which has recorded 1,755 Ebola infections and more than 1,000 deaths, making it one of the Congolese provinces worst-hit by the disease.
But he did not stay there long, crossing into Uganda later that day.
Uganda imposed restrictions on movement across its border with DR Congo shortly after the outbreak began in May.
The country has experience containing several Ebola outbreaks, including through surveillance, contact tracing and the isolation of suspected cases. It has had some cases this year - mostly among people travelling from DR Congo - but was declared free of the disease in August.
But the border between the two nations stretches for hundreds of kilometres through remote terrain, making it difficult to police.
It remains unclear whether the businessman passed through an official health checkpoint when he crossed the border.
Once he had, he travelled by road to the capital, Kampala, and then Entebbe International Airport, where he boarded a flight to Nairobi on 3 October.
Ugandan officials said his temperature was normal when he passed through airport screening. Health experts say his case highlights the limitations of relying on temperature checks and self-declarations.
Mankoula said investigators were examining whether the man's medication could have suppressed his temperature. He may have also not had a fever when he passed through the checks.
Kenya
Similarly, he was not flagged as a suspected Ebola patient when he reached Nairobi's Jomo Kenyatta International Airport, where a relative collected him and drove him directly to Nairobi Hospital, a private medical facility in the Kenyan capital.
By then, he was suffering from fever, chills, muscle pain, a sore throat and bleeding.
Laboratory tests confirmed that he had contracted the Bundibugyo species of Ebola - the same one responsible for the outbreak in DR Congo.
He was placed in isolation while his condition deteriorated. He died on 5 October and was buried the following day under strict infection-control measures.
The Kenyan government says it has now identified 66 people who may have been in contact with him after he arrived there. The WHO says the number is likely to rise as contact-tracing in Uganda and DR Congo continues.
The quarantine arrangements have also raised concerns among some healthcare workers, amid questions about how the patient was handled at Nairobi Hospital.
Kenya's health ministry says more than 652,000 travellers have been screened and nearly 5,000 healthcare workers trained to deal with Ebola, with five facilities designated to handle cases.
Ebola spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person who has developed symptoms, or through contaminated materials.
Its incubation period ranges from two to 21 days, meaning someone exposed to the virus may not become ill until several weeks later.
CDC advice
Mankoula urged travellers experiencing symptoms of Ebola to report them, saying early medical attention could improve their chances of survival.
"When you reveal any Ebola-related symptoms early, you're not only preventing the virus spreading to other countries but you're also protecting yourself first," he said.
The WHO has warned that stigma surrounding Ebola could discourage people from reporting symptoms or seeking medical care, potentially allowing the virus to spread undetected.
The agency says it is stepping up efforts to encourage this by reducing fear and misinformation about the disease - something that is a big problem in DR Congo, where some health workers have been attacked by people who claim Ebola doesn't exist.
