Why your Ring camera is still useful without a subscription
Patrolling your porch or pets doesn’t require a monthly fee.
Beyond serving as a fully functional doorbells, the Ring Camera lineup still offers plenty of solid use cases. Unfortunately, like most smart gadgets, whether fitness trackers or bird feeders, you'll need a monthly subscription to unlock all of its features.
With three tiers to choose from, starting at $4.99/month, keeping your home fully secure comes at an added cost that might put you off. On the bright side, you can get by without a subscription, unless you need to access saved footage for future reference. Ring cameras can still operate as a live intercom that'll come in handy whether you're home or on the go.
The company has garnered some bad press over the last year, but its security cameras still provide protection and some peace of mind for owners, with or without the monthly fee.
It's best for parents, pets and packages
The Two-Way Talk and Live Feed features help in many scenarios. Even when you're home and just waiting on someone, you can see exactly who's at the door and talk to them through the app before getting up to answer it.
Personally, whether dealing with weak water pressure or other household issues, there've been plenty of times when a maintenance technician waited outside my door and rang the bell, letting me speak with them through the Ring app so I could give an ETA for when I'd be back home. If you're a parent who wants to keep an eye on your young ones from another room, the free tier is a great choice.
Similarly, indoor Ring cameras do the trick for pet owners without a subscription. Using your phone, you can keep an eye on them when you're out for the day or ask "who's a good dog?" with Two-Way Talk. The association between pets and Ring cameras is a touchy subject, however.
If you travel often and want to make sure there's no funny business in or outside the house, or an eye on incoming packages, the free plan is a great choice. On the contrary, with porch pirates on the rise, subscribing to one of Ring's plans makes sense if you've had items stolen and want access to the footage.
What are some problems with Ring?
While they have benefits, Ring cameras also come with a fair share of privacy concerns, which both owners and disavowers have raised for years.
For starters, the Familiar Faces feature that debuted last year, which uses AI to recognize which friend, neighbor or relative is at your door, led to a recent lawsuit that suggested Ring and Amazon were collecting facial recognition information unbeknownst to plenty of people who walked by a Ring camera.
This suit follows widespread backlash of this year's Super Bowl commercial, which framed the AI-assisted Search Party feature as a way to find lost dogs. Of course, no one is complaining about seeking out missing pets, but people are worried about the mass surveillance.
The lawsuit and commercials came months after Ring partnered with Flock Safety in 2025, originally permitting law enforcement to request footage from Ring owners. Following widespread reactions to the pet-focused commercial, that deal was dismantled days after the Super Bowl.
In an effort to ward off negative reactions, the Amazon-owned company's recent TAKE software update (Throw Away the Key Encryption) asserts that "Ring videos are protected with unique, rotating encryption keys," putting people in full control of who can access footage. Ring likens it to a pair of house keys, as only the owner can decide who gets a spare.

Celebrity shark returns to South Korea canal after failed rescue
- Published
A famed dusky shark in South Korea has returned to the canal where she had been stuck for a month, just one day after authorities said they had successfully guided her out, local media report.
The shark, nicknamed Bukangi, became an unlikely sensation after she was spotted lingering in a canal in the south-eastern port city of Busan last month.
South Korea's oceans ministry said on Wednesday evening they had led Bukangi out of the canal into an open harbour - but reports later said the shark had swum back to the mouth of the canal, having apparently broken through a barrier installed by authorities.
Another operation to relocate Bukangi has been scheduled for Thursday.
It is thought that Bukangi might have been drawn to the canal by unusually warm waters and plenty of fish. With the sea getting warmer each year, experts say Busan may play host to more sharks in the future.
In recent weeks, more than 1.6 million visitors have descended upon a park in Busan to catch a glimpse of Bukangi, named after the canal in which she was spotted.
Her popularity gave a welcome boost to Busan's tourism, and the city has embraced her as an unofficial mascot.
But authorities were also concerned about Bukangi's well-being as she appeared to be injured and was not eating. There were concerns that she would be further weakened by falling water temperatures.
In a livestreamed operation on Wednesday, rescue workers took more than eight hours to delicately guide the three-metre-long (10ft) shark with a net towards open water in a harbour.
Hundreds of adoring fans cheered and waved goodbye to their shark, unaware that she would still be lingering in the canal by the next day.
Before Wednesday's operation, there had been two earlier failed attempts to guide Bukangi out of the canal with nets.

Here's how to test a CR2032 battery to see if it's good
You won't need expensive equipment or invest much time.
Your car key fob suddenly needs several presses to unlock the door. Your AirTag stops responding when you try to locate it. Before blaming either gadget, it's worth checking the battery inside. One common type is the CR2032, a 3V lithium coin cell also used in Samsung's SmartTag2 and some smart home sensors. Depending on the device and how often it's used, one can last way over a year.
A multimeter can help you check the battery's voltage, and it's a good addition to your toolbox if you don't already own one. There are cheaper ways to check, too, but don't mistake a voltage reading for a complete picture of battery health.
How to test a CR2032 battery with a multimeter
Begin by checking the battery itself. If you spot crusty residue, rust-colored patches, swelling or leakage, skip the test and replace it. Have a look at the device's contacts too, since corrosion there can cause trouble even with a good battery.
Remove the CR2032 and set your digital multimeter to DC voltage (V with a solid line over a dashed line). Plug the black lead into COM and the red lead into the V or VΩ port. If your meter doesn't automatically select a range, set it above 3V, typically 20V.
Hold the battery by its edges over a nonconductive surface. Touch the red probe to the broad face marked with a plus sign (+) and the black probe to the center of the smaller negative face underneath. Keep the probe tips from touching each other or bridging the battery's terminals. A negative reading simply means you've reversed the probes.
A fresh CR2032 typically reads around 3V, while a reading closer to 2.5V is a good reason to bring in a replacement. But don't give that 3V reading too much credit though. A multimeter draws almost no current, so a battery might look fine on the display but struggle when your key fob or tracker actually needs power. There's no single pass-or-fail reading for every device. If it keeps acting up, try a fresh CR2032 unit before assuming the device is faulty.
No multimeter? Here's how to check your AirTag or key fob battery
A dedicated coin-cell tester is another option. Some cost around $10, although certain models only measure voltage rather than how the battery performs under load. Basic multimeters can cost less than $20 and are good for checking other batteries or troubleshooting low-voltage electronics. Still, buying either just to diagnose one suspect $3 battery is a harder sell.
There's also the LED trick, assuming you have one lying around. A small red or yellow LED is a better choice than a blue or white one because it generally needs less voltage to light up. Touch its longer leg to the CR2032's positive side and the shorter leg to the negative side. If it lights up, the battery can supply some current. That's about all it proves. The LED won't tell you how much life is left, and one that stays dark doesn't necessarily mean the battery is dead.
AirTag owners can check Find My before opening anything. Select Items inside the app and tap your AirTag. If it says "Low Battery," or shows a depleted battery icon, skip the testing and replace the CR2032. Some CR2032 batteries have bitterant coatings that may prevent proper contact, even when they're brand new. Apple recommends packaging marked "Compatible with Apple AirTag" when replacing an AirTag battery, and says an AirTag's battery lasts more than a year, while Samsung rates the SmartTag2 for up to 500 days in normal mode.
After removing a CR2032, keep it out of children's reach and tape its terminals before taking them to a battery collection facility. If one is swallowed, seek emergency medical care immediately, as serious internal injuries can occur in as little as two hours.

The Japanese government highlighted the urgent need to fundamentally strengthen the country’s energy supply-and-demand structure to prepare for future emergencies in its fiscal 2025 white paper on energy, adopted at a Cabinet meeting on Friday.
The white paper noted that, in response to the deterioration in the Middle East situation, Japan was the first in the world to decide to release its petroleum reserves, contributing to stable energy supplies both domestically and internationally.
The government also said in the white paper that options for crude oil procurement had narrowed and that oil dependence on the Middle East had been rising again in recent years on the back of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and economic growth in Asian oil-producing countries.
With supply imbalances also having emerged for petroleum products, Japan’s energy supply-and-demand structure was shown once again to be vulnerable, it said.
Elsewhere in the white paper, the government included a plan to strengthen efforts to secure stable fossil fuel supplies while accelerating the use of nuclear power and domestic renewable energy in order to fundamentally strengthen Japan’s energy supply-and-demand structure.
The energy white paper is usually adopted by the Cabinet around June each year, but its compilation was delayed this year due to the deterioration in the Middle East situation.

Japan is known for world-class events - but the Asian Games were chaotic
- Published
From the Olympics to Tokyo's annual video game convention, Japan has a strong track record of hosting major international events. But this year's Asian Games in Nagoya and the wider Aichi Prefecture were marred by problems.
There were diplomatic blunders, transport errors and accommodation chaos. In comment fields online, some branded it the "worst Games in history" and urged a "full investigation".
Prof Kozo Tomiyama, who studies major sporting events at Osaka University, believes organisers were unable to handle the unexpected.
"If these problems damage international confidence in Japan's ability to operate sporting events, they could also affect Japan's ability to attract international competitions in the future," he warned.
The deputy director general of the Games, Takaaki Omi, admitted organisers had faced a range of unforeseen issues, but insisted they took on feedback and made improvements.
String of incidents
Before the tournament had even begun, participants were complaining about too few rooms and poor-quality accommodation.
Organisers had decided to forgo building a traditional athletes' village to cut costs, and were instead housing participants in hotels and container-style units across Nagoya. A top Korean basketball official said tall athletes housed in the containers were struggling to "stretch their legs out on the beds".
Last-minute additions to the total number of participants strained the city's capacity so much that an Italian cruise ship with 1,500 cabins was used to fill the gap.
The organising committee had initially arranged accommodation for up to 15,000 delegation members "in accordance with the host city contract", Omi told the BBC. But as other sports were added, the number grew by 2,000 to a total of 17,000.
Organisers initially claimed there was "simply nowhere" to put up the late influx and told them to make their own arrangements - before backpedalling and releasing a joint statement with the Olympic Council of Asia promising that all "17,000-plus" guests would get "Games-appropriate accommodation".
This was just the start of the problems.
Over the course of the Games, athletes were bussed to the wrong venues and the North Korean anthem was played for the South Korean men's hockey team. During the men's football gold medal ceremony, the South Korean flag was not raised properly. Taiwan's sports minister found himself temporarily barred from a flag-raising event.
In the last days of the Games, volunteers received an email inviting them to the closing ceremony free of charge. But later an organiser said the decision to distribute free tickets was still under review and had not been approved.
Omi admitted the string of incidents at the event - which was bigger than the Paris Olympics by number of participants - had caused significant inconvenience for some delegations.
"Hosting and managing an event of this scale was a major challenge for us, and each day involved addressing a range of unexpected issues and challenges," he said.
"During the Games, we also listened carefully to feedback from the athletes who were actually using the facilities and responded promptly with necessary improvements and measures."
'Overwhelmingly cheaper'
As soon as these issues began to surface, local media pointed fingers at the company managing venue operations: the Japanese subsidiary of France's GL Events.
GL Events had won the 63bn yen (£306m; $405m) contract over Dentsu Group, an advertising giant with a long history of successfully running sporting events in Japan that had been sidelined after a criminal bid-rigging conviction.
A source told Kyodo news agency that GL Events was "overwhelmingly cheaper" than alternative providers.
Last week the Tokyo Shimbun newspaper accused the firm of aggressively cutting corners on hiring, resulting in a shortage of experienced staff capable of managing the issues which arose. The personnel that were recruited were not properly trained, the newspaper alleged.
But organiser Takaaki Omi stressed that GL Events "has experience in international sporting events, including the Paris Olympic Games".
"We believe the necessary competition environment was in place by the start of competition, including thorough discussions and co-ordination with GL Events," he told the BBC.
Prof Tomiyama said he didn't think it was right to "simply conclude that GL events did not have sufficient experience with international competitions". He believes the issue stemmed from the "extremely broad" scope of responsibility they were given.
"Also, because this was a negotiated contract rather than a competitive tender, it's important to examine the criteria organisers used to assess the contractor's capabilities, as well as how they supervised the contractor after the contract was awarded," Tomiyama added.
GL Events did not respond to repeated BBC requests for comment.
Hopes for the future
Watching organisers play whack-a-mole as they rushed to address each new concern which popped up throughout the Games felt deeply out of line with what the world has come to expect from a major Japanese event.
It's far from the "omotenashi" spirit - Japan's whole-hearted hospitality that is almost an art form - they might have wanted to showcase.
Officials ended up having to send a formal apology to South Korea for the series of mishaps affecting that particular delegation.
But Olympic Council of Asia director general Husain al-Musallam was keen to highlight the 54 new world records achieved at the Games - in swimming, weightlifting, and shooting - as proof they were a hit.
"This achievement does not come without the best environment that the organising committee created for the athletes," he said. "The athletes cannot perform if they don't sleep good, the athletes cannot perform if they don't have good transportation."
While the Games may be over, the problems aren't.
Glitches have continued at the ongoing Para Games, where the wrong national anthems were played at three events. Nagoya Mayor Ichiro Hirosawa, who is also deputy head of the Games organising committee, called it "unacceptable" and offered his apologies.
Prof Tomiyama hopes organisers will take lessons from the past few weeks to deliver higher-quality sporting events in the future.

Sagawa Express has announced that up to about 53.23 million sets of personal information may have been compromised due to unauthorized access.
The unauthorized access occurred on its delivery tracking service, according to the transport company’s announcement on Sept. 30.
The affected data includes the names, addresses, and phone numbers of senders and recipients listed on shipping labels from June 21 to Sept. 30, as well as the addresses and phone numbers of corporate customers.
Sagawa Express said that the number of potentially compromised personal information sets does not necessarily reflect the number of affected customers, as there are many overlaps among the senders and recipients listed on the shipping labels.
The company has resumed the delivery tracking service, which it had halted since the unauthorized access. Some other services will remain suspended for the time being.

Iron Man
As everyone knows, Iron Man became the MVP at the end of the final Avengers movie, and he can pretty much repeat the history here in the Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. As an aerial Duelist, Iron Man gets a natural advantage and can only concentrate on nuking Thanos with his repulsor blasts and unibeam.
In case you didn’t know, his missiles received auto-tracking capabilities in Season 10.5 for the first time. So, players can keep sending out missiles in addition to his primary attacks. As Iron Man, your regular drill would be entering Armor Overdrive mode and keeping fire on Thanos to quickly charge your ultimate. Then send out the Invincible Pulse Cannon in Thanos’ way before he moves.
Moon Knight
The swarm of Chitauri, Chitauri Gorillas, and other minions on the battlefield are definitely annoying. But you can take advantage of this opportunity by picking Moon Knight in Marvel Rivals. The large number of enemies makes life easier for Moon Knight, as his Crescent Darts can easily ricochet between foes without any disturbance.
So, keep placing your Ankhs and spam your Crescent Darts to continuously attack Thanos and his mighty monstrous army at the same time. Since there isn’t any high ground here, it is a bit difficult to survive as Moon Knight. So, make sure to stay near healers or ask a friend to play a healer, if you can.
Scarlet Witch
Scarlet Witch, aka Wanda Maximoff, was a great pick for both Avengers: Age of Ultron PvE mode and Avengers: Infinity War PvP mode in Marvel Rivals. And her winning streak continues in Avengers: Endgame PvE mode.
Chaos Control, Scarlet Hex, Chthonian Burst, Sorcerer Supreme, etc., basically all the abilities in Wanda’s kit are deadly and are perfect for wiping out Chitauri squads and sucking Thanos’ life force. Although it is hard to rely only on Mystic Projection, you can surive for a long time on the battle arena if you play your cards right.
The Hood
It’s hard to survive as a Duelist or Strategist in the Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. So, the natural option is to pick a Vanguard who can withstand longer. Out of all the Vanguards in the game, The Hood remains the only solid pick for the new PvE mode. While most of the Vanguards are melee-focused, Marvel Rivals’ The Hood can obliterate with his accursed dual pistols.
Similar to how you play as The Hood in other game modes, keep dealing damage with his pistol to build up the Demonic Energy. Enter the Half-Demon state to get movement and attack boost which results in increased damage. Finally, you can easily hit your shots during The Hood’s Demon of the End ultimate ability, thanks to Thanos’ massive hitbox.
Ultron
The second-best Strategist after Jubilee in Avengers: Endgame mode is Ultron in Marvel Rivals. Ultron has all the same perks as an aerial Duelist. In addition, he can easily manage healing as he gets a better view of the battle from the top.
As Ultron, keep shifting your drones between the heroes in need of health and keep hitting Thanos with the Encephalo-Ray. Then make sure to use the Rage of Ultron ultimate ability When Thanos orders the spaceships to strike as well as when he uses the Infinity Stones to rescue the injured heroes.
Jeff the Land Shark
Last but not least, Jeff the Land Shark is one of the best characters for Marvel Rivals Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. His Joyful Splash has a great range, so you can heal your allies while also damaging the minions at the same time. Use Hide and Seek ability whenever you need to escape and you can use your Healing Bubbles to heal yourself and remain alive on the battlefield.
While you cannot use It’s Jeff, one of the best ultimate abilities in Marvel Rivals, to swallow Thanos, it is still good enough. The created healing water zone is helpful in healing allies and you can instead focus on swalling the members of Thanos army.
And these are our top 10 picks for the best heroes/characters for the ongoing Marvel Rivals Avengers: Endgame PvE mode. It is very easy to defeat Thanos by picking any one of the characters we have listed here.
That said, if you feel like any other hero deserves a spot on our list, let us know in the comments below.

Reduction in Indonesia gas supply amounts to less than 2% of Singapore’s total daily demand: EMA
Singapore's Energy Market Authority also said that it had contingency plans in place to deal with such reductions.
SINGAPORE: Indonesia’s reduction in gas exports to Singapore on Saturday (Oct 24) amounts to less than 2 per cent of the country’s total daily gas demand, said the Energy Market Authority (EMA).
In response to media queries, an EMA spokesperson said the total reduction of 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day amounts to 17 British thermal units per day (bbtud) over a period of 18 days.
"This is less than 2 per cent of our total daily gas demand of more than 1,000 bbtud," it said, adding that it understands that importers will pursue all relevant recourse in their contracts for the gas supply disruption, said EMA.
EMA also said that it had contingency plans in place to deal with such reductions.
It pointed out that in recent months, there were reductions ranging from 20 bbtud to 100 bbtud due to planned or urgent maintenance.
"These reductions were replaced with other gas sources without incident. Singapore GasCo is operationally ready to import more LNG at any time," it said.
"Besides Indonesia, Singapore imports natural gas from other sources around the world," it added.
"Power generation companies are further required to maintain sufficient fuel reserves for power generation, including diesel reserves. We therefore have sufficient energy supplies to meet our national demands," said EMA.
In response to CNA queries, gas importer Gas Supply, which sources natural gas from Indonesia, said its deliveries to customers had been affected by temporary reductions in supply from its upstream supplier in the country.
A spokesperson said: "We have been in direct communication with customers who are impacted and appreciate their patience and understanding during this period."
The company added that it was continuing to engage closely with its upstream supplier to manage the situation.
The statement did not specify how many customers were affected or how long the supply reductions were expected to last.
Indonesia began reducing natural gas exports to Singapore, in order to divert more supplies to domestic electricity needs, the country’s upstream oil and gas regulator SKK Migas said in response to CNA’s queries.
The diversion involves 31 million standard cubic feet of gas a day, comprising 15 million from Natuna and 16 million from Sumatra.
GAS SUPPLY DIVERSION
SKK Migas had said the gas from Natuna was being diverted to PLN Batam through the WNTS–Pulau Pemping–Batam pipeline. Supplies from Sumatra were being redirected through the TGI pipeline to meet electricity needs in Batam, Bintan and Sumatra.
The regulator said the move was intended to "safeguard the reliability of domestic gas supplies for electricity generation".
It cited Article 8, Paragraph 1 of Indonesia’s Oil and Gas Law as the basis for prioritising the use of natural gas for domestic needs, and said it would monitor developments daily.
Natural gas is used to generate about 95 per cent of Singapore's electricity.
CNA has also sent queries to Indonesia’s presidential palace but has yet to receive a response.
The move comes days after Energy and an Indonesian minister warned that Jakarta could review energy exports to countries that did not show it sufficient respect. SKK Migas’ response did not link the diversion to those remarks.
Singapore imports natural gas through pipelines from Indonesia and Malaysia, as well as liquefied natural gas (LNG) shipped in from international suppliers.
In 2025, piped natural gas accounted for 43 per cent of Singapore's total gas imports, while LNG made up the remaining 57 per cent.

PATNA: In a major political crackdown, the ruling Janata Dal (United) on Saturday expelled sitting Mokama MLA Anant Kumar Singh and his spouse, former MLA Neelam Devi, from the party for a period of six years.

Ukraine’s military has a “stable connection to Starlink”, the Ukrainian government has said, 10 days after its ability to use the satellite communications system was suddenly restricted.
The Starlink satellite terminals, which are produced by Elon Musk’s SpaceX but managed by the US government, are a key component of Ukraine’s military operations. Sudden speed restrictions on the terminals, which capped operations at speeds of 160km/h (99mph), led to the failure of several Ukrainian combat missions earlier this month.
The military’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones was hampered and some Ukrainian operations to strike behind enemy frontlines were cancelled. Russia was able to launch ballistic missiles at Ukraine without any advance warning from the US.
The speed restrictions coincided with the announcement by Donald Trump of a US deal to buy Russian diesel, although the US president initially denied that his administration was behind the decision to cut intelligence sharing with Ukraine.
“I don’t know if it was anybody, but it wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon,” Trump said, referring to Musk, SpaceX’s chief executive.
However, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, appeared to throw suspicion on Musk when he defended Trump last Wednesday. “The president has nothing to do with the decisions that are made by Starlink and Starshield and by Mr Musk,” Rubio said. “That’s a private company. The president doesn’t run that company and can’t direct that company to do anything.”
Musk was quick to blame the limits on Starshield on the Trump administration, writing on X last week that the systems were “owned and controlled by the US government”. “Any limits on speed or usage are decided by the US military and ultimately Potus [president of the United States],” he wrote.
The US vice-president, JD Vance, backed Musk on Thursday, saying the billionaire “doesn’t want to get in the middle of what is a war between two state actors without the United States government effectively directing him on what to do”.
Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, blamed both parties: “It was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed … And technically, SpaceX did it.”
There were no similar restrictions on Starshield terminals in EU countries and that they applied only to Ukraine, he added. “In other words, this is a planned operation.”
He said the decision would “bring a lot of human losses … of course people would die”.
Announcing the restoration of the system on Saturday in a diplomatic video address on the Telegram app, Zelenskyy expressed his gratitude to his US allies, including Trump and the US state department, for resolving the operational issue: “The most important development for today is that Starlink and Starshield have resumed operations at their pre-restriction speeds. The speeds are now at the level we need.”
The restoration began overnight. “By this morning, the speeds were already sufficient for operational use,” Zelenskyy said. “This is very important and significant for our frontline logistics and for defending Ukraine against jet-powered Shaheds.”
On Thursday, Trump had claimed the service was running again at full speed, but a European official speaking to the Associated Press denied the service was fully functioning.
When asked by reporters whether he would tell Musk to stop “messing around” with Ukraine’s access to Starlink on Friday, the US president said: “I’ve not spoken to him. I might have to … I’ve heard it was fixed. But if it’s not, I’ll speak to him … If there is a problem, I’ll get it straightened out.”
He then described Musk as a “very brilliant” and “very good” person.

Some of London’s top restaurants are opening branches in Dubai because of a “tax tsunami” in the UK and better work ethic abroad, according to a leading restaurateur.
James Robson, a co-owner of Fallow in St James’s Market, regarded as the capital’s hottest restaurant, serving 1,000 people a day, has just signed a deal to open an outpost in the Gulf.
Other restaurants have opened in Dubai, including the celebrity hotspot Scott’s in Mayfair, the two Michelin-starred Indian venue Gymkhana, and the upmarket Chinese restaurant Park Chinois. Isabel’s, a Mayfair institution enjoyed by politicians, has opened in Abu Dhabi. And the trendy Borough Market bakery Bread Ahead has branched out in Dubai.
Despite conflicts in the Middle East, including the US-Israeli war in Iran which caused Dubai to face bombardment and an exodus of expats earlier this year, restaurants continue to open in the emirate.
Speaking from Hong Kong, where he is looking at opportunities in Asia, Robson said: “East Asia, the States and the Gulf are key growth targets for us. America champions business, the Gulf actively encourages and assists, whilst east Asia has a work ethic and taxation system that puts the UK to shame. I’m incredibly keen to start working in these regions over the next few years.”
Fallow has risen to fame partially through Instagram, where it has 650,000 followers, and its striking dishes including a whole cod’s head drenched in a spicy butter sauce.
Restaurateurs have complained of the VAT rate for hospitality in the UK, which at 20% is one of the highest rates in Europe. The European average for restaurants is about 12%. In Italy, it is set at 10% for food sold in restaurants. Chefs are calling for Andy Burnham to use next week’s budget to cut the VAT rate.
“We have had a tsunami of taxes that have got to the point where taking business risk simply does not make sense in the UK,” Robson said, “Sadly the country has sleepwalked into multiple anti-growth taxations the last two budgets and likely more will be forthcoming next week.”
The entrepreneur has asked for VAT to be put more in line with Europe. “Add 25% corporation tax and 40%-plus dividend tax, then you start to question why do businesses any more.”
Jason Atherton, a Michelin-starred chef, spends a third of his time at his Dubai restaurant now and says it is easier to make a profit abroad than in London.
But human rights experts have warned of exploitation and poor worker protections in the Gulf. Felix Jakens, Amnesty International UK’s director of campaigns, said: “Dubai might look like an attractive place to do business, but the UAE has a very poor record on workers’ rights and protection from labour exploitation. The UAE has spent heavily on polishing its image in the UK, not least through Manchester City, but that glamour shouldn’t distract from how the people who keep its economy running are treated.
“Migrant workers, who make up the majority of the UAE’s population, remain bound by a sponsorship system that ties them to their employers and exposes them to labour abuse. They are denied the right to form trade unions, leaving them few ways to challenge unfair treatment.
“Any UK business expanding into the Gulf has a responsibility to carry out proper human rights due diligence, to make sure the people working in its kitchens are treated fairly, paid properly and able to raise concerns without fear of losing their job or visa.”
Some restaurants in Dubai are struggling: Dinner by Heston is temporarily closed and has been since the fallout from the war in the Middle East. The Michelin guide came under fire earlier this month because it included 16 restaurants that were either permanently or temporarily closed. It appears that some visits were undertaken by inspectors at the beginning of the year, before the war started.
Robson said he had no resentment paying UK tax. “I am incredibly proud of the taxes I pay and feel privileged that I can contribute to our country’s deficit and will continue to do so,” he said. “My point is UK growth simply does not have any risk-reward balance any more, therefore it’s play incredibly safe here and focus overseas.”

Park24 has announced plans to provide a consolation payment of ¥3,000 in cash or gift cards to Times Car vehicle-sharing service users affected by a recent data breach.
The company has confirmed that about 6.62 million user accounts were compromised. Of those accounts, eligible for the payment will be about 1.46 million accounts from which images of identification documents, including driver’s licenses, were externally transferred.

The total cost of the consolation payment is expected to be some ¥4.4 billion. The company plans to book an extraordinary loss of ¥5.5 billion for the year ending this month, including other expenses related to the data breach.
On Friday, it was also learned that Makino Law Office plans to organize affected users and file a damages lawsuit against the Times Car service operator and others.
Yuki Makino of the law office said that the payment amount is “too low” given concerns over identity theft and the burden on affected users of dealing with potential damage.
According to Makino, more than 90,000 people have registered online to participate in the planned lawsuit.

How to get better iPhone battery life without closing any apps
Apple has added a host of battery-management features to the iPhone over the years.
No matter how good your iPhone's battery life is, you probably wish it would last a little longer. Over time, even the best batteries degrade, and before that happens, the way you use your phone has a major impact on how long it holds a charge. It makes some sense to think that closing apps you're not using would mean your phone is using less power, but that's actually not the case. Instead, there are plenty of other ways to extend battery life without closing any apps.
Background apps may not be to blame for a dead battery, but there are some ways to limit the power those apps draw when you're not using them. When it's toggled on, the Background App Refresh setting lets apps pull data from the internet and update themselves even while suspended. Turning this off will prevent these processes and save power. Similarly, under individual apps' settings, you can choose to let them access location services only when you're using them.
Changing display settings is a good start
Apple recommends two options as the first steps to extending your battery life. First, manage your phone's brightness by manually setting it to the lowest level or turn on auto-brightness to let your phone manage it automatically. It's probably best to try auto-brightness first so you're not constantly fiddling with your settings or forgetting to turn the brightness down when lighting conditions change. Second, Apple recommends always keeping Wi-Fi turned on so you use as little data as possible, since connecting to a cellular network uses more power than connecting to a Wi-Fi network.
Aside from brightness, there are a few other display settings you can adjust to get more life out of your battery. Disabling Always-On Display is a great place to start, since it's a nice but not essential feature that puts a constant strain on your battery. Turning on Dark Mode can also save power as long as your phone has an OLED screen, since OLED turns off the parts of the screen where black pixels appear. Turning on Limit Frame Rate sets the phone's display to a 60 Hz refresh rate instead of ProMotion's 120 Hz, halving the number of times your screen refreshes during a day. The power savings might not be that noticeable for most people, though, and if you're used to 120 Hz, the change can be jarring.
Extend your iPhone's battery life with power settings
Finally, your iPhone has some settings to directly change how it handles charging and power draw. With Adaptive Power turned on, your phone will analyze your usage patterns, changing everything from screen brightness to background data to lower battery drain when you don't typically need your phone's full power. Turning on Low Power Mode forces similar changes, but tends to have a heavier impact on your phone's performance, so it's best used only when you really need it. With Adaptive Power toggled on, Low Power Mode automatically engages when your battery drops to 20 percent.
Over time, a phone's battery loses its ability to charge efficiently and hold that charge for as long. While some depletion is inevitable, turning on Optimized Charging will prevent some of that wear by stopping a charge at 80 percent until you really need it. Even better, you can set a charge limit yourself so that your battery never fills to 100 percent, which can reduce its life over time. In general, if you can keep your battery charge between 20 percent and 80 percent, rather than letting it fully drain or fill, you can extend your battery's life by a noticeable amount even before using any of these other tips.

The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum on 24-25 February 2025 brought together global partners from the humanitarian sector to discuss urgent health and humanitarian issues. It focused on advocacy for the survival, health diplomacy, well-being, and dignity of people affected by crises, as well as the security of aid workers. The forum, marking the 10th anniversary of the King Salman Humanitarian Aid and Relief Centre (KSRelief), witnessed key agreements and pledges aimed at addressing ongoing humanitarian challenges in the Middle East and beyond.
KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing funding agreements in response to humanitarian crises. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
WHO and KSrelief signed new agreements aimed at malaria prevention and cholera control in Yemen. This includes a US$ 12 million for malaria control and US$ 2.1 million to expand cholera treatment. Another agreement, worth US$ 3.6 million, was made between KSrelief and WHO Egypt Country Office to provide dialysis treatment for Sudanese refugees in Egypt due to the ongoing conflict in Sudan.
Read Press Release: WHO and King Salman Humanitarian Aid & Relief Centre expand life-saving health interventions with new agreements at Riyadh Humanitarian Forum
UNICEF Executive Director, Catherine Russel, KSRelief Supervisor-General, Abdullah Al Rabeeah, and Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, WHO Director-General signing the Global Polio Eradication Initiative funding agreement for US$ 500 million. Photo by: WHO/Karim Yassmineh
The Kingdom of Saudi Arabia reaffirmed its US$ 500 million pledge to the GPEI, initially made in April 2024. Two funding agreements were signed with WHO US$ 300 million and UNICEF US$ 200 million. This contribution will support efforts to vaccinate 370 million children annually, aiming to eradicate polio globally. The commitment highlights Saudi Arabia’s role in combatting polio, particularly in conflict-affected regions such as Pakistan, Afghanistan, and Gaza, where the virus has made a resurgence.
Read Press Release: Kingdom of Saudi Arabia confirms US$ 500 million commitment to global polio eradication effort
The Riyadh International Humanitarian Forum 2025 was a significant event that underscored the continued partnership between WHO and KSrelief, as well as with other international partners to address critical humanitarian health crises. The agreements made during the forum are pivotal in combating diseases like malaria, cholera, and polio, and ensuring better healthcare for displaced populations. The forum also highlighted Saudi Arabia’s ongoing commitment to global humanitarian efforts, reaffirming its leadership role in tackling some of the world’s pressing health crises.

New York – Japan’s National Governors’ Association held an event in New York on Thursday to promote famous sights and food cultures in six prefectures in the Asian country.
The six were Toyama, Shizuoka, Mie and Nagano, as well as Miyagi in the country’s northeast and Chiba.
The tourism seminar, aimed at travel agencies and media organizations, was held to expand sales channels for local products and attract travelers from North America as the Japanese market shrinks due to the decreasing population.
At the venue, “Kokiriko,” a folk song from the Gokayama rural district, a UNESCO World Heritage site in Toyama, was introduced together with a graceful dance performed to pray for a good harvest.
The event also included a presentation on the characteristics and history of Shizuoka tea, as well as an Iga-style ninja show representing Mie, which drew a cheer from the audience as the performers engaged in spectacular action sequences, wielding swords and other weapons.
“We want to showcase the unique appeal of our regions in New York, the world’s cultural and economic hub,” said Shuichi Abe, the association’s president and Nagano governor.
Over the weekend, an exchange meeting between prefectural governors and buyers, including trading house officials, is scheduled to be held, as well as a tasting event featuring prefectural products.
At a reception following the seminar, a business operator from Nagano gave a soba buckwheat noodle-making demonstration, while regional specialties were served, including Miyagi’s zunda mochi cakes of pounded rice topped with sweet green bean paste.

Lee Chang Dong’s seventh feature film, Possible Love, is inspired by true events from 2009, when a Korean conglomerate fired a third of its staff – 2,600 employees – after which many died by suicide. Possible Love is the latest in a long line of Lee movies that engage with themes of class or labor or religion or compressed modernity, that uniquely Korean affliction, without feeling didactic.
Lee Chang Dong ponders the ethics of the camera
In Possible Love, the director of Burning tackles labor struggle, human connection, and the nature of capturing others on film.
A different kind of movie would have captured the heat of that labor struggle. Possible Love picks up with the characters in the aftermath, a murkier time that defies easy understanding. The film opens with an epigraph: “Thou shall not covet.” What follows is a movie about characters who covet. They covet each other’s job, designer clothes, spouses, and positionality. Mi-ok (Jeon Do-Yeon) is the long-suffering wife of Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), her laid-off husband. At a funeral of a colleague who died by suicide, Mi-ok and Ho-seok meet another couple, documentary filmmaker Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) and her rich husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung). And off we go.
The Verge spoke with Lee during his trip to New York about how he arrived at his politics, porousness between people, the properties of the camera, and what it is like to work with Netflix. The interview was conducted in Korean and translated into English.
I am also from Daegu. I wonder how this fact shaped you? And more broadly, to whom or what do you owe your political education?
As you know well, Daegu is referred to as the heartland of conservatism in Korea. I went to school there, all the way through university, so I grew up steeped in that conservative disposition and was influenced by it. But until I graduated from college, in the spring of 1980, I didn’t realize how politically conservative Daegu citizens were.
That spring, in May of 1980, I participated in protests against the Chun Doo-hwan regime as a university student. It was on the streets that I met them, the citizens, and experienced their hardline sentiments in a visceral way. It was shocking to me. Afterwards, I thought a lot about how come the people in Daegu were so politically conservative. In light of all that, the thoughts of a person I perceive as myself, that person’s attitude towards the world, could only be bound with a certain kind of tension.
I was interested in how different directors respond to similar social forces in different ways – like Bong Joon Ho’s Parasite and Park Chan Wook’s No Other Choice. I imagine you know them both personally. What is the conversation between you all when working on your various projects?
We do know each other personally, but we seldom talk about our work. It might be the result of coincidence. Though of course, there might be a certain inevitability hidden within them. We lived through the same modern Korean history, and you cannot call that coincidence.
One thing does come to mind. A long time ago, I think before he made Mother, Bong Joon Ho told me over drinks that he had almost finished writing a script and wanted to show it to me. It was a story about a mother, and he was wrestling with how he could portray that person’s pain, whether he even had the right to. He said he wanted to show me the script. But once he sobered up, maybe he forgot, because he never showed it to me. Later, when I saw the film, I felt I might understand what he had been talking about.
Possible Love is concerned with similar questions: How can I portray another person’s story, another person’s pain? What position am I in? How much distance should I keep from them? You could say that these questions around the ethics of the camera are connected to the worry Bong Joon Ho had back then.
Like Ye-ji, I come from the so-called margins, and now report on that terrain, which is perhaps why watching her character pursue a near-vampiric level of access, I felt something close to repulsion. How were you able to represent the filmmaker–participant dynamic so accurately?
I can’t say how accurate it is. I don’t think Ye-ji’s attitude can be generalized. Not every documentary filmmaker has a rich husband. Nevertheless you can say Ye-Ji captures something universal about filmmakers, or those who deal in other people’s stories, directors such as myself, or reporters, in that they aren’t exactly the people they portray. Even if they came from a lower class, they are no longer of it. Their position in life has changed. And yet, in order to do their work, what do they do? When someone else’s suffering unfolds dramatically in front of them, are they to capture the moment on tape, or should they step away from the camera? Or maybe it isn’t unfolding dramatically in front of them, in which case, do they create a certain effect by producing the moment, by staging it?
I think those are basically properties of the camera. The moment you hold a camera you have power, and the camera operates according to that power.
It’s not so much that I portrayed it so precisely, but these properties of the camera are something worth thinking through together.
For us filmmakers, we don’t belong to the world of our subjects, nor are we on the side of capital either. We are in the middle where we are, it can be said, in a neutral, or perhaps cowardly position. Despite that, those who make movies, those who tell stories of others, in the end, can, through their efforts, bring about some small change.
In this film, Ho-seok ends up pouring out what’s inside of him in front of the camera, which functions as a kind of treatment, even if that isn’t what Ye-ji intended.
Possible Love is a collaboration between you and screenwriter Oh Jung-mi. How did you two come to work together, and what does that collaboration look like?
She is a student I met at Korea National University of Arts. You could say it’s a school that draws the most talented and ambitious students, and she was special even among them. By special I mean she was creative and wrote well, of course, but she also has a perspective, and the ability to take a step back and regard something, and find meaning in things.
As I get older, I grow duller and numb, and set in my ways, and she is a friend who reliably jolts me out of it, which is very precious to me.
I think I’m lucky. Not just with Oh Jung-mi but everyone around me that I work with is very precious to me, and I feel lucky to have met them.
The problem with Oh Jung-mi, though, is that while working together, I kept scrapping projects. So she suffered. But she never left. She stayed beside me, and even though she herself is someone who makes and develops films, she has given me a lot of help up to now.
Ye-ji documents in service of higher purpose. Mi-ok’s character snaps photos of the table spread for no purpose at all. The footage from the helicopter captures a moment of police brutality. How does the function of cinema compare to all the other instances in which we hit record?
Ye-ji has a desire to capture in her camera vanishing laborers [and] the value of their labor — not unlike her dry cleaner father. And yet, it is undeniable that she also regards their lives as source material for her own movie. As narrative filmmakers, stories of others in pain often is nothing but material for a commercial movie.
As for Mi-ok, she knows about the properties of the camera, but she, too, has a desire: to broadcast her pain, and her problems. She has a secondary desire, which is that she wonders if her husband’s traumas may not be healed through the camera, because she believes that his biggest issue is keeping all his problems, his despair and his anger, hidden.
So each has their own desires regarding the camera.
As a filmmaker, firstly, I had the goal of conveying the contents of the documentary Ye-ji was making, of capturing the sufferings of the laid-off laborers. I believed what Ye-ji tried to show, I had to show through my own film.
The group therapy session scene, for example, could be very long and tedious, and for some viewers it might be something that they cannot emotionally relate to, because they came to see a narrative film, not documentary. Despite that, I felt I had to convey it.
Regarding the crackdown scene, some of it appears through archival footage shot from a distance. But as someone making a fiction film, I also have a responsibility to convey Ho-seok’s subjective memory cinematically. So you could say within the narrative structure of Ye-ji’s documentary, multiple layers of roles and goals co-exist.
What are some notes you received from your American movie executives that felt unique to working in the American system versus Korean?
I didn’t feel that at all. From pre-production through post-production, Netflix, as the investor, never once interfered or offered unsolicited notes. Of course, I can’t generalize from that. I haven’t asked everyone else. But I had none of that. In that sense they absolutely guaranteed my independence and freedom as a director.
Now the film is finished and we are promoting it, and in particular part of what we call the Oscar campaign. I probably wouldn’t have gotten this kind of help without Netflix, that’s clear.
Possible Love was released in select US theaters October 23rd and will be available on Netflix globally on November 6th.

Barnes Ice Cap sits on the central plateau of Baffin Island, in the Canadian Arctic. It is the last surviving fragment of the Laurentide Ice Sheet, the largest of the Pleistocene ice sheets, which at its peak buried most of Canada under two miles of ice and locked away around 80 meters of sea level. That remnant has now yielded direct physical evidence that ice sheets might have reversed their retreat and started to grow again thousands of years ago.
In a recent Science study, researchers show that the Laurentide reached its smallest size about 3,600 years ago, then started re-expanding roughly 2,000 years ago, which the team interprets as the opening move of the next glaciation. Apparently, this brand-new ice age was on its way until about 1960, when human-caused climate warming reversed it.
Frozen to the bed
“Barnes is the last remaining piece of one of the domes of the Laurentide Ice Sheet,” says Nicolás Young, a geologist at Columbia University’s Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory and lead author of the study. As that enormous dome thinned through the Holocene, its margin withdrew up onto Baffin Island, and what’s left today is the deflated core of something that was once two miles thick. The reason Barnes can testify about its own history, Young explains, comes down to the temperature at its base.
Most glaciers are warm-based, meaning meltwater at the bed lets them slide, and sliding ice grinds up everything beneath it, erasing the record. Barnes is cold-based, and thus frozen directly onto the bedrock beneath it, which prevents it from sliding.
“If there is an ice event where you live and you have to go and scrape off your windshield, that ice that’s plastered to the windshield of your car, that’s a good example of how cold-based ice operates. It’s sort of just stuck to what it’s on,” Young says.
This stuck ice preserves what’s beneath instead of eroding it. As the Laurentide retreated across the plateau, tundra plants colonized the newly bare ground. When the ice came back later, it simply smothered them in place and held them there, intact, for two millennia. To pinpoint the exact moment of this turnaround, Young’s team used two independent dating methods.

Mumbai Indians announced Kieron Pollard as its new head coach for the IPL 2027 season on Saturday. Pollard, whose association with the franchise runs back to 2010, will take over from Sri Lanka’s Mahela Jayawardene.
Speaking about his role and expectations for next year, Pollard said his immediate focus was to bring a team-first mindset to help MI become a title-contending team again.
“I think my first task is about understanding what’s needed to be done. Again, and then when you get into that, bring that spirit and that energy. Talk about that. When you walk into the Wankhede Stadium, you are not seeing the yellows and the reds and stuff like that. You want to see that blue flag flying, and you want to see that passion and spirit from the fans. And that can only come from within us,” Pollard said.
“We recognize the fact that we have not been where we wanted to be in the last couple of years. So there’s no hiding, sort of from that.
“But what’s going to happen is that we’re going to try our best now to ensure that we continue to play for that badge, put the team above self, and then ensure that when the opposition comes, it’s something that they remembered from the past. Yes, it’s history, but sometimes in order to go forward, you have to go back a little bit and understand. And I think that’s where it’s going to start,” the West Indian added.
Mumbai Indians, the joint-most successful team in the IPL with five titles, has looked a pale shadow of its former self in recent IPL seasons.. The team failed to qualify for the Playoffs in two out of the last three seasons, and has not won the title since 2020.
ALSO READ | Kieron Pollard replaces Mahela Jayawardene as Mumbai Indians head coach for IPL 2027
Pollard also said his players would have complete freedom to express themselves, a personality trait that came to define the West Indian during his playing career.
“I think that’s very very important, and that’s something that has been leaving the game, and not true. Sometimes a lot of the guys wanted to show their personality and be free, but through the rules and regulations of the demerit points and all of these things, I think at times we have gotten a bit robotic in that sense.
“So, guys don’t actually sometimes try to show their true personality, and I think that is what is missing a little bit. So for us, as a Mumbai Indians team, I think it’s very important that we show personalities because each and every individual in our dressing room has something that people would not have seen that has gotten them to where they have got at the stage, and that is where you need bring it out,” Pollard added.
Pollard also spoke highly of Jayawardene, stating the Sri Lankan’s technical acumen has strongly influenced his understanding of the game.
“What stood out for me immediately from then was how precise he was from a tactical perspective in that in that sense.”
“Having to experience him as a coach playing under him, I think was even more fantastic for me. And then following that, being under him as an assistant, as well as a batting coach, the knowledge that I would have gained over that period of time, from someone like him, I have to say I’m blessed, to be able to be in that position, to be able to receive all that he had to bring from different perspective from opponent into the coaching setup,” Pollard said.
On how he would approach the head coach job, Pollard said it would involve player management and data driven decision-making.
“It comes down to the players. It comes down to conversations, one-on-one conversations. Yes, it comes down to the team talks and the team tactics. Also, with how much cricket has changed lately, data also becomes an important aspect, it helps with preparation.”

The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday (October 23, 2026), the head of the World Health Organisation said.
Also Read: Congo’s Ebola outbreak records more than 4,000 deaths
The DR Congo's worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600.
Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic.
Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo.
The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC's northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak.
"Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means 'hope' in Swahili," WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X.
"This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work," he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested.
"WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives."
Two vaccines in the pipeline
The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines.
The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection.
It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials.
One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the U.S.-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology.
Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and are expected to enter the trial "shortly", CEPI said in a statement.
"Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks," said CEPI.
The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials.
'Important step'
WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk.
"If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus — a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives," he said.
Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years.
"Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities," said Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, the DRC Ebola response incident manager.
The DRC declared its 17th outbreak of Ebola on May 15, and the WHO, two days later, triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level.

A magnitude-7 earthquake has hit China’s Tibet region, killing at least 16 people, injuring 54 and collapsing hundreds of homes in the northern regional city of Nagqu, official media said.
Search and rescue efforts continued after the collapse of at least 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds, the Nagqu media office said, citing city government officials.
More than 1,600 people from the local county were deployed for rescue efforts. Supplies including 1,000 prefabricated housing units and about 3,000 tents and folding beds as well as torches and winter clothing arrived in the region.
The US Geological Survey said the quake occurred at 10.33pm local time on Thursday, with its epicentre 191km (119 miles) east-northeast of Nagqu, in a sparsely populated, high-altitude area of northern Tibet. It put the earthquake’s depth at 18km.
The US agency recorded at least seven aftershocks with magnitude between 4.3 and 5.2, all of them with a depth of 10km, according to its website.
Videos posted by China’s national broadcaster CCTV said showed workers running out of restaurants and objects falling off shelves at supermarkets when the quake struck.
China’s official Xinhua news agency said on Friday that communication in some areas hit by the quake was down. Local railway authorities had taken emergency actions to halt trains passing through the region.
More than 300 police officers had been dispatched for relief work while the regional fire and rescue corps has mobilised almost 350 personnel to the affected areas, Xinhua reported.
Rescue workers clambered through damaged buildings, some with collapsed roofs, footage on CCTV showed.
The earthquake also caused rockfalls that had forced local authorities to close a section of national highway 317, allowing only emergency, rescue and official support vehicles through as crews worked to clear debris, according to Xinhua.
Intermittent snows were expected in the quake region over the next three days, Xinhua said. It was the biggest quake in the region in the past five years, CCTV said.
China’s leader, Xi Jinping, called for all-out efforts in rescue operations and medical relief work.
Nagqu is more than 300km north of Tibet’s capital, Lhasa.
Earthquakes are relatively common in China. In January 2025, at least 126 people were killed in one in Tibet’s rural Tingri county.
In December 2023, a quake in remote Gansu province in north-west China killed at least 134 people, state media said. That quake was China’s deadliest since 2014, when more than 600 people died in the south-western province of Yunnan.
A huge tremor in Sichuan province in 2008 left approximately 90,000 people dead or missing, including about 5,000 schoolchildren.

Jammu, Oct 24: The Jammu and Kashmir Congress on Saturday reiterated its demand for the restoration of full statehood, making it clear that the party would continue to stay out of the Omar Abdullah-led Cabinet until its concerns over statehood and constitutional safeguards were addressed.
J&K Congress working president Raman Bhalla said the party remained firm on its position that the restoration of full statehood was essential to ensuring justice for the people of Jammu and Kashmir and protecting their land, jobs and natural resources.
“The Congress has always maintained that the people of Jammu and Kashmir must get back their full-fledged statehood,” Bhalla told PTI, reiterating the party’s long-standing position on the issue.
He stressed the need for safeguards to protect the employment opportunities for the local youth, land rights and the region’s resources, saying these concerns remained central to the Congress’ political position.
“We need a full-fledged state, headed by a governor, with a single power centre rather than a dual power structure,” Bhalla said, adding that further decisions concerning the region should be taken after the restoration of statehood.
He maintained that the Congress had not deviated from its position and remained committed to securing the rights and safeguards of the people.
The Congress’ decision to stay out of the Omar Abdullah-led Cabinet has been linked to the delay in restoring full statehood to J&K.
Despite the National Conference (NC) and the Congress securing a comfortable majority in the Assembly following the 2024 elections, the NC formed the government while the Congress chose to extend support from outside rather than join the Council of Ministers.
Earlier in the day, Chief Minister Omar Abdullah said the Cabinet would be expanded and reshuffled next week.
Speaking to reporters after meeting Lieutenant Governor Manoj Sinha at the Lok Bhawan, Abdullah said he had requested time from the former to carry out the exercise.
“Yes, it certainly was discussed. I requested time from him for the expansion and told him that in the first two to three days of next week, I will carry out the expansion and make certain changes in my Council of Ministers,” Abdullah said.

Five years after being diagnosed with multiple sclerosis, actor Christina Applegate revealed this week that she had been misdiagnosed. Her experience puts a public face on one of the most consequential challenges in neurology: how to diagnose a complex disease early enough to prevent irreversible damage without sacrificing accuracy.
How MS is diagnosed has changed dramatically during my nearly four decades in the field. When I began my career, physicians often had to wait for symptoms to recur before they could confirm MS. Today, advances in imaging, biomarkers, and diagnostic criteria are helping us recognize the disease earlier, when treatment may have the greatest opportunity to prevent irreversible neurological damage.
But progress brings a critical responsibility. Too many people still spend years searching for an accurate diagnosis, while others are told they have MS when another condition is responsible for their symptoms. Applegate’s experience is a powerful reminder that the future of MS diagnosis cannot be about speed alone. Our goal must be both: diagnosing MS earlier and getting the diagnosis right.
The challenge is that MS does not look the same in everyone, and other neurological disorders can produce similar symptoms. Signs such as numbness, vision changes, fatigue, and difficulty walking can occur in many other neurological disorders. Even abnormalities detected on an MRI are not necessarily unique to MS.
The consequences of both misdiagnosis and delayed diagnosis can be substantial.
Someone incorrectly diagnosed with MS may receive treatments they do not need, potentially exposing them to unnecessary risks while delaying appropriate care for the condition actually causing their symptoms.
For people whose MS goes undiagnosed, time matters enormously. While there is not yet a cure for MS, there are more than 20 therapies that can help reduce disease activity and slow worsening for many people living with MS. Research has demonstrated the importance of initiating appropriate treatment early in the course of disease, before neurological damage accumulates. Every unnecessary delay can mean a missed opportunity to protect long-term neurological health.
Fortunately, decades of research have fundamentally changed what is possible.
Today, we have better diagnostic tools, more sophisticated imaging technologies, and a deeper understanding of MS than at any point in history. Yet significant challenges remain in ensuring that these advances reach the people who need them.
One of the most significant developments has been the evolution of the McDonald Diagnostic Criteria, the internationally recognized guidelines physicians use to diagnose MS. Working in partnership with the European Committee for Treatment and Research in Multiple Sclerosis, the National Multiple Sclerosis Society helped advance these criteria, contributing to progress that has shortened the diagnostic process from years to months in many cases. The latest revisions incorporate new imaging techniques and biomarkers designed to improve both the speed and accuracy of diagnosis.
One particularly promising example is an MRI technique that identifies the central vein sign, a feature that can help physicians distinguish lesions associated with MS from abnormalities caused by other conditions. Alongside progress in spinal fluid biomarker research, this technology offers the potential for earlier, more accurate diagnoses.
Artificial intelligence and sophisticated data analytics may eventually help clinicians recognize patterns in imaging and other clinical information, identify people who warrant further evaluation, and improve diagnostic precision.
These tools are still evolving, and they will require rigorous research and validation before they can be widely incorporated into clinical practice. But even the most sophisticated diagnostic tools cannot improve outcomes if patients cannot access the specialists and health care systems equipped to use them.
Access to neurological care across the country is uneven. Some communities face significant shortages of neurologists, particularly those with specialized expertise in MS. Patients may wait months for appointments, travel long distances to see specialists, or encounter lengthy referral processes before receiving the evaluation they need.
Clinician education is equally important. Primary care providers are often the first professionals to evaluate someone experiencing unexplained neurological symptoms. Helping them recognize potential early signs of MS and understand when to refer patients for neurological evaluation can make a meaningful difference.
Applegate’s willingness to share her experience has brought attention to an issue that extends far beyond any one person’s diagnosis. We have transformed our ability to recognize and treat MS over the past several decades, but scientific progress alone is not enough. The next challenge is ensuring that these advances translate into earlier answers, more accurate diagnoses, and better outcomes for everyone affected by the disease.
That will require continued investment in research to develop and validate better diagnostic tools, better education for the clinicians who first evaluate patients with unexplained neurological symptoms, and improved access to neurologists and MS specialists. Together, these efforts can help smooth the often difficult path from the first unexplained symptoms to an accurate diagnosis, while reducing the risk of both misdiagnosis and unnecessary delays.
The goal is not simply to diagnose MS faster. It is to get the diagnosis right, as early as possible, so that no one loses precious time, or the opportunity for appropriate treatment, while searching for answers.
Bruce Bebo, Ph.D., is chief research and medical affairs officer at the National Multiple Sclerosis Society. A cellular immunologist, he has dedicated nearly four decades to advancing research into multiple sclerosis, a commitment inspired by his mother’s experience living with the disease.

Jim Chalmers in a speech last week offered the scant encouragement that the economy would be “a bit better” in a year’s time.
Fast forward to Friday morning, and the treasurer revealed that his officials were busy downgrading their forecasts ahead of December’s mid-year budget update to show slower growth and higher unemployment.
In other words, things are getting worse, not better.
Overnight, a broadening Middle East conflict pushed the global benchmark oil price to US$113, and within sight of its April high of nearly US$120.
Motorists are paying 60 cents more for a litre of petrol prices than they were before the US and Israel attacked Iran. That’s an extra $36 to fill up a 60-litre tank. Do that once a week and a family’s monthly fuel bill is $144 higher than in February.
The New York Times overnight reported that the US and Israel have drawn up plans to restart attacks on Iran after the upcoming American midterm elections.
Westpac analysts have sketched out an “escalation” scenario for the Middle East conflict where oil climbs towards US$150, echoing warnings from the International Monetary Fund earlier this month.
That worst-case scenario would have huge implications for inflation and interest rates, even as we brace for a potential fifth interest rate hike on 3 November.
Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here
Meanwhile, the one bright spot that has helped paper over many of the cracks in the global economy – the huge spending associated with artificial intelligence – has hit some serious wobbles.
Investors are worried about the huge surge in debt among companies racing to build the infrastructure for an AI future – the trigger for another steep sell-off on Wall Street overnight.
Community opposition to the massive datacentre build-out could stall the headlong rush towards an AI future. That is likely a good thing in the longer term, but in the short term is another stress to add to the wall of worries. Rising chatter of a new tech stock bubble is naturally accompanied by talk of an imminent bust.
With all this going on, no wonder that the treasurer can only offer the thinnest of gruel for Australians hungry for any evidence of an end to years of disruption, and of wages that can’t keep up with high and rising prices.
High inflation, low growth and rising unemployment is a central banker’s “nightmare”, as the Reserve Bank’s Andrew Hauser has said.
It’s also a nightmare for a federal treasurer who is increasingly unpopular and desperate for a win in the court of public opinion.
“The pressures on people right now are very substantial and obviously that keeps me awake at night,” Chalmers told Politico.
“And there’s a number of reasons for that, some of them are outside our control, and some of them we have some influence over. You know, providing some cost-of-living help, managing the budget in a responsible way,” he said.
“Those are the things that we can do, but in lots of ways we’re hostage as well to decisions taken in DC or Tehran or in Eastern Europe about two wars which are pushing up inflation around the world and weighing on growth around the world.”
The high level of government spending is not helping the inflation fight, by any means – something the opposition is keen to point out at every opportunity.
Productivity growth is, if not dead, then resting, and shows no signs of springing back to its perch. That means more inflation at lower rates of growth as the economy hits its speed limits sooner.
But Chalmers is right when he says there’s a lot that is out of the government’s control.
His options to alleviate voter discontent are limited, which is why he frequently falls back on platitudes and lines to the effect of “you think we have it bad? You should see other economies.”
Sure, the government can lower petrol prices through another temporary cut to the fuel excise. But the billions of dollars that pumps into motorists’ pockets makes it harder for the RBA to bring inflation back under control.
Labor could go the other way and announce plans for big spending cuts in the December mid-year economic and fiscal outlook.
That would help the central bank’s job, but would drag on an already weak economy and push unemployment higher – would they win any plaudits for that?
This is Hauser’s “world of hard choices” – a world where the solution to one problem makes the other worse. A world with which Australians are becoming all too familiar.
