Why Zimbabwe tycoon 'Sir Wicknell' was loved and hated in Africa
- Published
Wicknell Chivayo, the Zimbabwean tycoon who died in a helicopter crash along with his wife Lucy Muteke last week, divided opinion in life and continues to do so in death.
He called himself "Sir Wicknell", a nod to the embellishment that epitomised his lifestyle - and a nickname some used for the 45-year-old who packed enough controversy into his short life to last several lifetimes.
He was relentlessly self-documenting, building much of his public persona on social media, where he posed with piles of cash and announced the cars and money he gave to people whom he considered deserving.
Chivayo delighted in displaying his access to heads of state across Africa and showing off his possessions, conducting video tours of his fleet of expensive cars, mainly Rolls-Royces, with vanity plates, watches and a vast collection of designer shoes.
His admirers saw a fabulously wealthy man sharing his good fortune. His detractors recoiled at the ostentatious displays, questioned the origins of his money and his political connections, and saw his lifestyle as a stark illustration of inequality.
But Chivayo remained tone-deaf to such criticism. As his fortunes rose, he became ever more unapologetic about flaunting his wealth in a country where nearly half the population lives below the international poverty line, according to the World Bank.
"He gave to those few on an island of wealth in a sea of poverty," Pedzisai Ruhanya, director of the Zimbabwe Democracy Institute think-tank, told the BBC, explaining how his donations were mainly to influential people.
He dismissed Chivayo's generosity as grandstanding for the ruling Zanu-PF party - an attempt to ensure the support of key politicians and even church leaders.
Nonetheless, there has been an outpouring of grief, especially from recipients of his largesse, and tributes from politicians, religious leaders and business figures.
Among the mourners gathered at the Chivayos' opulent home in the capital, Harare, ahead of their burial on Thursday, was Cleopas Mukungunugwa, a young and prominent Zanu-PF social media influencer and recipient of two luxury cars from Sir Wicknell.
Standing outside the mansion, where a massive poster of the couple is displayed, he told local media that he was devastated by his patron's death, external, explaining how "Sir Wicknell" often dictated what he should write in his posts.
"He was criticised by many on social media and our goal was to bolster his reputation as a philanthropist," he said.
Chivayo dropped out of high school aged 15 because his family could no longer afford the fees after his father died when he was 10.
His first job was as a wages clerk for a bus company. From there, he moved into his first independent hustle - selling mobile phones and dealing in foreign currency, often on the black market at the height of the country's hyperinflation crisis.
In 2005, he was sentenced to five years in prison for money laundering involving 837,000 South African rand (then worth $137,500, £72,000). He served three years at Chikurubi Maximum Prison after two years were suspended.
Details of his career following his release are murky, but he went into the energy business, becoming what one state-run newspaper described as a "tenderpreneur" -making money by getting government contracts.
He headed the firm Intratrek Zimbabwe, which partnered with Chinese electrical giant CHiNT Electric. This was at a time when legislation required all companies in the country to cede economic control to black Zimbabweans, under a policy known as indigenisation.
In 2014, Intratrek was selected to build a 100MW solar power station in the southern town of Gwanda. A contract worth more than $170m was signed the following year. It became one of the biggest controversies of Chivayo's business career.
Zimbabwe Power Company, the state-owned utility that awarded the contract, sought to terminate it when Intratrek failed to deliver, but the courts ultimately ruled that the agreement remained valid.
A parliamentary inquiry later described Intratrek as a "briefcase company" being used as a front to attract investment.
Chivayo acknowledged that Intratrek lacked expertise in solar construction, describing it as the local partner while CHiNT provided the technical muscle.
Intratrek received an advance of more than $5m for the Gwanda solar plant, but it remains unbuilt to this day.
Just weeks before Chivayo's death, Intratrek received a government notice to proceed with the project and was given 24 months to complete it.
As the accusations flew, the businessman just smiled and sweet-talked his way through the maelstrom - even winning over President Emmerson Mnangagwa, who was initially unimpressed by him when he first came to power.
In 2018, Mnangagwa cited Gwanda as a lesson in the dangers of doing business with "fly-by-night briefcase businessmen", adding ominously that "Chikurubi is not full". The state-run Herald newspaper reported that the warning was directed at Chivayo.
Yet within a few years, that relationship transformed into a bromance. In one of several photographs capturing the remarkable informality between them, Chivayo lounges, almost lying, on a sofa beside Mnangagwa, apparently entirely at ease in the president's company.
His access was not confined to Zanu-PF - he also posted photographs with opposition figures, including the late Morgan Tsvangirai and Nelson Chamisa.
But he became a conspicuous presence around Mnangagwa, speaking glowingly of the president and making no secret of his support for Zanu-PF.
He faced allegations over the procurement of materials for the 2023 elections, in which Mnangagwa was voted in for a second term.
Investigations alleged that South African supplier Ren-Form grossly inflated prices and subsequently paid hundreds of millions of rand to a company linked to him. Chivayo denied wrongdoing, and Zimbabwe's anti-corruption commission later said it had found no evidence linking him to procurement fraud. Ren-Form denied any wrongdoing.
In April, he offered the country's 360 legislators $10,000 each, prompting accusations that he wanted to influence an impending vote on a controversial constitutional amendment to extend what would have been Mnangagwa's final five-year term by two years to 2030.
He was forced to withdraw the offer following a backlash and denied it was intended to influence the vote.
When the legislation was signed into law several months later, Zanu-PF posted a video clip of him with the caption, external: "Billionaire Sir Wicknell Chivayo celebrates… singing '2030 Ndeya Emmerson Baba!' while cruising at 51,000 feet aboard his Gulfstream G550".
Access to power became part of Chivayo's social-media persona. In June, Eswatini's King Mswati III granted him citizenship of the southern African kingdom and a diplomatic passport - photographs and videos showed him kneeling before the monarch, external.
He had an impressive camera roll, with snaps of him posing with other African presidents such as Nigeria's Bola Tinubu, external, Tanzania's Samia Suluhu Hassan, external, Malawi's Peter Mutharika, external, Mozambique's Daniel Chapo, external, Zambia's Hakainde Hichilema, external and he was part of the delegation that met South Africa's Cyril Ramaphosa, external when he visited Mnangagwa's farm earlier this year.
Some relationships extended beyond formal meetings. In August, Chivayo and his wife attended the engagement of Kenyan President William Ruto's daughter Charlene at the president's family home.
Afterwards, Ruto personally drove the couple to their waiting helicopter. Chivayo filmed the journey from the passenger seat, external. True to form, he gloated: "Being driven by the president of the republic. God is the greatest."
Ruto wrote on X following the death, external: "I will remember him for his friendship, his energy, and his deep conviction in the possibilities of our continent."
But in Kenya the Zimbabwean businessman was viewed with great suspicion because of his closeness to Ruto - something expressed loudly on social media since his death.
Many of the comments are not printable but as Kenyan blogger Cyprian Nyakundi put it, external, listing some of the controversies surrounding Chivayo: "As a Kenyan, I distance myself completely from President Ruto's glowing tribute to Wicknell Chivayo. Those condolences and that 'dear friend' language are his own, not mine, as a Kenyan."
One commentator on X said his death had "united Africans in celebration", external.
"When a man's passing brings more relief than sorrow, the reaction itself tells a powerful story. It is time for those in power to reflect and reevaluate!"
At home there has also been pushback against those who say speaking ill of the dead is un-African - as the topic of the tycoon's death is the trending topic in Zimbabwe these days.
At a shopping centre in Harare over the weekend, Christabel Moyo voiced what many have been saying.
"What is African - getting rich from inflated state contracts and using that money to support Zanu-PF?" the 42-year-old accountant asked.
"He was busy doling out cars and cash to the rich while the Zimbabwean public health system is collapsing."
The extraordinary gifting spree for which he will be remembered began around 2023. Musicians, sports and business figures, politicians and religious leaders were among the beneficiaries of cars and cash in what some might see as a blatant attempt to buy support for the ruling party.
He started with relatively modest Toyota Aquas, but the gifts soon became dramatically more expensive.
Top musician Jah Prayzah, who is close to Zanu-PF was given three luxury cars, along with about $400,000, over three years.
The musician postponed his wedding - scheduled to take place last weekend - because of the helicopter crash, saying: "Wicknell was more than a friend to us."
Another key recipient was Bishop Nehemiah Mutendi, head of the Zion Christian Church that is fiercely loyal to Zanu-PF. The cleric received millions in cash donations and four luxury cars.
Chivayo regularly attended the Johane Masowe weChishanu African apostolic church, one of the biggest in Zimbabwe, whose followers can often be seen worshipping outdoors wearing white robes.
It also received scores of cars, buses and cash from the businessman as he pushed the influential sect closer to the ruling party, taking along Mnangagwa as guest of honour to a massive church gathering in August.
But not everyone accepted Chivayo's largesse. Eunor Guti, widow of Zimbabwe Assemblies of God Africa founder Archbishop Ezekiel Guti, declined a luxury vehicle and $250,000 in cash.
In 2024, veteran musician and government critic Thomas Mapfumo, who is based in the US, rejected Chivayo's offer of a luxury car and house, saying he could not be "bribed" and later describing his money as "dirty".
However, this year, he did accept $1m to perform at Jah Prayzah's wedding and Chivayo's birthday party in November.
Some long-time admirers of Mapfumo, who arrived in Harare on the eve of the helicopter crash, accused him on social media of compromising his principles, though this was denied by the 81-year-old musician.
Chivayo's generosity was not confined to individuals - he also donated 20 ambulances to Zimbabwe's failing public health system and gave buses and other assistance to schools.
Those close to him say his philanthropy was not always performed for an audience. Prominent lawyer Wilson Manase said following the tycoon's death that when he had fallen seriously ill in Dubai, Chivayo flew over to visit him.
In an interview with state broadcaster ZBC, the lawyer, who was promised a car in Chivayo's last tweet, described him as "pure hearted" and deeply religious.
The tycoon had two young children with his first wife Sonja Madzikanda, from whom he split in 2024 and was still embroiled in a messy court case over the divorce settlement.
He was also keen not to forget his roots. On the day he died, he had visited his rural home in Gandami, south-east of Harare, where he was building a $1m eight-bedroom mansion to be officially opened in November for his birthday.
He boasted it would bring "Borrowdale Brooke to Gandami" - a reference to one of Harare's most exclusive residential estates. He had also pledged $500,000 to improve the local primary and secondary schools and a clinic.
Chivayo's death leaves Zanu-PF without one of its most colourful campaigners.
But he also leaves behind unanswered questions - with many of his countrymen continuing to wonder how exactly he rose from such humble beginnings to becoming a multi-millionaire with the means to dole out such extravagant gifts.
Ish Mafundikwa is a freelance journalist based in Harare

The festive season, usually a time to splurge, is telling a different story this year. A smaller number of card transactions and weaker smartphone sales are hinting at consumers tightening their purse strings amid mounting pressure on household budgets. Early data from Redseer estimated that India’s online festive sales clocked $7-8 Bn in gross merchandise value (GMV) during the first leg, from October 8 to 18. Nearly 100 Mn shoppers placed more than 350 Mn orders, with consumption running at around three times the everyday rate. However, the data also pointed to a more cautious spending environment. According to Datum Intelligence, a market intelligence and consumer data analytics company, the online festive sales amounted to ₹29,800-₹30,900 Cr this year, down 7-10% from ₹33,200 Cr during the corresponding four-day period last year. Card spending, too, declined 12-15% YoY. The broader consumer picture was also subdued. LocalCircles’ ‘Mood for the Consumer 2026’ survey estimated that urban households would spend ₹1.97 Lakh Cr on festive discretionary purchases this year, down 6% from ₹2.10 Lakh Cr in 2025. The survey received more than 67,000 responses from urban consumers across 307 districts. The trends pointed to a central challenge for retailers: consumers continued to browse and buy, but rising expenses, uncertainty over earnings and jobs, and less compelling discounts made them more cautious about committing to expensive purchases. Shoppers Tune In But Spending Remains Muted Flipkart’s ‘Big Billion Days’ sale, which opened on October 8 and closed on October 19, recorded 6.3 Mn concurrent users in a minute during its opening hour. Listed Meesho’s ‘Mega Blockbuster Sale’, which went live on October 9 and wrapped up on October 18, also reported a 75% YoY rise in day-one orders and 60% growth in transacting customers. Over at Amazon, the ecommerce major said that its nearly two-week long ‘Great Indian Festival’ sale (stretching between October 8 and October 20) saw the number of products ordered during the first twenty four hours more than double YoY. Redseer’s assessment also highlighted the expanding reach of online festive shopping beyond major cities. Tier II and smaller towns accounted for around two-thirds of shoppers during the first leg, while the number of first-time shoppers from these regions doubled in 2026. Gen Z made up more than 35-40% of festive shoppers, with demand across gaming devices, creator cameras,wearables, sports footwear, grooming and beauty. Around 60% of Flipkart’s festive demand came from non-metro customers, while more than 72% of Amazon’s visits came from outside the top nine metros. Meesho also reported strong growth in orders through its Meesho Mall offering. However, traffic, visitors and orders measured different aspects of shopping activity. They did not, by themselves, establish how much consumers spent or whether the average purchase value increased. Datum’s card payment data offered another view. On October 9, the first day Amazon and Flipkart opened their sales to all shoppers, card transactions stood at 83.5 Lakh against 82 Lakh on the corresponding day last year. Yet, the value of those payments fell 18% to ₹6,594 Cr from ₹8,067 Cr. The figures point to lower spending despite a similar number of card transactions. Meesho’s order growth, much of which came through cash on delivery, also illustrated why order counts alone could not establish the value of sales. The year-on-year comparison, however, comes with an important caveat. The major online sales in 2025 coincided with the September 22 GST rate cuts, which reduced prices on several consumer products. The opening of this year’s sales did not have a comparable tax-led trigger. Fashion And Select Categories Find Buyers Category-level disclosures showed that consumers spent on fashion and certain premium products, even as electronics faced pressure. A Bank of America research note (dated October 20) found that Myntra’s daily active users rose around 40% during the first six days of its ‘Big Fashion Festival’, which ran between October 8 and October 25, compared with its September average. Myntra’s monthly active users stood at around 93 Mn (up 8% YoY), while Nykaa Fashion’s monthly active users grew 24% to around 17 Mn. Flipkart also reported a 42% YoY rise in beauty sales during the first hour of its sale, while its lifestyle category grew 12.5%, according to the company’s disclosures. Meesho also reported demand for festive décor and other lower-priced products. Redseer’s category-level estimates showed that large and small appliances recorded more than 20 times their average daily GMV during the festive period. Electronics ran over seven times the everyday level, while mobiles exceeded five times. These multiple compared festive daily GMV with the January - August 2026 daily average, rather than with the previous year. Amazon’s disclosures show that some premium categories performed well. Televisions measuring 55 inches and above accounted for 65% of its TV sales, while premium Android smartphones’ sales rose 70% YoY. The company also reported that high-end home theatre sold at 100X its regular day levels, while front-load washing machines with capacities of 9 kg and above sold at 80X. Fashion and beauty also recorded strong festive demand. Redseer estimated that fashion grew 20-25% and accounted for nearly a fifth of festive GMV, making it the second largest category. However, these numbers reflected performance in specific categories and do not establish a broad recovery in big ticket demand. LocalCircles’ survey provided another indication of household priorities. Among respondents who planned festive discretionary spending, 72% intended to buy clothing, footwear or accessories. Home appliances and furniture and travel and holidays were each cited by 45%. Only 22% planned to buy mobile phones, consumer electronics or gadgets. The findings suggested that expensive electronics were not a priority for most households planning festive purchases. Household Budget Under Pressure LocalCircles estimated that urban households would spend around ₹20,000 on festive discretionary purchases in 2026. While 57% of respondents said they intended to spend, 31% planned no discretionary festive purchases. The survey’s findings on how households planned to fund their purchases were equally telling. Around 83% of households intending to spend expected to use savings to some extent. About 34% expected savings to cover at least a quarter of their festive expenditure, including 16% who said they would fund the entire amount from savings. This came as retail inflation stood at 5.54% in September and food inflation at 7.74%, according to figures cited by LocalCircles. Higher everyday expenses left households with less room for purchases. LocalCircles founder Sachin Taparia said, “Household earnings are not rising, and inflation continues to rise.” He also pointed to concerns over AI and its potential effect on white-collar jobs, along with a lack of attractive deals on online commerce platforms. Discounts may also have done less to persuade shoppers to buy. The Economic Times reported that festive discounts were 35-40% lower than last year. The report also cited price increases of 30-40% for premium electronics in recent months. Smartphone Sales Exposed The Limits of Online Traffic Smartphones provided one of the clearest indications of the pressure on high-value purchases. Counterpoint Research’s early assessment found that smartphone sales fell 16% YoY during the first three days of Amazon’s and Flipkart’s festive sales, despite strong traffic on both platforms. The research firm had initially forecast a 12% decline in festive smartphone volumes. Its early assessment suggested that the fall could be steeper, although the figures available in the supporting documents did not establish the final full-season outcome. Counterpoint’s report identified higher device prices and fewer direct discounts as factors weighing on demand. Brands relied more on no-cost EMIs, bank cashback and exchange offers to make upgrades affordable without cutting listed prices sharply. Premium Samsung models, including the Galaxy S25 Ultra and the S25 FE, found buyers, but their performance did not prevent the overall decline in smartphone sales during the opening days. Entry-level devices faced greater pressure because even discounted models were generally more expensive than a year ago. “We had projected a 12% decline in smartphone sales, but based on the first wave of festive sales, we would not be surprised if the decline deepens to around 16%. Platforms have seen strong traffic, but conversions have been weak. Premium smartphones, however, continue to sell well, which could support revenue despite pressure on volumes,” Tarun Pathak, Research Director at Counterpoint Research. Counterpoint also noted that the opening days fell during Pitru Pakha, when some consumers in North India traditionally defer purchases. Navratri began on October 11, after the initial sales period, leaving the full festive effect on offline demand to pay out later. With the online sales campaigns now over, the early figures underline the difficulty retailers faced in converting strong digital engagement into higher-value purchases. Overall, with household budgets under pressure, rising product prices and fewer compelling discounts, shoppers appear to be prioritising essentials and selective purchases over expensive upgrades this festive season. Yash has explained why he is focusing on big-budget films and projects with a global reach, with co-star Sai Pallavi sharing a conversation that offered insight into his approach to filmmaking. During the making of Ramayana, Sai Pallavi asked Yash whether he would consider returning to the small, intimate love stories he worked on earlier in his career. His response highlighted his ambition to take Kannada and Indian cinema to a wider audience.
Yash on choosing big-budget films over small love stories: “I have the opportunity”
“I asked Yash if he’ll ever come back to making small cute love stories,” Sai Pallavi said. “He said, ‘I want to make my films big because I have the opportunity, and at the same time, I want to present Kannada and my South Indian and Indian cinema to the world.'”
Sai Pallavi shared the conversation during promotional events for Ramayana in Hyderabad. Her account comes as Yash continues to explore projects that aim to reach audiences beyond regional markets. The actor, who established himself in the Kannada film industry through a mix of romantic dramas, comedies and action entertainers, has increasingly taken on large-scale productions.
Before the KGF franchise brought him nationwide recognition, Yash appeared in films such as Googly, Mr and Mrs Ramachari and Kirataka. These projects helped establish his position in Kannada cinema, with stories largely rooted in romance, family relationships and everyday experiences.
His career took a different turn with KGF: Chapter 1, directed by Prashanth Neel. Conceived as a Pan-Indian film, it expanded Yash’s reach beyond Karnataka. The sequel, KGF: Chapter 2, went on to become a blockbuster, further strengthening his presence across the Indian film industry.
Following the success of the KGF franchise, Yash took up Toxic: A Fairy Tale for Grown-Ups, directed by Geetu Mohandas. Yash is also part of Ramayana and he is co-producing the film through his banner, Monster Mind Creations.
In Ramayana, Yash plays Ravana, while Sai Pallavi portrays Sita and Ranbir Kapoor plays Rama. Directed by Nitesh Tiwari, the film is being produced by Namit Malhotra’s Prime Focus Studios in collaboration with DNEG and Monster Mind Creations.
The film is scheduled to have its world premiere at the Academy Museum in Los Angeles on October 27, ahead of its worldwide theatrical release on November 5. Yash’s comments, as recounted by Sai Pallavi, underline his stated intention to use large-scale productions to introduce Kannada and Indian cinema to audiences around the world.

Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
- Published
Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease.
A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said.
Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added.
All the cases were within "one cluster, with no evidence of community spread", the ministry said.
More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease.
Kenya's latest victim was a "direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms" on 13 October, the health ministry said.
The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later.
Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner.
The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert.
Ebola is a rare but deadly disease, external caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding.
The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit.
The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment - though trials are under way.
With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread.
Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic.
Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival.
Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases.
Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital.
It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.

Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way.
He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus.
"We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending," Pate said.
Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria's first case crossed paths with Kenya's first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda's Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.

After a special executive magistrate court released CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka on October 11 after a one-day preventive detention, several pro-BJP social media handles claimed that the trio had been granted bail on the condition that they would not take part in any protest for a period of one year. Those making such claims included retired Major Manik M Jolly, Right wing Wire, and BJP-supporting troll handle RiseOfBurnol.
Subsequently, a copy of an alleged bond began circulating on social media, bearing the name of Abhijit Dipke and the seal of the executive magistrate of New Delhi district.
It was claimed that this Dipke had signed the bond at the time of his release. BJP leader Radhika Khera shared a photo of the said bond while quoting an X post in which Dipke had claimed that he had not signed any such bond.
Sharing this picture, Facebook user Riju Dutta, who claims to be a ‘politician’, took a dig at Dipke, remarking that these people are supposedly revolutionaries.
Several users shared the same image on social media platforms.
Fact Check
We first checked Delhi Police’s official X handle. In their post, Police stated that Deepke, Ranka and Das were placed under ‘preventive arrest’ on October 10, 2026, and were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, 2026. “A bond of ₹50,000 was furnished to ensure the maintenance of peace and good behavior for one year, and the Special Executive Magistrate Court released them.”
Preventive arrest u/s 126/170 BNSS of Sh. Abhijeet Dipke, Sh. Ashutosh Ranka and Sh. Saurav Das was done on 10.10.2026. All due legal procedures were followed and they were produced before the SEM Court, Delhi Cantt on 11.10.2026.
A bail bond as Surety Bond of ₹50,000/- was filled for maintaining peace and good behaviour, for a period of one year, and they were released by the SEM Court.
— Delhi Police (@DelhiPolice) October 11, 2026
Nowhere in this police statement was it mentioned that their release was conditional on Dipke or the other leaders not participating in any protest for one year. There is also no mention of Dhruv Rathee in the statement.
In other words, police did not state that Rathee was required to sign a bond. The YouTuber himself refuted the viral claim on his X account, stating that he did not sign any bond or undertaking to secure his release.
I did not sign any bond
I did not sign any undertaking
I did not sign any condition for release
For all the media houses ^
— Dhruv Rathee (@dhruv_rathee) October 11, 2026
Examining the viral document clearly, we noticed several discrepancies:
- According to the police statement, the three individuals were produced before the special executive magistrate (SEM) court, Delhi Cantt, on October 11, whereas the alleged bond bears the date of October 10.
- The SEM Court falls under the South West district of Delhi, while the alleged bond mentions the New Delhi district.
- The spelling of “Satyamev Jayate” in the center of the Executive Magistrate’s seal on the alleged bond is incorrect.
We checked the image using OpenAI’s ‘Verify OpenAI-generated content’ tool, which revealed that it was created with the help of AI.
Advocate Sautik Banerjee, who appeared for Deepke, Das and Ranka in the SEM court, told the media that the magistrate had not imposed any conditions on them. They were released on a personal bond with one surety.
Delhi: On the SEM Court releasing CJP leaders Abhijeet Dipke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Saurav Das, advocate Soutik Banerjee says, “The magistrate has not imposed any conditions on them. They have been released on a personal bond with one surety” https://t.co/UI6OgPt2nL
— IANS (@ians_india) October 11, 2026
Speaking to Alt News, Banerjee explained, “Breach of peace refers only to activities that are not sanctioned by the Constitution and do not enjoy protection as fundamental rights. If the Constitution grants the freedom of speech and expression, the right to form associations and hold assemblies, or the freedom of movement, then restrictions can be imposed on these rights only within the scope of ‘reasonable restrictions’ that are rational. As the Supreme Court has repeatedly stated, peaceful protests are permitted, and one is always free to organize or participate in them; this cannot, under any circumstances, be considered a breach of peace.”
Sautik Banerjee sent us a bail bond format from the special executive magistrate (West District), Delhi, which looks entirely different from the document in the viral image.
Overall, the claim that Sourav Das, Abhijit Deepke, Ashutosh Ranka, and Dhruv Rathee were released on the condition that they would not participate in any protests for a year is false. Furthermore, the image of the bail bond bearing Abhijit Deepke’s name, which was shared by several individuals, including BJP leader Radhika Khera, was generated using AI.

NASA does not have, nor want, nuclear weapons. But when it comes to a particular metric that is part of the Artemis Program to land people on the Moon, NASA guards a particular number like they are trying to prevent outsiders from cracking nuclear codes.
I am speaking of the number of Starship launches required to fuel a Starship-based lunar lander in low-Earth orbit such that it can fly out to the Moon, land there, and return to lunar orbit.
This number has been a moving target over the years. The general response from NASA has typically been, ‘We don’t know for sure, so we’re not going to say.’ In 2023, for example, the then-director of NASA’s Human Landing System, Lisa Watson-Morgan, told Ars, “We have a general idea, but I’m reluctant to say exactly what that is.”
Later, she said the number was in the “high single digits to the low double digits.” That suggests about a dozen launches, which is a lot. SpaceX would need to launch a “depot” Starship, and then 11 “tanker” Starships to fully load it with liquid oxygen and methane propellant for a lunar voyage. Other officials have said “high teens.” The hope has always been that SpaceX would dramatically improve the lift capacity of Starship to bring down the number of tanker flights.
But now there are concerns among some NASA officials that this might not be happening, or at least not happening soon enough to allow SpaceX’s Starship rocket to play a meaningful role in returning humans to the Moon for NASA as part of Artemis this decade.
A new estimate emerges
On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon.

India condemns ‘heinous’ attack that killed 8 in Jordan church, reaffirms ‘fight against terrorism’
External affairs minister S Jaishankar said India stood with the government and people of Jordan during the difficult hour.
India strongly condemned the deadly shooting at a church in Jordan’s Karak that killed eight people and injured 34 others on Friday. Ministry of external affairs (MEA) spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal expressed condolences to the victims’ families on Saturday as he reiterated India's fight against terrorism.
“India unequivocally condemns the heinous attack at a church in Karak, Jordan on 23rd October 2026, which resulted in the tragic loss of several innocent lives and injuries to many others,” Jaiswal shared a statement by the MEA on X.
He extended condolences to the bereaved families and wished those injured a speedy recovery. He also reaffirmed India’s solidarity with the Jordanian government and people. “We also reaffirm our strong commitment to the fight against terrorism in all its forms and manifestations,” the statement read.
Jaishankar condemns attack
External affairs minister S Jaishankar also condemned the shooting. On X, Jaishankar said India stood firmly with the government and people of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan during the difficult hour.
"Deeply shocked at the heinous attack at a Church in Karak, Jordan yesterday, which resulted in the tragic loss of several innocent lives and injuries to many others. Our heartfelt condolences to the bereaved families and wish a swift recovery to those injured.
India stands firmly with the government and the friendly people of the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan in this difficult hour. We also reaffirm our strong commitment to the fight against terrorism in all its forms and manifestations," he wrote on X.
Gunmen open fire during funeral
Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church in Karak, around 180 kilometres south of Jordan’s capital, Amman, on Friday. The attack initially left seven people dead and around 40 injured, the Associated Press reported. Reuters later updated the death toll to eight.
Footage aired on Jordanian state television reportedly showed two gunmen approaching the church and firing pistols. A third individual, apparently carrying a semiautomatic rifle, was then seen opening fire. All three were subsequently seen moving towards the church.
Authorities said the search for the attackers was ongoing. They added that it was too early to establish whether the assailants had links to any known groups inside or outside Jordan. No group has so far claimed responsibility for the attack, Reuters reported.
Jordan vows tough action
Jordan’s King Abdullah II strongly condemned the attack and vowed to confront the “terrorist act” targeting Karak with the harshest penalties. He also offered condolences to the victims’ families and wished those injured a speedy recovery, AP reported.
The shooting drew condemnation from several countries across the region, including Lebanon, Syria, Egypt and Oman. Iraq also expressed solidarity with Jordan and reaffirmed its support for the country in its fight against terrorism.

US’s top group of OB-GYNs release first-ever rules for GLP-1 use and pregnancy
The percentage of new mothers receiving prescriptions for the drugs has leapt in the past seven years

New, first-of-their-kind guidelines are advising pregnant women and new moms about how to safely use GLP-1 weight loss and diabetes drugs.
The guidelines aim to help OB-GYNs, who have seen GLP-1-use surge in the U.S. in recent years but lacked comprehensive instruction on whether or not to recommend the drugs.
Women should forgo taking GLP-1 drugs during pregnancy, according to the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists guidelines published Friday.
Doctors should recommend women stop taking the medications one to two months before they plan to get pregnant, the guidelines stated.
But taking the shots might be okay while breastfeeding, after a baby’s first month, the nation’s leading organization for obstetricians and gynecologists notes.
While as many as 1 in 300 women are exposed to the drugs before pregnancy, lead author Dr. D. Yvette LaCoursiere said, there still isn’t enough data to know what effects the medication could have on a pregnancy or a fetus.
“This is a fast-moving area of research, so for now we need to proceed with caution and reassess as more data becomes available,” the University of California, San Diego professor explained in a statement.
The guidelines aren’t necessarily an endorsement of taking a GLP-1 while breastfeeding, either, LaCoursiere told The Wall Street Journal. They support having a discussion with a healthcare provider.
“We know that GLP-1s have an impact on caloric and nutrient absorption. How does that impact the breast milk? We don’t know,” she said.
“I think this guideline allows providers to follow the data as they are released and have a discussion with their patients so that they can make a decision,” LaCoursiere added.
New moms’ use of GLP-1s
The guidelines follow research released earlier this month showing more new moms are taking GLP-1s in the U.S.
The percentage of new mothers receiving prescriptions for the drugs saw a 24-fold increase over the course of seven years from 2018-2025, researchers at the University of Southern California said.
The majority of Americans are now taking the drugs for weight loss, instead of to treat diabetes or other health conditions, a survey published Thursday by Boston consulting group EY-Parthenon showed.
Effects of the drugs postpartum have not been studied widely. The new guidelines do not say if and when postpartum women should take the drugs if they did not qualify for a prescription before their pregnancy. The guidelines will be updated as research evolves, the authors said.
Preliminary research suggests GLP-1s aren’t likely to show up in breast milk, though the guidelines say people who are breastfeeding should avoid oral forms of the drugs.
And taking the drugs during the first trimester of pregnancy does not appear to substantially increase the risk of adverse outcomes, a June study from the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health found.
However, the study doesn’t shed light on the safety of GLP-1 use after that period.

The Port Adelaide AFL club has said it will honour Daniel Stewart at the first home game of 2027 after the former Power forward's death at the age of 37.
Stewart, who played 36 games and kicked 31 goals for Port Adelaide between 2010 and 2013, died suddenly yesterday.
The tall key forward was drafted by the Power in the 2009 rookie draft and promoted to the senior list at the end of that season.
Originally from Victoria, Stewart was recruited from SANFL team North Adelaide after playing for the Eastern Ranges and AFL Queensland club Labrador.
His best AFL return came in the final round of 2010 at Docklands against Richmond, where Stewart kicked four goals in a 10-point win for the Power.
"On behalf of everyone at the Port Adelaide Football Club, I extend our deepest condolences to Daniel's family including his mum Donna, dad Byron, wife Laura, his two sons Bernie and Lando and his brother Leigh," Port Adelaide chief executive Matthew Richardson said in a statement.
"We also extend our thoughts to his friends, including his close friend and former teammate Matt Thomas, and to all those at North Adelaide and Labrador who knew him.
"Daniel was part of the Port Adelaide football family, and he always will be. A sudden passing like this is devastating and our thoughts are with everyone who loved him, and with the teammates, coaches and staff who shared the journey with him here at Alberton.
"The club will provide support to those affected by Daniel's passing, including his former teammates and the people who worked alongside him."
The club stated it would honour Stewart by wearing black armbands at their first home game at Adelaide Oval next season.

On October 12, the Centre informed the Supreme Court that it had decided to cap trade margins at 30% for anti-cancer medicines. The Bench of Justices Vikram Nath and Sandeep Mehta questioned why similar restrictions could not be extended to other medicines and medical products. Citing steep differences between the prices at which products were supplied and those charged to patients, the court asked the government to work out broader measures for regulating medicine prices. The matter is scheduled to be heard again on October 27.
While high trade margins are not necessarily illegal, overcharging beyond regulated prices violates the Drugs (Prices Control) Orders (DPCO), which govern medicine pricing in India. Both, however, raise questions about the costs borne by patients. The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA), the government’s drug-price regulator, continues to pursue companies over past cases of overcharging. Although established in 1997, the NPPA’s records cover cases dating back to 1979. As of March 31, 2026, ₹10,029.8 crore had been demanded, including interest. Under the 2013 Order, certain pricing violations can also attract penalties. Of the total demanded, ₹1,582.4 crore had been realised, leaving ₹8,447.4 crore outstanding. The NPPA notes that the figures are subject to reconciliation.
The scale of the issue matters because medicines make up a significant share of household hospitalisation costs. According to the National Statistics Office’s Household Social Consumption: Health survey, conducted in 2025, medicine expenditure averaged ₹6,368 per hospitalisation case in rural areas, out of a total of ₹32,884. This accounted for 19.4% of the total. In urban areas, medicine expenditure averaged ₹6,948 out of ₹46,774 per hospitalisation case, accounting for 14.9%.
However, when hospitals charged a single package price and households could not specify expenditure on individual items, the amount was recorded as a lump sum under the ‘package component’. Since these packages may include medicines, the actual share of hospitalisation costs spent on medicines could be higher than the separately reported figures of nearly 20% in rural areas and 15% in urban areas.
NPPA’s recovery record
The outstanding amount is more than five times the amount realised and accounts for about 84% of the cumulative demand. Moreover, these figures cover only cases in which the NPPA has raised demands against companies for overcharging. They do not include cases that may have gone undetected or have not been pursued by the regulator.
The NPPA’s year-wise data show that the number of cases has varied considerably between 2009-10 and 2025-26. The highest count in this period was 268 cases in 2015-16, followed by 224 in 2017-18. The number fell to 38 in 2020-21 before rising to 148 in 2022-23. In 2025-26, the regulator recorded 133 cases.
The annual entries add up to approximately ₹5,265 crore in demands, including interest, of which about ₹4,460 crore remained outstanding and ₹805 crore had been realised. For the period before 2009, the NPPA recorded 731 cases, with ₹4,764.75 crore demanded and ₹3,987.5 crore outstanding. The amount realised refers to recoveries against demands raised in these financial-year cohorts, not necessarily money collected during the respective years, as recoveries may take place later.
Outstanding amounts were highest in 2015-16, at ₹1,003.3 crore, followed by ₹576 crore in 2017-18. In 2025-26, ₹45.1 crore remained outstanding against a demand of ₹72.2 crore.
Of the total outstanding amount, More than ₹5,800 crore is tied up in litigation, including cases referred to Collectors and contested by companies in court. Another ₹200 crore relates to cases referred to Collectors for recovery, while ₹2,369.3 crore remains under process.
Importantly, recovering money from pharmaceutical companies is distinct from compensating patients who paid higher prices. In a Lok Sabha reply on July 23, 2019, the Department of Pharmaceuticals stated that “there is no mechanism to compensate the consumers for the amount overcharged.” However, the NPPA accepts complaints from consumers and other stakeholders through its Pharma Jan Samadhan portal and the Pharma Sahi Daam app. Complaints can relate to medicine overpricing, shortages or non-availability, new drugs being sold without prior price approval, and refusal to supply or sell medicines. The regulator examines complaints and takes appropriate action where warranted.
Source: The National Pharmaceutical Pricing Authority (NPPA) and NSS Report no. 596: Household Social Consumption: Health (2025)

Peak on consoles, hockey roguelites and other new indie games worth checking out
Plus, Steam Next Fest, food-based horror games and a bunch of Dispatch updates.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
Welcome to our latest roundup of what's going on in the indie game space. There are some neat new games you can play this weekend and we'll take a look at a few that are on the way. However, much of the attention this week is on Steam Next Fest. The latest edition of the event, which includes thousands of demos, runs until Monday.
The week ran away from me, so I haven't played too many demos yet. I did enjoy playing a chunk of Emberville recently, and the whole prologue's now available for you to dive into. Progress carries over into the full game, which is out on October 27.
I absolutely had to carve out time to check out the demo for Golden Retriever Simple Life, which I've had on my wishlist since I first saw it last year. This is an FMV life sim in which you take care of a golden retriever named Pichu. The demo runs for a week of in-game time, during which you'll feed, pet, play with, train and go on adventures with this very good boy. Mechanically, it's pretty light, but I absolutely do not care because this game is utterly lovely so far. I can't wait to play the full thing in February.
I'm planning to check out other demos this weekend, including one of the big hits of this edition of Next Fest, the cyberpunk shopkeeping sim Probably Stolen. Also on my to-do list are the Backrooms-style puzzler Geodyssey, propeller plane schmup Iron Skies, 2D Metroidvania with no jump button Moonbrella and comedy game My Arms Are Longer Now, in which you pull off heists with a very long arm.
On the news front, there was an ID@Xbox Showcase this week, along with one from Critical Reflex. The former included release dates for A Game About Digging A Hole Together (December 4) and Mouthwashing on consoles (October 29), as well as a release window (March) for Croak, a platformer I've had on my radar for a while.
As well as platform updates, demo announcements and something we'll get to later, Critical Reflex Time included two wild game reveals. In the surreal RPG amFM, you'll hop between dimensions and create machines to defeat your enemies. To survive in Keykruncher, your character has to eat keyboards. Gosh, I love indie games, don't you?
New indie game releases
Peak
Developer: Team Peak
Publisher: Aggro Crab, Evil Landfall?
Platforms: PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Nintendo Switch 2. Already on Steam
Price: $10
One of the biggest indie hits of 2025 is now on consoles. Co-op climbing game Peak is a collaboration between developers from Aggro Crab (Another Crab's Treasure) and Landfall (Content Warning). Players work together to ascend mountains with layouts that change every day. Peak blends survival and chaos to great effect, and it has a terrific canvas for viral, funny moments. It's mostly about friends helping (and sometimes hindering) friends, and the inclusion of cross-play should help with that.
When Peak debuted on Steam last year, it cost $8, though an initial discount to $5 helped it take off — it has now sold more than 23 million copies. The console versions will run you $10, however.
Nick Kaman, one of Peak's developers, told Game File the team has doubled how much content is in the game since its initial release, "which necessitates that we double the perceived cost of the game from 5 bucks to 10 bucks, even though the game price for consoles is only literally going up by 2 bucks. If we were really smart we'd go to 12 bucks which is basically 10 bucks, but we decided to have mercy."
Tape to Tape
Developer/publisher: Excellent Rectangle
Platform: Steam (Windows; Steam Deck Verified; leaving early access), PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch
Price: Usually $20, with a 10 percent discount on Steam until October 30
Tape to Tape is an arcade hockey roguelite in which you'll unlock abilities, players and other upgrades that will help you on your quest to stop a team of "evil golfers" from destroying one of Canada's national sports. Those scoundrels!
After choosing a squad (each of which has its own rules and playstyle), you'll take on an array of opponents that includes a soccer team and "farting princesses." You can find synergies between abilities that could help make your team feel unstoppable. It's hockey, so you'll get into fights too. Your buds might be able to help out, as here's co-op support for up to 10 local players.
Until this week, Tape to Tape had been in early access since 2023. The developers say they've upgraded the audio and visuals, revamped the campaign, and improved gameplay mechanics.
I much prefer arcade sports games to sims, so I might give this a bash. Also, I adore the name of the developer, Excellent Rectangle. That's a killer Parks and Recreation reference.
Mycopunk
Developer: Pigeons at Play
Publisher: Devolver Digital
Platforms: Steam (Windows; leaving early access), PS5
Price: Usually $15, with a 50 percent discount on Steam until November 3. Also on PlayStation Plus Extra and Premium
I've played a few missions in Mycopunk, a stylish co-op looter shooter. I dig the grungy, Moebius-inspired art direction and the fast, frenetic action. The gist is that you're helping to wipe out a fungus that's taken over a planet. The infected enemies are modular, so there's some strategy involved as you try to focus on certain parts you want to disable first. However, you'll need to account for other baddies, as they can pick up and use dropped weapons.
I really like the weapon upgrade grid, as it offers many ways to experiment with off-the-wall builds. There are lots of other smart, thoughtful touches here, including a hub that's actually fun to explore and mess around in. Mycopunk doesn't quite feel sticky enough for it to slot into my regular rotation just yet, but I've flown solo thus far. Maybe it'll feel different if I can pull a squad together and jump in with them.
Cucina Stellata
Developer: Filthy Eden
Publisher: Critical Reflex
Platform: Steam (Windows; Steam Deck Verified)
Price: Free
Perhaps you're trying to save cash for the next Steam sale or a certain blockbuster that's out on consoles next month, but you're looking for something new and scary to play in the run up to Halloween. Cucina Stellata might check the boxes, especially because it's free. It was announced and released during the Critical Reflex Time showcase.
This is a short psychological horror game set in the Italian countryside in the 19th century. The trailer doesn't give too much away of the game's scary side outside of some squelchy sound effects, but the cooking aspect looks interesting. If you'd like to support the developer, there's a $5 "supporter pack" DLC. It offers illustrations as well as recipes from Cucina Stellata that you can put together IRL.
Grease Trap '99
Developer/publisher: James Muirhead
Platform: Steam (Windows)
Price: Usually $5, with a 10 percent discount until November 4
Here's a good reason why it's smart for developers to promote their games in every relevant space they can think of. I found out about Grease Trap '99 after its creator posted about it in r/Scotland on Reddit this week. I'm glad James Muirhead did that, because this game looks right up my street.
It's a horror mystery with a dash of comedy that takes place in a fish and chip shop in the Scottish Highlands. At first glance, the setting looks like every "chippie" I frequented while I was growing up, but here something is growing beneath the floor. It's up to you to deduce what's what. Grease Trap '99 has retro, low-poly visuals and it's a short game that should take less than an hour to complete. It's fully voice-acted in Gaelic, which I speak maybe two words of. There are English subtitles, thankfully, so I plan to eat this one up.
Upcoming indie games
Dispatch
Publisher/developer: AdHoc Studio
Platforms: iOS, Android. Already on Steam, Switch, Switch 2, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Xbox on PC, Luna
Release date: December 9
Price: $20, though the first four episodes are free on mobile
AdHoc Studio had lots of Dispatch news to share for the game's first anniversary, including the mobile release date. The superhero workplace comedy from ex-Telltale Games developers now has a commentary mode (with 16 hours of cast and crew commentary) and an option to play the entire game with storyboard animatics. Those modes are available as part of the deluxe edition. You can upgrade to that from the standard edition for $11.
Elsewhere, a one-off concert of music from the game will take place in Los Angeles on December 3. A hardcover art book from Lost in Cult is on the way too.
Faraway
Developer: Steph Thirion
Publisher: Annapurna Interactive
Platforms: Steam, Epic Games Store, PS5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch
Release date: November 5
Price: $10
I first learned of Faraway during a Day of the Devs showcase in December 2024, but it had been in the works for many years by that point. Developer Steph Thirion announced it for the iPhone in 2010. I'm glad it's almost here, even if it's arriving during an incredibly dense slate of game releases.
This is a procedurally generated arcade game. You take control of a shooting star that connects stars into a constellation and draws energy from them to keep going. It's said to be easy to pick up, but hard to master as you swing from one star to the next. I love the aesthetic, and I'm hoping Thirion has found a fine balance between making the game relaxing and challenging.
Payday: Aces High
Developer/publisher: Fast Travel Games
Platforms: Steam (SteamVR), Meta Quest
Release date: November 5
Price: $25
Out on the same day as Faraway is something entirely different, a Payday spinoff. Up to four players can squad up in this first-person shooter and carry out heists. After you assemble your crew, you can plan out the job, gear up and then try to sneak your way to the loot (and back out undetected) or go in all guns blazing.
As you might imagine, you'll be able to expand your inventory and unlock new skills by spending cash. There are four characters to choose from, each named after an ace in a deck of cards (hence the title). They have distinct specialties, ranging from planning missions to taking charge of gadgets. You don't necessarily need to wait until next month to jump into Payday: Aces High, as the final playtest is live on both Steam and Quest until October 26.
Nyra and the Garden of Moros
Developer/publisher: Resting Relic
Platform: Steam
This trailer popped up a little too late for me to include in last week's edition, but I wanted to mention it. Nyra and the Garden of Moros is an open-world action adventure from solo developer Joe Winter. It looks heavily inspired by Shadow of the Colossus, but that's not a complaint. I think there should be more games about clambering all over giant beasts.
In order to lock a god of doom back up and cure a curse that's taking over the world, Nyra must overcome a dozen of these creatures. It's up to you whether to take them down or opt for a more difficult approach to cleanse and save these Keepers. Nyra gets around the world with the help of Rama, a wolf companion inspired by Winter's late husky. The developer also drew inspiration from his wife's strength and compassion while creating Nyra.

Get your daily dose of health and medicine every weekday with STAT’s free newsletter Morning Rounds. Sign up here.
As I pondered potential Halloween costumes, I was particularly tickled by an Instagram influencer dressed up as Elizabeth Holmes dressed up as Karen from Mean Girls (both of whom have been played by Amanda Seyfried). Send me your punny costume ideas, though no “You Can See Everything” spoilers until tomorrow.
Medicaid’s messy work requirements
Yesterday, I was in the Boston federal courthouse for a hearing on a case filed by two dozen states challenging the implementation of new Medicaid work requirements. The arguments presented echo a lot of other legal challenges to the administration’s health policy decisions.
The states argued that health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. exceeded his authority in determining who qualifies for exemptions to the work requirement, and that the way the rule was implemented is arbitrary and capricious (an argument that has also been used to challenge the administration’s vaccine policy changes and research grant terminations). The DOJ, in turn, said Congress’s writing of HR1 afforded Kennedy the latitude to make the determinations. The judge left the courtroom after an “interesting morning” saying he would rule in the coming weeks.
While I was in court, Isa Cueto was at a conference of the National Association of Medicaid Directors, taking the temperature of the people responsible for implementing those sweeping changes in just about 70 days. The vibes were frantic, she writes in a story with O. Rose Broderick. Part of the confusion lies with the fact that the midterm elections could change the makeup of Congress, which could lead to new policies or pauses. So, too, could the aforementioned lawsuit making its way through the court. The mood of the room was “very anxious,” one staffer told Isa.
A top MAHA adviser is leaving the White House
A top MAHA adviser to Kennedy is departing the Trump administration, reportedly over frustrations that the implementation of some of Kennedy’s initiatives were being stalled. Calley Means initially joined the administration to work with Kennedy at the Department of Health and Human Services, but more recently moved to a position at the White House.
“The past two years have seen historic policy and cultural change to confront the chronic disease crisis and healthcare incentives that profit from us being sick. This movement is in the first inning and just getting started,” he told Chelsea Cirruzzo. His departure just days before the midterms adds to the questions swirling around MAHA’s salience to the electorate. You may also want to revisit this profile by Isa about Means and his sister Casey (who was nominated for surgeon general before having her nomination pulled), which served as my introduction to the Meanses before they rose to MAHA royalty.
80%
That’s the percent of Americans who support an ultra-processed food labeling policy, according to an Annenberg Public Policy Center survey released yesterday.
And coincidentally, STATs Sarah Todd has a story on such a policy making its way through the Trump administration. Officials had scheduled an event in August to announce a proposed definition of ultra-processed foods, but cancelled it at the last minute. Now, more than 80 nutrition experts are signing a petition for the White House to release its definition.
The Food is Medicine Institute at Tufts University, led by cardiologist Dariush Mozaffarian, is scheduled to meet with the Office of Management and Budget on Friday to present the petition. Mozaffarian said that HHS wants to release a definition before the midterms, in part to notch a victory for the MAHA movement amid their aforementioned angst.
Data on Merck and Moderna’s personalized cancer vaccine leaked ahead of ESMO
Our colleagues Drew and Adam are on the ground in Madrid for the European Society of Medical Oncology conference. Things are off to a quick start: an oncology news site published eagerly anticipated data from Merck and Moderna’s personalized cancer vaccine trial two days before it was scheduled to be presented. The leaked numbers sent Moderna’s stock price tumbling 24%, even though the findings were generally good.
The site removed the report, and ESMO subsequently released the data, which Janice Mehnert, professor of medicine at NYU Grossman School of Medicine and an investigator in the INTerpath-001 study, told STAT was “very satisfying.” Beyond Adam’s story, you can revisit Jason Mast’s write up of a panel with Merck and Moderna from our STAT Summit last week, and sign up for our ESMO newsletter.
A new Huntington’s drug shows promising results
Alnylam Pharmaceuticals announced the results of a small but promising study, suggesting that its experimental drug for Huntington’s disease can partially silence the mutant gene that drives the neurological disorder. Huntington’s is the result of a three-letter repeat, and researchers have spent years attempting to lower the levels of the RNA and protein this gene produces. Several drugs have failed, and while the new drug from Alnylam seems to lower levels of that protein, it’s unclear if that will ultimately slow disease progression.
Jeff Carroll, an investigator at the Allen Institute who was not involved in the study, said the reduction in mutant huntingtin “looks great,” and “the safety signals so far look as good or better than” other similar drugs. Read more from Jason Mast and Elaine Chen here.
‘You Can See Everything’ that STAT has been thinking about this new movie
Lastly, a fun one to send you off into the weekend. It seems like everyone is talking about “You Can See Everything.” And as you can imagine, our staff had BIG feelings about the movie.
So resident cinematographer Alex Hogan brought together five of our colleagues to talk about the movie. “I’ve never seen anything quite like it,” he reports from outside his local AMC. Do watch his hourlong debrief of the movie (which I only started to avoid spoilers).

Melania Trump says she has secured a ceasefire for a Ukrainian city that was until now cut off from the world and facing starvation.
The Russian-occupied city of Oleshky is located at the frontline and is made up of 2,000 residents who have faced an ongoing blockade restricting food and aid.
But the First Lady said on Friday that Russia has agreed to pause all military action in the town to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway, according to the White House.
The localised ceasefire is set to begin on 29 October.
“The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a frontline war city on the brink of disaster,” she said. “Oleshky’s remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, medicine, food, and clean water.
“The people of Oleshky have limited electricity, live amid mined roads, and endure regular military attacks. It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible.”
Melania and her representative are said to have worked directly with both Russian and Ukrainian leadership in order to define the terms of the agreement.
“Non-military civilian leaders from both countries will work together to visit Oleshky residents in their homes and determine the level of assistance they require,” she said.
”Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination. I anticipate some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine.”
The Kremlin confirmed the agreement on Friday and said they were working on dates to implement the ceasefire.
Kyiv’s human rights ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets told Reuters that the First Lady’s personal involvement made the humanitarian mission in Oleshky possible. He said that Ukraine is working to expand the mission to other settlements.
Lubinets added that the multi-staged mission will involve de-mining the roads to Oleshky, organising food deliveries and evacuations.
According to the United Nations Human Rights Monitoring Mission, the area was one of many frontline communities in Kherson that have faced food shortages and interrupted aid.
“People can’t get out, food can’t get in, and sick and injured are not getting the medical assistance they need,” said Danielle Bell, Head of HRMMU in June.
Residents said that the town’s last grocery store had stopped operating back in January.
The news follows weeks of discontent between the Ukrainian and American leadership, with both President Donald Trump and Volodymyr Zelensky taking shots at each other in public statements.
Tensions escalated when Trump agreed to lift sanctions on Russia in order for Vladimir Putin to export diesel globally. Around the same time, Ukraine reported restrictions to its military-grade Starlink terminals.
SpaceX billionaire Elon Musk claimed that the decision to limit the use of the satellite service was down to the US government and Trump. However, it was later reported by the Wall Street Journal that Musk had ordered the restriction.
On Thursday, Zelensky said that full service was yet to be restored while Trump reported that Musk had ensured it was up and running again.
On Friday, Trump said that he had not spoken to the X owner but told reporters that he would fix any Starlink issue in Ukraine.
US-brokered talks had been taking place before Trump and Israel chose to launch a war on Iran, which has largely stalled discussions. Trilateral discussions are set to continue next month.

Can Trump block the Alaska Senate election?
Why the DOJ is suing over two Dan Sullivans running for Senate.
Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is getting a head start on litigating the midterms.
What’s happening? The administration is asking a federal district court in Alaska to potentially block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate race, should incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, a Republican, lose to his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola.
It’s the first major lawsuit of the 2026 midterms aimed at directly challenging the results, and very likely a sign of things to come after polls close on November 3.
What is the administration arguing? Sullivan is currently in a close race against Peltola, a former US representative who polls suggest may hold a slight lead. But the race is complicated by the presence of a second Dan Sullivan, Daniel J. Sullivan, on the ballot (no relation).
According to the lawsuit, which names Alaska’s state elections director and several state elections entities as defendants, the election could be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan.”
The suit asks that “Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” which it defines as a loss by the incumbent Sullivan in the event that the other Sullivan attracts enough votes to alter the outcome of the election.
What’s the context? The second Dan Sullivan’s appearance on the ballot has already been litigated. After he was initially disqualified from the ballot, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he should be included, and he finished third in the state’s August primary (the top four vote-getters appear on Alaska’s general election ballot).
How worried about this should I be? For now, not very. Trump filing lawsuits disputing election results was all but inevitable, even if it’s surprising to see him start this early.
None of that means he’ll succeed: Trump and his allies filed dozens of election lawsuits in 2020 and were largely laughed out of court. (Plus, this particular lawsuit has been assigned to a judge appointed by President Barack Obama.)
And with that, it’s time to log off…

Worldwide, traditional medicine is used by billions of people for their health and well-being. At a signing ceremony in Geneva, the Government of India committed US$ 85 million over 10 years, 2022–2032, to support the programming of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre. India’s 10-year financial contribution will support a cross-sectoral program of work to strengthen the evidence base for traditional medicine by providing data and evidence on traditional medicine policies, practice, products, and public use.
The WHO-India donor agreement is part of a US$ 250 million investment from India in support of the establishment of the WHO Global Centre of Traditional Medicine in 2022, which includes financial support for the workplan of the Centre, interim premises and a new building. This support will scale up WHO’s capacities on traditional medicine across technical divisions and regions in the spirit of global collaboration and solidarity. Part of this substantial contribution from the Government of India will also be included in WHO’s Investment Round to resource WHO’s core work during 2025–2028.
Photo: WHO/Lindsay Mackenzie
“India’s commitment and leadership in expanding the evidence-based contribution of traditional medicine to the health and well-being of all people and the planet, comes at an opportune moment,” said Dr Bruce Aylward, Assistant Director-General of the Universal Health Coverage and Life Course division of WHO. “Traditional medicine, supported within national health systems, can allow us to reach those most often left behind. Integration of traditional practice and knowledge is critical to achieving health for all.”
“The signing of this donor agreement is a major milestone towards achieving the shared vision of Honourable Prime Minister of India Shri Narendra Modi and WHO Director-General Tedros for the development of the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre at Jamnagar in India,” said Vice Minister Vaidya Rajesh Kotecha, Secretary of the Ministry of Ayush, Government of India.
“India remains committed to supporting WHO in its work to strengthen traditional medicine systems globally for achieving universal health coverage and serving the entire humanity, especially through this Global Centre in Jamnagar, which would help focus these efforts to benefit all Member States,” said Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, Permanent Representative of India to the UN and other International Organizations in Geneva.
The WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre is is a knowledge hub focusing on five inter-connected areas of work: research and evidence; primary health care and universal health coverage; Indigenous Knowledges and biodiversity; digital health applications; and the biennial WHO Global Traditional Medicine Summit and collaborations. The Centre is led by Dr Shyama Kuruvilla, Director a.i.
The first WHO traditional medicine global summit was held in August 2023 in Gujarat, resulting in the a multistakeholder action agenda, the Gujarat Declaration. The next WHO Global Summit is planned for November 2025, following up on the anticipated launch of the 2025–2034 Global Strategy for Traditional Medicine at the 78th World Health Assembly in May 2025.
India’s support for traditional medicine has been expressed through a variety of long-standing partnerships with WHO. In 2023, India signed a five-year agreement to support the technical work of WHO’s Traditional, Complementary and Integrative Medicine (TCI) unit. The unit is supporting the development of the Member State-requested new WHO traditional medicine global strategy (2025 - 2034), and publishes key benchmark documents, standardized terminologies, and other evidence-informed technical products to support the safe and effective integration of traditional medicine in national health systems.  
The Centre and TCI collaborate closely with teams across WHO to advance WHO’s multisectoral agenda on traditional medicine, including through regular meetings of the WHO Technical Expert Network, coordinated by the WHO Global Traditional Medicine Centre and TCI, to promote a One WHO approach on traditional medicine across headquarters, regional and country office.

Making politics 'fun, trendy, sexy': How Gen Z could shape Kenya's next election
- Published
Ademba Allans is making it "cool" to vote in Kenya.
The student journalist turned civic mobiliser launched a voter registration drive on social media earlier this year, using snappy selfies infused with music and humour to target young people.
The result astonished him and many observers of Kenyan politics – by the time the registration period ended, 2.6 million new voters across the country had signed up. He is aiming to get another 2.3 million on board in the next round.
"It was the Gen Z way of doing politics," he tells me. "Fun, trendy, sexy, fashionable. Because of how we created the hype around it, people had the fear of missing out. Everybody wanted to be involved."
Gen Z, the term used to describe people born in the late 1990s and early 2000s, burst onto the scene two years ago with mass protests that forced the government to retreat on a widely unpopular tax bill. But their victory was followed by a police crackdown that killed and injured dozens of demonstrators.
Now many young Kenyans are planning to move from the street to the ballot box, angry with a political establishment they accuse of corruption and police brutality.
And they have the numbers to make a difference - more than 30% of voting-age Kenyans are younger than 35.
Polls suggest President William Ruto is looking vulnerable.
[The youth] just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created"
But can Gen Z convert a decentralized digital-led rebellion into organised political power?
"These youth-led movements are a wild card, in that they are unpredictable," says political analyst Tom Mboya.
"They don't require much in the way of resources and can pop up at any time. The finance bill protests were political in nature, but the movement has not been tested at an overtly political level. So if they decide to support a candidate, then he's likely to do fairly well."
One of the strengths of the digitally savvy Gen Z activists is that they have been able to mobilise outside the party structures and ethnic allegiances that anchor Kenyan politics.
Allans has been careful not to advocate a particular candidate or party – emphasising leadership rather than politicians, marshalling a new force, he says, outside traditional tribal voting blocs.
"There has never been a case where there is a bloc that is not affiliated to any person or any party. They just want to vote in the right leaders, and this is what we created," he says.
"It's more of a swing vote because you cannot tell who we are going to vote for."
Ruto and his United Democratic Alliance (UDA) are facing strong head winds with less than a year to go before the August 2027 vote.
More than three-quarters of respondents to a survey conducted in June felt the country was moving in the wrong direction, with two-thirds saying their personal economic situation had worsened since Ruto was elected in 2022.
But analysts argue that the president does not necessarily have to be popular to win. He is a master political organiser with the resources of the state, they say.
Ruto's political rivals are also fragmented, and it is not yet clear whether they can form a united opposition to take him on.
One man who has captured the attention of many Gen Zs is Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. He has emerged as the leader of a movement called Linda Mwananchi (Protect the Citizen), which is getting strong support from disaffected young people.
Sifuna first caught their attention when he tried to stop police from shooting at protesters who were storming parliament during the 2024 demonstrations.
