  - Published28 April 2025
Now he is championing a "people-led" movement that promotes the protection of human rights and rule of law as enshrined in the constitution.
He has yet to officially declare a run for the presidency, but is already on the road rallying support. The BBC caught up with him on a recent trip to Meru county in central Kenya, a region that voted strongly for Ruto in the last election.
"Young people want us to create an environment where everybody feels that they can compete fairly," he told me before starting out on his raucous road show.
"We need to absolutely dismantle the system so that everybody has a fair chance at life, a fair chance at education, a fair chance at employment, and the opportunities to grow themselves.
"This election in 2027 is when this theory that the young people are advancing will be put to the test," he said. "Our challenge as a leadership is to ensure you have a compelling message that then encourages people to come out, let them see the vision for the new country."
Ruto also had a compelling vision for the country when he came to power in 2022.
He promised to transform the economy from the bottom up, with a focus on lifting the marginalised. His government has since introduced changes including landmark reforms that widen access to public healthcare, but many young people felt betrayed by his austerity measures and tax hikes.
"I'm here to participate in a revolution change that we want a new Kenyan youth leader who knows the common problems that are facing the young people," 23-year-old Brandon Muremi told the BBC.
I found him in a relatively quiet corner of the final stop in a hectic day of a "rolling rally" – Sifuna's convoy visited four locations, sometimes blocking traffic as he and local politicians climbed on top of their vehicles and delivered rousing speeches at ear-splitting volumes.
They promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths"
"We are looking for a leader who sticks to his plans, not just talking the promises that he makes," agreed Conrad Mutangili, a 19-year-old mechanical engineering student who had come out of curiosity.
"We are looking for somebody who can actually accomplish and actually bring to the people what they are talking about," he said. "Because they promise sweets, but we don't feel any sugar in our mouths."
"We want immediate results," said a 22-year-old computer science student, Yvonne Kileme, acknowledging that the results of government projects may be more long-term. "And one thing that we want as youths is employment, employment, employment, employment."
Ruto argues strongly that his government is delivering jobs, and says the high rate of youth unemployment is a problem that predates his presidency.
He has reached out to Gen Z with various programmes that offer grants and loans to small business and youth-led enterprises, technology hubs and digital work opportunities.
The national youth leader of Ruto's UDA, Kariuki Ngunjiri, told the BBC he was confident of winning the election with an overwhelming majority.
"The president is a listening president and he's been able to now come down to the youth, get what their concerns are, give them jobs, and that has absolutely, even for the party, given us a head start," he said.
"We are not worried about the social media buzz because we are people who actually engage the young people on real, actual, tangible development. What you see mostly on sponsored hashtags and sponsored headlines does not really concern us."
He was speaking as a senior sports official promised to expand the stadium-building programme with another venue, at a packed UDA town hall meeting in Kangema, about 100km (60 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi.
Like so many others, 23-year-old Shintah Mutahi was job hunting.
"I came to listen to what they were saying," she said, "maybe find an opportunity for a job. I think they can give me a chance, they should just be given some time to do that."
John Kiragu, a local UDA youth leader, said he understood the grievances that had driven young people to protest.
"There have been challenges," he said, "but now the government is really trying hard to consolidate the youth. The government is implementing programmes that will really uplift their lives."
Kiragu told me he was involved in a programme to deal with youth alcoholism – a real problem in this region. Many of the young men who attended the morning town hall meeting were already drunk on a cheap local liquor.
The captain of the local football team, Calvin Ware, also turned up to hear the stadium announcement. He said he had heard similar promises many times before, especially before elections, and this one was not going to influence his vote.
"We have already made our mind," he said. "The whole government should go home. We want to build a new Kenya, new youth, new people, fresh people from all over the country, and we are not basing on tribal [allegiances] or anything else. We just want a change, a change, and a change. Nothing else."
As we were speaking, we heard a loud cheer – the event had ended and people were lining up to receive cash handouts – 350 Kenyan shillings, about $3 (£2.20).
It is common practice to pay people to attend political meetings in Kenya, and politicians can use much larger sums to try and influence votes.
"More so than many other parts of the world, money talks in an election here," says political analyst Mboya. "The cost of politics is significantly higher than in other parts of the world."
Less than a year to Kenya's election, it does feel like politics might be changing, that the race could be shaped by youth disillusionment with the political establishment. But while the Gen Z movement has rejected the "old politics" based on ethnic group and money, those have been the building blocks that win elections in Kenya.
Nobody yet knows what the energy of Gen Z voters will mean at the ballot box.

Revival Rugs is turning 9 this month, and evidently, the birthday girl is feeling generous. The rug retailer is taking 20 percent off everything sitewide (exclusions may apply, as always). But don’t dillydally—the party ends Sunday, October 25.
Sure, Black Friday is around the corner, and there will be deals aplenty. But will they be sitewide and stackable? Revival’s 20 percent stacks, meaning it also applies to marked-down and clearance items. Will the rug you’ve been eyeing for months still be available in November? Are you willing to risk it? I wouldn’t.
Why We Love Revival Rugs
Revival is a retailer we love here at WIRED, mainly because of its lovely selection of hand-knotted and handwoven wool rugs at reasonable prices. The company imports rugs from Turkey, Morocco, and India, and also works with its own supplier in Oakland, California. Revival also offers a variety of washable rugs, à la Ruggable (which, by the way, is having its own October Hosting Sale). Not every Revival rug is machine washable, but many are easy to maintain with spot cleaning and a low-suction vacuum.
WIRED reviewer Nena Farrell has the Bronto Hand-Tufted Rug in her toddler’s bedroom, and they are both fans. Farrell appreciates how soft it is and how it makes the room feel playful without looking tacky. Meanwhile, her son is mostly here for the giant dinosaur, which, honestly, is fair. WIRED operations coordinator Molly Higgins has the Garland Washable Area Rug in her living room, where its Turkish-inspired folk-art pattern adds plenty of color and disguises everyday stains. WIRED commerce director Cooper Fleishman just bought a vibrant marmalade wool rug for his new office from the Birthday Sale; sadly, it’s sold out, but this tonal design is a close cousin.
As with any sale, there are a few exclusions. Swatches and gift cards aren’t included, and be sure to read the terms and conditions for more information.

Before 24 July, a person I will call R was preoccupied with the ordinary routines of teenage life: experimenting with makeup, grumbling over mathematics homework and hanging out with friends at a tea stall.
That month, as the fever of student protests spread across the country, the 15-year-old watched on her phone as young people poured into Jantar Mantar, the designated protest site in Delhi, demanding education reform. She went too. But an 11-second video clip from the protest site, in which she made crude and profane remarks about the prime minister, Narendra Modi, upended her life.
“I feel like a criminal, as if I murdered someone,” R said in her first interview about life since the backlash. “I didn’t get a chance to make amends. In my own country, I am being treated like an enemy.”
It’s been 86 days since that protest, but R doesn’t leave home over safety concerns, trapped in the reality the ordeal created.
The summer agitation had for weeks demanded the ousting of the then-education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan, over repeated examination paper leaks. But after a violent police crackdown on a student march the anger spilled over to the Modi government.
I went to Jantar Mantar every night that week as people from all walks of life streamed in. Protest signs once directed largely against Pradhan now increasingly targeted Modi and his powerful deputy, Amit Shah, whose ministry controls Delhi Police.
The language was often profane and sexualised, and was quickly seized on by government supporters to condemn the protesters. Pro-government media channels ran heated debates about the disrespectful language and questioned the motives of those gathered. Women were singled out; BJP supporters identified them from social media clips and doxed them.
R found herself at the centre of this storm. A police case was filed against her for insult intended to provoke a breach of the peace, and statements that could lead to public mischief and defamation. The complainant told Scroll, an independent news organisation, that she had called R and asked her to publicly apologise.
After Pradhan resigned, Modi posted on Instagram about the use of vulgar abuses against him by “some mischievous children”, saying: “It is a cultural shock. How can our daughters speak like this?” Modi added that the children must be forgiven, instead of being punished.
Meanwhile, R issued an apology to Modi. In a grainy video filmed in low light, R stands against a dull white wall wearing a striped T-shirt, her hands folded in a namaste. “I am so ashamed of saying those things that I am not even able to raise my eyes. I apologise to the whole nation for it. This is my first and last mistake,” she said. (Local media reported that the complainant withdrew the police case after R’s video was posted.)
“I cried after making that video,” she told me. “I was feeling so helpless.”
But her apology did little to stem the abuse. She received rape and death threats, abusive phone calls, incessant warnings on text, knocks on doors and cars outside her apartment building in a Delhi suburb.
“I couldn’t understand what was happening,” R said, her eyes misting up as she recalled the initial days after the incident. “People older than my mother were calling me randi (prostitute), aatankwadi (terrorist), deshdrohi (enemy of the state). Others were offering Rs11,000 to find me and Rs21,000 to beat me.”
With her phone and address leaked, R and her mother were compelled to leave their home. They struggled to find landlords willing to rent them a place to stay. They found one apartment, then another and then another. Her mother, a single parent, lost the income she earned from tutoring. To pay for the repeated moves, she sold her gold jewellery. That money is keeping them afloat. She estimates it will probably last another four months. As the clock runs out, her mother is desperately searching for work.
During this time, R has not been to school and can no longer imagine returning. Some friends have cut off contact, leaving her increasingly isolated.
Despite her apology video, pro-government media continued to hound her, she said. In late August, frustrated and angry at yet another media crew showing up, she uploaded a video to social media laying bare what she was going through.
“Modiji, my life has become hell,” R said addressing the prime minister. “Now I can’t go anywhere, neither do I have any freedom. I can’t live anywhere. I have to live hiding my face,” she said.
R told me she wants people to understand how traumatising her experience has been. “To make someone homeless overnight is a big deal,” she said.
Now, stuck indoors, she is watching another wave of protests unfold. This time it’s over the controversial electoral rolls revision that has removed 130 million voters from the register. (If you missed it, read last week’s newsletter about this issue.)
R feels solidarity with the students getting brutalised and detained. There have been moments she has felt tempted to join them. But the thought of her mother and their uncertain housing situation have held her back.
“I am not scared any more. I have gone through the worst already,” she said. But she doesn’t want to put her mother through more pain.
Days before the protest, R had been planning her 15th birthday. She wanted to cut her birthday cake inside an autorickshaw, to remake a trend she had seen on social media.
It’s been a couple of months since she turned 15. I asked her what she wants or hopes for now. She paused and then said: “My past is not in my hands. I can’t change that. Now, I just want to look ahead and do well in my board exams.”

Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With the chief justice of India criticising citizen journalist covering the recent protests, veteran television reporter Ravish Kumar, who now hosts a YouTube show, recommends a relevant book.
“I had just finished reading Vineet Kumar’s book Media Ka Loktantra (Democracy of Media) when the chief justice’s statement came out, saying that if every citizen becomes a journalist, it will create problems for all of us. Published in 2024, Vineet’s book discusses the idea of do-it-yourself journalism. He shows how, when mainstream journalism began silencing the voices of ordinary people, they picked up cameras themselves and started practising journalism. They are becoming journalists to also assert their citizenship and rights guaranteed to them by the constitution. The mainstream media has a problem with journalism emerging on social media platforms because stories that it refuses to report – such as those concerning the electoral rolls – are being covered by others. The conflict between the media and DIY journalism has only now reached the courts. But it began a long time ago.”

A number worth knowing

Close to 45% of thermal power plants in India – as many as 84 out of 191 – were critically low on coal stocks (£) as of early October. At the same time, the country’s demand for power grew by 10% this year, the highest year-on-year increase in the past 10 years.
Vibe check
Artist Sagarika Sundaram has spent a decade working with wool, transforming it into felt for expansive sculptural pieces that feel almost otherworldly. Her latest exhibition, Reservoir recently opened at the Henry Moore Institute, in Leeds, and runs until 10 January.
“There’s a clearer commitment to sculpture in this body of work, even though I’m still working with felt. I’m thinking spatially and making large volumes that explore what cloth can do: bend, collapse, gather, turn inward and support or surrender to its own weight,” she said of her latest works. Among them is Blue Mountain, which stretches almost seven metres long, creating a cave-like space that viewers can move through. That’s what I find compelling in the way her works are presented: they are not static objects offering a single perspective.
The New York-based artist finds it exciting to give up a degree of agency during the making process, allowing the material to determine, in part, how the final form will unfurl. “Wool is a wonderfully responsive material. It can be soft and pliable but also dense, strong and structural. Wool takes dye exceptionally well and I can be quite expressive with colour and mark-making,” she said.

It feels like Apple’s Welcome Home event just happened. And the iPhone Duo announcement isn’t all that far in our rearview mirror, either. Yet, the company is back with another launch, focused on the MacBook Pro, it looks like. Its “Pro and tell” event is scheduled for October 28th at 1PM ET in Los Angeles. While obviously nothing is confirmed yet, it sure seems like we’re finally going to get that long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro.
What to expect from Apple’s ‘Pro and tell’ event
Apple’s long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, an OLED iPad Mini, and more.
Beyond that? There could be an OLED update for the iPad Mini, plus M6 updates across other devices, following the M6 debut with the Mac Mini in August.
A touchscreen MacBook Pro
A MacBook Pro with an OLED touchscreen has been a fixture of the rumor mill since at least early 2023. But now, in late 2026, it may finally come to fruition. The name MacBook Ultra has been floating around, but Apple is unlikely to rebrand its flagship laptop line.
This will be the first touchscreen laptop and the first OLED laptop from Apple. It will supposedly feature an iPhone-esque Dynamic Island, but don’t expect a dramatic revamp of the macOS interface — The touchscreen MacBook isn’t going to be some sort of iPad hybrid. It may include a few flourishes, like a magnification effect when you touch the screen or new gesture controls in native apps. But that’s it.
It’s also going to stick with the M5 series of chips for the time being — specifically, the M5 Pro and M5 Max. There might not be an M6 Pro or Max, even. Instead, Apple may wait to upgrade its higher-end processors until it introduces the M7 next year.
M6 MacBook Pro
That doesn’t mean there won’t be an M6 MacBook Pro, however. The base model of the MacBook Pro could be getting a bump from the M5 after the M6 debuted in the Mac Mini earlier this year. It might also get a slight redesign, including a hole-punch style camera. Unfortunately, they’re also expected to come with a price increase as component shortages reverberate through the Apple lineup.
M6 iMac
The iMac is also expected to get an M6 update, nearly two years after its last revision. Apple’s all-in-one desktop appears like it’s going to skip right over the M5. Don’t expect any real changes beyond that, though. But at least we might get some new color options, just like we did with the M4 model.
OLED iPad Mini
Another long-rumored device that might finally be making its debut on Wednesday is the OLED iPad Mini. Other than the iPad Pro, the tablet lineup has stuck with LCDs until now. The new OLED iPad could kick off a broader transition for the product line. The screen upgrade may add $100 to the cost, though. Otherwise, it likely won’t be a significant redesign, but expect a processor upgrade from the aging A17 to the A20 that debuted with the iPhone 18.

Climate change is exposing food workers to intensifying health and safety risks, from extreme heat and toxic wildfire smoke to hazardous pesticide exposure, even as poverty wages and inadequate labour protections leave many unable to protect themselves, a new global report by the International Panel of Experts on Sustainable Food Systems (IPES-Food), has found.
The report, released on October 5, says that nearly 1.4 billion people work across the global food system, but 30% (about 416 million people) earn below a living wage. It identifies climate change, corporate concentration, and widespread informal employment as forces deepening the exploitation of workers who grow, process, transport, sell and serve food.
A dangerous sector
Agriculture is among the world’s most dangerous sectors, accounting for one-third of all occupational deaths globally. Workers face hazards including extreme weather, long shifts without breaks and contact with harmful pesticides and chemicals. Heat stress is already the most common occupational health threat in agriculture, the report says, and climate change is escalating the risks into potentially life-threatening conditions.
Many farmworkers lack basic protection from extreme weather, including access to shade, rest breaks and drinking water, the report notes, adding that international labour standards are often ignored, while weak enforcement leaves workers exposed to dangerous conditions.
“Climate change is becoming a workers’ rights crisis,” said Mamadou Goïta, an IPES-Food panel expert in a webinar at the launch of the report. Farmworkers already face poverty wages, toxic pesticides and gruelling working conditions, which are being compounded by rising temperatures and other climate impacts, he said.
India’s climate-linked risks
The report highlights how climate-related livelihood losses in India can reinforce labour exploitation. Drought-driven crop failures have pushed tens of thousands of landless farmworkers into cycles of high-interest debt and bonded labour, it says. These debts can extend across generations, trapping families in exploitative working arrangements.
It also cites a study covering five Indian States that found farmer suicides increased significantly following droughts. The report links climate distress to the financial pressures faced by farming communities, particularly where workers lack adequate social protection.
Evidence from across India also points to how climate-related risks are affecting the health and livelihoods of workers in agriculture and fisheries. A study published in January 2026 in the Journal of Occupational and Environmental Medicine examined 200 male agricultural workers harvesting paddy in West Bengal during the summer of 2024 and found that the proportion experiencing dehydration rose from 16.5% to 33% over the observed work period. Higher heat exposure was also associated with greater physiological strain.
Meanwhile, a study published in April 2025 in the International Journal of Bio-resource and Stress Management examined the climate vulnerability of 400 small-scale fisher households in Ernakulam district, Kerala. It found that female-headed households had a higher livelihood vulnerability index (0.40) than male-headed households (0.37), showing how climate-related risks can intersect with gender inequalities and economic insecurity.
Health risks across the food chain
The IPES-Food report’s concerns are not limited to agricultural workers. Food workers across processing, hospitality and delivery face occupational hazards alongside insecure employment and limited access to basic protections.
Informal employment compounds these risks. Around 90% of agricultural employment and 60% to 80% of non-agricultural food employment worldwide is informal, the report notes. Informal workers earn, on average, only 56% of the monthly wages of formally employed workers and often lack access to health coverage, social security and labour protections.
Women, migrant workers and other marginalised groups face disproportionate risks, often working in the least protected jobs. Migrant workers may be reluctant to report unsafe conditions or abuse for fear of losing their jobs or facing immigration-related consequences, the report observes.
Raj Patel, an IPES-Food panel expert, in the webinar during the launch of the report, said the people who produce and deliver food were among the most exploited workers globally. Farmworkers, cooks and delivery riders face low pay, unsafe conditions, abuse and insecure work, he said, while powerful food corporations benefit from keeping labour cheap and workers powerless.
What is needed
The report calls for stronger labour standards, collective bargaining, better enforcement of workplace safety rules and equal rights for migrant workers. It also urges governments to address corporate concentration and hold companies accountable for abuses across food supply chains.
For food workers facing intensifying climate hazards, the report’s central concern is that those who sustain the food system are often left to bear its risks without adequate safeguards. It calls for a food system that does not depend on poverty wages, dangerous working conditions or the absence of basic labour protections.

Narendra Modi’s heavy-handed crackdown on protests over electoral rights in Delhi appears to have backfired. Over the weekend, his government tried to crush demonstrations led by the gen Z Cockroach Janta party (CJP). It locked up thousands of young people, detained journalists and shut down the capital as if he had declared emergency rule. Abhijeet Dipke, who launched the CJP in May after India’s chief justice compared jobless youths to “cockroaches”, was detained with other leaders when he landed in Delhi. Those who did take to the Indian capital’s streets were roughed up by police or taken into custody. Even when the usually deferential supreme court ordered peaceful assembly be protected, Mr Modi’s government showed its authoritarian contempt for fundamental constitutional rights.
This was less a display of strength than a government showing its fear of voters it claims to represent. But the actions did not stop the protests. On Monday, thousands marched in Delhi, demanding the resignation of India’s election chief over reports that the names of more than 130 million voters were deleted from the electoral roll to benefit Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) in recent elections. It’s a charge that India’s election commission denies, although some commissioners have raised concerns over voters’ names being removed without their knowledge.
Demonstrators’ demands for electoral fairness deserve answers, not arrests and intimidation. The BJP won state elections in West Bengal, where Muslims make up roughly 27% of the 100m population, for the first time ever after 2.7 million voters had been officially struck off the rolls. In many seats won by the BJP, the number of deleted or disputed voters exceeded the margin of victory. The courts said that the missing voters could cast their ballots next time.
Mass voter deletions and a brutal crackdown are fuelling distrust. Daily protests by student organisations, political parties and the Cockroach movement have been taking place in the capital for weeks. The world’s largest democracy ought to be protecting constitutional rights and finding responses to its critics. A crisis is growing because of repeated cycles of government failure, official denial and resistance to accountability. The Cockroach movement was born of anger over indifference to exam leaks that benefit connected insiders. It has become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Clearly, many are now challenging a government that they say denies them opportunity and accountability. Repression risks hardening their frustration into wider resistance.
This latest episode reveals that Mr Modi has significantly weakened the public’s faith in independent institutions like the election commission and the courts. That may be by design. It’s hard not to think that India’s prime minster bets he can survive the public’s anger as long as the protesters cannot turn it into leverage over his government – and the institutions meant to hold power accountable refuse to act. But what happens when the state makes correcting mistakes impossible? Without a democratic release, the ire builds up to a potentially volatile confrontation.
There is still reason for hope in India. The Indian Express newspaper revealed officials had raised objections to scrubbing voter lists. The resulting political mobilisation has raised the cost of ignoring such dissent. Mr Modi can’t wave this issue away. In 2011, corruption scandals became evidence that the Congress-led government had lost its moral authority. Mr Modi rode the wave of public disgust into power three years later. Now, allegations about electoral rolls could unite people around the belief that Mr Modi has betrayed them. Silencing young people with martial law-like tactics only helps to dramatise the grievance.

OpenAI says it's cutting off internet access for frontier model training
The company is trying to avoid another Hugging Face incident.
OpenAI will train frontier AI models without internet access moving forward, the company announced in a blog post, in an attempt to protect internet infrastructure and limit other safety risks. The decision was inspired by OpenAI's own rogue AI incident: In July, the company shared that agents it was testing hacked Hugging Face, just the first in what has turned into a series of reports of AI misbehavior from OpenAI, Anthropic and Google.
"Based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no internet access," OpenAI says.
The company said that restrictions on what agents can access is "paramount" to its new approach. The company allows agents to access browsers, computer-use tools and code environments they need for training tasks, but in a secure environment that's not connected to the live internet. Communication is also limited to only agents with authorization.
Everything else remains out of reach, including the live internet, which the company says isn't necessary for training and "most evaluation." Because many of its recent models are meant to power agents like Dots, which browse and use apps for you, OpenAI built an "offline world" of indexed and cached web material for agents to use without touching live websites.
Even with those restrictions, OpenAI says the red-teaming agents it dispatched to test security safeguards found vulnerabilities that allowed them to escape the virtual machines (VMs) used to isolate agents from their host system. Agents also found a way to communicate with each other by manipulating data in a processor's cache and timing how long it took to load. To address both, OpenAI says it's disclosed and fixed vulnerabilities in several VMs and added checks to its monitoring systems to spot when models try to collaborate.
OpenAI paused frontier training in September. In announcing this new internet-free process, the company shared that it restarted training on October 1. OpenAI plans to continue frontier training without internet access until improvements in existing safeguards "justify broader internet access," but it didn't share what those improvements would look like.

An immunization worker gets set up to receive her wages on her mobile wallet in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
Campaigns in Africa to stop polio and other diseases have a more stable, better-motivated workforce thanks to WHO’s collaboration with countries and partners to pay frontline health workers through their mobile phones instead of in cash.
“Over 80 percent of workers are saying they prefer the digital payments,” said Ahmed Hamani Djibo, head of WHO’s Digital Finance Team.
WHO has been leading among international organizations in moving away from the unwieldy, less-secure practice of disbursing salaries in cash. Over the past few years, the Organization launched its Digital Finance Team and joined the Better Than Cash Alliance, an 80-member United Nations partnership with a mandate to develop the digitization of payments and expand financial inclusion – activities that support the UN Sustainable Development Goals.
Since it was established in 2020, WHO’s Digital Finance Team has designed and implemented digital payment solutions in 24 countries in Africa, including, last year, in Benin, Botswana, Madagascar, Rwanda, Togo and Zimbabwe.
“WHO has successfully digitized payments for more than two million health workers across Africa,” said Tidhar Wald, Managing Director, a.i., at the Better Than Cash Alliance. “With these inspiring results, WHO is taking a clear leadership role in accelerating the digital transformation in the provision of health outcomes globally.”
A polio immunization team on the job in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Credit: WHO
“A really big difference in speed”
Workers surveyed in Côte d’Ivoire, Liberia and Tanzania said they appreciated the security of not carrying cash, the convenience of no longer having to travel to a disbursement site to receive their wages, and above all, the speed of payment – as short as half an hour after finishing work compared to waits of weeks or even months.
The surveys, funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, linked timely compensation to better morale and worker retention.
“There is really a big difference in speed,” said Jean-Luc, a health worker interviewed in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) at the end of a polio immunization campaign. “We finished the campaign mop-up yesterday and received a text notification the next evening. I’m going to pay my child’s school fees. Now we can relax.”
Digital payments also save time and money for health campaign organizers, including the burden and expense of transporting large sums of cash and completing documentation.
“When you have 300 to 500 volunteers to pay, doing accounts and signing receipts takes a lot of time,” said Saïdi, a polio team leader in DRC.
WHO first used the new digital payments in polio immunization campaigns in Côte d’Ivoire. Although outbreaks of vaccine-derived polio were on the rise, vaccination campaigns were having trouble getting off the ground. In the first quarter of 2020, almost half the polio campaigns in WHO’s African Region were postponed, saw workers drop out, or suffered other detrimental effects stemming from delays in cash disbursements.
As WHO and partners worked to develop the nuts-and-bolts aspects of a digital payment ecosystem (registering workers into a database, verifying their profiles with the mobile network operator and more) the benefits of a cashless approach became more apparent.
"There is substantial evidence that digitizing payments can support people, especially women, to gain access to financial services and increase control over their earnings,” said Maria May, Senior Program Officer, Inclusive Financial Systems, at the Gates Foundation. “Over the past four years, the World Health Organization has utilized the growing presence of mobile money across Africa to ensure that the courageous frontline vaccinators in polio outbreak campaigns are paid completely, quickly, and securely.”
Alain Labrique, director of WHO’s Department of Digital Health and Innovation, said that “digital payments are one of the key pillars of Digital Health Public Infrastructure currently strongly encouraged within WHO’s guidance to member-states on Digital Transformation.” WHO views digital payments as a foundation for many more digital development activities, together with Data Exchange and Digital ID Infrastructure. He added “we are delighted to work with partners in the digital space and add our voice to this celebration of WHO's joining the Better Than Cash Alliance”.

“The world needs the BBC more than ever. It might be a different size and shape. It’s not going to be a so-so Netflix or a me-too YouTube. It’s going to be a better BBC.”
That was the message Matt Brittin left ringing in the ears of BBC staff when concluding a town hall last month. The director general was attempting to lift the gloom after being beset with questions from anxious employees about job losses, service reductions, and general retrenchment.
He has an uneviable task. Brittin is grappling with a financial crisis that is precipitating some of the most painful cuts in the BBC’s history. He is also attempting to cement the BBC’s position as Britain’s premium media brand in an era of unprecedented competition.
These two objectives are not obviously compatible, but Brittin’s pitch to staff is that they are not incompatible. It’s why, when he announced the closure of linear networks BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra on Tuesday, he said the decisions were necessary to both “respond to immediate cost pressures and reinvent the BBC for a changing world.”
Watch on Deadline
It’s not an easy sell to an unsettled workforce that is all too aware that worse is yet to come. The BBC must save £500 million ($670M) by 2028 after hemorrhaging more than two million licence fee payers since 2020. Despite relentless internal memos about layoffs and content cuts since the summer, the BBC has only announced £200M of its half-billion goal. In other words, it’s not even halfway through the cuts.
Closing BBC Three, BBC Scotland and Radio 4 Extra may seem substantial, but the reality is that switching off these services in spring 2027 will only save around £10M, according to two insiders. In the case of BBC Three, the network spectrum from which the channel broadcasts will continue to be an expense because it also houses CBBC, the children’s network that airs between 7AM and 7PM.
Deadline can reveal that BBC leaders did discuss merging CBBC with the corporation’s other children’s network, CBeebies. The BBC would have banked a more significant saving alongside the closure of BBC Three, but executives dismissed the idea because they did not wish to call into question the corporation’s commitment to kids’ public service media.
A senior insider, who spoke on condition of anonymity, said the closure of CBBC was deemed too “politically dangerous” when the BBC is negotiating its funding settlement and charter with the UK government. A second source added that Lisa Nandy believes BBC children’s services should be protected — perhaps unsurprising after her first visit to the BBC as culture secretary involved meeting Hacker T Dog, CBBC’s resident puppet.
BBC Sounds Under Threat?
That the BBC even contemplated CBBC’s future is revealing of the agonizing decisions facing Brittin as he attempts to put the broadcaster on a surer financial footing.
Speculation internally has turned to the future of another service: BBC Sounds, the radio and podcast streaming service launched in 2018. Deadline hears that the BBC has held tentative discussions about whether Sounds could be folded in with iPlayer to create a single streaming service for video and audio, not unlike Netflix and YouTube. A BBC insider said it is symptomatic of the BBC “having to dig much deeper and be more radical to find savings.”
Although no decisions have been made and Sounds is not under immediate threat, there are signals that point in this direction. During an internal all-staff call earlier this month, Brittin said he wanted iPlayer to be an “entertainment destination,” and asked Manon Dave, a product designer, to demonstrate a reimagined iPlayer where audio and video dovetailed. A further clue came this week, when BBC content chief Kate Phillips merged TV and audio commissioning teams in comedy and arts.
Somewhat counterintuitively, BBC Media Tech, the division that powers online platforms, is among the hardest hit by the cuts. The unit must save £102M by next year, but the talk is that a smaller team will focus on fewer products, which also fits with the emerging narrative around a single streaming service.
The BBC has announced around 1,200 job cuts in recent months, which is 800 shy of its intended target. Some think the BBC could exceed 2,000 redundancies. Few are immune. On-screen presenters like health editor Hugh Pym are expected to leave the building as BBC News contributes at least £51M to the savings pot.
Staff morale is low amid the drip-drip of redundancy announcements, which follows the BBC’s workforce contracting by 10% since 2020. The BBC is also navigating fraught negotiations over a staff pay deal, with the corporation infuriating unions by bundling in changes to terms and conditions, such as curbing cab usage for night shift workers. Many think industrial action is likely.
“There’s a lot of anger and bitterness,” said one insider. “If we all took work-to-rule [industrial action] and refused to do overtime, and turned our phones off for our lunch break, it would cause them a real headache.” Another spoke of a “f**k it feeling” internally: “The longer cuts get drawn out, the more uncertain everything feels. You think, God, do I really want to be sticking around for whatever this might end up being?”
A former Google executive, Brittin is trying to inject more Silicon Valley spirit and speed into the BBC’s culture. He is known to be disarmingly direct in meetings, unapologetically taking team members to task if they do not support their assumptions with audience data. “I’d like us to celebrate activity less, and outcomes more,” he told colleagues this month.
BBC Three Not Mourned
The closure of BBC Three, BBC Scotland, and Radio 4 Extra has not provoked significant backlash. When BBC Three was first taken off air in 2016, campaigners rallied to save the channel and two producers, Hat Trick boss Jimmy Mulville and Avalon co-founder Jon Thoday, made a serious offer to acquire the network. A decade on, Thoday is unmoved by the switch-off.
“I don’t think the BBC should have got rid of BBC Three in the first place. I don’t think they should have brought it back in the second place. And I’m not going to lose any sleep over them getting rid of it now,” said Thoday, who produces HBO’s Last Week Tonight with John Oliver.
“All I hope is that the cancelation of BBC Three for the second time results in the BBC increasing its spend on content for young people. It’s really important that the BBC increases and leads on comedy investment and lets comedy bring young viewers to the BBC.”
A former BBC executive added that the “terrible” decision to reinstate the channel in 2022 had harmed BBC Three, which was hit by low linear ratings for flagship shows. “It killed it,” they said. RuPaul’s Drag Race UK, The Rap Game and I Kissed a Girl/Boy have all been cancelled recently, meaning there is space for a creative refresh of the brand on iPlayer. The BBC has committed to increasing investment for younger audiences, but offered no detail on the value and scope of this ambition.
Perhaps the most ominous thing for the BBC is that it is not in control of what comes next. Funding talks with the government are progressing slowly, despite Westminster press briefings about enthusiasm for a so-called “Netflix tax,” which would involve charging consumers extra for subscription streaming services to help pay for the BBC. Ministers like this idea, and the BBC has not dismissed the solution, but there are those at the corporation who are skeptical that it will solve its funding crisis.
The protracted talks leave the BBC with no visibility over its finances beyond the end of next year, an extraordinary situation for any organization that relies on £3.9 billion of public income. The BBC expects the government to publish its policy position before the end of the year. As director-general Matt Brittin looks to forge a “sovereign” streaming service from a smaller BBC, clarity can’t come soon enough.

To strengthen Karnataka’s organ transplantation programme and increase deceased donor transplants, the State Health Department will constitute an Organ Transplant Visionary Committee under Nagesh Hegde, who heads the State-run Institute of Gastroenterology Sciences and Organ Transplant (IGOT), Health Minister U.T. Khader said on Thursday.
Mr. Khader said the decision was taken at a progress review meeting with the State Organ Transplant Advisory Committee, which he chaired.
The proposed committee will recommend measures to raise public awareness about organ donation and improve access to transplantation, with a focus on strengthening infrastructure and streamlining procedures across the State, he said.
Brain death certification
One of the key priorities would be to facilitate brain death certification and organ retrieval at all district hospitals and government medical colleges. The committee would also recommend measures to expand organ transplant facilities in government hospitals, Mr. Khader said.
“Most hospitals do not want to obtain licences for organ retrieval due to the long process of paperwork. To avoid this, we are proposing that all hospitals with 50–100 beds capacity should automatically become organ retrieval centres. If they do not wish to, they can apply to get it cancelled,” he said.
The early launch of a new software system for organ allocation and tracking would be another priority, aimed at improving the efficiency of the process. The government would also focus on renewing registrations of transplant centres whose approvals had lapsed, he said.
Waitlist
Mr. Khader said 6,291 patients were awaiting organ transplants in Karnataka and stressed the need to encourage more people to pledge their organs. One deceased donor could help save multiple lives, he said.
The Minister urged the public to pledge their organs through the Jeevasarthakathe portal at https://jeevasarthakathe.karnataka.gov.in.
He said the proposed measures were intended to strengthen the State’s organ donation network, expand transplant services in government hospitals and improve access to life-saving organs for patients on the waiting list.

France mobilised a massive security force on Saturday as protests over school funding, wages and soaring living costs spread across the country, a week after violent unrest left shops looted, cars burned and public buildings damaged.
Authorities restricted a major march in Paris to the city’s southeastern edge, closed prominent museums and banned demonstrations in several cities to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence.
Up to 70,000 police officers deployed
Before the protests began, interior Minister Laurent Nuñez had said that up to 70,000 officers would be deployed nationwide, supported by helicopters, armoured vehicles and water cannons. Security was tightened in Paris and other major cities after more than half a million people took to the streets the previous Saturday.
These massive security arrangements came in the backdrop of last weekend when around 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted during last weekend’s unrest. Nuñez acknowledged on Monday that police had lost control in some cities during the violence. He offered to resign, but President Emmanuel Macron refused.
Hundreds arrested
French police arrested 135 people in connection with protests and seized various weapons, French iterior minister Laurent Nuñez said, as authorities stepped up security amid fears of renewed violence.
Paris march restricted to city’s southeastern edge
Paris police changed the route of a union-organised march on Friday, replacing the planned Bastille-to-Nation route with one between Porte d’Italie and Porte de Vincennes on the capital’s southeastern edge, reported AP.
At Bastille, the original starting point, police used a megaphone to instruct people to leave or face a 135-euro fine. The route restrictions were imposed to keep demonstrators away from central areas affected by last weekend’s violence.
Paris police ordered a union-organised march to be moved at the last minute from central Bastille to Porte d’Italie on the capital’s southeastern outskirts. Unions reluctantly agreed to the change, while the Yellow Vests, the protest movement that staged disruptive demonstrations against Macron eight years ago, indicated they would defy the order.
Major museums close as shopkeepers board up stores
Major Paris landmarks, including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais, were closed on Saturday amid security concerns. The Grand Palais is hosting a major Cézanne exhibition.
Art Basel, a prominent contemporary art fair, opened to the public on Friday but cancelled its weekend programme because of the threat of unrest.
Shopkeepers across Paris also boarded up storefronts ahead of the demonstrations. Near Saint-Lazare train station, contractor Akram Ahmed, 34, was securing an optician’s shop on Saturday. “I got the call last night,” he said. “The owner seemed desperate. He said I was saving his life.”
Some demonstrations banned, teargas used in Lyon
Protest marches were scheduled in Paris and Marseille, while local authorities banned some rallies in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier. French media reported that police used tear gas in Lyon on Saturday morning to disperse demonstrators.
Trade unions criticised the bans, describing them as violations of freedom of expression, a right protected by the French constitution.
The restrictions came as authorities sought to prevent a repeat of last weekend’s violence, which saw masked groups target businesses and public buildings across the country.
Thousands rally  in Orléans
Thousands of people marched in Orléans, about 110 kilometres (70 miles) south of Paris to protest against the far right. The demonstration took place alongside a two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s National Rally party ahead of next spring’s presidential election.
The rally added to a day of demonstrations across France, where public anger over living costs and public services has increasingly intersected with political tensions.
Students and workers demand better schools, higher wages
The protests began last month over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris but have since expanded into a broader movement over living standards.
Student groups are demanding 250,000 additional higher-education places and an end to selection through Parcoursup, France’s national university admissions system. Their joint 10-point plan also calls for more teachers and repairs to schools and universities.
Students are seeking additional financial support, including an extra 200 euros a month in student grants and a rent freeze in public student housing. Workers and unions are demanding higher wages and pensions to help households cope with rising costs.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people,” said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. “And it’s not possible anymore.”
Macron faces pressure as protests widen
The demonstrations have added to pressure on Macron during the final stretch of his current presidency, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017.
Macron met high school representatives on Friday, who said he had promised to overhaul the university admissions system. However, they called for protests to continue until concrete measures were formally announced.
The government has defended restrictions on demonstrations as necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, as France faces mounting anger over living costs and public services.
Europe on the boil: Protests in Italy, Spain & Albania
Italy deployed an additional 500 soldiers to Milan ahead of fresh protests on Saturday, a week after looting and clashes with police. The deployment, announced by Premier Giorgia Meloni, came alongside tighter security measures, including drone surveillance, railway station checks and rapid-response units. Around 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel were expected to support security operations in the city.
In Rome, authorities tightened security around luxury shopping streets and major public spaces ahead of planned demonstrations, including an anti-war march and a rally by right-wing students. Protests were also scheduled in several other Italian cities amid concerns over possible violence.
In Albania, student-led protesters planned a fresh anti-government rally in the capital, Tirana, on Saturday after days of violent unrest. Demonstrators have demanded better education facilities, lower tuition fees and action against corruption, while also calling for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama. More than 300 people, including police officers, have been injured since the protests began, according to AFP. Although tensions had eased in recent days, organisers urged students and other groups to join the latest rally.
Meanwhile, thousands of retirees and supporters marched in Spain capital to demand protection for public pensions ahead of next month’s snap election. In Lisbon, protesters prepared to march for affordable housing, opposing government measures they say could leave tenants more vulnerable to rent increases and eviction.

Five Israelis wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed in West Bank shooting
- Published
Five Israelis have been wounded and two suspected Palestinian attackers killed by Israeli security forces following a shooting in the occupied West Bank, Israeli officials say.
Footage verified by the BBC shows an intense gun battle between soldiers and the gunmen, at a military checkpoint at the entrance to the city of Hebron.
In response, Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he had ordered the military to prepare for a full lockdown of the West Bank, beginning later on Friday.
The attack comes at a time of high tensions, with extremist Jewish settlers targeting Palestinians during the annual olive harvest, and Israel's general election taking place in four days time.
The two injured Israelis are in critical condition, according to Israel's ambulance service.
The Israeli military said it had found a large quantity of ammunition in the attackers' vehicle, and that they believe the gunmen had intended to carry out a much larger attack on the nearby Route 35, but ran into the checkpoint - so instead decided to open fire there.
Unverified CCTV footage shows two gunmen exit a car armed with what appears to be a handgun and an assault rifle and start firing on soldiers at the checkpoint, before coming under return fire.
The Israeli military said it had begun raids on the homes of the attackers, while far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich said he had ordered the demolition of several Palestinian buildings adjacent to the site of the attack.
It is common practice for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis.
Netanyahu, who has built his election campaign on promising security for Israelis, said that his Likud party would cancel campaign events for the morning.
The West Bank was already expected to be placed under lockdown for the election on Monday and Tuesday, according to Israeli media.
At least 96 Palestinians have been killed by Israeli forces or settlers in the West Bank since the start of the year, according to the UN.
Four Israelis, both security forces and civilians, have been killed by Palestinians there over the same period, the UN says.

The Chamber of Trade and Industry (CTI) has appealed to Congress MP and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha Rahul Gandhi to defer INDIA bloc's November 1 rally at Ramlila Maidan to a date after November 10, stating that the event could disrupt business during Delhi's peak festive shopping period. In a letter to Gandhi on Saturday, CTI chairman Brijesh Goyal suggested holding the rally after Bhai Dooj, which will be celebrated on November 10 this year. The traders' association pointed out that Delhi's retail markets witness heightened commercial activity around Dhanteras, Diwali and Bhai Dooj, with preparations, purchases and sales gathering pace well before the festivals, according to ANI. The letter noted that Dhanteras will be observed on November 6, Diwali on November 8 and Bhai Dooj on November 10. It also estimated that Dhanteras alone generates business worth approximately ₹25,000 crore in Delhi across several sectors, including gold and silver, utensils, electronics, garments, dry fruits, sweets, automobiles and furniture, among other goods. The CTI also referred to business losses incurred by traders in October because of road closures and traffic diversions around Connaught Place, India Gate and other parts of central Delhi. It claimed that these disruptions had already resulted in losses of nearly ₹3,000 crore for the trading community. The traders' body further noted that 20 major wholesale and retail markets operate within a five-kilometre radius of Ramlila Maidan. These include Chandni Chowk, Sadar Bazaar, Khari Baoli, Bhagirath Palace, Dariba Kalan, Kashmere Gate, Nai Sarak, Mori Gate, Tilak Bazaar, Daryaganj, Jama Masjid, Chawri Bazaar, Karol Bagh, Nabi Karim, Azad Market and Lajpat Rai Market. According to the letter, traffic restrictions, metro station closures and barricading arrangements during the rally could affect commercial activity across these markets. Such measures could also cause inconvenience to traders and customers travelling to Delhi from neighbouring areas and other cities. The CTI also drew attention to the location of Old Delhi Railway Station and New Delhi Railway Station near Ramlila Maidan. It said traffic restrictions and congestion during the rally could inconvenience commuters and visitors coming to the capital for festive shopping. While recognising the right of political parties to organise rallies and public gatherings, the traders' association urged Rahul Gandhi to take into account the concerns of Delhi's business community and consider postponing the event. The letter expressed hope that Gandhi, in his capacity as Congress MP and Leader of Opposition in the Lok Sabha, would acknowledge the traders' concerns and agree to hold the rally after November 10. The opposition rally is intended to intensify pressure on the government over allegations of "vote chori" and demand the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. Earlier, on October 12, opposition leaders, activists and members of civil society staged a 'March for Democracy' in Delhi, taking their protest against the alleged "vote theft" to the doorstep of the Supreme Court. The march was held along a route secured with heavy barricades, while participants also filed a joint petition challenging the SIR. A day later, Gandhi hosted leaders of the INDIA bloc at his residence for a meeting over the issue. Israeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families, in collective punishment for a militant attack on an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.
The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.
Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.
People said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.
The large-scale demolitions follow an attack on Friday on an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20 minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.
The attack came four days before Israeli elections, and the prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.
Netanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.
Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.
A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.
A Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”
Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.
“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”
The Israeli army was approached for comment on the operations and on videos showing extensive devastation.

Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."
This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.
Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.
OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."
Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.
The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.
"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.
As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.
Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.
In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."
Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.
Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.
"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "

Bracknell Football Club coach Josh Adams charged with three counts of rape
A former northern Tasmanian football coach has been charged with three counts of rape, leading to the resignation of the football club's president.
Police confirmed a 44-year-old man from northern Tasmania had been charged with the offences that were alleged to have occurred in April last year.
The man is believed to be former Bracknell football coach, Josh Adams.
He is scheduled to appear in the Launceston Magistrates Court early next year.
In a statement, Northern Tasmanian Football Association (NTFA) president Peter Gutwein said the association had recently been informed that a coach had been charged with "a serious criminal offence".
But he said the NTFA would not provide further comment as the matter was now before the courts.
News of charges being laid against Adams were first published by an independent media outlet.
Its reporting detailed private messages exchanged between Bracknell Football Club president Nicole Jones and the mother of Adams's alleged victim
Yesterday, Ms Jones announced via social media that she would be "standing down as president and all official club duties with immediate effect".
"I acknowledge that what I said [in the messages] was disrespectful, inappropriate and wrong, and I unreservedly apologise for these comments,"
she said.
In his statement, Mr Gutwein said the league was "deeply concerned" by the content of the private messages.
"The NTFA has referred the matter to the AFL for independent consideration and acknowledges that the President has unreservedly apologised for those comments and stood aside from all official club duties with immediate effect," he said.
"The NTFA recognises that individuals who report allegations of sexual violence must be treated with dignity, compassion and respect."
Adams had not re-committed to coaching Bracknell as of last month.
It is understood he has since been stood down from the role, and will be replaced.

Will the Alberta referendum feed a more polarized immigration debate?
Immigration was on the ballot in Alberta. Now attention turns to the Carney government
Referendums tend to raise as many questions as they answer. And so it may be for the 10-part questionnaire that Alberta Premier Danielle Smith put to her province — although with a series of no's Albertans have seemingly foreclosed on a number of possibilities.
"I am well aware that not every grievance Alberta has with Ottawa has been resolved," Smith told Albertans on Tuesday night. "There are still many political and constitutional battles ahead of us."
On the question of whether Alberta should remain in Canada the answer was not close. The 75 per cent of voters who chose the first option is decidedly more decisive than the 1980 referendum in Quebec.
Of the 25 per cent who voted for another referendum, it is also fair to ask how many genuinely want secession. According to Abacus Data, making Alberta an independent country was the primary motivation for just 32 per cent of Albertans who favoured Option 2.
Whatever Smith's appetite for future constitutional battles, Albertan voters also proved to be unenthusiastic: all four questions about whether Alberta should pursue constitutional amendments were answered with a "no."
Not even a question about abolishing the Senate — possibly the most-maligned public institution in Canada history — was able to muster even a simple majority of Albertans.
"There's a reason to be skeptical that some constitutional amendments would be worth the effort and ... what I'm seeing is that Albertans would just rather that we spend our time focusing on things where we can make some meaningful change," Smith said at a news conference on Wednesday (at the time, two of the four constitutional questions were being answered in the negative as results were still being tallied).
"That's why I think the numbers were so different on the immigration questions versus … perhaps the constitutional ones."
Beside Smith's own political future, the most unresolved questions raised by her referendum concern immigration — and one of the questions now is whether they will feed into a more polarized national debate on Canada's immigration policy.
Immigration on the ballot in Alberta
Of Smith's 10 questions, four concerned either immigration or potential new rules for newcomers. On its official referendum website, Smith's government claimed that "unsustainable immigration levels over the past 10 years" had "a profound impact" on Alberta's ability "to fund and effectively deliver social services like health care and education — directly impacting Albertans' access to these services and costing taxpayers billions of dollars."
Alberta NDP Leader Naheed Nenshi argued Smith was "scapegoating" immigrants.
"The reality of the matter is even if you took all the young, healthy temporary foreign workers out of the health-care system, even if you denied public education to refugee children, it's not going to make the emergency room lineups any less," Nenshi told CBC's Power & Politics this week. "It's not going to make your classrooms any smaller. It's not going to make anyone's life better."
Just under 55 per cent of voters supported the proposition that the Alberta government should take "increased control over immigration for the purposes of decreasing immigration to more sustainable levels."
Three questions that floated possible limitations on how or when newcomers or temporary residents can access health care, education and other social services in Alberta were supported by narrower majorities of 52.4, 53.1 and 52 per cent.
Smith's government has a majority in the Alberta legislature and it didn't need a referendum to pursue any of these initiatives. But the results — notably, none of the immigration questions won a majority in Calgary — may give Smith reason to hesitate.
At her news conference on Wednesday, the premier suggested she was prepared to act quickly on the first question, but she would "proceed with caution" in response to questions two, three and four. She said she did not want to impact anyone who was already residing in Alberta.
While Prime Minister Mark Carney raised some eyebrows when he repeated the "no to the nine" slogan before Alberta's vote, he had also suggested he was inclined to give all provinces more input on immigration.
"To be candid, I don't need a referendum to tell us to co-operate more with the provinces on immigration," Carney told Global News a few days before Alberta's vote. "I think that's where we're headed."
But Alberta's immigration questions also caught the attention of Conservative Leader Pierre Poilievre.
An increasingly polarized debate
"I thought it was inappropriate for the prime minister to tell Canadians and tell Albertans that they should vote to continue to give deluxe taxpayer benefits to people who are illegally here," Poilievre said. "And for the prime minister to suggest that Albertans vote in favor of continued mass, unvetted, out of control immigration was a mistake."
The Conservative Party also sent a fundraising appeal to supporters on Tuesday that promised a Conservative government would "dramatically reduce immigration."
The Carney government argues that it has immigration "under control" after steps were taken to curb the intake of international students and temporary workers. The Conservatives obviously disagree.
But the Alberta referendum also landed between two triggers for renewed debate about immigration to Canada.
First, in discussing immigration policy during an interview with the New York Times last month, Carney said, "now the question starts to become: When do we resume some controlled increase in the population, which is the nature of Canada? So that will happen, and we just want to make sure that we've got it under control."
Now the federal government is due to table its latest immigration levels plan, which sets out targets for the next few years for both permanent and temporary arrivals (technically, a new plan is due by Nov. 1, but last year's plan was included in the fall budget).
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Carney said his government "will not budge from overall levels that are sustainable." But what constitutes "sustainable" is likely a matter of debate.
At a news conference on Thursday, Conservative immigration critic Michelle Rempel Garner argued "mass immigration" was suppressing wages and driving up rents, to the benefit of corporate profiteers. Conservatives, she said, will "vigorously oppose any attempt by Mark Carney to continue to raise and sustain high immigration levels" and "will push him to lower them."
Claims that the "Canadian consensus" on immigration has been broken are sometimes overstated. Canadians still believe immigration is a net-positive for the economy, but they also believe recent immigration levels have been too high, driven in large part by concerns about the availability and affordability of housing.
Polling by the Environics Institute has also shown a growing gap along the political spectrum, with Conservative voters much more inclined to say there is too much immigration. And the parties themselves may be getting further apart.
That is not the most stable foundation on which to build significant new increases in immigration, however much such increases might be necessary.
If the goal remains to be as open and welcoming as possible — if there is an economic imperative to being so — "proceed with caution" might be good advice for all sides.

Nature vs. bulldozers: The environment minister's balancing act at UN nature summit
Julie Dabrusin heads to COP17 in Armenia looking for ways for Canada to have 'leadership role'
Canada is showing up at this year's international nature summit in Armenia with pledges to protect swaths of land bigger than most countries. But it's also facing criticism for advancing major projects that put those protections in jeopardy.
Environment and Climate Change Minister Julie Dabrusin spoke to CBC News about the work she hopes to advance in Yerevan and responded to critics who say the government's actions on the nature file are "incoherent."
Dabrusin is heading to COP17, the United Nations biodiversity conference, on Saturday.
"Canada is the second-largest country in the world. We have the longest coastline in the world. So whatever we do has a real global impact," said Dabrusin before departing to Armenia.
She said international environmental conferences are "real moments" for Canada to have a "leadership role" in "pushing the world" to protect nature and reduce global emissions.
The environment minister attends COP17 on the heels of making a series of announcements to conserve lands and waters.
In October, Dabrusin announced that Canada is conserving an area of forest and peatlands near Kapuskasing, Ont., that's 1.3 times the size of Toronto.
In 2025, the minister said Ottawa would support the conservation of an area of land that's the size of Japan. As part of the initiative Northwest Territories: Our Land for the Future, the Canadian government is funding one of the world's largest Indigenous-led projects, conserving 380,000 square kilometres of land and water.
Policy 'incoherence': Greenpeace
But Dabrusin's attendance at COP17 comes as the Carney government receives sustained criticism for changes it's making to Canada's environmental laws.
"I think the big headline specifically for Canada is policy incoherence," said Salomé Sané, the nature and biodiversity campaigner for Greenpeace Canada.
The Building Canada Strong Act, or Bill C-39, is making its way through the House of Commons. The omnibus bill is proposing to amend several pieces of environmental legislation in order to fast-track pipelines, power lines, mines and other projects that fall under federal jurisdiction.
- Critics accuse Carney government of proposing 'sacrifice zones' for the environment
- Liberal MP calls for more safeguards in new bill to fast-track development projects
"We have the same federal government pushing for a very destructive bill under C-39 that will allow development projects to be built by bypassing, amongst other things, environmental regulations," Sané said.
"So our question to the government is, which is it? Are we protecting nature or are we destroying nature? Because going to COP to talk about nature protection and not defending nature at home will not allow us to deliver nature recovery."
Debrusin responded to that criticism noting the government didn't move forward with some of the amendments it was contemplating due to pushback. She added the bill focuses on how projects get assessed, not weakening environmental standards.
"There's nothing in the policies we're putting forward that reduces our environmental standards," Dabrusin said.
Canada co-hosted with China the UN biodiversity conference in 2022. Countries signed the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which set a target of the world conserving 30 per cent of lands and waters by 2030.
Since setting those targets, global progress has been slow according to UN Secretary General António Guterres.
"Even if current national commitments are met, only 26 per cent of terrestrial, and 12 per cent of marine ecosystems would be protected by 2030. That is well short of the promise made in Montreal," Guterres said in the Armenian capital last week.
