In 2018, anatomists at the Toho University Graduate School of Medicine, Tokyo, Japan, performed a sleep deprivation experiment on lab mice. Mice usually sleep for 12 hours a day. In this experiment, researchers induced sleep deprivation using the ‘gentle handling method’ during sleep hours so that the mice could sleep only for six hours daily.
They discovered that liver fat content in sleep-deprived mice increased without total weight gain compared to another group who were allowed to sleep normally. The liver cells were stressed, and the activity of certain genes that escalate insulin resistance and fat content within liver cells also increased with sleep deprivation.
Experiment on rats
Three years later, a group of Chinese researchers at the Xinjiang Medical University went one step ahead. In this experiment, rats were severely sleep-deprived, turning into insomniacs. Liver enzymes, blood, and liver fat increased substantially. None of these changes were notable among rats who were allowed to sleep without distractions.
They also found the reason for increased liver fat in insomniac mice — the sympathetic nerves that supplied the liver, best known for their role in responding to stress and danger, were hyperactive. When insomnia was treated with a sleeping pill in these stressed rats, the liver fat was reduced with adequate sleep.
There are lessons here, of mice and men. Sleep is an underrated activity among humans. Sometimes, the intentional and forced lack of sleep ‘to increase productivity’ is advertised by men in power to showcase their self-proclaimed metahuman nature. During an interview in 2011, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he had become a workaholic and hardly slept for 3.5 hours in a day, and that yoga and pranayama routine kept him energised and awake.
But medical science has a different story to tell. A study of nearly 55,500 people from Europe showed that those who slept 7-8.5 hours daily had higher life expectancy than those who slept less than seven hours. In those between ages 50 and 75 without sleep disturbances, the expectation of living longer without chronic disease development was significantly higher.
And yoga interventions improved overall sleep quality, efficiency, latency, and duration, contrary to all claims.
Healthy sleep
Sleep is a vital function of human life and accounts for up to one-third of the lifespan. Contrary to normal belief, during sleep, the brain is not ‘resting’ but is engaged in various activities necessary to improve well-being, increase life, and especially impact the liver. The minimum required duration for ‘healthy’ sleep is seven hours.
When 10,000 persons with sleep disorders were followed up for one year, incident fatty liver disease was noted in 14, while in those without sleep disorders, it was only six. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease association was significantly higher among persons with shorter sleep duration (less than six hours per night) and excessive daytime sleepiness. A high-quality study showed that inadequate sleep duration was strongly associated with an elevated risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and adequate sleep helped prevent it. With every one-hour decrease in sleep time from the recommended seven-eight hours, the risk of fat deposition in the liver increased by 24% compared with those who slept adequately.
However, when people who lost sleep during the weekdays caught up on the debt during weekends (known as weekend catch-up sleep), the development of fatty liver disease reduced significantly. Compared with non-nappers, long daytime nappers (more than 60 minutes) had a higher risk of developing non-alcoholic fatty liver disease.
Identification
Correlation may not be causation, but with non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, which is associated with other conditions such as obesity, high blood pressure, increased waist-hip ratio, low functioning thyroid, and high blood cholesterol, studying and identifying independent associations make realistic sense.
In people who sleep less than six hours at night, have a persistently poor sleep quality, or nap more than one hour during the day, independent of other disease conditions, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease development was a strong association. The next time someone brags that sacrificing time and quality of sleep is an achievement associated with success, know that success comes with fatty liver disease. And it is not worth it.
(Cyriac Abby Philips is a senior consultant and physician-scientist at the Liver Institute, Rajagiri Hospital, Kochi)

Three released without charge after fatal arson attack
- Published
Three people, who were arrested in connection with a suspected arson attack which killed four family members in the Republic of Ireland, have been released, gardaí (Irish police) have said.
Philip and Kim English and two of their children - nine-year-old Jayden and 12-year-old Callum - died after their home in Birch Avenue, on the outskirts of Waterford was set on fire earlier this month.
A man aged in his 20s and a woman in her 30s were previously charged in connection with the attack.
On Saturday, gardaí said three people - two women in their 30s and a man in his 50s - who were arrested on Tuesday have been released without charge.
A fourth person, a man in his 20s who was arrested on Thursday, remains in custody.

Measles strategy works – Now it must expand to more countries
Cape Town Measles Declaration pledges to cut measles deaths by half
At a landmark World Health Organization (WHO)/United Nations Children’s Fund (UNICEF) meeting in Cape Town, leading players in the fight against measles spelled out what it will take to stop 2000 children dying every day from this preventable disease. Together with UNICEF special ambassador Angelique Kidjo, they issued a call for intensified efforts and the resources necessary to ensure all children are protected against measles.
“We can do it – we’ve done it before – in Afghanistan, Angola, in countries devastated by conflict and drought and every other form of disaster,” said Carol Bellamy, Executive Director, UNICEF. “In just three years, and against great odds, we’ve cut the number of children dying from measles by almost 25%. It’s one of the most dramatic declines in disease mortality in history. But the next 25% will be harder. With the political and financial support of donors and governments around the world, we can together save many more lives.”
The “Cape Town Measles Declaration” calls on governments to take strong action against one of the world’s most vicious and prolific vaccine-preventable childhood killers – a disease which kills 745,000 children every year. We must control this disease to meet the Millennium Development targets of a 67% reduction in under-five mortality by 2015. The world leaders are well aware of the urgency. Last year, the UN General Assembly Special Session on Children set a 2005 target date to reduce measles deaths from 1999 levels by 50%. This year, the World Health Assembly, which includes 192 member states, endorsed the WHO and UNICEF measles strategy to combat the disease.
“When 30 million children are affected and 745,000 children die every year, you have to think big,” said Dr. LEE Jong-wook, Director-General of WHO. “Since the launch of the WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths in 2000, we have delivered measles vaccine to more than 200 million children globally. We know the strategy works. An additional half a million children are alive today because of all the partners’ efforts. But if we’re to prevent more deaths, we must do more. And we’ll need help from governments and from the international community.”
The campaign against measles has been dramatic – hundreds of thousands of children saved, the virus almost banished from the Americas and transmission cut drastically in many African countries, where the Measles Initiative Partnership has been the driving force behind the campaign. WHO and UNICEF have identified 45 countries as the highest priority for mortality-reduction strategies, accounting for 95% of global deaths from measles.
“It has been astonishing to see the results of the immunization programme in Africa,“ said Dr Mark Grabowsky, Senior Technical Officer, American Red Cross. “Now we have proof that we can reduce measles mortality even in countries torn apart by conflict, if governments are committed, communities are engaged and we have the support of donors, NGOs and volunteers. What we have accomplished so far through the Measles Initiative Partnership gives great hope for the future, and the many thousands of children we can still save.” The foundation of the measles mortality-reduction strategy is the re-invigoration of national immunization systems. At the Cape Town meeting, delegates discussed strategies with governments and policy makers for strengthening routine immunization services and making the life-saving measles vaccine available to all children as a matter of course.
”It’s not just about reducing childhood deaths today. We need to be in this for the long haul and this means a sustainable reduction in childhood deaths, which only a strong national health system can guarantee,” said Dr Stephen L. Cochi, Deputy Director, National Immunization Program, Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). ”This kind of international focus and commitment gives us the opportunity to build that strength – boosting safe routine immunization services, establishing international laboratory networks and increasing surveillance to detect and respond to outbreaks.”
“Today the call to action is clear,” said Mr Nick Farrell, Senior Programme Officer, International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies. “ We have to ensure every child receives a second opportunity for measles immunization in these 45 countries, no matter how remote or marginalized, regardless of barriers of conflict, culture and poverty.
“To date we have seen tens of thousands of health workers and volunteers trek across mountains and deserts in all kinds of conditions to find these children to ensure they receive the life-saving vaccine,” said Timothy E. Wirth, President of the United Nations Foundation. “We are witnessing incredible commitment from ordinary people. They need – they deserve to be backed up by the world’s political will and financial support.”
Ms Angelique Kidjo, Special UNICEF ambassador, believes that the Cape Town Measles Declaration indicates a clear path towards a giant achievement in children’s health.
”The world has committed, to drastically reducing the devastating, pointless waste of young life,” she said. “If we reach our targets for measles, we will have taken a huge step towards keeping that promise. I believe we can get there – but only if we make it a priority to turn this declaration into action. This goal deserves all we can give. We must do whatever is necessary.”
Further information:
- Of all the vaccine-preventable diseases, measles remains the leading childhood killer. Measles is an important cause of overall under 5 childhood mortality.
- Measles affects over 30 million children. More than 745,000 die each year from measles – more than half of them in Africa.
- A safe, effective and inexpensive measles vaccine has been available for over 40 years.
- Measles accounts for an estimated 50% of vaccine-preventable deaths among children.
- One million measles deaths are already being prevented each year with existing immunization efforts. With the successful implementation of the WHO-UNICEF measles strategy (including routine immunization and periodic supplementary immunization activities), an additional 500,000 measles deaths can be prevented each year.
- Measles is a highly contagious vaccine-preventable disease caused by the measles virus. It is one of the most readily transmitted communicable diseases and probably the best known and most deadly of all childhood illnesses. Measles causes a high fever, rash, cough and can kill. It affects mostly children, but also young adults. Children usually do not die directly of measles, but from its complications such as pneumonia and diarrhea which attack their weakened immune systems.
- It costs less than a dollar to immunize a child against measles.
- A critical goal is to reduce measles mortality by 50% by 2005 (compared to 875,000 deaths in 1999).
- The WHO-UNICEF strategy to reduce measles deaths includes: achieving and maintaining high routine measles immunization coverage – ‘the first opportunity’ to infants; Providing a ‘second opportunity’ for measles immunization for all children through periodic supplementary immunization campaigns; Ensuring high quality measles surveillance is in place to detect and respond to outbreaks; and improving management of complicated cases.
- Collaborating partners include: WHO, UNICEF, the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the United Nations Foundation, humanitarian and non-governmental organizations, including the American Red Cross and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, governments of countries affected by measles, development banks, donor governments (e.g. Canada, Japan, the United Kingdom and the United States of America).
- The importance of developing long term immunization planning cannot be underestimated. This includes ensuring measles activities are fully integrated with other national health goals, establishing high quality surveillance, mobilizing necessary human and financial resources and planning for financial sustainability of measles mortality reduction activities.

How to stop a pastime from becoming an unhealthy obsession
A new hobby can be satisfying and fulfilling especially when one gets good at it. But when does spending too much time on an activity border on obsessive?
Last year, while training for an overseas marathon, I developed an ankle injury that forced me to pull out of the race.
I was deeply disappointed, not least by having to scrap a holiday to Japan with a hefty flight cancellation fee to boot.
What upset me more was all the wasted time and effort I had invested in preparing for the race, including sacrificing time with friends and family to wake up early for training sessions.
Lately, however, injuries have not been the only source of frustration in my running journey. As I get older, I have found myself increasingly discouraged by the lack of improvement in my race timings.
Unlike in my university days, when I first took up cross-country running, these improvements no longer come as easily, no matter how hard I train.
When I wake up for runs, I now find myself wondering: Why is a hobby that is supposed to relieve stress and keep me healthy having the opposite effect?
And when did the pursuit of a passion stop being enjoyable and instead start to take a toll on my mental health?
Experts I spoke to said that most hobbies, when taken seriously, can be beneficial, but like most things may also be detrimental if taken too far.
"A dopamine rush comes because of accomplishment," said Mr Edgar Tham, sports and performance psychologist at SportPsych Consulting.
"You have a positive reinforcement, and therefore it makes you motivated to do it again because it gives you a positive result mentally and emotionally."
But the danger comes when the "rush" is taken away through bad results, or when an individual is sidelined due to factors such as injury or an inability to complete a more complicated skillset, such as playing a favourite but more complicated song on the guitar.
"When you take it away from them, they have no other sources of dopamine rushes, so to speak ... you can see where that potential addiction can come from in the long run," he added.
"It's something people don’t speak up enough about ... people don’t want to admit that there's an addiction to a hobby."
SERIOUS HOBBIES ARE BENEFICIAL BUT WHEN DO THEY CROSS THE LINE?
Taking up a hobby and being serious about it is in itself not a bad thing, said experts.
Founder of mental health service Therapy-Help Juliana Pang said that hobbies and interests help children with their cognitive, social, emotional and physical development, and this extends to adulthood.
"With a hobby, usually there's some structured practice, some knowledge to learn mastery and skills," she said.
This not only provides personal satisfaction and fulfilment but also helps individuals connect with people with similar interests and be part of a community.
Artistic hobbies like painting allow for emotional expression, while physical interests like sports can improve fitness and lower health risks, she added.
"Overall, there is a benefit to having not just a passing interest in hobbies, but a commitment or a passion for it," she said.
Negative feelings towards a hobby, however, can emerge when there are setbacks or perceived failures.
"If our disappointment is hooked to our sense of achievement, performance, and self-identity, then we might have feelings of anxiety, maybe shame, for not being able to perform well vis-à-vis our peers,” said Ms Pang.
      
    If our disappointment is hooked to our sense of achievement, performance, and self-identity, then we might have feelings of anxiety, maybe shame, for not being able to perform well vis-à-vis our peers.
Disappointments can also come when hobbyists take on a "perfectionist" mindset as they achieve more in their interests.
"You are in this space where you have no idea of what failure means or is, and so the expectation is now broken or not accomplished when things go wrong," said Mr Tham.
But even if our hobbies are going well, could we unknowingly be going overboard?
Mr Tham said one sign that an obsession with a hobby is out of hand is when it begins to affect day-to-day function.
"It affects the mood, your daily habits and lifestyle, your work, your school, almost anything, because it's now weighing you down," he said.
In my case, whenever I am deep into a training cycle, I tend to take a "run at all costs" approach, which means going so far as to skip quality time with loved ones to fit in a run.
Ms Pang said that the compulsion to continue an activity despite its negative effects is a red flag to watch out for.
"When it becomes a compulsion, meaning that there's already negative impact, and you're still insisting on doing that rather than trying to balance out your time and attention, that's indicative of some problem," she said.
Indeed, if I end up missing the run for one reason or another, I tend to get moody, and sometimes those closest to me can sense it.
People who become overly obsessed with their hobbies often exhibit signs and symptoms similar to those facing stress at work, said Dr Jay-Lee Nair of Dr Jay-Lee Psychology Practice.
She said that among her clients are athletes who entered their sport with no expectations, before realising they had an aptitude for it, thus becoming more serious by entering competitions and even hiring a coach.
"They come to me because they feel really anxious about the experience, they suddenly have expectations that they never had before, and they feel a lot of pressure to suddenly make it a performance exercise and very results-oriented," said the sports and performance psychologist.
DOES SOCIAL MEDIA EXACERBATE THE PROBLEM?
A common joke among runners is that a marathon doesn’t count if you don’t post about it online.
While the line is meant as a joke, many runners, myself included, do indeed have a tendency to share our achievements and shiny new personal bests online.
And it's not isolated to sporting achievements: there are many who have also created accounts to share their various interests, be it baking, pottery, or even support for a football club – with some gaining a substantial following.
But while sharing one’s progress in their hobby can feel good and possibly inspire others, there are downsides as well.
Dr Jay-Lee said that those who constantly post about their progress on social media could end up in a cycle of being dependent on external validation in the form of likes or encouraging comments.
"That can lead to a lot lower satisfaction over time, simply because they're not really doing it for the intrinsic value, and they need the validation from the outside world to confirm that this is something they're doing well," she said.
Agreeing, Ms Pang said that some individuals also feel the pressure to continually post about their progress on social media.
"When there's a loss of perfection, the feedback, comments and the rapid loss of popularity can be quite devastating on some individuals if they had built their self-identity and their self-worth based on that initial popularity and validation," she said.
HOW TO FIND THE RIGHT BALANCE
The first step in managing an obsession with one’s hobby is to recognise that there is an issue.
"Are you painting because you love painting, or because you know you want to sell the painting for a million dollars? Are you interested in running because running brings you joy, or are you trying to strive to get that popularity?" said Ms Pang.
"Understanding the purpose for which you do the activity is helpful."
She added that looking to friends and family for feedback is crucial as well.
"Have a good inner circle that gives you good constructive feedback ... these people might share with you (that) there may be something that's not quite right with the way you are pursuing a certain activity," she said.
Feelings of disappointment related to hobbies are not unhealthy but how one deals with those feelings is key, added Ms Pang.
"We can use a setback to look at other strategies to get better at our hobbies, look at it with what is typically known as a growth mindset."
A growth mindset is the belief that one’s skills can continually improve through learning lessons from failures and working on weaknesses.
      
    Understanding the purpose for which you do the activity is helpful.
Another strategy is having a close friend or family member with whom to share disappointments, preferably someone who has experienced similar setbacks.
"These setbacks are then normalised and it is okay and you can recover from it, and I can try to learn from different experiences from different people," she said.
While not as damaging to someone’s health and relationships as vices like gambling and alcohol, addiction to one’s hobbies can also warrant professional intervention if it disrupts daily functioning.
Dr Jay-Lee said that 10 years ago, 2 per cent of those who sought help from her clinic were amateur athletes trying to better manage their sport. More recently, this has grown to 10 per cent.
Ms Pang said that it is often not obvious to seek professional help for matters regarding our hobbies, as hobbies are seen as intrinsically good.
"The hobby itself is not the problem. It's the obsession," she said.

French protests kick off amid heavy security blanket
PARIS: French police arrested more than 130 people and fired tear gas at some protesters on Saturday (Oct 24) as fresh demonstrations started, but the government said there were no early signs of the street violence that marred protests last weekend.
Authorities deployed 70,000 security forces across the country as nationwide marches were held against the cost of living.
"There has been no major incident" as of midday (6pm Singapore time), Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said, adding: "We will not tolerate any violence or any disturbance of public order."
Protesters' anger has been stirred further by President Emmanuel Macron's government banning non-union-led demonstrations. Several groups slammed what they called an attack on the right to protest.
Macron has blamed "ultra-left" groups wanting to "bring down the republic" for the worst of last weekend's violence, when public buildings were vandalised and hundreds of shops looted.
POLICE QUICK TO REACT
After being caught flatfooted by that unrest, police this time had armoured vehicles, helicopters and water cannon ready to respond to the slightest provocation.
"The police are really mobile ... They come and disperse marches before they even form," said a 21-year-old student in Lyon, speaking on condition of anonymity.
Police in Lyon fired tear gas to disperse about 150 protesters near the city center who had tried to block a road, an AFP journalist saw.
Nunez said 135 people had been arrested as of midday Saturday.
He added that weapons including metal balls, lead pellets, fireworks, slingshots, steel balls, improvised weapons, a katana sword and airsoft weapons had been confiscated.
"These seizures clearly demonstrate the determination of certain far-left and radical left-wing groups to turn a number of demonstrations violent," he said.
The minister spoke as the main march in Paris started. Police at the last minute changed the route from central Paris to the southern rim of the capital.
Murielle Guilbert of the Syndicale Solidaires union said it had been "outrageous" to ban non-union protests.
"We're here because there is obvious public anger" over low salaries, she said.
The march started in a calm and festive atmosphere.
Claire, a 26-year-old nurse who did not want to give a last name, said: "Not everyone is out to smash things up. Some of us are simply here to say we disagree and that we just want a better future."
BOARDED-UP SHOPS
Another protester, Aurore, 35, said that "people need to understand that the anger is real. We’ve been walked all over for 10 years".
Ynyane, a 19-year-old wearing a Dragonball Z costume, added: "Taxes are a bit too high, and I have to support people who are struggling."
Many retailers in Paris boarded up their windows or closed, fearing a return of looters on the margins of demonstrations who stripped stores last weekend.
Some 2,700 people were arrested after last weekend's violence, and the retail sector said shopowners were left with damage and losses totalling hundreds of millions of dollars.
The Louvre and the Musee d'Orsay museums were closed on Saturday for the new demonstrations.
PROTEST AGAINST LE PEN'S PARTY
Adding to tensions, Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party held a congress in Orleans to launch her campaign for a presidential election in six months.
Thousands of people yelling anti-fascist slogans marched against Le Pen, and President Emmanuel Macron, a pro-business centrist who cannot stand again. "Macron resign. Le Pen in prison," the crowd yelled. Police put their numbers at 11,000 while organisers said 26,000 took part.
The unrest highlighted tensions in France ahead of the vote, in which Le Pen leads in surveys.
Inflation in France, particularly for fuel, has surged since the start of the Middle East war in February.
Protests have also been taking place in Italy, Belgium, Spain and Portugal over different issues, yet with some overlap on inflation and education problems. Italy has mobilised 500 troops to Milan after street violence there.
While French unions reluctantly complied with orders banning marches from central Paris, Marseille and other cities, they and other groups decried a perceived "authoritarian drift" by the government.
The Yellow Vests, who staged disruptive protests against Macron eight years ago, called for more demonstrations on Oct 31 for "the freedom to protest".
A shopworker in the city of Rennes told AFP: "Bans are sometimes worse. Protesting is a right, and when you ban it you make it even more tempting."
Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, who marched in the Paris rally, said Macron "is going to understand that this is going to repeat itself every week".

The World Health Organization (WHO) and the Republic of Korea have a long-standing partnership spanning over 75 years. As a result of their fruitful collaboration, there has been significant progress in health and development all around the world. The Republic of Korea has gone from being a donor-recipient country to a donor-country and is now a leader in global health and playing a critical role on the world stage.
Dr Catharina Boehme, Assistant Director-General for External Relations and Governance (WHO) and Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination (Ministry of Health and Welfare, Republic of Korea), together with counterparts from WHO and the Government of the Republic of Korea. © WHO
To further strengthen this partnership and our commitment to working jointly to address global health challenges, WHO and the Republic of Korea convened their second Strategic Dialogue in Seoul from 28 to 29 August 2024. Dr Hye-Jin Kim, Deputy Minister for Planning and Coordination, Ministry of Health, led the Republic of Korea delegation and was joined by senior officials including Dr Young-Mee Jee, Commissioner, Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency, as well as senior counterparts from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, and the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety.
In addition, in line with WHO's work to enhance collaboration with parliamentarians, the WHO delegation also met with various Members of the National Assembly that are championing the global health agenda.
The recently concluded two-day meeting resulted in an alignment of priorities and paved the way for enhanced collaboration between WHO and the Government of Korea.

The Irish traditional musician Dónal Lunny has died at the age of 79 from cancer.
Lunny rose to prominence in the trio Rakes of Kildare alongside his brother Frank and Christy Moore. He went on to play in bands such as Planxty, Moving Hearts, the Bothy Band and Coolfin among others and toured the world.
A post on his Facebook page confirmed that Lunny died in St James’s hospital in Dublin on Friday morning.
“We are heartbroken to confirm that our beloved Dónal passed away peacefully this morning in Dublin following a short stay in St James’s hospital,” the post said. “Thank you for helping us to remember and celebrate his immense contribution to music, to culture and to so many people’s lives all over the world.”
The Irish president, Catherine Connolly, expressed her “deepest condolences to the family, friends and many musical collaborators of Dónal Lunny”.
In a statement, she said: “Dónal was one of Ireland’s greatest musical figures, a wonderfully talented musician and producer who was central to so many of the most influential moments of the last 60 years of Irish music.
“Dónal will be particularly remembered for his long partnerships with fellow musicians such as Christy Moore and Andy Irvine and for the innovative music he has left behind both as a musician in groups including Planxty, the Bothy Band and Moving Hearts and also as a renowned producer.
“This rich musical legacy, including his central role in the introduction of the bouzouki into Irish music, was appropriately recognised by his fellow artists in Dónal’s membership of Aosdána, as well as the well-deserved recognition which he received in being awarded a lifetime achievement award at the 2025 RTÉ Radio 1 Irish folk awards.
“Beyond his music, Dónal will be remembered for his warmth and the strong connection which he had with audiences all over Ireland and beyond. He will be deeply missed.”
The post ended in Irish, saying his likes will not be seen again: “Ní bheidh a leithéid arís ann.”
Lunny was born in Tullamore, County Offaly, and was a multi-instrumentalist but was best known for his mastery of the bouzouki. He was a talented melody writer and considered central to the revival of traditional music as he produced 17 albums under his record label Mulligan Records.
The taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said he was “deeply saddened” to hear of Lunny’s death. “A colossus of Irish music, as a performer, songwriter and producer,” he wrote in a post on social media.
“Uniquely gifted, Dónal carried traditional and folk music to new audiences through Planxty and his many other endeavours.”
Sinn Féin’s president, Mary Lou McDonald, also paid tribute online, saying: “Deeply saddened to hear of the passing of Dónal Lunny. A giant of Irish traditional music, Dónal helped shape the sound of Irish music for generations, bringing our rich musical heritage to audiences at home and around the world. His contribution to Irish music and culture will never be forgotten.
“Ar dheis Dé go raibh a anam [May his soul rest in peace].”

ED officer, head constable held in Lucknow for demanding ₹5 lakh bribe from complainant: CBI
The CBI has arrested an ED officer and head constable posted in Lucknow for allegedly demanding a ₹5 lakh bribe to help a complainant’s father in an Enforcement Directorate case.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) has arrested an Enforcement Directorate (ED) officer and a head constable for allegedly demanding a ₹5 lakh bribe from a complainant, the anti-corruption agency said on Friday.
The two officers were identified as enforcement officer Deepak Kumar, and head constable Manoj Dwivedi, both posted at the Lucknow Zonal Office of the ED. Dwivedi was deployed in the agency on deputation from Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and is not an ED’s cadre officer.
Both were charged under the Prevention of Corruption Act.
“The CBI registered the case on Friday against the head-constable of the enforcement directorate, Lucknow and unknown officials of the ED, Lucknow based on a complaint,“ the CBI said in a statement.
“It was alleged that the accused head constable (Dwivedi) demanded a bribe from the father of the complainant for helping him in the ED case in which he received two summons in the month of August and September 2026 from the ED Lucknow Zone,” the statement added.
A trap was laid and Dwivedi was caught while while demanding and accepting ₹5,00,000 on behalf of Kumar for favouring the father of the complainant in the ED case, the CBI said.

An interview with Sylvester Stallone from October 16 is going viral thanks to some candid comments the Tulsa King actor made about the casting of his daughter Scarlet Rose Stallone.
Stallone has a blunt message to naysayers: “Of course it’s nepotism, you idiot.”
The subject came up as Stallone was reflecting on comments he’s heard about the casting. “First they go, ‘Nepotism is terrible,’” he told USA Today. “I said, ‘Oh please, you’re not a good parent if you haven’t performed a little nepotism. Then obviously you don’t care about your kids, because they come first.’”
Stallone added, “‘Of course it’s nepotism, you idiot. That’s why we’re parents. We want the best for our children. So obviously, we let them have every advantage.’”
Watch on Deadline
The “nepo baby” charge has increased in visibility in recent years, as the offspring of Hollywood celebrities grow in prominence. Ryan Murphy alone has provided a home base for many: Billie Lourd (Carrie Fisher), Emma Roberts (Erik Roberts), Lily Rabe (Jill Clayburgh), Kaia Gerber (Cindy Crawford), Charlie Hall (Julia Louis-Dreyfus), Homer Gere (Richard Gere) and Ella Beatty (Annette Bening and Warren Beatty) have all featured in various Murphy series.
Stallone, though, points out that parents can only do so much. “Can they maintain that level of excellence?,” he asks in the USA Today article. “That’s out of our hands. But if you can open the door, we’ll see if they have the ability to go through it.

The National Council of Educational Research and Training (NCERT) has released a 20-hour introductory module on computational thinking (CT) and artificial intelligence (AI) for students of Classes 9 to 12. The activity-based module aims to help students understand how AI works, identify deepfakes, protect personal information and use AI tools responsibly.
Developed by faculty members from the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, IIT Jodhpur and NCERT, the module is aligned with the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020. It is designed for students with no prior knowledge of AI and focuses on practical learning rather than memorising technical concepts. The initiative is a welcome step towards preparing students for a world where AI is increasingly becoming part of everyday life.
Five Units To Build AI Awareness
The module is divided into five units covering AI in daily life, machine learning, AI errors, data privacy and the responsible use of modern AI tools. Students will learn how AI-powered applications work, why they sometimes produce incorrect information and how to verify their responses.
The first unit introduces students to AI systems they encounter regularly, including smartphone keyboards that predict words and applications that recommend music. It explains pattern recognition through familiar examples, such as identifying a friend in a crowded school canteen or recognising a song after hearing just three notes. Students are taught that while AI can identify patterns, it often lacks the context that humans naturally understand.
Learning How Machines Think
The second unit explains how machines learn from examples. Students will train an image classifier to identify everyday objects and then deliberately test its weaknesses. The exercise demonstrates how the quality and variety of training data influence an AI system’s performance.
The third unit, titled When AI Gets It Wrong, focuses on misinformation, deepfakes and AI hallucinations. Students will examine why AI-generated answers can sound convincing even when they are incorrect. They will also learn a five-step method to verify information before trusting or sharing it. This is particularly important as students increasingly encounter AI-generated content online.
Data Privacy And Digital Safety In Focus
The fourth unit introduces students to personal data protection, consent, fairness and digital safety. It also familiarises them with India’s Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023. Students will examine the privacy policies of applications they use and understand what information is collected, how it may be shared and how long it can be stored, Hindustan Times reports.
The module specifically warns students against sharing sensitive information with AI tools, including Aadhaar and PAN numbers, passwords, one-time passwords and personal documents. Teaching these precautions at the school level could help students develop safer digital habits before they begin using AI tools more extensively.
AI As A Helper, Not A Replacement
The fifth unit focuses on using AI tools effectively without becoming dependent on them. Students will learn to write and improve prompts, evaluate AI-generated responses and identify errors that require correction. The module promotes a “helper-stance”, encouraging students to use AI to improve their work while retaining responsibility for their own thinking.
Students will also maintain a “Curious Notebook”, recording their observations, reasoning and reflections throughout the five units. The module encourages experimentation and learning from mistakes instead of relying only on classroom lectures.
“This is not a module to be memorised. It is a set of habits to be practised,” the module development team states in its Letter to the Students.
Flexible Learning For Schools
The suggested teaching schedule covers 20 classroom hours and offers three ways to conduct activities. Students can use individual or shared devices, participate in teacher-led demonstrations on a common screen or complete exercises using paper and classroom discussions.
The third option, described as “unplugged” learning, allows schools with limited access to computers or internet connectivity to conduct the core activities. This flexibility is an important feature, as it allows students to learn fundamental AI concepts without depending entirely on digital infrastructure.
School Principals Welcome The Move
The introduction of the module has been welcomed by principals and representatives of schools affiliated with the Central Board of Secondary Education (CBSE). They believe that teaching AI concepts from Class 9 will help students develop skills needed in a technology-driven environment.
Praneet Mungali, trustee at the Sanskriti Group of Schools in Pune, described the move as a significant step towards preparing students for the future. He said early exposure to AI could strengthen critical thinking, creativity, logical reasoning and problem-solving skills. He also stressed the importance of helping students understand where AI can be used and what its limitations are.
Human Judgement Remains Essential
Dr Jyoti Arora, principal of Mount Abu Public School in Delhi, said the module would promote responsible technology use while improving students’ critical thinking, creativity and problem-solving abilities.
She said it would help students become “future-ready global citizens who use AI as a tool for innovation, guided by human judgement and values”.
NCERT also emphasised the importance of keeping human judgement at the centre of learning. “The module encourages students to become informed, confident, and responsible users of technology, while reinforcing that human judgement, creativity, and ethical responsibility remain central to learning,” the council said in a press release on Friday.
In the foreword, NCERT Director Dinesh Prasad Saklani underlined the same principle, stating that “technology can extend human capability, but judgement, creativity, responsibility, and ownership of learning remain with the learner”.
AI Education Expanding Across Classes
The latest module follows an earlier initiative by CBSE to introduce computational thinking and AI education for younger students. On April 2, the board launched a structured curriculum for Classes 3 to 8 to build AI awareness from an early age.
The curriculum recommends 50 hours of learning annually for Classes 3 to 5 and 100 hours for Classes 6 to 8. It aims to introduce computational thinking and AI concepts gradually, according to students’ age and learning abilities.
With AI education now extending across different school levels, the focus is shifting beyond simply teaching students how to use technology. The more meaningful goal is to help them question AI-generated information, recognise its limitations and make informed decisions while using it.

Vijayawada custodial death: CBI takes over probe, begins questioning of cops
A team of eight CBI officials visited the police station on Friday evening and examined the second floor, where the victim was reportedly kept in custody.
The Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI) on Friday took over the investigation into the alleged custodial death of 25-year-old Gade Sai Krishna from Krishnalanka in Andhra Pradesh’s Vijayawada from the special investigation team of the state police, people familiar with the matter said on Saturday.
The CBI’s Hyderabad unit registered a fresh First Information Report (FIR) and inspected the Krishnalanka police station, where Sai Krishna was allegedly detained and interrogated.
Also read: Demand for students' union, row over ‘slogans’ trigger tensions in Jamia Millia Islamia
A team of eight CBI officials, led by Additional Superintendent of Police Narendra Dev, visited the police station on Friday evening and examined the second floor, where Sai Krishna was reportedly kept in custody. The investigation is being supervised by CBI deputy inspector general Shiva Subramani.
A senior police official aware of the matter said the CBI team on Saturday started collecting technical evidence at the police station with the help of experts from the Central Forensic Science Laboratory (CFSL), Hyderabad.
On October 16, the state high court, which heard arguments over a habeas corpus petition filed by Sai Krishna’s mother Gade Vijayalakshmi on June 4, ordered a CBI investigation into the custodial death of Sai Krishna. The high court also directed the state government to pay ₹25 lakh compensation to Vijayalakshmi within four weeks.
Also read: Farooq Abdullah's remarks on Pakistan, Kashmiris spark row; BJP demands apology
It also ordered disciplinary proceedings against the erring police personnel. The high court directed the CBI director to immediately register a regular criminal case and entrust the investigation to a senior officer. It ordered that all officials found responsible for custodial violence should be proceeded against and prosecuted in accordance with the law.
On Friday, the CBI took possession of the case records and evidence collected by the SIT, including witness statements, other relevant documents and remand reports of the accused.
The CBI submitted a copy of the newly registered FIR to the court of the Fourth Additional Judicial Magistrate of First Class (in-charge) on Friday and also filed a memorandum in a sealed cover.
The CBI also sought details from the Crime Control Section (CCS) about the number of criminal cases in which Sai Krishna was an accused and the number of pending non-bailable warrants against him. The agency is also expected to question Sai Krishna’s mother in this regard.
The CBI also approached the court seeking permission to search the residences of two accused — Gulivindala Suresh Kumar (A4), a friend and close associate of suspended inspector SSVV Nagaraju, and Venkataraju (A7). The court is learnt to have granted permission for the searches.
The SIT already filed a chargesheet in the local court, identifying the roles of 13 people in the case. Apart from the police personnel allegedly involved in the incident, the SIT named Suresh Kumar, a close associate of Nagaraju, and subsequently added three more individuals as accused during the investigation.
The CBI will examine the existing chargesheet and the evidence collected by the SIT while independently investigating the allegations, the police official quoted above said.
According to the charge sheet, Sai Krishna was apprehended at Markapuram around 3 am on May 6 in connection with pending non-bailable warrants and brought to Krishna Lanka Police Station around 7 am. He was not produced before a magistrate, and his whereabouts subsequently became unknown.
On June 4, Gade Vijayalakshmi filed a habeas corpus petition before the Andhra Pradesh High Court, seeking directions to the authorities to produce her son before the court.
Subsequently, the Vijayawada police registered a case on June 19, and the state government constituted a SIT, led by Inspector General Ravi Prakash. The SIT arrested inspector Nagaraju and several police constables on June 23.
After detailed investigation, the SIT filed a chargesheet on September 19, confirming that Sai Krishna was subjected to custodial torture and was beaten to death by the Krishnalanka police at an abandoned building in Vijayawada on May 12 and his body was cremated on the same night.

Retired WWE icon Ric Flair is reportedly recovering at a Florida hospital after falling outside a Tampa restaurant yesterday, Friday, October 23. The incident itself came just hours after the 77-year-old former wrestler canceled a Seattle appearance due to a blood clot in his leg.
Flair’s daughter Charlotte Flair provided an update on her father’s condition last night, posting on X, “Not my dad telling the doctor he fell bc of warrior dropping him on his head…(ps: he’s going to be ok).”
The ex-wrestler’s accident was first reported by TMZ, which published photos Friday of Flair on the ground surrounded by medical workers and also being lifted into an ambulance. The outlet reported that Flair was “bleeding extensively” and seemed to have cut his head and his eye in the fall.
Earlier yesterday, Flair posted an Instagram message apologizing to fans attending the Washington State Horror Con in Seattle.
Watch on Deadline
“Unfortunately, I am dealing with a blood clot in my leg, and my doctors have limited my travel to 3–4 hours. Seattle falls outside that range, and as disappointed as I am, I have to put my health and recovery first. Blood clots are extremely serious and can be life-threatening. We have seen this recently with Jalen Hurts and the complications involving blood clots in his lungs. It is a reminder that this is not something to take lightly, and I must follow medical advice.”
Flair continued, noting that he is scheduled to have a procedure on the affected vein, which his doctors say will clear the way for travel. “I look forward to getting healthy and seeing you all down the road.”
Flair, full named Richard Morgan Fliehr, is considered one of the most successful WWE pro wrestlers ever, with a career spanning 50 years and at least 16 championships. He retired from active wrestling in 2022.

Good morning and welcome to our live coverage of events in Europe – we will be closely following protests across the continent today.
In France, hundreds of thousands are expected at rallies across the country, with high school students, unionists, “yellow vest” demonstrators and others turning out for a fourth weekend of protests demanding more government funding for schools and measures to help with housing and the cost of living.
Desperate to avoid the looting and property damage seen on the fringes of some protests last weekend, French authorities have ramped up restrictions on where protesters can march and which groups are “authorised” to do so. They’ve increased policing 20%, mobilising 70,000 police officers and soldiers to the streets, including both elite units and trainee officers.
Many of Paris’s metro stations and major museums and tourist sites are shut today, while across the country, shops and businesses have been urged to close their doors.
Community tensions are also high following a deadly shooting on Friday west of Paris where the gunman targeted non-white people, killing one person and injuring five others including a child. The French president called it a “racist terrorist attack”.
Meanwhile, Marine Le Pen’s anti-immigration party is also due to hold its national conference in the central city of Orléans. The far-right National Rally’s meeting is expected to draw up to 30,000 counter-demonstrators.
Protests are also being held in Italy, Spain, Austria, Portugal, Albania and Ireland today.
Tension was also high in the town of Orléans on Saturday as Marine Le Pen’s far-right, anti-immigration National Rally party gathers for its annual congress and the official launch of her presidential campaign.
The police presence in the city has been stepped up as around 5,000 party members and officials gather on Saturday and 10,000 attend Le Pen’s first campaign rally on Sunday.
A protest march by the left has been organised against “racism, fascism and imperialism”. Between 20,000 and 30,000 people are expected to demonstrate against the far-right in the city.
Several political personalities on the left were to attend the Orléans march including the leader of the Socialist party, Olivier Faure, the head of the leftwing CGT union, Sophie Binet, and the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko, from the party La France Insoumise.
The capital’s authorities have shut down the stations in a bid to contain crowds and curb movement throughout the city today.
The affected stations are: Argentine, Assemblée Nationale, Bel Air, Champs-Elysées – Clemenceau, Charles de Gaulle – Étoile, Cluny - La Sorbonne, Concorde, Daumesnil, Dugommier, Franklin D. Roosevelt, George V, Mabillon, Maubert – Mutualité, Miromesnil, Odéon, Picpus, Rennes, Rue du Bac, Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Saint-Sulpice, Sèvres - Babylone, Solférino, Tuileries and Varenne.
We’ve seen other attempts by authorities to restrict movement in cities across France for this weekend; Marseille authorities earlier this week said they would suspend public transport services on Saturday; they were forced to reverse the decision following outcry.
In Orléans, which is hosting the far-right National Rally congress, the tram lines are suspended and bike-sharing rentals have been removed from the city centre.
All through the night in neighbourhoods in the centre and east of Paris, the sound of sawing, drilling and hammering rang out as wooden boards were hastily secured into place to cover windows and shop-fronts.
Businesses being boarded up included opticians, supermarkets and pharmacies as well as trainers and handbag stores.
Hundreds of shops were smashed and looted over two nights last weekend in Paris, and thousands more in cities across France, including Marseille and Bordeaux.
At a public meeting at Paris city hall this week, some shop-owners had cried as they spoke of their fears of businesses being smashed and looted again this weekend.
“I’m afraid there isn’t enough wooden board left to protect shops and the demand is making it so expensive to board up shops,” one optician near Châtelet in the city centre said. “We’ll close up and take all our stock of glasses out of the shop.”

New Delhi, Oct 24: A special NIA court in New Delhi has ordered a trial against Yasin Malik, Zahoor Ahmed Shah Watali, Abdul Rashid Sheikh, Shabir Ahmad Shah, Naval Kishore Kapoor, Trison Farms and Construction Pvt Ltd, and Masarat Alam Bhat in Rs 8.9 crore money laundering case, according to a report in The News Mill.
According to the report, the accused received the said amount through hawala channels from the Pakistani establishment.
The charges stem from a case initially registered by the National Investigation Agency (NIA) in 2017. The accused are charged under Sections 120B, 121, and 121A of the Indian Penal Code (IPC), as well as Sections 13, 16, 17, 18, 20, 38, 39, and 40 of the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act (UAPA).
Special NIA Judge Prashant Sharma, as per the report, ordered the trial to begin, with prosecution evidence recording scheduled to start on November 19. The hearing was conducted in a closed courtroom. Malik appeared via video conferencing from Tihar Jail and denied the charges, stating he will contest the case.
In September, the court had framed charges against Malik and six others under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act (PMLA). It is alleged that the accused received funds from the Pakistani establishment and other terrorist organisations to support secessionist activities in Jammu and Kashmir. The court found sufficient prima facie evidence to charge all seven accused under Section 3 of the PMLA, punishable under Section 4.

Israeli PM pledges massive military operation after West Bank checkpoint attack
The Israeli military is demolishing homes and forcibly removing hundreds of Palestinians from a neighborhood in the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank following an attack by Palestinian gunmen on an Israeli checkpoint that killed two soldiers and wounded three others.
In response to that attack yesterday, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces a tough election on Tuesday, vowed to launch a military operation in the West Bank "on a scale not seen since the Six Day War," when Israel first occupied the West Bank almost 60 years ago.
"We will act to demolish this place, to change it completely," Netanyahu said in a televised speech from the location of the attack, close to the Palestinian city of Hebron.
He likened the plan to an Israeli military assault against two long-standing Palestinian refugee camps in the northern West Bank last year in which the Israeli army displaced tens of thousands of Palestinians. Human Rights Watch said those expulsions amounted to war crimes, a charge that Israel rejects.
On Friday afternoon, the Israeli military had already begun bulldozing homes close to the site of the shooting. The Israeli human rights group B'Tselem is calling on foreign governments to act to prevent "another wave of ethnic cleansing and war crimes."
Commenting on the attack, the Israeli military told NPR that soldiers were positioned behind concrete barriers at the checkpoint when two gunmen opened fire on them. A firefight continued for about 20 minutes before Israeli soldiers killed the attackers.
This comes amid a surge of violence and land seizures by Israeli settlers against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. The United Nations Human Rights Office for the occupied Palestinian territory has described it as a "new level of dehumanization of Palestinians."
Israel imposed widespread closures in Hebron on Saturday, making movement difficult in and around the most populous city of the occupied West Bank. Israel regularly imposes restrictions on movement across the Palestinian occupied territory with some 925 checkpoints, roadblocks, earth mounds and other barriers.
Analysts tie the wide-scale Israeli response to Friday's attack to the Israeli national elections on October 27, claiming this is an effort by Netanyahu to appear strong to voters. According to polls, Netanyahu and his main opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, are neck and neck in the race. Neither candidate currently has enough support to form a government.
"For Netanyahu, his ticket before the election is, 'I'm Mr. Security,'" Danny Citrinowicz, a senior researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies in Tel Aviv, told NPR. "In order to show that he is the protector of Israel, he will take harsh measures in order to show the Israeli public that he supports them and he's defending them."
This is a view shared by other analysts, who see this latest military action more as an effort by Netanyahu to remain in power than a closely thought-out strategy to improve Israel's long-term security. Citrinowicz called Netanyahu's response — to evict families from their homes in the neighborhood the attackers came from, without evidence of a connection to the gunmen — "collective punishment."
"The way to prevent [more attacks by Palestinians] is not collective punishment. It's by giving hope," Citrinowicz said. "Distinguish between those who want to commit terrorist attacks and arrest them and those who just want to live peacefully and help them to live peacefully, with an economy that works, with everything they need for stability.
Daniel Estrin in Tel Aviv and James Hider in Washington, D.C., contributed reporting. This story was edited by Samantha Balaban.

BJP accused Farooq Abdullah of echoing Pakistan's narrative and questioned his comments on the country's role in Jammu and Kashmir.
NEW DELHI: The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday strongly criticised National Conference chief Farooq Abdullah's remark claiming Pakistan was “protecting” the people of Jammu and Kashmir by repeatedly raising the "Kashmir issue" at international forums. BJP leaders accused Abdullah of echoing Pakistan's narrative.BJP Jammu and Kashmir leader Ravinder Raina called his remarks an “act of treason” and questioned how Pakistan could be considered a well-wisher of Kashmiris. Raina termed Abdullah's statement “highly condemnable and unfortunate”, alleging that Pakistan had supported terrorism in Jammu and Kashmir for decades.“The statement made by Dr Farooq Abdullah regarding Kashmir and Pakistan is highly condemnable and unfortunate. In fact, Dr Farooq Abdullah has committed an act of treason," Raina said."Pakistan is the killer of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. Over the last 35 years, Pakistan has sought to turn Jammu and Kashmir into a graveyard and a cremation ground. This is the very same Pakistan that has fostered terrorism within Jammu and Kashmir—providing training, bombs, guns, pistols, ammunition, and grenades to terrorists. How could Pakistan ever be a well-wisher to the people of Jammu and Kashmir?" he added.
BJP condemns Farooq Abdullah's statement
Uttar Pradesh minister Suresh Kumar Khanna also accused Abdullah of exploiting Kashmiris throughout his political career. He said the region's integration into the national mainstream under the Modi government was in the best interests of its people.“It is people like Farooq Abdullah who have exploited Kashmir throughout their lives. Farooq Abdullah is responsible for reducing Kashmiris to second-class citizens, and he ought not to be making such statements. It is precisely because of India’s diversity that Kashmir is now integrated into the nation’s mainstream, and every citizen of Kashmir enjoys the same rights as those in the rest of India. Therefore, the current situation in Kashmir—brought about by the Modi government—is what is truly in the best interest of the Kashmiri people. Today, the people of Kashmir are at their happiest, thanks to the Modi government,” Khanna said.BJP leader Altaf Thakur also condemned Abdullah's remarks, calling them an attack on India's unity and integrity. He demanded action against the National Conference chief.“This is an open rebellion against the country. His statement is against the unity and integrity of the country. The National Conference has always been anti-country. The statement made by Farooq Abdullah is completely an anti-country statement. Action should be taken against him,” Thakur said.Chhattisgarh deputy chief minister Vijay Sharma questioned Abdullah's allegations about the Centre's intentions towards Jammu and Kashmir, asking whether he considered himself separate from India.“If we point out that they lack love for the country, they immediately start complaining that such things are being said about them. He himself served as chief minister, and now his son is chief minister. He has full access to all resources—from across India and everywhere else. Yet, he still makes such accusations. If he claims that India’s intentions were not good, does that mean he views himself as separate from India? He should learn from his own son, Omar Abdullah,” Sharma said.
JD(U) questions echoing Pak's narrative
Janata Dal (United) state president G M Shaheen also criticised Abdullah, questioning why he continued to echo Pakistan's narrative despite having held several constitutional positions.“When a leader like Farooq Abdullah makes such a statement and supports Pakistan, what else can I call it but a misfortune? He has served as a chief minister, a member of the Rajya Sabha, and a member of parliament; he has worked within the framework of the country’s Constitution, yet, he chooses to speak the language of Pakistan. It is truly shameful. If Jammu and Kashmir is safe, it is because of India. Why does he always echo Pakistan’s narrative? The militancy that has plagued Kashmir since the 1990s was, in part, a consequence of his government. Whenever these people have come to power, they have invariably begun to speak the language of Pakistan. “You must have the courage to stand by the truth. Speaking the truth is not easy, but unless you speak the truth and stand firm by it, your future will never be secure,” he said.Apart from his comments on Pakistan and the Centre, Abdullah raised concerns about the mandatory two-year service requirement for doctors who pursue MBBS, MD or MS courses in Jammu and Kashmir. He alleged that a file related to the policy had been pending with the Lieutenant Governor for a year.“Doctors who come from outside Jammu and Kashmir to pursue MBBS, MD, or MS courses, as well as students who study medicine here, are required to serve for two years in villages, hospitals, and other areas across the region. If they fail to fulfil this requirement, they must pay Rs 50 Lakh to the administration. This is a region where a file has been pending with the Lieutenant Governor for a year, yet it has still not been approved. This is the state of affairs here. What can you expect from Delhi? Arsenal relieve pressure with Spurs win - can they kick on now?
- Published
Arsenal's victory over Tottenham on Saturday meant more than usual.
It was not just a win against their rivals at the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, but a first in six Women's Super League matches and a huge release of pressure.
Upon hearing the final whistle, confirming their 2-1 success, Arsenal's players ran towards their supporters in the away end to celebrate passionately.
It was a visible show of emotion, a moment of relief and a sense things could finally be turning in their favour after a disappointing WSL start where they had beaten only Brighton.
Could it now be the catalyst to repair a campaign that looked to have been derailed in just two months.
'Pure joy and happiness'
Arsenal started the day in the bottom half of the table, four points off fourth-placed Tottenham and 12 points behind leaders Manchester City.
With their title ambitions in ruins, manager Renee Slegers was facing weekly questions about her future and defeat by Spurs could have been the last straw.
Confidence was at an all-time low and a high-stakes north London derby was not the ideal game to go into with no momentum.
The nerves were obvious as there were misplaced passes, poor clearances and sloppy errors in a disjointed first half.
Tottenham had even taken the lead, although they held it for just four minutes as Georgia Stanway's powerful strike cancelled out a header from Cathinka Tandberg.
When asked what she said to the players at half-time, boss Slegers revealed: "I just gave constructive and tactical things that could help us to get the win, and remind us about the fight and intensity on the pitch.
"It was a real derby. The team were in a good place and were finding solutions themselves. It was just constructive messaging."
Arsenal were much better in the second half, putting more pressure on Tottenham and getting the winning goal they needed.
Referee Phoebe Cross pointed to the spot when Lisa Baum's shot bounced off the post and Tandberg's clearance hit the outstretched hand of her Spurs team-mate Ella Morris nearby.
Alessia Russo, who had failed to convert a big chance just moments earlier, made no mistake the second time around and slotted the ball past goalkeeper Lize Kop.
She roared in celebration and sprinted towards the away fans - an outburst of emotion that was replicated at full-time by England team-mate Leah Williamson.
Slegers stood back as her players enjoyed the adulation from supporters. They had finally delivered a win and the fans had something to sing about.
"I'm so happy we got it for them. We said we would play for the fans. We played for them and connected with them," said Slegers.
"We sold out the away section, they came in the rain and sang and fought with us throughout the game.
"At the end, it was scrappy and it was game management and they were all there with us.
"You could see how the team responded and how they were with the fans. It was pure joy and happiness. We want to capitalise on these emotions."
'This will definitely energise us'
It was the perfect result, but never easy.
Former Arsenal defender Gilly Flaherty told BBC One the visitors were "causing their own problems" in an unconvincing first half and they took time to settle.
They showed nervousness and had to cling on at the end, relying on a stroke of luck and a controversial refereeing decision to get them over the line.
But it was not undeserved and Slegers made the decision at full-time to show their feelings and celebrate with supporters in a different way, having abandoned their familiar post-match team huddle in the centre of the pitch.
"The fans were on our minds. We wanted to play for something bigger, not only for ourselves. That is always a balance," she said.
One Gunners fan told BBC Sport at half-time: "It's 1-1 but Arsenal look very nervy in and out of possession. Another week, another formation, another different starting XI. All feels so desperate and out of control."
Slegers showed understanding of their frustration as she added: "We normally do a huddle on the pitch but we decided to just go to the fans instead.
"Actions speak louder than words. There was not much more talking to do so we just wanted to celebrate with them.
"We had a run of games where results haven't been good enough. It was frustrating for everyone. This will definitely energise us."
Slegers is pleased Arsenal are set to embark on a busy period with their next game in the Women's Champions League on Wednesday against Benfica.
They have four home games in November and a trip to Barcelona - all good opportunities to build momentum.
Their WSL title hopes may be gone, but a top-three finish is imperative to secure European football next season.
"We need to back this up in the next couple of games. There were some really good things for us on the pitch," said Slegers.
"We want to be more consistent but this was a really good step. It's positive energy we want to capitalise on, but it's only a step."

This is not a list of edgy MAGA influencers sharing hot takes on X, or podcast hosts on Rumble boosting wild conspiracy theories. No, this is a list of some of the Republican candidates running for attorney general in states across the US.
A WIRED review has identified a slate of GOP attorney general candidates in more than half a dozen states, including key swing states, who have repeatedly expressed their belief that the 2020 election was stolen. If elected, several have said, they are willing to relitigate 2020 once again—and all will potentially play a key role in the 2028 presidential election.
“Any attorney general should be dedicated to upholding the rule of law,” Christina Beeler, senior counsel for the Chicago Lawyers’ Committee for Civil Rights, tells WIRED. “The office of attorney general is a powerful office, and it is deeply important that anyone in that role is dedicated to upholding the rule of law and the results of elections.”
The role of attorney general in the administration and protection of elections differs from state to state, but in general, as their state’s chief legal officer they are required to be a check on both the governor and the federal government. The functions of the role have been highlighted in recent months, as attorneys general across the country have repeatedly stood up to President Donald Trump and his administration's efforts to take control of elections, seize ballots, and obtain voter rolls containing sensitive information on US citizens.
Here, WIRED has looked at GOP candidates for attorney general in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, and Kansas, where some have openly espoused baseless allegations about the 2020 election.
Arizona
Warren Petersen, an Arizona state senator, was one of the most vocal supporters of Trump’s baseless claim that the 2020 election was stolen. In 2020, he signed a document that asked Congress to accept 11 alternate electoral votes for Trump, and later signed another demanding the US Senate reject Arizona’s slate of electors.
Petersen was also central to getting the bogus audit in Maricopa County approved, a process run by a firm called Cyber Ninjas. The audit ultimately showed that Joe Biden had won by more votes than originally thought. The whole process cost Arizona taxpayers millions.
Earlier this year, Petersen complied with a grand jury subpoena, handing over files on the Cyber Ninjas audit to the FBI as part of its investigation into the 2020 election in Maricopa.
And the lawmaker has also signaled a possible desire to relitigate the 2020 election if he’s elected, calling for an expansion of the attorney general’s Election Integrity Unit. “People will know we’re serious about it,” Petersen said during his primary campaign in July. “Just like they know the Trump DOJ is serious about it right now.”
Polls show Petersen tied with his Democratic opponent, Kris Mayes.
Georgia
In Georgia, the focus of much of Trumpworld’s conspiracy theories about elections, the GOP’s nominee for attorney general is Brian Strickland. In 2020, as a state senator, Strickland shared a press release that called for officials to consider launching an investigation into “fraudulent activities” in the 2020 election, a forensic audit of the election in Georgia, and new voting laws in the state.
Strickland has also signaled his willingness to fall in line with the Trump administration’s continuing efforts to investigate the 2020 election. When FBI officials raided Fulton County’s election offices earlier this year and seized ballots from the 2020 election, Strickland called it a “transparency” measure. “Fulton County can't run elections,” Strickland wrote on X in February. “That's the simple truth. An Atlanta Journal Constitution poll published this week shows Strickland in a tie with his Democrat opponent Tanya Miller.
Kansas
Unlike the other election deniers on this list, Kris Kobach is already in the position he’s running for in November, having won the attorney general’s race in 2022.
A long-time promoter of baseless conspiracy theories about fraudulent elections, Kobach previously served as Kansas’ secretary of state from 2011 to 2019. During his time in office, Kobach claimed that an estimated 18,000 noncitizens were on the state’s voter rolls based on non-peer reviewed research that initially found six people who may have attemped to register or registered to vote. In the wake of the 2020 election, Kobach was an adviser to Texas’ effort to overturn the results and assisted a member of the Michigan Board of State Canvassers who tried to rescind her vote to certify Michigan’s 2020 presidential election results. In 2022, Kobach was announced as a headliner at a Kansas rally with prominent election denier Lindell.
Recent polling suggests Kobach is in a tight race with his Democratic opponent, Chris Mann.
Michigan
In Michigan, Eaton County prosecutor Doug Lloyd won the GOP nomination for attorney general earlier this year, in a race that had once included Matt DePerno, a lawyer facing felony charges for undue possession of a voting machine and conspiracy in the wake of the 2020 election. (DePerno pled not guilty to the charges, and the case is still pending in the district court.)
Unlike DePerno, Lloyd is not typically labeled as an election denier, and he has claimed to be more moderate than his Democratic opponent, Eli Savit. But in a recent podcast interview reviewed by WIRED, when asked about “credible concerns raised by voters about the 2020 election,” he signaled his willingness to relitigate the six-year-old issue.
“I believe the attorney general has the ability to actually use their investigative officers within their office or the Michigan State Police to actually go back and look at those items,” Lloyd told the MI True Red podcast. “And so as I look at it, you know, I want to take those things in.”

In Nevada, Trump has endorsed lawyer Adriana Guzmán Fralick for the position of attorney general. That may be because she has said she would push for Nevada’s version of the SAVE Act, which Trump has failed to force Congress to approve on a federal level. The act would impose severe restrictions on eligible voters by requiring those registered to produce a passport or birth certificate, documents that tens of millions of Americans readily do not have.
"President Trump is fighting for secure elections—but DC keeps dragging its feet,” Guzmán Fralick wrote on Facebook earlier this year. “Nevada shouldn't have to wait. As your Attorney General, I will push for the SAVE Nevada Act to remove non-citizens from our voter rolls, count all ballots on Election Day, and end universal mail-in voting. What Washington won't finish, Nevada will.”
Experts have repeatedly said the SAVE Act would disenfranchise millions of voters.
Guzmán Fralick has also touted the endorsement of Joey Gilbert, a far-right boxer turned MAGA influencer who gained fame for spreading conspiracy theories about the Covid-19 pandemic. Paris shuts museums and police deploy in big numbers for new protests across France
Major museums in Paris are closed as authorities deploy a large police force for new protests across France
PARIS -- Major museums in Paris closed and authorities deployed a sizable police force for a round of new protests Saturday across France, hoping to prevent a repeat of last week’s violent unrest that shocked the country.
Scenes of looting, burned-out cars and attacks on public buildings left the impression that the government had lost control, as groups of masked vandals targeted businesses in Paris and other city centers.
Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said as many as 70,000 officers will be deployed nationwide, along with helicopters, armored vehicles and water cannons.
A massive turnout is expected again after more than half a million took to the streets last week.
Major museums including the Louvre, Orsay Museum, Picasso Museum and Grand Palais — where a major Cézanne exhibit is on display — are closed Saturday. Art Basel, one of the world’s most prestigious contemporary art fairs, opened to the public Friday, but only for the day, with the threat of unrest prompting organizers to cancel the weekend program.
Parisian shopkeepers have been barricading their stores all week. Near Place de la République in Paris, one of last weekend’s hot spots, a bank branch and other businesses were boarded up with wooden panels to deter potential looters.
Following the unrest, Paris police prefect Patrice Faure urged Parisian shopkeepers to hire security guards. He later clarified that protecting business owners and their establishments is the responsibility of the government.
Some 3,000 shops across France were damaged or looted last weekend.
Protest marches are scheduled in Paris and Marseille, but some other rallies, including in Lyon, Nice and Montpellier, have been banned by local authorities. Cities outside Paris were hit hard by the unrest. In Limoges, a suspected arson nearly destroyed the 19th-century city hall.
Trade unions have criticized the bans, calling them violations of freedom of expression, which is protected by the constitution.
President Emmanuel Macron, a centrist, entered the crisis in the final stretches of his term, with his popularity at its lowest since he took office in 2017. He has said that the measures are needed to protect city centers, businesses and public buildings.
Saturday’s demonstration in the city of Orléans, about 110 kilometers (70 miles) south of Paris, will also be closely watched.
About 50 organizations have called for a protest against the far right on the sidelines of the two-day congress of Marine Le Pen’s nationalist, anti-immigration party ahead of next spring’s presidential election. Organizers include labor unions, left-wing parties, student and anti-racism groups.
The demonstrations first erupted last month in a high school southeast of Paris over a lack of staff.
From there, class boycotts and demonstrations spread to other Paris suburbs and nationwide, including smaller towns. High school students have raised concerns about underfunded schools and staff shortages, particularly in lower-income neighborhoods. Some also called for a reform of the university admissions system, seen by many as unfair.
With the government seemingly unable to respond to students’ demands, the movement has morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, just months before the vote to choose Macron’s successor.
“The money is now concentrated in the hands of very few people," said Victoria Ambrosini, an art critic and art teacher at Saint-Denis University. “And it’s not possible anymore.”

Bhopal (Madhya Pradesh): Bhopal Municipal Corporation (BMC) will take a loan of Rs 493 crore to complete projects under AMRUT 2.0, abandoning its earlier plan to raise Rs 200 crore through bonds. The proposal was approved amid uproar and questions by a majority vote during the municipal council meeting on Saturday.
AMRUT 2.0 covers several projects, including water supply, four sewerage packages and the rejuvenation of Upper Lake, Kaliyasot Lake and Shahpura Lake.
Later, mayor-in-council member Ravindra Yati said to add other remaining water bodies of Bhopal while addressing the concern raised by the Congress councillors over sewage dumping in all other water bodies.

The BMC had earlier planned to raise Rs 200 crore through bonds but has now decided to borrow the entire outstanding amount. According to the proposal, the Centre will contribute 25% of the project cost, the state government will put in 58% and the corporation the remaining 17%.
