It’s a great time to buy a rug. The floors are getting cold, and you need to be prepared for your winter hibernation. Fall is also hosting season, which means making your place more presentable for the holidays. Maybe you’ve moved, like many do this season, and are still furnishing your new space. Fortunately, home goods sales are plentiful this time of year.
Ruggable’s October Hosting Sale is one of my favorite excuses to redecorate, with up to 30 percent off select styles. It runs through October 25, so your window is closing as I type. Keep reading for more reasons I love Ruggable, plus a few of my favorites currently on sale.
For People Who Make Messes
I adore Ruggable. The entire WIRED Reviews team adores Ruggable. I have the Pamir Moroccan Flatwoven runner under my kitchen sink, and it's gorgeous, but I don’t panic when spills and stains happen. In fact, I welcome them. The beauty of a washable rug is that you can actually live on it, which feels almost radical when so much home decor seems designed for childless, pet-free people who never eat or drink.
WIRED editor Harry Rabinowitz has a toddler and a cat, both of whom have peed on his hallway rug. Both times, he was grateful he could toss it in the washing machine and dryer and move on. Commerce executive director Cooper Fleishman was debating between the Wendel Ochre Rug by Anthropologie, the bohemian Yara Navy & Bronze Rug, and the Berber-inspired Enya Multicolor Rug for his office. Reviewer Simon Hill has the Santiago Persian Tufted Rug in his home in Scotland (yes, they ship to the UK and Europe) and recommends the Mandalore Tufted Rug for any Star Wars fans out there.
Ruggable has thousands of designs to choose from—2,122 to date. It’s a blessing and a curse. The brand also regularly offers alternatives to discontinued styles, so all is not lost if you were eyeing a piece you can no longer find. Note that the sale does exclude the new Easy Care Wool collection, along with gift cards, spot cleaner, and rug pads. Read the terms and conditions before you buy, and don’t delay; the sale ends October 25.
Is Ruggable Worth It?
While we stan Ruggable, it’s not without its shortcomings. WIRED editor Kat Merck has the Jonathan Adler Venom Flatwoven Rug in her kitchen; the edges curl up, and it drives her nuts. I will say my Ruggable’s nonslip pad has betrayed me more than once. It shifts around the kitchen and is the occasional tripping hazard. Aligning a rug onto the pad is also two-person job, but it’s not impossible if you live alone. Customers online have also reported issues with prints fading over time, but that’s practically a given with high-traffic, machine-washable rugs.
We also like Revival, which has an assortment of hand-knotted and woven imported wool rugs at reasonable prices. Plus, the company is having its own 20-percent-off sitewide sale that ends on Sunday.

Austria expels 4 Russian diplomats linked to espionage, official says
Austria has ordered four Russian diplomats to leave the country, accusing them of espionage
VIENNA -- Austria on Friday ordered four Russian diplomats to leave the country after accusing them of espionage, an Austrian official said.
Austria — and particularly Vienna, its capital — has long been considered a hotbed for spying because of lenient espionage laws and a high concentration of diplomats, given the many international organizations based in the city.
The Austrian official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter, said the expulsions were linked to espionage and that the diplomats were told to leave in the coming days.
Austria’s Foreign Ministry said that three of the four were diplomats at the Russian Embassy in Vienna while the fourth was based at Moscow’s mission to the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe.
The ministry, in a brief statement, said the Russian diplomats had “engaged in activities incompatible with their diplomatic status” and had therefore been declared personae non gratae. The ministry did not provide further details about the diplomats or their alleged activities.
Russia’s Deputy Foreign Minister Dmitry Lyubinsky told the state-run Russian news agency TASS that “a reaction is unavoidable.”
The move brings the number of expelled Russian diplomats since 2020 to 18.
In May, Austria expelled three Russian Embassy employees who were suspected of espionage by using antennas on Russian diplomatic buildings, according to the Austrian Foreign Ministry. The installations allowed Russia to intercept data transmitted by international organizations based in Vienna via satellite internet, Austria's public broadcaster ORF reported at the time.
European nations and Russia have expelled each other’s diplomats on several occasions since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Austria has given aid to Ukraine but not military equipment since it has a policy of military neutrality.
Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger and her liberal Neos party have frequently called for taking a tougher stance on Russian espionage in Austria, including calling for an overhaul of Austria’s espionage legislation.
The legislation now in place punishes espionage by foreign services only if it targets Austrian interests.
An overhaul of the legislation is still being worked out and negotiated by the Austrian government, which aims to expand the punishment for espionage to include actions directed not only against Austria itself but also against international organizations.
Austria is a European Union member that has a policy of military neutrality.
Vienna is host to several U.N. agencies, including the International Atomic Energy Agency and the U.N. Office on Drugs and Crime, as well as other international groups such as the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe and OPEC.

Revanth Reddy said Telangana aimed to emerge as the country’s largest industrial hub for the defence industry, calling upon domestic and global companies to step up investments in defence manufacturing, aerospace, space technology, cybersecurity, artificial intelligence (AI) and drone technology.
Addressing the curtain-raiser for Raksha Expo-2026, he said the State had the necessary ecosystem, skilled human resources, research institutions and industrial capabilities to play a leading role in strengthening India’s defence manufacturing sector.
The government would soon unveil its Aerospace and Defence Policy 2.0, aligned with the Telangana Rising Vision 2047, he said.
Mr. Revanth Reddy said Hyderabad occupied a strategic position in India’s defence ecosystem, being home to several important research institutions and strategic establishments associated with the Indian Army and the Indian Air Force.
Although Telangana is the only landlocked State in southern India, it continued to make significant contributions to the Indian Navy, he said, referring to the very low frequency (VLF) naval radar facility being constructed in the Damagundam Reserve Forest in Vikarabad district.
He stressed that India should move beyond importing technologies required for warfare and become a country capable of exporting advanced defence technologies. Strong defence capabilities were necessary not only to fight wars but also to preserve peace by deterring adversaries from initiating conflicts, he said.
The Chief Minister said Telangana had been working towards realising this vision but needed greater participation from industry leaders and investors to achieve more ambitious targets. He urged companies to double their investment plans in the State and assured them of the government’s cooperation in addressing their requirements.
“Tell me what support you need from me to achieve this objective. I am ready to extend all necessary assistance,” he said, emphasising that the government was committed to creating a conducive environment for investment.
No policy paralysis
Stating that there was no policy paralysis in Telangana, Mr. Revanth Reddy said political and ideological differences would not come in the way of investment and development. The government had a clear approach and strong determination to advance economic growth, he said, urging industry leaders to think big and explore opportunities across strategic sectors.
While the State accounted for more than 2.5% of India’s population and contributed about 5% of the country’s gross domestic product (GDP), he wanted Telangana’s share in the national economy to rise to 10% by 2047.
Defence manufacturing, aerospace and allied industries would play a crucial role in achieving this objective, he said.
The Chief Minister also invited investors to participate in the second edition of the Invest Telangana Global Summit, scheduled to be held at Bharat Future City on December 7, 8 and 9.

Donna Nelson's family ecstatic she is home after prison transfer from Japan
In short:
Donna Nelson's daughters say they were told at the last minute of the prison transfer deal that brought their mum home from Japan.
Nelson, who was convicted of drug smuggling after being duped in a love scam, is now serving out her time in Western Australia.
Her family say they are grateful to have her back home.
Grandmother Donna Nelson was greeted with lots of hugs — and her favourite cappuccinos — on her return to Perth from Japan under an international prison transfer her daughters say has "lifted a weight" out of their lives.
The 60-year-old was arrested in January 2023 at Narita International Airport and charged with trying to import almost 2 kilograms of methamphetamine after she was tricked by a love scammer into carrying a bag filled with drugs.
Loading...
She was found guilty of drug smuggling and sentenced to six years in jail, three of which she has already served at a Japanese prison.
The former Greens candidate and Aboriginal health advocate is now being held at Bandyup Women's Prison in Perth, an outcome two of her five daughters say they and their mother could not be happier with.
"She's so happy, she's ecstatic. She's so happy to be able to have a cappuccino again," Ashlee Charles said of her mum.
"She's missed her cappuccinos. She was a regular cappuccino drinker… and she never had one all this time (in Japan)."
Ms Charles said in addition to indulging in her favourite coffee, her mother also enjoyed a lot of time with family and met her youngest grandchild for the first time.
"She hasn't had a hug this whole time,"
Ms Charles said.
"She got at least 10 hugs yesterday. She got so many hugs. We tried to make up as much as we could."
'Breathing the same air'
The prisoner transfer that brought Nelson home began last year after she abandoned her final avenue for appeal.
Daughter Kristal Hilaire, who had visited her mother in Japan, said the process of bringing her home had been stressful.
"It's been very secretive and we've had to put a lot of trust in our government and the Japanese government," she said. "That's been hard."
The family said they only found out when their mother would return at the last minute, and could not stop crying with relief once she contacted them from Perth.
"It's like a weight was lifted that you'd forgotten was there, because it became normal to be wearing that weight and today you wake up and you're feeling renewed," Ms Hilaire said.
Ms Charles said she was looking forward to having her phone "blow up again" with calls from her mother, who used to call her daughters at least once a day but was unable to contact them on any regular basis from jail in Japan.
"It's weird to think that we are breathing the same air as her now and we literally can just drive past where she is," she said.
Nelson's family are uncertain about the future, but hopeful she could be up for parole in February.
For now, they are just grateful to the authorities for bringing her home.
"We can't thank them enough, they've made our family whole again,"
Ms Charles said.

For Mugdha Kalra, a parent of a special needs adult, financial planning has consumed the past few years. The question for her is, who will take care of her son when she is no longer there? She is planning to set up a trust fund that will help him reside at a support home. Ms. Kalra is not alone: for parents of children of special needs, the question of ‘who after me?’ is constantly at the back of their minds, a question made difficult by the fact that there is very little in the way of State-funded support services in the country.
“Even the basic facilities cost ₹50,000/month. A parent must make a lifetime plan for their child to be able to have this support once they are old or too incapacitated to take care of their child. Many people with autism also have comorbidities or other health conditions and money is needed for this too. Parents need to start planning early and set up trust funds for the child,” says Ms. Kalra, who is also an autism advocate.
Understanding autism
Autism is a diverse group of conditions related to development of the brain. The World Health Organization estimates that as of 2021, 1 in 127 people globally had autism. Exact numbers for India are hard to come by, but up to 1.8-2 million children in India are thought to have ASD, as per figures cited in a paper published in Cureus in 2024.
Not everyone who is on the autism spectrum has the same level of needs or abilities. Some people with autism may face several difficulties in their day-to-day lives, while others may only need help with specific tasks. Those with higher needs may require assistance from a caregiver to function and live a life of dignity. In India, as in many other countries, caregiving responsibilities fall on the parents, and predominantly on mothers. But this then raises the question of long-term planning: how to ensure their child is provided for, and care for, after they are gone or unable to care for them anymore.
“My son will outlive me; a facility for neurodivergent individuals is the only option,” says Sutapa Bose, senior special educator, India Autism Center (IAC), a non-profit organisation based in Kolkata. Her son has just turned 19 and she is planning to set up a trust fund for him soon to help in his future care and living. “Financial stress is always there; care has become expensive. But his health and safety are also major concerns for us,” she adds.
Guilt, sibling and caregiver burnout
Caregiving is no easy task. It take a toll, both physically and mentally. “There is always guilt about not doing enough for our children even though our personal lives are affected,” says Ms. Bose, adding that their parents’ mental health inevitably suffered, an aspect of caregiving that is not much attention is paid to.
An unfair amount of the burden of caring for a person with autism also falls on the sibling, if there is one, who is younger and more able than the parent, so an unsaid expectation lies on them to offer lifetime care, Ms Kalra added.
This is what happened in the case of the Chatterjees. Jharna Chatterjee’s son lived and grew up during a time when she was the only breadwinner in the family and also took on caregiving responsibilities. Her son, Sanjib Chatterjee, passed away 16 years ago due to comorbidities. She did not have the financial resources to send him to a care facility.
“It hurts my soul to think that my son passed away, but in a way, as a mother I can die in peace knowing that my son led a dignified life and was cared for. How would I ensure that if he lived after I passed away? My elder son had spent half his life caring for my younger son, who was autistic. It drained our finances, we lost our house, and my elder son lost his business while taking care of his brother. Life felt unfair, but we had no choice,” said Ms. Chatterjee, who is now 87.
Little support
Parents, caregivers and experts point out that what makes their caregiving harder, is the lack of support from both the government and the society in caring for people with autism.
Ms. Kalra notes that even when support homes are available, the basic facilities are sometimes below average and may not always offer a dignified life.
“Once we are not there, we hope to ensure our children are in a place where they have a dignified and structured life and are cared for. However, the government does not do much: India has individuals and NGOs trying to make small changes. That is not enough. We need to have structural and policy-based change in the country to make the society more inclusive for people on the spectrum,” points out the parent of twin boys with autism.
The IAC, in this regard, recently brought out a white paper to seek GST exemption for disability support services. The institute argued that taxing therapy and rehabilitation increases the financial burden on families and sought a service-based approach instead of disability severity thresholds. Representatives of IAC also met with the Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman and presented the paper to her and put forth their demands. According to Sakhi Singhi, a governing board member of IAC, the Finance Minister acknowledged the issue and assured them that they would look into the matter.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has asserted that Tehran retains full control over the Strait of Hormuz and accused two oil supertankers carrying more than 4.5 million barrels of crude oil combined of striking naval mines while attempting to use what it described as an unauthorised route through the strategic waterway, ANI reported.
The claims come amid escalating tensions between Tehran and Washington, with US officials discussing the possibility of military action against Iran even as diplomatic efforts continue.
The IRGC said maritime security was being maintained under Iranian regulations. Its navy alleged that the two supertankers attempted to navigate a southern route that had not been authorised by Iranian authorities.
According to a statement from the IRGC Navy's Public Relations Office, reported by Iranian state broadcaster Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting (IRIB), explosions and fires in the vessels' engine rooms disabled the tankers and forced their crews to abandon ship.
Iran has also warned that it would not permit US military vessels to enter the Persian Gulf, rejecting Washington's assertions that Iranian military capabilities had been significantly weakened.
Major General Ali Abdollahi, chief of the general staff of Iran's armed forces, said Iranian forces had rendered the US Navy ineffective in the region, according to Iranian state broadcaster Press TV.
"The US president must only dream of their military and army entering the Persian Gulf again. They will take this wish to their graves," Abdollahi said, adding that Iran would not allow US military vessels to enter the Gulf.
He also challenged US President Donald Trump's repeated claims that Iran's nuclear facilities had been destroyed, questioning why Washington continued to raise concerns about Tehran's nuclear programme if the facilities had already been eliminated.
Abdollahi accused the US president of making statements intended to mislead public opinion.
The competing claims over maritime security come as the Strait of Hormuz remains central to concerns about global energy supplies and international shipping.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Friday that oil exports from the Persian Gulf had risen above pre-conflict levels despite Iran's attempts to disrupt maritime traffic.
In a post on X, Bessent said exports were "roaring back" and had surpassed pre-conflict levels. He added that Iran's threats had failed to stop the flow of energy to global markets.
Iran, meanwhile, has maintained restrictions on maritime traffic through the strait and warned that vessels attempting to pass without coordinating with its authorities could face serious consequences.
The waterway is a critical route for global oil shipments, making any disruption a potential concern for energy markets and shipping operators.
Uncertainty over the possibility of further military action has added to tensions between the two countries.
US Ambassador to Turkiye Tom Barrack said on Friday that a US strike on Iran could take place over the weekend, although he said Trump remained open to a diplomatic agreement.
Barrack said diplomatic discussions involving regional countries, including Pakistan and Qatar, were under way. The issues being discussed included the Strait of Hormuz, uranium enrichment, sanctions relief, the unfreezing of Iranian assets and security commitments towards Israel.
Trump appeared to distance himself from the ambassador's remarks when asked about the prospect of an imminent strike after arriving in Florida.
Later, during an election rally in Florida, Trump warned that Washington could launch "another little Epic Fury" against Iran if Tehran failed to reach an agreement.

The New York Knicks organization sent employees a phishing email promising free championship rings in a test of its staff’s ability to detect scams, The New York Times reported yesterday. “Congratulations, your Employee Championship Ring is here,” the email sent in late September said, instructing employees to click a link to make a selection from two ring designs.
Madison Square Garden employees who clicked that link “were forced to attend a mandatory cybersecurity class to help satisfy some of [owner James] Dolan’s growing cybersecurity concerns,” the report said, citing team sources. Dolan is the owner of the Knicks, the New York Rangers, and Madison Square Garden.
It’s common for corporations to send phishing emails to find out which employees don’t pay attention to clues that an email is a scam. A cybersecurity-test email often appears to be from the company itself but includes telltale signs of phishing. For example, Ars Technica owner Condé Nast sends phishing-test messages from email addresses with a misspelled domain, “condenest.com.”
It’s not difficult for the typical Ars Technica reporter or editor to spot this kind of tell, but we haven’t received any offer as valuable as a free NBA championship ring. We can hardly blame a Knicks organization staffer for being fooled or at least greatly annoyed by a fake offer of a ring commemorating the basketball franchise’s first NBA championship in more than half a century.
We don’t know whether the Knicks email had any obvious signs that it was a phishing test, such as a misspelled domain name. The offer wasn’t implausible, either. “Typically, most employees for NBA teams receive rings, even if they are not as fancy and expensive as the ones the players receive,” wrote Joe Vardon, senior NBA writer for The Athletic, which was bought by The New York Times in 2022 and then merged into the parent news organization.
Phishing email and empty ring boxes
Vardon’s article was primarily about how Knicks assistant coaches did not get rings on Tuesday when the team raised its first league championship banner since 1973. The assistant coaches were handed boxes without rings inside, though they are expected to receive rings later on.

After deadly shooting, Israel forcibly evicts hundreds of Palestinian families from Hebron homes
Israeli forces have forcibly evicted hundreds of Palestinian families from their homes across several neighbourhoods after a shooting on Friday near the Farsh al-Hawa checkpoint west of Hebron, in which two soldiers were killed and three others wounded.
As part of what it termed an "operation to thwart terrorism", the Israeli military said the operation was launched in the city of Hebron, in coordination with the Shin Bet (internal security service) and the Border Police in the West Bank.
The two suspected Palestinian attackers were also killed by Israeli forces, according to the military.
The army said it was conducting searches to locate and dismantle what it described as “terrorist infrastructure” and weapons, while interrogating dozens of suspects.
It said the operation was focused on the area from which the alleged attackers had operated and that residents could leave through designated exits.

But residents described being ordered from their homes at gunpoint, with little time to gather belongings and no clear information about when they would be allowed to return.
The families who spoke to Middle East Eye said they were evicted on Saturday morning from the neighbourhoods of al-Jalada, Ein Deir Bahha, Wadi al-Maghariba and Shi'b al-Milh.
The al-Jalada neighbourhood is home to the families of the two alleged perpetrators of the shooting, Ahmad and Hamouda al-Joba, who were killed by Israeli military fire after they reportedly killed two soldiers and wounded others.
Abdul Hamid Shahada, a resident in the neighbourhood, told MEE that the Israeli military stormed the area shortly after the attack on Friday morning.
A large number of soldiers, accompanied by several military vehicles, took up positions near the homes of the Joba family.
During the incursion, the Israeli military distributed a map designating homes and adjacent buildings for evacuation and compelled a number of families to leave their residences.
'Until further notice'
Shahada and his family said they watched the unfolding events from their windows.
“We watched them forcing families out of their homes; they even beat one of the men."
"We stayed in our building, waiting anxiously, and packed small bags with essentials: medicines, mobile phone chargers, and important documents. We didn't sleep all night," he said.
At 9am on Saturday, soldiers stormed the family’s building and ordered Shahada to tell all the residents, about 54 people, mostly children, along with his 79-year-old ailing mother, to leave at once.
"They gave us only five minutes. Although we had anticipated an evacuation and tried to prepare the children, they were trembling and crying. Even the women wept as we were being led out," he told MEE.
"The soldiers ordered us to keep our hands behind our heads and forbade us from taking any clothing or belongings other than our small personal bags," he added.
The soldiers directed the families along a specific route toward Al-Salam Street.
From there, some went to stay with relatives, while others sought shelter at the Child Happiness Centre, which the municipality had opened to accommodate them.
The soldiers didn’t tell Shahada and his family when they might be able to return, saying only "until further notice", though they did inform some other families that they would be kept out of their homes for six months to a year.
Shahada and his family say they cannot stop thinking about the fate of their homes, especially after seeing the houses of their neighbours left with doors and windows wide open and being ransacked and vandalised by the soldiers.
Emergency plan
The forcible displacement has coincided with demolitions targeting residential buildings, commercial shops and industrial facilities in Farsh al-Hawa, west of Hebron. Local sources reported that around seven dunums of land had been levelled.
Israeli forces also imposed a broad closure on the city of Hebron and its surrounding villages, towns and refugee camps, blocking main entrances and roads. Simultaneously, they raided homes, conducted searches and carried out arrests.
Local sources reported that at least 13 Palestinians were arrested in the city, while dozens were detained for several hours and subjected to field interrogations.
In response to the repercussions of the operation, the Hebron Municipality announced the activation of an emergency plan.
This includes the preparation of shelters for families forced to leave their homes, as well as the establishment of an operations centre to monitor residents' needs amid concerns that the scope of evacuations may expand and the number of families requiring shelter could rise.
Khaled al-Qawasmi, deputy mayor of Hebron, told MEE that the Israeli military began its operation in the area around midnight, giving residents one hour to vacate their homes.
He said that the evacuation included both adults and children, and that residents were not permitted to remain in the area.
Approximately 250 families have been forced to leave the area so far, Qawasmi said, noting that this figure is not final, given the ongoing military siege and the possibility that more families may be evacuated.
"Families evacuated during the first wave sought refuge in the homes of relatives, while the Hebron Municipality worked to open centres to accommodate those affected, including family guesthouses, the Childhood Happiness Centre, the Korean Centre and several other facilities," he said.
Qawasmi warned that if the military operation continues and expands, it could lead to a crisis in finding shelter, given the limited capacity of the centres already opened to accommodate any additional people.
"The military operation has not ended, and the closure is not limited to the targeted area; it extends to the entrances and gateways of Hebron, with Israeli forces continuing to be deployed across various parts of the city," he said.

BJP alleges Sanjay Raut faked AI audio on ₹500 crore payout to Jarange; Sena UBT leader claims BJP MLC leaked clip
The BJP alleged that the recording was part of an attempt to advance Rahul Gandhi's agenda and create divisions within the ruling alliance.
The political row over an audio recording alleging a ₹500 crore payment to Maratha quota activist Manoj Jarange intensified on Saturday, with the BJP accusing Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut of fabricating the clip using artificial intelligence (AI). The BJP alleged that the recording was part of an attempt to advance Rahul Gandhi's agenda and create divisions within the ruling alliance.
Raut rejected the charge, claiming that a BJP member of legislative council (MLC) had leaked the recording amid what he described as "cut-throat competition" within the party. Meanwhile, Jarange, who has denied receiving any money, called on Maharashtra Chief Minister Devendra Fadnavis and Deputy Chief Minister Eknath Shinde to ensure a thorough investigation and hold everyone involved accountable, news agency PTI reported.
The controversy escalated after Fadnavis ordered a forensic examination of the audio clip on Friday. The recording, released by Jarange on Thursday, purportedly features BJP functionaries discussing an alleged payment of ₹500 crore to the activist through Shiv Sena MP Shrikant Shinde, Eknath Shinde's son.
BJP alleges Sanjay Raut fabricated audio using AI
BJP spokesperson Navnath Ban called for a case to be registered against Raut, if required, and demanded an investigation into whether he had received money from Rahul Gandhi to carry out the alleged conspiracy.
Ban claimed that Raut had coordinated the operation from a purported war room in Vashi, Navi Mumbai, and alleged that he had taken up a task from Rahul Gandhi to discredit the BJP.
"Sanjay Raut orchestrated the conspiracy from a war room in Navi Mumbai's Vashi. The contract to defame the BJP has been taken by Raut from Rahul Gandhi. Raut has been consistently pushing Gandhi's agenda over the past few days," Ban claimed.
Raut claims BJP MLC leaked recording
Responding to the allegations, Raut said Fadnavis should first register a case before ordering a forensic examination of the recording. He, however, claimed that the investigation would not produce any results.
"The clip was leaked by a BJP MLC. He was involved in the talks with Jarange. The CM treated him with a lot of affection, which has backfired," Raut said without identifying the lawmaker.
Raut maintained that internal rivalries within the BJP had led to the leak and described the incident as evidence of a "cut-throat" contest within the party. He also alleged that the BJP had become the target of a sting operation.
"If an internal audio clip is getting leaked, then the Home Department has gone against you (the CM)," Raut said.
Fadnavis also heads the state's Home Department.
Raut further alleged that tensions between Fadnavis and Shinde had intensified, claiming that their "cold war" had reached its peak and that both leaders could go to any length to politically finish each other off.
What does the viral audio clip allegedly contain?
Jarange released the recording on Thursday, claiming that a conspiracy had been hatched to silence him and weaken the Maratha reservation movement.
The purported conversation features BJP functionaries discussing an alleged ₹500 crore payment to Jarange through Shrikant Shinde. A woman is purportedly heard claiming that the money had been delivered to the activist through the Shiv Sena MP.
The recording also allegedly contains a discussion about ways to counter Jarange's growing political influence in the Marathwada region ahead of the 2024 assembly elections.
The allegations contained in the clip have not been established, and its authenticity is the subject of the forensic probe ordered by Fadnavis.
The controversy emerged amid allegations by Shiv Sena leader Ramdas Kadam that BJP insiders were working with Jarange to politically "finish off" Shinde, the Shiv Sena chief and Deputy CM.

Personalized mRNA vaccines against melanoma—the deadliest form of skin cancer—reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42 percent compared to standard treatment in a late-stage trial, pharmaceutical partners Merck and Moderna announced Thursday.
The results are a significant advance in melanoma treatment; Merck and Moderna are already engaging with regulatory authorities to get the vaccine approved. More broadly, the vaccine’s success bolsters hope that mRNA vaccines and individualized cancer-targeting medicines offer a new paradigm for cancer therapies.
“From the beginning, we believed mRNA technology could make it possible to develop cancer treatments uniquely matched to each patient’s tumor,” Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in a statement. The trial results “mark a defining moment for that vision and show what’s possible when we rethink how medicines are made.” They also “reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer,” he said.
In August, Moderna and Merck reported that the vaccine has succeeded in the trial, but held off reporting details until the data could be presented at an upcoming scientific conference. That conference is the European Society of Medical Oncology, starting now in Madrid, Spain. The data was scheduled for presentation on Saturday, but after an oncology news site reported the results early, breaking the embargo, the companies released the top-line results. The full data has been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine.
As Ars reported earlier, the Phase 3 trial included 1,137 patients who had stage IIB–IV melanoma that had been surgically removed prior to entering the trial. Patients were randomized 2-1 to receive either a combination treatment including the personalized mRNA vaccine with a standard treatment, or the standard treatment alone. The standard treatment was Merck’s established monoclonal antibody cancer treatment Keytruda.

Two local Japanese lenders in Osaka and nearby Shiga prefectures are poised to merge to create the biggest regional banking group in Kansai region, according to people familiar with the matter.
Senshu Ikeda and Shiga Bank are in talks to consolidate their operations, with an announcement expected to come as soon as next week, said the people, who asked not to be identified discussing a private matter. Nikkei reported the news first.
Both banks confirmed the talks in exchange filings late Friday but added that nothing has been decided.
The move came after a capital and business alliance between the two firms in April, in which they took a small stake in each other. Senshu Ikeda and Shiga have been in the spotlight after Japanese hedge fund Ariake Capital took 10.8% and 6.48% stakes in them, respectively.
The combined assets of the two lenders will amount to ¥14.6 trillion ($93.1 billion), making them the biggest regional banking group in the Kansai region, surpassing Kyoto Financial Group Inc. Shares of Shiga have rallied 73% this year while Senshu Ikeda’s stock is up 17%.

More than a week after allegations that Greens senator Jordon Steele-John had behaved inappropriately towards women made headlines, his position in the party remains in limbo and its new leader’s handling of the issue in question.
David Shoebridge’s first major challenge at the helm of the federal Greens came earlier this month when the Nine newspapers reported a three-page letter had been sent to him urging an independent investigation into Steele-John.
It referred to secondhand allegations that the Western Australian senator had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
As a progressive party that prides itself on taking such matters seriously and fairly, it made sense that Shoebridge announced the 32-year-old’s leave amid an independent probe into the claims.
But the process quickly became more complicated. Days later, a defiant Steele-John rejected the allegations against him, denied he agreed to take leave from parliament, and accused an internal faction within the WA Greens of playing “nasty political games” in its decision to release the letter to the media.
Steele-John said he made a public statement because he didn’t want his silence on the letter’s claims to be perceived as guilt.
While Shoebridge insists Steele-John agreed to take leave, he acknowledges he alone does not have the power to force the senator to do so.
Only if two-thirds of the party room – or more than seven members – decided to expel him in a secret ballot would Steele-John have to comply.
Such a move would be nuclear. Even if the WA Greens’ independent investigation clears him of any wrongdoing, Steele-John’s standing in the party room would be shattered.
The week ahead under scrutiny
On Monday, Shoebridge’s ability to deal with the matter will be on show.
Senate estimates is a time for members of the upper house to have their moment in the spotlight. For the Greens, it’s a chance to extricate answers about government policies from carefully trained bureaucrats to drive home a political point.
With the NDIS undergoing major changes between now and the decade’s end, the Greens will have to decide whether their disability spokesperson, Steele-John, who is championed and well-liked within the disability community, should be allowed to attend. Perhaps, virtually.
For many supporters within and outside the Greens, the optics of allowing a federal party member accused of sexual misconduct – even though a complainant has not directly come forward to make those allegations – to continue public duties will be a tough pill to swallow. Particularly as the “manosphere” phenomenon and backlash against the #MeToo movement gain momentum in mainstream society.
The question over whether the allegations were politically motivated by adversaries of Steele-John looking to gain advantage in the state’s pre-selection is a part of the equation.
But the fact remains that the rumours have persisted over the senator’s time in office. Even if they are malicious, as Steele-John contends, the simpler option would still be to stand aside and settle them while they are investigated.
The decision over whether to force Steele-John to take leave will be as much about Shoebridge’s leadership as it is about the party’s processes.
The party room, and its membership more broadly, prides itself on being a movement based on consensus decision-making.
Shoebridge will need the support of the party room to take the expulsion route. How he handles this issue will also set the tone for the rest of his leadership and, depending on his actions, could prompt an ugly battle with Steele-John.
It’s a quagmire – politically, legally and ethically.
There are unlikely to be any winners.

UPI provider super.money reported a net loss of ₹263.8 Cr in FY26, 78.5% higher than ₹147.8 Cr loss incurred in the previous fiscal year. Its operating revenue more than tripled to ₹292.4 Cr from ₹88.8 Cr in FY25. Its loan marketplace contributed around 84.7% of its revenue. Combined with other income of ₹90 Lakh, its total income amounted to ₹293.3 Cr. super.money did not report any tax expenses or exceptional items, resulting in a total comprehensive loss of ₹262.9 Cr. super.money was launched by the Walmart-owned Flipkart in 2024 and is led by founder and CEO Prakash Sikaria, who was the senior vice president at Flipkart, helming its ads business, Shopsy, Cleartrip and Yantra. super.money’s core business is enabling UPI payments and is the fifth largest player in the market. In September 2026, it processed over 40.51 Cr UPI transactions, collectively worth more than ₹19,613.3 Cr. Besides, the startup has now also ventured into loan facilitation, connecting borrowers with banks and NBFCs. It also enables users to book fixed deposits and partners with banks to offer co-branded credit cards. Where Did super.money Spend? super.money’s total expenses in FY26 surged 130% YoY to ₹557.1 Cr from ₹241.8 Cr in the previous fiscal. Let’s dive into a breakdown of its spending. Business Promotion Expenses: This was the biggest expenditure, rising 3.34X YoY to ₹341 Cr in FY26. Employee Benefits Expense: Employee costs grew 73.8% YoY to ₹138.1 Cr compared to ₹79.5 Cr in the year-ago period. Marketplace Charges: Spending on this line item fell 64.2% YoY to ₹15.6 Cr from ₹43.5 Cr. Finance Costs: super.money’s finance-related expenses skyrocketed to ₹11.1 Cr in the year under review from ₹0.1 Cr in the previous year. Other Expenses: Other operating expenses including outside contracted services and communication charges increased 177.2% YoY to ₹47.9 Cr in FY26 compared to ₹17.3 Cr in FY25.

Companies change course in good times and bad. For Zetwerk, the key turn came after it raised $150 Mn from D1 Capital Partners in August 2021 when Indian startups raised a record $42 Bn in the calendar year. And what began as a platform to connect manufacturers to vendors and suppliers, turned into a full stack manufacturing play on the back of a bevy of acquisitions in 2021 and 2022. The company, founded in 2018 by Amrit Acharya, Srinath Ramakkrushnan and Vishal Chaudhary, made its stock market debut today (Friday, October 23) with that full-stack promise at the centre of its pitch. No longer is this a marketplace, but a full-fledged platform that manages everything from procurement, supply, manufacturing, specifications and delivery. While the listing itself was not at a massive premium like some other new-age tech stocks, that’s besides the point when looking at the business model and the sector. The thesis around manufacturing remains strong for years to come as companies in key segments such as electric vehicles are looking to bring more of their component sourcing to India including in vital areas like precision machined parts. This was the opportunity that Zetwerk wanted to capture with its shift from marketplace to manufacturing. In FY26, its revenue from operations rose 40.4% YoY to ₹15,913 Cr, from ₹11,331 Cr in the previous fiscal. Yet, its consolidated net loss widened to ₹1,606 Cr from ₹371 Cr in FY25. This loss includes an exceptional charge of ₹836 Cr from continuing operations and a ₹453 Cr impairment related to its discontinued civil infrastructure business. Those are the realities of working in the manufacturing space. Opportunities come and go and companies have to react in terms of pivoting their operations. The impairment itself is not a major number, but what could worry investors is that adjusted EBITDA stood at a mere ₹421 Cr, translating into a margin of just 2.65% against the revenue. Plus, cash flows present another challenge. Zetwerk’s cash outflow from operations widened to ₹682 Cr in FY26 from ₹386 Cr a year earlier, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.4% to ₹12,370 Cr. A larger order book offers revenue visibility, but fulfilling those orders requires the company to fund procurement, production and logistics, while managing payments to suppliers and collections from customers. Let’s dive deeper into this as this is what investors will look at. The Two Revenue Pillars Zetwerk operates through two main business segments: manufacturing and ecosystem. The latter operates under the Terra91 brand and supplies industrial raw materials such as steel, aluminium, copper, zinc, lead and bitumen. The manufacturing business, which focuses on custom-made industrial products and related projects, is the largest of the two. Together, the two businesses generated ₹15,913 Cr in revenue from continuing operations in FY26, up 40.4% YoY. Manufacturing accounted for ₹9,375 Cr, or 58.9% of revenue, while ecosystem contributed ₹6,539 Cr, or 41.1%. Simply put, the manufacturing business earns revenue by working with third-party manufacturers and Zetwerk’s own facilities to fulfil orders across energy products, precision machined products and capital goods. Its earnings depend on the price charged to customers relative to supplier payments, materials and fulfilment costs. More complex work, such as precision manufacturing requiring tight tolerances, can command a higher take rate than relatively less complex products. Notably, Zetwerk doesn’t disclose these margins and fees as it is likely to depend on the product and client needs, since this is how the industry functions. In an earlier Inc42 interview, cofounder and CEO Acharya said the company does not consider commission when accounting for revenue. He described the model instead as a take rate for services. He said rates vary across product categories depending on the complexity of the work. The manufacturing segment reported a standalone EBITDA of ₹565 Cr in FY26, translating into a margin of 6.03%. The other side is the ecosystem, which has grown considerably since 2022 as we indicated in the beginning. Unlike manufacturing, where Zetwerk coordinates production, the ecosystem segment aggregates demand for industrial raw materials, procures them in bulk and resells them to customers. Its economics are driven by the spread between procurement and selling prices, after accounting for logistics and other fulfillment costs. The segment’s Adjusted EBITDA stood at around ₹81 Cr, giving it a margin of approximately 1.24%. The thin margin means that changes in commodity prices, sourcing costs or delivery expenses can have a significant impact on profitability, which we will see soon. Plus, the margin is considerably thinner than in manufacturing. These segment-level margins offer a view of Zetwerk’s economics, but the company has not disclosed commission rates or order-level profitability. Zetwerk’s revenue from operations includes the sale of products, income from construction and project contracts, sale of services and other operating revenue. Product sales cover manufactured goods, products sourced from third-party suppliers and industrial raw materials sold through the ecosystem business. Construction and project contract income relates to projects involving broader execution responsibilities, while service revenue includes activities such as job work and related services. Here’s the key difference from any other marketplace: Zetwerk acts as the principal in these transactions rather than simply connecting buyers and suppliers for a fee. It takes responsibility for sourcing, quality and delivery, meaning the revenue it reports reflects the value of goods and services sold, while procurement and fulfillment costs are recorded separately. This is precisely the turn that Zetwerk’s 2021 fundraise and subsequent expansion allowed. Zetwerk’s Big Opportunity Having said that, as we mentioned in the beginning, the problem for the company is that it operates with razor thin margins. Even as the adjusted EBITDA margin has improved year-on-year, it’s still not quite robust enough. Fulfilling industrial orders starts with a substantial procurement bill and procurement costs almost always escalate when there is a disparity in the order book. The key thing for Zetwerk will be to double down in one or two categories which will allow it to maximise the arbitrage revenue. Economies of scale will drive arbitrage revenue in the manufacturing business, especially when Zetwerk owns and controls the procurement side of the business. So manufacturing cannot drive profits on its own and Zetwerk will have to flesh out both sides of the business at the same time. Owning procurement removes third-party broker fees, distributor markups, and structural inefficiencies. The company captures the full margin that middle-men usually take. Add to that, sourcing inputs from low-cost regions which allows you to absorb fixed costs of logistics, customs, and compliance. And as the procurement side of the business scales up, Zetwerk will also have leverage for exclusive, long-term low-price contracts. But it’s not a flick of the switch, buying in extreme bulk can exponentially increase warehousing, insurance, and inventory carrying costs. Moreover, commodity price volatility is another factor since companies can get locked in to massive forward contracts even as market price shifts. So any arbitrage advantage gets flipped here. In FY26, the company spent ₹9,880 Cr on purchases of stock-in-trade and another ₹3,964 Cr on materials consumed, making these its two largest expense heads. Together, they accounted for nearly 86% of its total expenses of ₹16,142 Cr. Purchases of stock-in-trade largely represent goods bought from suppliers and resold to customers. This expense head rose 45.3% YoY to ₹9,880 Cr in FY26 from ₹6,800 Cr in the previous fiscal. The cost of materials consumed includes materials used in manufacturing and project contracts — which increased 31% YoY to ₹3,964 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹3,036 Cr. The two expense heads reflect the procurement-heavy nature of Zetwerk’s business, where revenue growth requires the company to source goods, materials and manufacturing capacity to meet customer orders. Why Revenue Growth Is Not Translating Into Cash Zetwerk’s cash flow numbers point to the pressure of achieving the balance between procurement and manufacturing. In FY26, its net cash outflow from operating activities widened to ₹682 Cr from ₹386 Cr in FY25, even as its manufacturing order book grew 43.3% year-on-year (YoY) to ₹12,370 Cr. A growing order book provides visibility into future business, but it does not immediately translate into cash in the bank. Zetwerk still needs to source materials, pay suppliers and coordinate production to fulfil orders, while customer payments may come in only after goods are delivered or project milestones are met. This gap between spending on fulfillment and collecting revenue can tie up cash as the business expands. The company’s procurement-heavy model means it’s particularly important that Zetwerk gets this balance right. As order volumes rise, the company may need to deploy more working capital to support the procurement, manufacturing and fulfillment needs, even if each order itself is profitable. The challenge is therefore not simply to grow revenue or expand the order book, but to wring out inefficiencies in terms of arbitrage price, production bottlenecks and generally save costs through tech and AI. This will help the company mitigate the risks of delayed cash inflows and receivables. In FY26, Zetwerk’s trade receivables increased by ₹336 Cr, while its other financial and current assets rose by ₹715 Cr. Zetwerk’s ability to improve cash conversion will depend on how efficiently it manages inventory, supplier terms, production timelines, fulfillment and customer collections as it scales. Converting the order book pipeline into cash remains a big test of its business model. Which is why Zetwerk is looking to capture more value by taking on design and engineering responsibilities, rather than simply manufacturing products to customer specifications. Its original design manufacturing (ODM) contracts accounted for 13.93% of manufacturing gross merchandise value (GMV) in FY26. Such work can offer better margins because it involves design and co-development, while also making customer relationships harder to replace. Zetwerk is also trying to balance its supplier network with greater control over complex manufacturing. It operated 26 manufacturing facilities across four countries as of June 2026, while continuing to rely on third-party manufacturers for most of its manufacturing business. Products sourced from third-party suppliers accounted for 80.46% of manufacturing segment revenue in FY26, down from 96.51% in FY24. This suggests that Zetwerk is gradually reducing its dependence on external capacity, but has not moved away from the model that helped it scale without investing in every stage of production. But is scale alone enough to improve profitability? And now as a public company, Zetwerk will have to answer this tricky question.

During the festive season, shoppers tend to splurge more, drawn by a host of offers and steep discounts. However, not every deal is a good bargain. In a statement on Friday, Delhi Chief Minister Rekha Gupta announced that the capital's food safety department had seized over 322 kg of ghee amid concerns over quality and pricing. The inspections targeted stores promoting deals on social media, including ‘Buy One, Get One Free’ offers and discounts of up to 60 per cent. According to PTI, food safety officials inspected the shops to assess compliance with food safety rules and check for adulterated, substandard, expired, or incorrectly labelled products. During inspections at Maxcart Store and Aggarwal Store in west Delhi's Vikaspuri, officials collected five enforcement samples of ghee from several brands, along with samples of other food products. Over 75.5 litres of ghee were seized. Similarly, at Aggarwal Store in Hastal village, officials collected three enforcement samples of ghee from the Shri Shan, Vrinda Farms and Avtar brands and seized 246 kg of the product. In separate inspections, the department also collected samples of other food items, including two samples of sugar-boiled confectionery from a store called Sahib Sons in Azad Market, which was operating under the trade name Vicon International. The samples were collected over suspected labelling irregularities. Additionally, samples of makhana and turmeric powder were collected from Jain Store in Lajpat Nagar, while samples of different types of biscuits, soft candy and sugar-based candy were collected from Yug Basket Private Limited in Rithala. The food safety department stated that the findings would be assessed alongside laboratory test reports before any further action was taken. It added that inspections had revealed lapses in adherence to food safety standards at the establishments and that further action would follow. The development comes days after the food safety department carried out an inspection drive last week and found several ghee samples unfit for consumption. According to reports, the department found that 19 of 59 desi ghee samples were unfit for consumption, while four others were substandard. Samples from different brands were collected from markets across the capital, including Naharpur, Posangipur, Laxmi Nagar, Preet Vihar, Rampura, Tagore Garden, Kalyanpuri, Krishna Vihar and Kondli. Separately, frozen green peas, Greek yoghurt, soft drinks and eggless chocolate-chip brownies were among the items found stocked for sale at warehouses and dark stores despite being past their use-by dates. Following the inspection drive, Gupta said in a statement, “The food safety department has been directed to tighten monitoring of markets, food storage facilities and establishments supplying food products through online platforms. Action must be taken in accordance with the rules wherever food safety standards are violated. The govt’s objective is not merely to identify deficiencies, but also to ensure a system in which every family in Delhi has access to safe and quality food. Protecting public health and ensuring accountability in the food trade remain govt priorities.” Following the seizure of over 322 kg of ghee, Rekha Gupta on Friday urged consumers to check the quality and packaging of food products, along with their manufacturing and expiry dates, before purchasing them. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) has outlined a home test to detect starch adulteration in ghee. Place half a teaspoon of ghee in a clear glass bowl and add two to three drops of iodine solution. A blue colour may indicate the presence of starch, potentially from mashed potato or sweet potato. However, the absence of a colour change does not establish that the ghee is pure or free from other adulterants. Remember Popcorn Time, the app that served as an easy-to-use front end for streaming torrents of movies and TV shows? Development of the MPAA’s least-favorite app of the 2010s has been abandoned for years, but the “Netflix of Piracy” software is still installed on millions of devices that are just waiting to join a bot army. Researchers at Eye Security found the updater for a Popcorn Time fork called “Time4Popcorn” still running on tons of Windows, macOS, and Android devices located around the world, phoning home to now-abandoned web domains over unencrypted HTTP and running an outdated, insecure version of Chrome.
Abandoned Popcorn Time apps had to be disabled to prevent a zombie army
What old and vulnerable software might be running on your PC right now?
Eye Security’s Niels Teusink says the updater could have been used to install and run basically any kind of software with full privileges, easily enabling someone to create a botnet just by taking over one of the domains, using a man-in-the-middle attack to target specific devices, or perform surveillance by identifying the machines running the software.
Their solution was to register one of the domains and use it to send their own update that instructed the updater to disable itself. Despite ethical concerns about the fix, the researchers say their only alternative “was to do nothing,” pointing out, “The update process wasn’t doing anything functional anyway, it was only creating risk for users.”
Eye Security said on Windows devices, their update “simply stops and disables the service via the Service Control Manager” without deleting any files or anything else. On macOS, it uses a shell script to execute a command that blocks the update process from starting. They didn’t address the software on Android devices, where installing the update would still require actual user interaction first.
They had to tweak their update after it was uploaded to VirusTotal, causing security programs to flag it as malware and block it while leaving the vulnerable updater running. It’s unclear exactly how many devices were at risk, but Eye Security says it “sent out over 2 million update downloads” by March, when they stopped sending the update and transferred the domains they used to the Shadowserver Foundation, a web security non-profit.

The Union Agriculture Ministry had created 11 crore unique digital identity cards for farmers as of Friday (October 23, 2026), five months ahead of a deadline set for March 31, 2027. The IDs are expected to enable “transparent, efficient and timely” access for farmers to government schemes, bank credit, crop insurance and disaster relief. It will also reduce paperwork and repeated verification, according to the government.
The milestone has been achieved under the Digital Agriculture Mission implemented by the Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, Union Agriculture Minister Shivraj Singh Chouhan said on Saturday (October 24, 2026). The creation of 11 crore Farmer IDs was successfully completed by the night of October 23, he said.
“The Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers’ Welfare, State governments, and field-level officials worked in coordination to achieve it five months ahead of schedule,” Mr. Chouhan said, congratulating farmers across the country on the achievement. The Minister described the Farmer ID as their own digital identity, and an important step towards making agriculture more efficient, transparent and prosperous through modern technology.
“Earlier, farmers often had to provide documents repeatedly to access various benefits, resulting in a loss of both time and money. With Farmer IDs, access to several key services is expected to become simpler and more transparent,” the Minister said in a statement, adding that the initiative intends to improve transparency and accountability in agricultural service delivery, and ensure eligible farmers could access government support with fewer procedural hurdles.

A GOP congressman voted to cut Medicaid. It covers 62% of his district. Can he win?
Ulises Hernandez, of Bakersfield, Calif., has had health coverage through Medicaid for as long as he can remember.
But he had never waited as long for care as he did in September after a dental crown slipped down his throat during a procedure. He spent eight hours in an emergency room waiting for care and more than two days without food.
Sitting in his wheelchair to protest looming federal Medicaid cuts outside Republican U.S. Rep. David Valadao's Bakersfield office, Hernandez described his wait as a foreshadowing of what's ahead.
"I couldn't eat, I couldn't drink, I couldn't do anything, and I was in pain," said Hernandez, who had been discharged from the hospital a few days before. "I'm livid."
Hernandez, 41, said Valadao "should be ashamed of himself" for voting for the Republicans' One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The law is expected to reduce Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion through 2034, with provisions such as stricter Medicaid eligibility rules and reducing federal money to states.
Hernandez plans to vote for challenger Randy Villegas in hopes that this Central Valley toss-up district, where roughly 6 in 10 of constituents are enrolled in Medicaid, can help give Democrats control of Congress.
Villegas, a political science professor, has embraced the progressive rallying cry for "Medicare for All" and called out Valadao for a vote "that is going to rip away healthcare from Valley families," since many working-age adults may not satisfy new work requirements and twice-a-year eligibility checks that, by political design, start after the midterm elections.
Valadao defends his vote on the GOP bill. During a televised Oct. 6 debate, he said "there are no actual cuts" to Medicaid.
An estimated 60,000 more residents of his district could be without coverage by 2034 due to the tax and spending bill and the expiration of enhanced premium tax credits for Affordable Care Act insurance plans, according to the left-leaning Center for American Progress think tank.
Researchers estimate that those new rules will push more than 2 million Californians statewide off their coverage and that the state stands to lose about $30 billion a year, more than any other state.
Fertile Ground, High Unemployment
Bakersfield is an oil town, and it wears that identity proudly. Pump jacks nod in the distance. Streets run wide. The Kern River's bed lies dry, its water siphoned to feed the agricultural fields.
Sitting partially in the southernmost portion of the contested congressional district, this city produces much from the land, but unemployment is high.
Democrats have outnumbered Republicans in voter registrations by double-digit percentage points in Valadao's district since he was first elected to the U.S. House in 2012, yet he has won six of his seven congressional elections.
Valadao has survived by focusing on local issues such as water infrastructure and distancing himself from the Trump administration, said Jeffrey Cummins, a political science professor at California State University-Fresno. Valadao is the last remaining Republican House incumbent who voted to impeach Trump after the Jan. 6, 2021, riot at the U.S. Capitol who is running for reelection to Congress.
"This is an area where, even when we see the registration advantage for Democrats, that they are moderate Democrats who tend to be concerned with agricultural issues, and Valadao in the past has successfully appeased those voters," Cummins said.
But California's congressional map was redrawn last year as part of a national mid-decade redistricting fight, and Valadao's Central Valley seat is considered more favorable for Democrats than before. Cummins said a different mix of voters, coupled with anger toward incumbents, could flip the seat.
"Valadao knows that he's on notice," Cummins said.
Nationwide, healthcare costs remain a top affordability concern for voters, and they trust Democrats over Republicans by a 2-to-1 margin on the issue, according to a September KFF poll. Valadao lost in 2018, when Democrats targeted his votes to repeal the ACA, as well as his alliance with Trump.
On Nov. 3, he faces Villegas, a populist backed by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) who favors a single-payer universal healthcare system.
"The system that we have now, we pay twice as much as other countries across the world, despite the fact that we have worse healthcare outcomes," Villegas said during the debate.
At campaign event, no mention of healthcare
On Sept. 30, Valadao held a $1,000-a-ticket fundraiser. It was hosted by House Speaker Mike Johnson, who is campaigning across 22 states in six weeks as Republicans try to hold the chamber.
Afterward, press were allowed at an invitation-only reelection event in Bakersfield, held in an office building just outside of the new district Valadao hopes to represent. Arches of red, white, and blue star-shaped balloons framed the small stage.
Neither lawmaker mentioned Medicaid or the rising cost of healthcare when they spoke to the audience.
After brief speeches, Valadao repeatedly refused to answer KFF Health News' questions about his vote for the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and its impact on his constituents' Medicaid coverage, saying, "I think you are distorting the truth."
Of the half dozen attendees KFF Health News approached among roughly 50 in the room, none lived in Valadao's district.
They came anyway. Retired nurse Charlotte Brandt lives in the neighboring Republican-held district but follows Valadao's votes closely. She called him "a hero for the Central Valley," citing his work on water, oil, and agriculture, which she said sustain Kern County as the "breadbasket of the world."
Her daughter, Allison Brandt Oliver, who also lives in Republican Vince Fong's district, said she favored the stricter Medicaid eligibility rules Republicans put into place, saying her concern is whether spending is going to U.S. citizens who contribute to the economy.
A few days later during the televised debate, Valadao said he was among the negotiators who secured community engagement provisions in the law, which will require certain adults on Medicaid to prove they're working or completing other activities such as job training or volunteering.
"It's not an actual cut," Valadao said. "We need people to actually put in and make a fair effort to try to cover their expenses and be a part of their community. This is not an unreasonable ask."
$32 million in campaign ads for one swing district
In a sign of how vital this district is, Republicans and Democrats have each booked more than $16 million in ads here through Election Day, according to data compiled by AdImpact.
"When you start getting over $10 million of spending total in the district, I would say that that's pretty high," Cummins said.
Some of the ads are reaching voters in unexpected ways.
Outside a local library, Seslie Maese, a stay-at-home mom from Bakersfield, said her 7-year-old, who often watches Lego videos on YouTube, runs to her whenever a certain ad plays.
"David Valadago is going on vacation again, Mom," he'll tell her, mispronouncing the congressman's name. Her son doesn't realize the ad, paid for by a Democratic political action committee, means that as a criticism.
Maese is undecided. Even though she's a registered Republican, she said what she has heard about Valadao doesn't sound positive, such as that he went back on his pledge not to cut Medicaid for vulnerable populations by voting for the federal tax-and-spending law.
For Maese, a politician who says one thing and does another is a deal-breaker.
"He just hasn't come through with anything he said," she said, "especially since he cut off a lot of Medicaid."
This story comes from NPR's health reporting partnership with KFF Health News, a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

There is now proof for what we have suspected all along: What you eat will determine your quality of life. A new study that was conducted by Chennai-based Madras Diabetes Specialties Centre and the University of Reading, U.K., has found a link between quality of diet and the Asian Indian predisposition to high cholesterol. High and uncontrolled cholesterol levels are associated with a high cardiovascular disease profile.
The study, Low diet quality increases the genetic risk of high blood cholesterol levels in Asian Indian adults [CURES–165], was published last week in the international peer-reviewed journal PLOS ONE, and are considered to advance the understanding of how diet and genetic factors interact to influence cholesterol levels.
The researchers analysed data from 1,020 adults (25–80 years), comprising 452 men and 568 women, who participated in the Chennai Urban Rural Epidemiology Study (CURES). The study examined three genetic variants of two genes :TCF7L2 and FTO, with a known association with diabetes and other metabolic disorders.
Researchers found that a poor quality diet amplified the genetic susceptibility to high cholesterol. Study participants who already had a higher genetic risk and who consumed a poor-quality diet had significantly higher total cholesterol and LDL cholesterol levels. Conversely, researchers proved that among participants consuming medium- or high-quality diets, there were no significant differences in cholesterol levels between the high- and low-genetic-risk groups were not observed. Individuals with higher genetic risk had significantly higher fasting blood glucose and HbA1c levels.
Among the key messages is that genetic susceptibility alone does not necessarily translate into adverse cholesterol levels under all dietary conditions. Naturally, these findings support the role of sticking to healthy diets to counter cardiometabolic risk. This is particularly significant in India, witnessing a literal explosion of cases of diabetes, rising cholesterol levels and cardiovascular disease. Researchers said there could be a role for precision nutrition, The findings also open up new possibilities for precision nutrition, where dietary advice is tailored to an individual’s genetic and metabolic characteristics.
Commenting on the results of the study, V. Mohan, Chairman, Madras Diabetes Research Foundation, who was also a co-author of the study, said the key message is that our genes alone “need not determine an individual’s metabolic destiny.” With adjusting of the diet, it is possible to lower the risk, even when the genetic load is present.

Jordon Steele-John has confirmed he will not attend parliament next week as the embattled Greens senator releases a letter detailing the allegations against him.
After days of confusion following historical complaints about alleged misconduct were publicly aired in the media, Steele-John posted a statement to social media late Friday night.
In the statement, the Western Australian senator said he considered attending Senate estimates virtually but was told it would be “unacceptable”. He will instead focus on seeing through an independent investigation to its conclusion, he said.
“Over the past few days there has been a growing chorus calling on me not to attend parliament next week. I have explored attending digitally but have been informed that would also be unacceptable,” Steele-John said.
Steele-John said a precedent of keeping parliamentarians out of parliament after “allegations of allegations” are made had now been set.
“Had an allegation or complaint been made against me, I would have taken these actions immediately,” he said.
The 32-year-old senator’s attendance in parliament for the remainder of the year had been uncertain after a public stoush with the party’s leader, David Shoebridge, over whether he was on leave while an investigation was undertaken into allegations he had acted inappropriately towards women between 2017 and 2025.
The complaints are now subject to an independent investigation commissioned by the WA Greens and have been referred to the Independent Parliamentary Standards Commission.
Shoebridge claimed Steele-John had requested leave and he accepted it last week after seven party members penned a letter to the leader urging an investigation into the claims.
The three-page letter sent on 13 October, and first published by the Nine newspapers, said the authors had been “made aware of multiple allegations of serious misconduct” against Steele-John about his “behaviour in the presence of women”.
The letter referred to an allegation of sexual harassment at a Greens campaign event in 2024 that the alleged victim had not reported out of fear and backlash. The letter provided no further detail.
In another, the authors referred to an allegation of “serious sexual misconduct” in 2025.
Also contained in the letter was a reference to a disparaging nickname for Steele-John – “feels on wheels” – which the authors said implied he had a reputation for acting inappropriately.
“To be clear, all signatories to this letter know that an allegation does not equate to a fact and/or guilt. We simply believe that it is in the party’s best interests to ensure that every allegation is investigated thoroughly, in alignment with community and member expectations,” the letter’s authors wrote.
Steele-John was defiant in a lengthy statement last Sunday, rejecting the allegations against him, denying he agreed to take leave from parliament and accusing an internal faction within the Greens of playing “nasty political games” in their decision to release the letter to the media.
Steele-John said any claims of his alleged behaviour should be investigated “fairly and thoroughly” but accused an “unofficial faction” within the WA branch had released the complaint letter to the media in a bid to oust him from the Senate.
Guardian Australia has confirmed the WA police told Steele-John the investigation was closed in May with no charges.

Hero dad who killed Oregon school shooter said children were ‘pleading for their lives’
In his first interview since stopping the gunman at Silver Rail Elementary, Kaylub Giamanco spoke with Oregon Public Broadcasting about the split-second decisions he made that afternoon

A father who intervened during a deadly rampage at an Oregon elementary school said he was haunted by the memory of young students begging for their lives as he crawled toward an active shooter.
Kaylub Giamanco, 36, confronted a 16-year-old gunman who opened fire at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend where three children and a teacher were killed, and two other people were severely injured. Police have said that Giamanco’s actions prevented further loss of life at the 400-student campus, and President Donald Trump praised him as “a great hero that went in and did the business.”
In his first interview since the incident, given to Oregon Public Broadcasting, Giamanco recalled the moment he entered the building after following the armed teenager onto the grounds.
“That’s when I started hearing children pleading for their lives,” Giamanco told OPB. “I started hearing gunfire and I just started army crawling faster and faster, and I told myself this is probably the last thing that I’m ever going to do.”
Giamanco, a local carpenter, was driving home to eat lunch when he spotted a male dressed in black firing a shotgun at a passing pickup truck and toward a worker on the school grounds. After watching the teenager toss the firearm over a perimeter fence and scale it, Giamanco retrieved a .40-caliber handgun from his truck console, loaded a magazine and instructed his phone to dial 911.
He informed emergency operators that he could not stay on the line to answer questions.
“I said, ‘I’m sorry, I have to go in. People are going to die,’” Giamanco told OPB.
Looking inside, he witnessed a teacher wrestling with the teenager. Giamanco opened the door and fired his weapon. The teacher fled the room after both dropped to the floor, but Giamanco discharged two additional rounds when the gunman reached for his weapon again.
“He was scrambling for his weapon,” Giamanco said. “I looked at him and I shot him two more times to make sure that he couldn’t move because I was afraid of him shooting anybody else.”
Giamanco acknowledged the emotional toll of having to fire multiple times at a teenager.
“It was split second decisions while gunfire was going off, while children were losing their lives,” Giamanco told OPB, adding that he frequently thinks about the young gunman. “Sometimes there’s a child out there that didn’t have the love that they deserved. But I do want to believe that if he had more love in his life and better parenting, that this could have been prevented.”
When police arrived on the scene, Giamanco placed his firearm on the floor and stepped out with his hands raised. He then called his family to inform them he was safe before contacting his mother.
“She was just like, ‘Okay, baby, calm down. You did the right thing. You’re a hero. You saved lives.’ And I was just like, ‘I didn’t save everybody. I didn’t get them all,’” Giamanco told OPB.
Despite praise from local law enforcement and the public, Giamanco told the news station that he remains overwhelmed by grief for the victims he could not protect.
“I want to apologize for not saving their babies,” Giamanco told OPB. “The gratitude for saving people’s children is awesome, but there were ones that I didn’t save.”
He added that he has not yet spoken to the teacher who engaged the gunman and does not know her name, though he expressed respect for her actions.
“I would love to give her a hug because that’s a real true hero,” Giamanco said.
Giamanco, whose two daughters attend the school, credited informal training he received years earlier from Iraq War veterans for enabling him to react quickly during the crisis. He said that his family has temporarily relocated from their home, which overlooks the school, and that his daughters would not return to the campus for some time.
Uncertain if he will return to his previous line of work, Giamanco told OPB that he hopes to advocate for enhanced security infrastructure in classrooms.
“I feel like I was put on this earth to do something more than just fix houses,” Giamanco said.
He said he decided to share his story publicly because he felt a responsibility to use his platform for broader change.
“I’ve always wanted to change the world, but I’ve felt small,” Giamanco said. “I’m just a carpenter from Bend, Oregon. I was a nobody other than to my friends and family.
“I feel like if I’m going to have a voice, then I’ll be damned if I’m not going to use it to change this world, to make it a better place.”
