Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
- Published
When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks.
But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful.
"Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow?
"Those thoughts haunt me every night."
Nastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze.
Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas – an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire landmass of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone.
But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.
As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five.
"The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week.
"I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them."
Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body.
Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death.
Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air.
"Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body – specifically the brain – doesn't get enough oxygen."
Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate.
In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Nastiti says this is unrealistic.
"I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here."
Nastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside.
"With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house."
Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks – from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange – she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors.
Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air.
Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm.
"If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option."
The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities.
Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke – from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires.
"At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).
"It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can."
But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground.
For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. On the surface, the flames are out – but underground, smouldering blazes continue to burn through a deep understory of carbon, vegetation and peat.
"It is truly exhausting," he says, describing how the relentless smoke has produced in him a shortness of breath, a persistent cough and an unshakeable pain in his eyes. When asked what he needs, he says "air".
"The haze makes it hard to breathe," he explains. "We are just hoping for heavy rain."
Thousands of others across Indonesia and Southeast Asia have spent the past several months hoping for the same.
Seasonal wildfires are not new to Indonesia but this year, a so-called Super El Nino has amplified drought conditions and delayed the kind of rainfall that is critical to extinguishing peat fires. It has also made things exponentially harder for those at the coalface, like Juni, who have spent months battling a seemingly irrepressible fire front.
Dr Novita explains that conditions on the ground have become much harsher even in recent weeks, as the prolonged drought makes water increasingly scarce.
Fauzi Rahman, another firefighter in Palangkaraya, highlighted this as one of the main difficulties confronting him and his peers.
"Peatland fires are hard to put out because they require a lot of water and a long time," he says. "On regular land we can clear 20 hectares in a single day, especially with a large team... On peatland, it can take months.
"We really have to inject water deep down, all the way to the bottom, which requires a huge amount of water. And right now, water is hard to find."
What's more concerning for Dr Novita, however, is that her team has reported fires spreading into areas where there has been no history of fire before.
"So we're not only dealing with fires in the usual hotspots but also seeing them emerge in new areas," she says.
In Palangkaraya, people are growing desperate for an end to this apocalypse. But it will likely take a force of nature for that to happen any time soon.
Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office, tells the BBC that "hopefully, with all the extraordinary efforts from the community, the military, and the police working together, the fires can be put out".
"However, as of right now, the fires are still burning," he adds. "So what can we hope for? Our greatest hope is that Almighty God will bring us rain soon."

Pathos, an artificial intelligence-driven drug development company, announced on Friday it is raising $237 million in a Series E fundraising round led by Bristol Myers Squibb. The deal brings Pathos’ valuation to approximately $3 billion.
Pathos is also expanding from oncology to neurological conditions with new datasets from Tempus AI and a partnership with BMS that will first focus on Alzheimer’s treatments.
Most drugs that enter clinical trials never reach patients, but Pathos’ pitch is that AI can improve the odds. Its proprietary model, Foundry, operates thousands of agents that calculate the probability of success for its clinical assets. The agents analyze clinical data, genomics, biological specimen data, and competition from other developers. This information guides Pathos’s decision-making on which drugs to pursue, what populations to test them in, and how to design the clinical trials.

How worried should I be about the AI hacking panic and “Black October”?
Whether the cyber-pocalypse is here or not, it’s time to change your passwords.
Are we living through “Black October”? Maybe, according to cybersecurity experts who are raising the alarm about AI’s increasingly sophisticated and far-reaching hacking abilities.
This week alone has seen a string of alarming incidents where AI uncovered previously unknown security flaws deep in the infrastructure of the internet. The most concerning involves something called PHP — a programming language that, according to The Atlantic, is used by “as much as 70 percent of websites.” Cybersecurity researchers used AI to locate a major security breach in the technology.
It’s the kind of thing that, when it’s working, is practically invisible. When it stops, though, you really notice it: Government websites in the UK and Europe briefly went down earlier this week after the PHP vulnerability was discovered, as did some sites in the Wikipedia family, the Internet Archive, and many others.
The outages weren’t actually the result of a hack, but rather preventative action as web engineers took sites down to fix the vulnerability before it was exploited. But not every PHP-like issue will necessarily be uncovered before it can be exploited by someone using AI tools less ethically, and older websites relying on PHP might go unpatched.
The problem doesn’t stop there, either: Concern is also rising around AI cybersecurity risks to ubiquitous conveniences like online banking. As Axios reported on Thursday, banks are detecting more and more “unauthorized third-party AI agents” operating inside of their systems.
Those agents are mostly unauthorized by the banks, Axios explains — the holders of the bank account might have given them permission — but it still creates a security risk that executives described as “horrifying,” in part because banks can’t necessarily tell if an agent doesn’t have permission.
It’s a lot to take in, all of it moving extremely quickly, and it’s hard to tell what any of us can do about it as AI labs continue to forge ahead with ever more competent AI models and agents. Luckily, my colleague Adam Clark Estes has some simple recommendations to shore up your own cybersecurity.
How do I respond right now?
One problem with hackers — even those that happen to be AI agents — is that they can be unpredictable. You won’t know to, say, lock down your Quest Diagnostics records before a breach happens. But whenever you find yourself wondering if your data is safe, that’s a good time to double check that you’ve at least covered your bases.
The National Cybersecurity Alliance, a nonprofit dedicated to the safe use of technology, maintains a list of basic online safety practices that everyone should follow. In no particular order, here’s what to pay attention to now:
- Keep your guard up. AI makes it difficult to know the difference between humans and robots. It’s a fact of life in the year 2026. So be extra careful to avoid engaging in potential phishing scams. Don’t reply to unknown texts, and do due diligence on texts or emails that look like they’re from people you know but just seem off. Don’t click weird links. Don’t give out personal info over the phone, even if it sounds like it’s someone you know. They might be scammers using AI to clone a loved one’s voice.
- Update your software. Yes, it’s annoying to pause your phone or computer use for a few minutes to update your software, but this is one of the best ways to get rid of vulnerabilities. Companies like Apple and Google employ huge teams of security experts to spot these in their software and fix them with software updates. Do the updates.
- Use a password manager or, even better, passkeys. Each of your online accounts should have a unique password that’s at least 16 characters. Yes, it’s impossible to remember that many passwords, so you should also use a password manager like 1Password or the app built into your iPhone or Android device.
- Turn on multifactor authentication. Just in case you don’t already do it, make sure you use multifactor or two-step authentication for all your accounts, including email and social media. It can be annoying to type in a code or check your email while logging in, but hackers, including AI agents, will have a much harder time getting into your accounts if you take this step.
Taking all these measures is not a one-time affair. You have to be vigilant in keeping yourself safe online. Security experts have a term for this that’s almost too specific: cyber hygiene. Like brushing your teeth or taking a shower, take good care of your online life, and do it often.

➨ Is it still possible to ban gerrymandering? The current US Supreme Court is very, very hostile to getting politics out of congressional map-making. But if Democrats win back power, that doesn’t mean they shouldn’t try. My colleague Ian Millhiser gamed out how they could do it in a way that survives the Court — as well as some approaches that almost certainly wouldn’t fly. But, he writes, the real trick will be finding a solution that functions the way Congress wants it to and can’t be exploited by mapmakers.

The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has discussed preparations for the upcoming Graduates’ MLC elections and Greater Hyderabad Municipal Corporation (GHMC) elections at a meeting of its State leaders and office-bearers here on Saturday.
The meeting, chaired by State BJP president N. Ramachander Rao at the party’s State office, reviewed the prevailing political situation in Telangana and discussed the party’s organisational activities in nine districts falling within the GHMC limits.
Party leaders outlined strategies to secure victory in the Graduates’ MLC elections and called upon cadres to mobilise workers at the booth level and intensify public outreach.
The meeting also discussed the BJP’s ‘Loktantra Bachao – Bheedtantra Hatao’ (Save Democracy – Remove Mobocracy) campaign against what the party described as actions undermining democratic values. It was decided to intensify grassroots-level protests against the Congress government’s policies in Telangana.
BJP State in-charge Sunil Bansal, co-in-charge Abhay Patil, State organisational general secretary N. Madhukar, State joint organisational general secretary Dashrath, MPs, MLAs, MLCs and presidents of the nine district units attended the meeting. Rekha Sharma was also present.

Srinagar, Oct 24: Jammu and Kashmir Chief Minister Omar Abdullah on Saturday said his government would consider using its own budget to help bring back pilgrims stranded in Saudi Arabia because of flight cancellations and a sharp increase in airfares.
Omar said the issue was being taken up with the Union Ministry of External Affairs, adding that pilgrims who had booked tickets with budget airlines were struggling to afford replacement tickets.
“We are taking up this matter with the Ministry of External Affairs because it is not that flights are not operating at all,” Omar told reporters.
“But the problem now is that ticket prices have increased substantially. Those who are stranded there and had booked their tickets with budget airlines are finding it difficult to book fresh tickets at the new prices,” he said.
The chief minister said the government would explore ways to facilitate the pilgrims’ return in coordination with the Centre.
“We will speak to the Ministry of External Affairs and find some way to resolve this,” he said.
Omar said the Jammu and Kashmir government could step in financially if assistance from the Centre was insufficient.
“If the Ministry of External Affairs does not have the budget to bring our people back or help them with their tickets, we will set aside some money from our own budget and make arrangements to bring them back,” he said.
The chief minister noted that the problem was not limited to pilgrims from Jammu and Kashmir, with people from several states reportedly stranded in Saudi Arabia following flight cancellations.
“I know this is an issue, a problem, and it is not just our pilgrims who are stranded. People from different states across the country are stuck in Saudi Arabia because of flight cancellations,” he said.
His remarks indicate that the state government is considering financial assistance for affected pilgrims, particularly those unable to afford the higher cost of replacement tickets.

The son of Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi has been allowed to speak to the detained former democratic leader for the first time in more than five years.
“Today, I was finally able to speak with my mother, Daw Aung San Suu Kyi, after more than five years. Hearing her voice again means more than words can express,” Kim Aris said in a post on Facebook on Thursday.
Aung San Suu Kyi is under house arrest in the capital, Naypyidaw, according to Myanmar authorities, where she has been sequestered since being unseated in a 2021 military coup.
Images accompanying his Facebook post appeared to show Aris, who lives in the UK, standing outside the Myanmar embassy in London.
“I am deeply grateful to everyone who has stood by my mother and me. I believe your voices helped make this moment possible,” he said in the post. “But my mother is 81 and remains unjustly detained. One conversation is not regular family access.”
Myanmar’s military has held the Nobel peace prize laureate in almost total seclusion since the February 2021 coup, which ended a tentative decade-long experiment with democracy. But in recent months authorities have increasingly advertised the loosening of her detention and published photographs of her taking private meetings, as supporters have demanded “proof of life”.
On Monday, authorities said she received a package from Britain’s King Charles, including two books about soil and a “sealed diplomatic communication” from the monarch. Buckingham Palace did not comment on the contents of the communication.
Myanmar authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi was moved from a prison in Naypyidaw to house arrest in April, and in August they published images of her meeting the nation’s Red Cross representative.
After ruling Myanmar as military chief since the coup, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year.
Analysts described the election that put him in office as a charade, and said he could be loosening restrictions on Aung San Suu Kyi in an attempt to court international legitimacy.

For years, one of my patients lived with chronic pelvic pain that felt like a hot poker in her vagina. After I performed a targeted nerve block with numbing medication, her pain disappeared. Through tears, she told me something I have heard from patients again and again: “I forgot what it’s like to not have pain. Thank you.”
A peripheral nerve block delivers numbing medication around a nerve to interrupt pain signals. It can help identify the source of pain and, for some patients, provide relief that lasts well beyond the few hours before the numbing effect wears off.
But beginning in late October, new Medicare policies issued by five regional Medicare Administrative Contractors (MACs) — which determine local oversight of 37 states and several U.S. territories — will restrict coverage for millions of patients with severe pain, including my patients, by cutting access to many peripheral nerve procedures used to diagnose and treat chronic pain.
The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services writes and oversees the Medicare rules. But because Medicare claims are so big, MACs are private companies that operate much of the machinery to apply those rules to individual health care providers and claims.
The final policy is slightly less restrictive than the proposal released in 2025, an important response to patients, physicians, and advocates who spoke up. But it still leaves patients with high-impact chronic pain at risk of losing access to treatments used for decades in pain care that can restore something as basic as the ability to sleep, go out and buy groceries, or spend hours every day without being consumed by pain.
The final policy excludes therapeutic procedures targeting nerves such as the pudendal nerve and ganglion impar, interventions used for some forms of severe pelvic pain. I have used these interventions to provide relief to patients who previously never had a break from pain, people for whom sitting, putting on a pair of pants, having sex, or simply getting through the day can be excruciating.
As a pain medicine physician, I worry that we are forgetting one of the central lessons of the opioid epidemic: People with chronic pain need alternatives to opioids and more individualized treatment options. Peripheral nerve interventions are not used in isolation. They are part of multimodal and multidisciplinary pain care, helping patients participate in physical therapy, restore function, decrease medications, avoid emergency room visits and hospitalizations, and sometimes delay or avoid more invasive procedures or surgery.
CMS contractors have a legitimate concern. In evaluating these procedures, they point to limitations in the evidence, including small studies, short follow-up periods, and uncertainty about whether benefits last. For several procedures, they concluded that the evidence was insufficient to support coverage.
But chronic pain presents a particular challenge for this style of evidence gathering. Pain is by definition a subjective experience, and every patient experiences pain differently. A treatment that produces limited benefit on average across a study population may provide profound relief to an individual. Population-level evidence matters, but it cannot always capture which patients experience a clinically meaningful benefit. And for the 1 in 4 U.S. adults living with unrelenting pain, even a few weeks or months of decreased suffering can help them feel like themselves again.
My mother taught me that long before I became a pain physician. She is a brilliant cancer research scientist who has lived with chronic migraine and abdominal pain and, like so many patients I now see, often struggles to find physicians who understand her pain or know how to help her. She inspires me to keep looking for answers for patients who have spent years doing the same.
One of them was a remarkably healthy 87-year-old with severe bladder pain. By the time she came to see me, she had been passed from one doctor to another and was in despair. “I see it in their eyes,” she told me. “They don’t know what to do with me, and they look like they are trying to leave the room. I’ve never felt this way; people always want to be close to me.”
In my clinic, I meet patients no one knows how to help. And sometimes, the procedures I perform can be life-changing.
Some may question whether these procedures are used too often, whether the evidence supporting them is strong enough, or whether financial incentives influence their use. Those are fair questions. Not every nerve block works, and Medicare should not pay indefinitely for treatments that do not help.
We need better evidence, including larger studies, longer-term patient follow-up, and federal funding to support this research. The answer to gaps in evidence is to seek that real-world evidence while at the same time preserving appropriate access to effective non-opioid treatments
But absence of perfect evidence should not be confused with absence of meaningful patient benefit.
One of my patients developed chronic pain after gynecologic surgery. After a pudendal nerve block, she told me: “I did not realize how different my life was because of the pain until you gave me the injection that took my pain away. I was able to wear pants, sit in a chair, and spend my day without being distracted by horrible pain.”
That may sound like a modest victory. To someone living with chronic pain, it is anything but. In a few weeks, this pain relief will no longer be accessible to her.
Individualized pain care should not depend on luck, who you know, your insurance coverage, or what is in your checking account. Pain does not always fit neatly into an insurance box of “approve” or “deny.” Effective pain care requires a broad treatment toolkit. That toolkit is meaningless if patients cannot access it.
As these new policies take effect, Medicare contractors must reconsider restrictions as new evidence emerges, while researchers, clinicians, and specialty societies build and identify funding for the larger, longer-term studies Medicare says it needs. We need coverage standards that recognize clinically meaningful benefit while continuing to demand better evidence. We should not put the tools physicians use to relieve suffering out of patients’ reach.
Antje M. Barreveld is chief of pain medicine and anesthesiologist at Newton-Wellesley Hospital (Mass General Brigham) in Newton, Mass.; associate professor of anesthesiology at Tufts School of Medicine; and immediate past president of the American Academy of Pain Medicine.

Enabot Ebo Max FamilyBot for $600: I’m usually a big fan of Enabot’s pet tech—especially its line of pet cameras, which are generally affordable and work consistently well without needing a pricey add-on cloud storage system. While acting as a pet camera, the robot also entertains (or scares or confuses) your pet by making animal noises, doing tricks like spinning and zigzagging, and displaying “emotions” via its front screen. It also has a built-in laser toy that my cats actually played with, along with key features like 24/7 video recording with smart playback, motion detection, and activity alerts.

The laser toy is supposed to auto-engage when motion is detected, but this often didn’t happen during my tests. When the laser did work and caught my cats’ attention, the feature turned off quickly. Plus, because the camera needed to sit high on a shelf to see the area, the laser was often too high for the cats to attempt to catch. You can manually play with the cat using the laser through the app, although it’s often laggy, and my cats ended up more perplexed than playful when the laser was on. It’s a solid camera, but the toy aspect falls a bit flat.
Furbo Mini for $25: I love this super-affordable, 360-degree-rotating basic pet camera. Furbo’s app is easy to use, the 1080 HD feed is clear, it can be mounted on a wall, and it has two-way audio. It’s powered via USB, but it works only with 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, so beware. As with most other pet cameras, to access the full features—like smart detection, alerts, and access to historical video footage—you’ll need Furbo Nanny, the paid subscription service. Luckily, Furbo offers a 14-day free trial to see if the service is a good fit.

It also includes an easily detachable plastic treat dispenser that holds up to 1.5 pounds of kibble. You can toss treats remotely from the app, and you can also control the amount and distance. With the subscription service, the app alerts you when the device detects motion or sound and logs it with playback video. I like the customization options and clear video feed, but—like other Petcube devices—you need the extra Care plan to unlock all the best features.
Enabot Rola PetPal Robot Pet Companion for $200 (treat dispensing): A pet camera on wheels, this rolling model has the best of intentions, but the sometimes glitchy app makes the combo pet camera/toy/feeder a little unpredictable. Through the app, you can watch your pets on the security camera and drive the robot around, pressing buttons to do tricks and dispense treats. You can watch the camera feed live in the app, and you can also schedule recordings, which are viewable via cloud playback. It also assembles a 30-second “day in the life” compilation. The robot is also supposed to detect abnormal movement or sounds, like barking or broken glass, and send a smart alert to the owner with a timestamp while away from home. Through AI-powered pet recognition, the bot can also snap a picture of your pet, but the AI features were unreliable when I tested them.
Petcube Cam for $32: It's simple, compact, and doesn't have all the bells and whistles like more advanced models do, but it’s a great price for a reliable, basic pet camera. Like others in Petcube's lineup, it has a 1080p HD camera, night vision, and two-way audio. It sits on hinges and can angle up and down, with the option to flip the video feed in-app if you want to lay it horizontally. You'll need the brand's subscription Care plan to access any features beyond the live feed. You can set a “motion zone” to receive notifications only in a specific area, and you can connect your phone’s location to the app so you’re alerted more often when you’re away. You can also share the camera feed with others so they can watch remotely, and specify the footage you want to share. This camera is basic, but it delivers a high-quality camera feed and advanced extras that make it a steal at this price.
Catit Pixi Smart Mouse Camera for $51: This cutie looks like a miniature mouse with oversized, magnetic feet that attach to a metal stand. The mouse legs hinge so you can adjust the camera’s height and angle. While adorable, it’s expensive for what it is: The lens doesn't move, and it requires a microSD card to capture video beyond a live feed. With the SD card, you can scroll through recorded video to see activity from past days, record live footage, and save photos and videos to your smartphone’s camera roll. Even with the SD card, though, it was hard to pinpoint the exact time when reviewing footage. The live video feed can be laggy, and there were connectivity issues a few times. It’s a tad expensive at this price point for its (lack of) capabilities.
Closer Pets TreatView with Pet Camera for $100: With an HD camera, two-way communication, motion detection, a built-in memory card, and a one-cup storage for kibble or treats, which you can schedule or dispense at random—on paper, this pet camera has all of the bells and whistles. The video feed was always clear, though the audio was a bit laggy and hard to hear. The treat portions were huge, dispensing a heaping handful of kibble even at the lowest setting. The dispensing alert was super jarring, and my pets were frightened by it—there was no way to silence it. Because of the kibble-dispensing hole's placement, the camera is angled low, making it hard to see the area I wanted. This is an okay pet camera, but its additional features become a burden rather than an asset.
How I Tested
To find the best pet cameras to test, I first looked for security cameras with extra pet-specific features. I set up each camera individually, noting any difficulties with initial setup, Wi-Fi configuration, and the camera feed's speed and reliability. I tested each camera for at least a week (most for much longer) in various spots around my house, and I rigorously tested the extra features available on most of the cameras, like scheduled feedings, food-dispensing, playtime, and scheduled recordings, noting any issues I experienced. Over the months of testing, I went out of town several times and completely relied on these cams to keep an eye on my two children—I mean, cats.
So, Is There Really a Difference Between Security Cameras and Pet Cameras? Sort Of
Security cameras let you keep an eye on your house (and pet) while you’re away, but pet cameras often include additional pet-specific features, such as the ability to dispense treats and interact with your furry friend via a two-way speaker. These cameras with special features can help ease common pet issues like separation anxiety or boredom. The Enabot Rola PetPal Robot Pet Companion, for example, has attachments that let you remotely give your pet a treat or engage in “playtime.”
That's not to say you can’t use a security camera as a pet cam, but like any other smart home device that connects to Wi-Fi, it could be hacked and compromise your privacy. Make sure your Wi-Fi password is strong, and set up two-factor authentication in your camera’s app. It’s also a good idea to keep it turned off when you’re home, as an extra precaution.

Chorbagan Durga idol immersed without customary rituals Debi Boron or Sindoor Khela a week after stampede
Chorbagan’s Durga idol was immersed in the Hooghly under police watch, a week after the stampede that killed 19, without Debi Boron and Sindoor Khela.
The Durga idol of Chorbagan Sarbojanin Puja was immersed in the Hooghly River on Saturday, a week after a stampede at the pandal claimed 19 lives, with the farewell taking place without the customary 'Debi Boron' and 'Sindoor Khela' rituals.
The immersion remained uncertain even after the end of the festivities until retired judge Anindita Roy Saraswati, who heads one of the special investigation teams (SITs) probing the tragedy, cleared it, provided the main structure of the pandal was preserved for the investigation.
Also read: Three months too short to submit stampede probe report, will strive to meet deadline: SIT head
The massive idol was brought out of the pandal through a section of the entrance gate that had been cut on Friday to facilitate its removal.
The idol remained on Central Avenue for some time as residents gathered to bid it farewell, while a large police contingent supervised the immersion process.
Several residents stood along the route as the idol was taken out. Women bowed before it, while some locals walked ahead carrying candles.
A black banner displayed in front of a truck conveyed condolences to the families of those killed and injured in the stampede.
An elderly woman from the neighbourhood was seen folding her hands before the idol, tears rolling down her cheeks.
"So many people died before our eyes. So many homes have lost their loved ones. May we never have to witness such a terrible time again," she said.
Another resident said the cries of people and the scenes of death from the evening of the incident continued to haunt them.
"I pray to God that we never have to see such a day again," the resident said.
"This year, there was no 'Debi Boron'. We could not even find out whether there had been any shortcomings in the puja. Mother, please forgive us," Sananda Roy, a resident, said while expressing their grief over the tragedy.
'Debi Boron' is a traditional ritual of the Bengalis, in which women, preferably married, offer sweets, sindoor and other items to Maa Durga before bidding a final farewell to the goddess.

The immersion was carried out under police supervision, with no members of the Chorbagan Sarbojanin puja committee present during the proceedings.
Nineteen people were killed in the stampede at the Chorbagan puja pandal on October 17.
So far, nine people, including two announcers, have been arrested in connection with the incident.
Two separate SITs have been constituted to investigate the tragedy.

Malaysia's Johor schools to reopen on Oct 26 after weeks of haze-related closures
Authorities cited improving air quality and expected rainfall, with health and safety measures including mask-wearing to accompany the reopening.
JOHOR BAHRU: All educational institutions in Malaysia's Johor state will reopen on Monday (Oct 26) as haze conditions improve, said Johor education and information committee chairman Muhammad Naqib Md Ghazali.
Muhammad Naqib said the decision followed a review of air quality readings and health risk assessments by relevant agencies, local media outlet The Star reported on Saturday.
"The decision takes into account the downward trend in Air Pollutant Index (API) readings across Johor over the past five days," he said in a statement.
"Changes in wind direction beginning Oct 24, increased humidity and expected rainfall are also anticipated to help reduce the effects of the haze," he added.
The reopening also takes into account year-end examinations and preparations for Malaysia's national secondary school examination.
Muhammad Naqib said health and safety measures, including mask-wearing and monitoring school activities based on prevailing API readings, would be implemented.
"The state government and relevant agencies will continue to closely monitor the haze situation, and any changes or further action will be announced through official channels," he said.
Schools in Johor were initially closed on Oct 8 and 9, with the closures subsequently extended until Oct 23 due to the haze.
The prolonged closures affected 1,198 schools and more than 617,000 students across Johor, according to an earlier report by The Star.
On Oct 15, Malaysia's education ministry raised the API threshold for school closures to above 200, while outdoor school activities must be suspended when readings reach 100 or higher.
Previously, schools were required to close when API readings exceeded 180 or remained above 150 for three consecutive days.
Meanwhile, Singapore continues to grapple with haze from regional fires.
Air quality deteriorated across Singapore early on Saturday, with the 24-hour Pollutant Standards Index (PSI) reaching the unhealthy range in all five regions.
At 7pm, PSI readings ranged from 108 to 152, with the highest recorded in western Singapore.
Singapore's National Environment Agency (NEA) said showers were expected over the weekend, while a shift in wind direction from Sunday could help reduce the amount of smoke haze reaching the country.
However, smoke from fires in Indonesia's Sumatra and Kalimantan regions continues to pose a risk to air quality in Singapore and neighbouring Malaysia.

My friend Steve Jones, who has died aged 77, had a working life devoted to humanitarian causes, with a particular focus on Bangladesh and India. In retirement he then dedicated a sizeable portion of his time to charity work, helping people with the lung disease pulmonary fibrosis get the help and treatment they needed.
Steve was born in London to John and Lettie, who were both teachers and shared the surname Jones. After secondary school in Crawley, West Sussex, he studied geography at Bristol University, worked for a short time as an economist for a company that became part of British Airways and then embarked on further studies at Cambridge University, where he gained a certificate in anthropology and began a PhD.
While there he became involved with Operation Omega, a group that smuggled humanitarian aid across the border from India to Bangladesh during its war with Pakistan in 1971. This led him to cut short his studies so that he could begin work as a consultant economist and project planner. Over the years he worked on many projects, including for the University of New South Wales from 1984 to 1986 in the Solomon Islands on a smallholder project and a post-cyclone survey.
In 1989 his work took him back to Bangladesh, where he was employed by the World Bank to develop a flood action plan. Fourteen years of his life, from 1992 to 2006, were then spent with the Department for International Development, working on ways to help tackle the social and economic problems related to rural poverty in India.
He was also particularly proud of a cyclone recovery and reconstruction project he worked on in 2007 for the World Bank, which led to the building of cyclone shelters in Bangladesh.
In 2006 he became a trustee and then chair of trustees of the Humanitarian Centre in Cambridge, which later became the Centre for Global Equality. Two years later he had to leave work after being diagnosed with pulmonary fibrosis, but eventually he was lucky enough to receive a lung transplant that prolonged his life considerably.
That allowed him to focus on being a trustee, chair and patient president of the charity Action for Pulmonary Fibrosis, giving over the last decade of his life to fighting on behalf of people with the disease so that they can be provided with better diagnosis, care and treatment. He was also president of the European Pulmonary Fibrosis Federation.
In 1976 he met Hilary Gretton, a nurse, and they married five years later. She survives him, along with their children, Rosie, David and Euan, and seven grandchildren.

What is Theater Mode on your Apple Watch and when should you use it?
The easiest way to stop your watch from distracting you at the movies.
Apple Watches do a lot more than tell the time, granting their wearers many of the iPhone's perks in addition to a suite of biometric data. However, they also possess an assortment of extra traits with more niche, but valuable, use-cases. One of these underrated Apple Watch features is Theater Mode, which is perfect for when you need your watch to quieten down.
Theater Mode is a neat little toggle designed to help you tone down your watch in a similar manner to Do Not Disturb mode. The setting launched with watchOS 3.2, meaning even the original Apple Watch, which first hit stores back in 2015, can utilize it. Therefore, if you want to make notifications as subtle as possible, without blocking them entirely, you can simply activate this nifty mode on any Apple Watch you might have.
How Theater Mode works and how to enable it
Activating Theater Mode will dim the Apple Watch's bright lights and hush it down; it will turn off the display, silence the device and disable visual notifications. In addition, it will also keep the display from waking whenever you raise your wrist, meaning you'll need to tap the screen or press either of the Apple Watch's buttons to turn the display back on.
The big difference between this mode and the total serenity of Do Not Disturb (besides the disabled display) is that Theater Mode will allow you to keep haptics on, meaning you'll still be able to feel the vibration from a notification.
If you want to turn this feature on, you only need to tap your watch's side button (the flat oval button) to bring up the Control Center. From there, you can toggle Theater Mode by tapping the icon resembling the theatrical comedy-tragedy masks. Unlike Do Not Disturb, however, there are no conditionals for disabling Theater Mode after a certain duration or event, so you'll need to toggle the mode manually.
The best times to use Theater Mode
Obviously, this mode is great for venues where being quiet and considerate is key, whether watching a play or a movie on the big screen. It's also a nice feature for when you're attending meetings or other social events that demand your full attention. In either case, the mode will block any distractions that might irritate anyone in your surroundings, while subtly keeping you in the loop.
Theater Mode also carries a few extra benefits that make it even more useful. Chiefly, it can reduce battery drain by stopping your watch from waking up at the slightest gesture. You can also choose to suppress certain biometric readings, such as blood oxygen readings, while your watch is in this mode. To toggle this, you can simply head to Settings and click on the reading you want to keep on or off during Theater Mode, if applicable.

“Bacchon, police ki maar ka bura nahi maante. Yeh aapko samjhane ke liye kari gayi hai” (Translation: Children, don’t take offence at being beaten by the police. This was done to teach you a lesson.)
This is what a Delhi Police official had to say after protesters were allegedly subjected to a vicious assault inside a prison van fitted with ‘cages’, while being taken to a detention centre at Pandwalan Khurd, a village in the Kapashera tehsil of Najafgarh in South West Delhi, on October 11.
One detainee was called in. Then came the screams. Another followed, and the screams came again. Inside the pitch-dark van, protesters were allegedly punched, kicked and beaten by police personnel before being shoved into cramped, grille-enclosed compartments. They could hear the violence unfold but could barely see who was inflicting it.
Two detainees who were in the same van spoke to Alt News, recounting what they described as a nightmare that would haunt them for the rest of their lives. Each detainee, they said, was made to board the vehicle one at a time, assaulted and then forced into one of the cages inside.
Their offence: Joining a protest on the streets of Delhi against alleged electoral malpractices and supporting the call for the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
An Evening of Unspeakable Horror
Twenty-three-year-old Tarang Balani, who works at an e-commerce startup, saw a video posted by Neha Bora urging people to reach R K Ashram at 2:30 pm. “I saw that post at 2. So I reached Connaught Place (CP) directly because I thought if they’re marching from R K Ashram towards Jantar Mantar, and if I’m reaching late, I should definitely find the march somewhere around CP. I reached around 3:30 pm,” he said.
With several routes blocked in the area, Balani had to take multiple detours. He eventually came across a group marching towards Jantar Mantar and joined them. “We were told to form a human chain in case the police came to detain us,” he said.
The group was marching past Chilli’s restaurant and about to turn left when the police moved in to detain them. “As soon as police came, half the crowd had dispersed around, trying not to get detained, and 10-15 people sat down and locked hands with each other to form a human chain. I saw male police officers pulling the women protesters. Then women police officers arrived and did the same thing.”
After a tussle with the police, the protesters were forcibly made to board a Delhi Transport Corporation (DTC) bus.
In the video below posted by BBC, as Hemansh speaks, a policeman inside the bus can be seen slapping or punching a young man in the face.
View this post on Instagram
“Soon after, they stopped outside the Pind Balluchi restaurant in CP and some police officers started asking us to deboard,” Balani said. The protesters refused to get off the bus since the area was teeming with security personnel and there were no media persons around. “We felt that the media should be able to document what was happening.”
“But if three people are trying to get hold of one person, there’s not much you can do,” he said. According to Balani, police officers began pulling a female protester by her wrists, breaking her bangles and leaving her wrists bleeding. She then clung to the window grille as the officers pulled at her trousers and shoes, leaving her almost suspended in the air. Two women police officers approached her from outside the window and pulled her hair, forcing her to let go. “I saw it happen in front of me,” he recounted.
Outside Pind Balluchi, the protesters were separated by gender. The women were made to sit in a van and taken away, while the men were made to sit on the street for at least half an hour before the next ordeal began.
“If anyone took out their phones, it was immediately snatched, even if they were not recording. They were asking them to open their gallery and delete all media files from the day, even from the recently deleted files. We were told that if we just co-operated, nothing was going to happen to us. So most of us were just sitting quietly,” Balani said.
A Journey that Turned into a Nightmare
Half an hour later, another police van arrived, and the men were asked to board it. Twenty-seven-year-old IIT graduate Hemansh Kashyap recounted how the police allegedly assaulted detainees one by one as they entered the vehicle.
“Some of the policemen started playing good cop, saying that nothing would happen to us if we boarded it. People were taken in one at a time. An official was collecting our phones at the entrance. The first person went in, and then came blood-curdling screams. Then the second person went in, and the same thing happened. We realised that they were being assaulted.”
“We said we wouldn’t board, but the cops said: ‘Aur nahi marenge’ (We won’t hit anymore). But it obviously wasn’t true, and there wasn’t a lot we could do. When I went in, I was immediately slapped very hard, repeatedly, so hard that my glasses flew off. I was shoved into my compartment, and the cops gave me my glasses back,” he said.
Balani said the van had four compartments separated by grille partitions, with a narrow aisle that could accommodate only one person at a time. The vehicle was completely dark, making it impossible for him to see clearly.
“I was beaten up right there in the narrow passage by three policemen. Initially, two of them started beating me up; they punched me and kicked me. And then somebody said, ‘Iska chashma utaar’ (Take off his glasses), and so they took out my specs and started beating me again. I couldn’t even see their faces in the dark; I just saw policemen without name tags,” he recounted.
“I really thought they had confused me with someone else because I was quiet from the start. I was protesting peacefully. As I tried to save myself from the blows, they kept beating me, and beating me, and I just kept pleading with them (to stop). Once they realised that the regular punches and kicks were not working, they started using their elbows. One of them kicked my knee, and I fell in the aisle, and then they hit me more.
“Once I started screaming, that is when they opened the compartment where they pushed me in and just threw my specs. They closed the door behind me and locked it. As soon as I sat down, another person came; he was not wearing glasses, so they literally just took his face and smashed it into a pole in that aisle. I saw it because I was sitting right next to the division between the aisle and my compartment. There was one guy who refused to surrender his phone, and he was beaten by the police as if they had a personal grudge against him,” Balani recounted.
Both Balani and Hemansh Kashyap told Alt News that each of the blocks or cages inside the police van could accommodate six people at most. Each had two benches facing each other, with space for three people on either side. However, 10–12 detainees were crammed into each block, forcing some to sit on the floor and others to sit on fellow detainees’ laps.
The van was completely dark, making it difficult for detainees to even check the time on their watches.
What emerged from both testimonies was the methodical nature of the violence — perhaps its cruellest aspect. One detainee was taken in, beaten and shoved into a cage; then the next was called. The screams were followed by more screams. There was no frenzy, no confusion, but a grim, repeated sequence, with each person left to await their turn, knowing what awaited them in the darkness of the van.
Families Lose Contact as Detainees’ Phones Go Dead
Both detainees had shared their live locations with family members. Kashyap had shared his with his partner, Barshana, who is currently in the United States.
“At 3:45 am Pacific Daylight Time (4.15pm IST) on October 11, Hemansh called me and said he had been detained. He had been detained the day before as well and was held at a farmhouse in Chhattarpur for about six hours before being released. There wasn’t much explicit violence then, so I wasn’t too worried.
“We texted for a while as he told me he was on a bus, and he even sent me a few videos from it. But soon there was complete silence from his side. After two hours of no contact, my calm gave way to worry. I kept checking his location, but it stayed parked at CP for a long time.
“Soon, I received a message request on Instagram from an unknown account. It was Hemansh sending a message from someone else’s phone informing me that he was in a police van and had been assaulted. He told me that his phone was possibly with the cops, and also asked me to track his location. I noticed that the van was moving very fast, heading towards the Haryana border. At around 7 am PDT, the location stopped updating. I had checked, and his battery was at 40%, so it couldn’t have died. I guess the phone was switched off. His friend, who was with him in the van, was also not getting his WhatsApp messages delivered, so both phones seemed to have met the same fate.”
“I kept texting the Instagram account, which, I later found out, belonged to a detainee who had managed to sneak in a phone, but I couldn’t bombard it with messages, as the same phone was being used by thirty others. At around 7:27 am PDT, he called me for a minute, told me they had been brought to a detention centre in the middle of nowhere, and shared the location with me. That is when I mobilised my lawyer and activist friends, who reached the spot to get him out.
“The entire ordeal, from the time he was detained to the time he returned home, lasted about eight hours. It was extremely worrying for me,” Barshana recounted.
Tarang Balani, too, said his brother, with whom he had shared his live location, lost track of him when the police van reached Raota in Delhi. “I’m guessing it was because someone switched it off. An app installed in my phone still shows 70% battery in brother’s phone. The location update was stopped between 6:36 pm and 6:40 pm,” he said.
Kashyap also recounted the assault of a young man, around 19–20 years old, inside the police van. The man allegedly screamed that the police had assaulted him on his private parts and manhandled him. “(He) fell on the ground while being assaulted, and the police started hitting him in between his legs. He told his cellmates after the van started moving. He was probably the first or second detainee to be taken into the van, and he was beaten up brutally. We told him, ‘Don’t get too agitated; they’ll beat you up even more.’ It was very scary,” Kashyap said.
Neither Kashyap nor Balani has got back his phone yet.
Both of them told Alt News that four minors were inside the police van and that all four were assaulted.
Locals Come to Detainee’s Aid at Pandwalan Khurd
The van dropped them at the detention centre around 7:30 pm. The detainees expected their phones back but were told by CRPF personnel that Delhi police had not handed over the phones.
One detainee with a fractured arm received medical attention only at 9:15 pm. “There was just one canister of water, and it ran out pretty quickly. There was no food or medical help. An AIIMS doctor finally came after someone contacted them through their connections,” Hemansh said.
Initially, lawyers were not allowed to enter the detention centre. Meanwhile, a crowd began gathering outside, with some villagers, including children, reportedly protesting the detention.
“They were recording us from outside the gate. We told them to go away or they would get beaten up, but they seemed quite aware of their rights and started asking questions like, ‘How can they beat us up?’ They went away for a bit and came back with their parents, I think. These were ordinary people from the neighbourhood. They came back with water and fruits. Later, when we were released, a man was going around giving everybody 100-rupee notes if they needed to get home,” Kashyap said.
At around 9:30 pm, another van arrived, and some detainees, including 51-year-old journalist Raj Shekhar, were offered the chance to leave. The detainees unanimously refused to go without their phones. The police allegedly told them they could collect their phones from Connaught Place, offering no accountability for their confiscation. Lawyers who had reached the detention centre advised the detainees to call the emergency helpline 112 and submit written applications and complaints.
Between 10:30 pm and 11 pm, buses were arranged to take the protesters to Dwarka More metro station. Unsure whether the buses would actually drop them at Dwarka More, Balani chose not to board one. Instead, he left in a car provided by volunteers, who had been sent sent by journalist Meghnad S to help detainees return home. Kashyap, too, left with lawyers who were present at the scene.
Balani also noted that most Delhi Police personnel involved wore no name tags; only officers with two or three stars had them. He identified one officer as Ashutosh Bishnoi, who, while the detainees waited outside Pind Balluchi, had repeatedly assured them that nothing would happen to them.

New York City was home to my husband and me for six years before we had kids and moved to Asheville, and it will forever be a place that holds so much for us. That's why when the timing, cost, and opportunity aligned for our family of four to vacation there for a week recently, I was chomping at the bit to return, enthusiastic at the prospect of sharing this colossal, important place with our 4- and 6-year-old daughters.
It was easy to have high expectations for a trip down memory lane, but the reality is that any trip with kids will be what it will be, and we can only hope that something along the way — a bump in the road, a detour, a singalong — cements into their memories and crystallizes into sentimental gemstones that they turn over and over in their minds with time.
I created a full itinerary for our trip
Leading up to departure, I planned a weeklong itinerary with suggestions for each day on where to go, what to eat, who to see, and what to do. Knowing my kids would need some rest and recovery, I built in plenty of downtime — or so I thought. Still, as with all things parenting, I was rudely reminded that even with my experience and expertise as Mom, I could not foresee every breakdown.
By midweek, my daughters hit a physical, mental, and emotional wall. I had planned to take them to the Met, but instead, I was met with loud, convincing pleas to spend a couple of hours in the hotel room. Crestfallen, I agreed. They didn't know about the daydreams I'd had of walking them through the museum to see the Temple of Dendur, the Medieval Sculpture Hall, and rooms where Degas's ballerinas, Monet's water lilies, or Van Gogh's self-portrait lived. Sigh. I'm an art lover — I enjoy meandering through vast halls and admiring human creativity and intellect. It brings me great peace and joy.
I was disappointed that we didn't go to any museums
A few days later, I found myself in the same situation at the Whitney. My generally agreeable kids protested once again, so we switched gears. We took a stroll on the High Line, grabbed pizza from Chelsea Market, and landed at the Diller — von Furstenberg Sundeck & Water Feature between 14th and 15th Streets. There, they were all smiles — delighting in the sun, in the relief of cool water, barefoot, holding up their dresses, splashing, squealing, happy.
My kids are still young — 4 and 6 — and have only experienced small art museums. They don't even know what they're missing! So, naturally, when it was clear that we weren't going to visit any art museums, reality stung. This is one of the painful aspects of parenting: accepting that the things you really want to do just don't happen for one reason or another. Of course, you could force your child to do what you'd like to, but what memory does that create? What good does that serve?
However, I realized that there would be other trips and was grateful for the time we had
I let out another deep sigh and told myself, It's OK. There's always next time — hopefully. I smiled, thinking about the next time, and I began to daydream once again. All was well. What mattered most to me on this trip was visiting the place we once called home and introducing it to our girls — acquainting them with the place their mother and father made countless memories, befriended incredible people, grew stronger in their marriage, became parents during a pandemic, and tearfully bid adieu.
Parenting continues to be one wide and winding journey, where I'm constantly toeing the line between curating memories and allowing memories to make themselves in the most ordinary of places: on the 32nd floor of a hotel room, on a playground in Central Park, on a Subway train, on a city bus, on an airplane in the clouds.
In addition, I'm still learning that parenting is mostly a selfless act. Yes, there are moments we get to share with our kids that allow them to see what fills us up as human beings, but it's often an unwieldy and imperfect balance.
Many of the decisions we make come at a cost, and, for this trip (and future trips), I'd rather the cost be one that I pay — not them. Their joy is my joy. And, in this chapter of life, it's bigger, grander, more powerful than any selfish indulgence that life has ever afforded me, and, honestly, I'm here for it. I'm grateful.

Singapore's tap water safe to drink despite haze, says Grace Fu
Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu's comments came after videos of blackish rainwater were circulated on social media.
SINGAPORE: Minister for Sustainability and the Environment Grace Fu reassured the public on Saturday (Oct 24) that Singapore's tap water remained safe to drink despite the haze, following the circulation of videos showing blackish rainwater on social media.
In a video filmed at national water agency PUB’s water quality laboratory, Ms Fu said rainwater collected during hazy conditions can be more acidic and have higher levels of particles and organic matter.
However, rainwater in Singapore’s reservoirs goes through several stages of treatment to remove dirt, tiny particles and other impurities, she said.
“Our water treatment processes can filter out particles up to 100 times smaller than PM2.5,” she said.
PM2.5 refers to fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter, and is usually the dominant particle during haze episodes in Singapore.
“Rest assured that the PM2.5 haze particles will be removed during this comprehensive treatment process,” said Ms Fu.
She cautioned against using rainwater for drinking, cooking or personal hygiene.
“During this haze period, PUB has also stepped up checks on our water quality as added precautions,” said Ms Fu, adding that the tests found no unusual changes in Singapore’s treated water quality.
“While the blackish water seems worrying, our tap water remains clean and safe to drink,” she said.

The Supreme Court has expressed displeasure over States and Union Territories not responding to the Centre on how its judgment declaring menstrual hygiene as a part of the fundamental right under Article 21 of the Constitution is being implemented.
“If what we have said in the judgment is only going to remain on paper, how are the Union and states/UTs going to give effect to this fundamental right?” said Bench of Justices J.B. Pardiwala and R. Mahadevan.
It said the apex court had declared menstrual hygiene/menstrual health as one of the facets of Article 21 of the Constitution, which deals with the protection of life and personal liberty.
The Bench said that on September 1, it had directed the States and UTs to take into consideration the deficiencies highlighted by it and report in that regard by the next date of hearing.
In a significant judgment delivered on January 30, the apex court said that the right to life under Article 21 of the Constitution includes the right to menstrual health.
During the hearing in the matter on October 13, Additional Solicitor General Aishwarya Bhati, appearing for the Centre, told the Bench that the Union of India has taken up this issue very seriously with all the states and UTs to respond to what manner the judgment is being implemented.
“Unfortunately, the states/UTs have not responded to the Union so far. We fail to understand that once the Union calls for the necessary information, why do the states/UTs not respond?” the Bench said.
Also read: Menstrual health is a public health issue
“We are sure that the Union, the states/UTs have realised the importance of the judgment that we delivered, declaring menstrual hygiene as a part of the fundamental right,” it said.
The Bench said the apex court’s verdict was in the interest of young girls who were giving up education, more particularly in remote parts of the country because of the problem of menstrual hygiene, etc.
“We direct the Union to take up this issue very seriously with each state/UT and call for the necessary information in writing as to what steps they have taken so far for giving effect to the judgment delivered by this court,” it said.
The Bench said the Centre should study the verdict once again and accordingly call for information on each and every aspect of the matter.
“On the next date of hearing, if we hear from the Union that some of the states/UTs have not responded, we shall proceed to issue a contempt notice to the concerned chief secretary,” the Bench said.
While granting one last opportunity to do the needful, it posted the matter for the next hearing on December 14.
In its September 1 order, the bench had said the focus should be on the number of schools that lack gender-segregated, functional toilets with usable water connectivity, ensuring accessibility and privacy.
The Centre had then informed the top court that 30,458 gender-segregated toilets with washing facilities had been constructed in schools across the country, while 4,236 were under construction.
In its judgment delivered in January, the apex court had directed the states and UTs to ensure that every school, whether government-run or privately managed, in both urban and rural areas, was provided with functional, gender-segregated toilets with usable water connectivity.
The top court had also directed the states and UTs to ensure that every school provides sanitary napkins to girl students free of cost.
The judgment was delivered on a plea seeking pan-India implementation of the Centre’s ‘menstrual hygiene policy for schoolgoing girls’ in government and government-aided schools from classes 6 to 12.

Barack Obama will campaign Saturday with Democratic candidates for the U.S. Senate in Ohio and Michigan, both highly competitive states that will help determine control of the chamber, as the former president ramps up his involvement in the midterm elections.
Obama's first event is in Cleveland with former three-term Ohio Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is looking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted. Amy Acton, a Democrat running for governor against Republican Vivek Ramaswamy, will also appear at the rally.
Although Ohio has become more reliably Republican, it's been a hotly contested battleground this year.
Quick answers to key questions
Obama is campaigning in Cleveland with Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is challenging Republican Sen. Jon Husted. In Detroit, he will rally for Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who is running against Republican Mike Rogers.
Both states have highly competitive Senate races, and their outcomes could help determine which party controls the Senate.
The article says Obama’s appearance in Detroit, a city that is three-quarters Black, could bolster El-Sayed’s support among Black voters.
His campaign appearances may help Democratic candidates, but the article does not predict whether Brown or El-Sayed will win. Both races are described as competitive.
President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have both visited the state in recent weeks to drum up support for Husted and Ramaswamy.
Obama then heads to a rally in Detroit for Abdul El-Sayed, a former public health official who is working to unite the Democratic base in Michigan after winning a divisive primary by less than a percentage point. El-Sayed is running against former Rep. Mike Rogers, a Republican.
Obama’s appearance in the city, which is three-quarters Black, could bolster support for El-Sayed among Black voters. In the primary, his opponent Haley Stevens won Wayne County, which includes Detroit, by about 6 percentage points. Former Vice President Kamala Harris, the first Black and South Asian vice president, campaigned for El-Sayed in September.
El-Sayed criticized Obama after his 2012 reelection for not following through on all of his progressive campaign promises, writing that Obama “was not the right choice — he just wasn’t the wrong one.”
El-Sayed told reporters earlier this month he appreciated the former president, calling him “foundational” to his ability to run for office, but there were still elements of Obama's presidency he disagreed with.
“It’s a normal thing to love somebody, to really appreciate all that they’ve done, and to say, ‘Hey, here are some things I would have done differently,’” El-Sayed said. “But they still did some important things to create opportunity for you.”
El-Sayed spoke with Obama on the phone shortly after his primary win in August.
Michigan also has open races for governor, attorney general and secretary of state. Jocelyn Benson, the Democratic nominee for governor, is slated to appear along with others down the ballot. Benson is running against Republican Rep. John James.
Obama will headline a rally in Georgia next week with Sen. Jon Ossoff and candidate for governor Keisha Lance Bottoms. Trump is slated to speak in Georgia Saturday.

SAT Hospital in Thiruvananthapuram, Keralam, the premier tertiary-level child health institution in the State’s public sector and one of the chosen Centres of Excellence for Rare Diseases in the country, has found itself in the eye of the storm following allegations about “clinical trial drugs” being given to spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)-afflicted children.
With Opposition political parties intent on carrying forth with the campaign that “experimental drugs” were used on SMA patients, the Superintendent of SAT Hospital, I. Riaz, appealed to all and sundry not to undermine the government’s efforts to make the drug for SMA available to a larger number of patients.
According to him, the decision to provide SMA patients with a less expensive, generic version of the original molecule against SMA, in place of the imported original drug costing several lakhs of rupees for a single vial, had been taken by a technical committee comprising experts in the field.
The purchase procedures initiated during the previous government’s time were completed by the present government. The drug meets all regulatory requirements and quality norms, Dr. Riaz added.
‘Unfounded rumours’
Dr. Riaz appealed to all to stop spreading unfounded rumours about the generic SMA medicine and push patients and their families into an anxious state. He pointed out that the medicine had been available in the open market for nearly a year and was already being used by several SMA patients. To raise the argument that it was an experimental drug, just when the government begins to distribute it free of cost, was preposterous.
Several health experts pointed out that quality generics were the only way to make expensive medicines accessible and affordable to a large number of people. If people can willingly accept generic oncology drugs, then to find fault with the generic version of SMA drug alone was just hypocrisy.
Financial assistance
The superintendent also condemned attempts by vested interests to link the financial assistance extended by Natco Pharma under their corporate social responsibility (CSR) initiative to renovate one of the wards in SAT Hospital, to the distribution of generic SMA drug.
SAT Hospital Health Education Society (SATHHES) regularly receives corporate social responsibility funds from various agencies, public and private-sector institutions, and individuals to undertake development projects related to patient care at the hospital
On March 25, 2026, the then Superintendent of SAT Hospital had written to Natco, seeking their assistance to renovate the isolation ward in the hospital
Following a site visit and assessment by company representatives, Natco Pharma transferred ₹25 lakh as the first instalment to the SATHHES account. The company representatives subsequently visited the hospital in the first week of August to meet the Health Minister and hand over a certificate related to the contribution.
The attempts being made to portray this in relation to the generic SMA drug of Natco given at SAT Hospital is malicious and ill-intended, Dr. Riaz said.
It was common for agencies, companies and public-sector institutions providing CSR funds to hand them over and take photographs in the presence of the Health Minister or the Chief Minister, he added.
Instead of spreading baseless allegations, the efforts of the government and SAT Hospital to safeguard the welfare of patients with SMA should be given more support, Dr. Riaz said.

Did you know that an Indian woman scientist had a notable role to play in the development of anti-epileptic drugs and anti-malarial drugs? That the same woman also told us most of what we needed to know about the medicinal plants in the subcontinent?
By the standards of her time, unlike other women scientists, Asima Chatterjee did get recognition for her research while she was alive, but it cannot be said that she received the adulation and celebration that her male peers did. That doesn’t make Asima Chatterjee any less tall a figure in the history of Indian science, and the nation must be grateful for her pioneering work in organic chemistry and the sub category of phytomedicine – using plant extracts to treat various conditions, even prevent them.
109 years ago, Asima Chatterjee was born, on September 23. Her love affair with chemistry began at a young age and she went on to pursue this, with a Bacherlor’s degree and a masters in the subject. At a time when few women were able to take up higher education, she went on to complete her Doctor of Science degree in pre-independent India, specialising in phytochemistry. History records her as the first Indian woman to be awarded a Doctor of Science by any Indian university. She went on to gain expertise in research methodology at the University of Wisconsin, Madison and the California Institute of Technology, working with international experts in the field before returning to India.
She took a great interest in a sector that sought to harness the natural plant biodiversty of India and phytochemistry skills to develop newer compounds and drugs that could be used to treat people. Today plant-based extracts form key elements of critical drugs. Plant-derived drugs range from pure compounds extracted from herbs to complex botanical extracts approved as prescription medications. Chatterjee sank herself into the development of clinically useful drugs from indigenous plants – striking success with isolating the chemical constituents of Marsdenia tinctoria – which led to the formulation of the anti-epileptic drug later marketed as Ayush- 56.
Chatterjee also made huge breakthroughs in developing anti-malarial drugs derived from plant extracts. But the greatest achievement that she is credited with is her extensive research on the chemistry of alkaloids found in Caranthus roseus, or the Madagascar periwinkle, which contributed leaps to the understanding of compounds with anti-cancer properties. No less important is the foundation she laid for modern pharmaceutical chemistry, utilising physical and chemical methods to to determine the complex molecular structures of numerous organic compounds, and recording her methodology meticulously.
Beyond her pioneering work in the lab, Chatterjee was also an ace institution builder and educationist. During her academic career, she served as a professor of chemistry at the University of Calcutta at a time of intense gender barriers in academia, and was later appointed as the Khaira Professor of Chemistry, a prestigious chair in the varsity.
Her work in science was recognised with a Padma Bhushan in 1975, Chatterjee creating a record here too, being the first woman scientist to achieve this honour. She was the first female scientist to be elected as the General President of the Indian Science Congress Association and was also a Fellow of the Indian National Science Academy. No wonder then that she was the first female recipient of the Shanti Swarup Bhatnagar Prize in Chemical Sciences (1961), India’s top science award, introduced in 1958. She was also awarded the prestigious CV Raman Award and PC Ray Award.
Today, as the debate rages about bringing scientific vigour and scientifically validating traditional systems of medicine in the country, Chatterjee was a beacon even in this area, her work bridged the gap between traditional Ayurvedic knowledge and modern rigorous chemical analysis, to benefit humanity. Legacy
But Asima Chatterjee’s achievements cannot be confined to just the scientific arena, her immense achievement must also be counted at a time when formidable gender barriers stood in the way of female achievements, breaking the glass ceiling and making it possible, even inspiring, generations of women scientists to make their bold foray into the sciences. Being that rare Indian women scientist who got substantial recognition during their lifetime, in the scientific world, and yet she was largely missing from mainstream narratives, and global histories of science.
But today, we say her name, properly celebrate her legacy. Asima Chatterjee, exceptional chemist, phytochemist and extraordinary pioneering scientist who opened the portals the world of science for generations of women. Say her name, say Asima Chatterjee.

Bigg Boss OTT 3 winner Sana Makbul appears to have taken another dig at Mahhi Vij amid the ongoing controversy surrounding their equation. The actress recently hit back at a social media user who labelled her a “homewrecker” for allegedly spending time with Jay Bhanushali, Mahhi’s estranged husband. Sana questioned the claim and asked the troll whose ex-husband she was supposedly hanging out with.
Sana Makbul hits back at troll
Sana shared a screenshot of a social media post accusing Mahhi of playing the “bechari” card. Reacting to it, she clarified her equation with Mahhi, writing, “Firstly let’s start here, she is not my best frnd, she was just a frnd fyi.”
A user wrote on social media, “Not interested in Sana she is mad she is roaming with jay all the time she could homewrecker.” Responding to the comment, Sana said, “Hanging out with Jay? When and where trollers be like? Mujhe bhi batao? Please whose X husband i m hanging out with?”
Mahhi Vij broke down emotionally on Bigg Boss 20 while opening up about the challenges of single motherhood following her separation from Jay Bhanushali. Speaking to fellow contestants, the actress revealed that she had neither accepted alimony nor asked for maintenance from Jay, despite him being willing to support her financially. “I didn’t take a single penny in alimony or even ask for maintenance. I’m here on my merit, only so that my daughter’s life is secured,” she said. Mahhi further recalled that the judge had urged her four times to reconsider her decision, but she stood by it because she believed the money was hard-earned by Jay. “It’s his hard-earned money,” she explained, adding that Jay had never refused to help her and that “his entire locker is open for me.” The actress also spoke about how her life revolves around their daughter, Tara, while Jay encourages her to step out and live her life.
