Leaders in the US Space Force would like to have a new spaceport up and running in four years, adding a third heavy-lift launch site to relieve pressure from bases in Florida and California that have shot rockets into orbit for nearly 70 years.
The obvious problem with that ambition is 2030 is four years away, and Pentagon officials have not determined where the new spaceport should go or how to acquire land for it.
Air Force Secretary Troy Meink first mentioned the service’s search for a third launch base in May. A congressionally mandated study of the Space Force’s launch infrastructure identified the need for “another site that’s capable of heavy and super heavy launch capability,” Meink said in a House Armed Services Committee hearing.
The Trump administration released a space transportation policy in August that endorsed the construction of more launch and reentry sites for commercial and military missions. This week, the Space Force general responsible for procuring launch services for the military laid out an “aspirational” timeline for a new launch site.
“We need this capability by 2030, but I’m also a pragmatist,” said Lt. Gen. Philip Garrant, head of Space Systems Command. “That is not an inconsequential demand to build a spaceport when you factor in orbital regimes, safety, access to commodities, the Americans that live near it. In many ways, it’s much like an airport, but even louder. So there’s a lot of consideration.”

Four Philippine Air Force pilots were killed after two military training aircraft collided midair and crashed at an air base south of Manila, the Philippine capital, on Friday, officials said on Saturday.
The two SF-260 aircraft collided while flying at a low altitude during a training flight on Friday afternoon before crashing at Fernando Air Base in Lipa city, located in the coastal province of Batangas, reported the Associated Press (AP).
There were no injuries reported on the ground, according to the news agency. One of the two-seater aircraft crashed near the barracks housing military personnel at the air base.
Two Philippine officials familiar with the incident confirmed that the aircraft collided in midair. The four pilots aboard the two planes died in the crash.
The Philippine Air Force has temporarily grounded all its remaining SF-260 aircraft following the accident as authorities investigate the circumstances surrounding the collision.
The air force did not disclose how many SF-260 aircraft remain in its inventory. The planes, which were acquired from Italy, are used for training purposes.
The investigation is expected to examine the circumstances leading to the midair collision. No further details about the cause of the accident were immediately available.
The latest crash has renewed concerns about the safety of military training flights, particularly as the Philippine Air Force continues to operate ageing aircraft while working to improve its operational capabilities.
Friday's accident follows two other fatal crashes involving Philippine Air Force SF-260 aircraft in recent years.
In May, an SF-260 aircraft crashed in the northern mountain province of Benguet during a navigation training flight involving several other aircraft of the same type. Both pilots aboard the aircraft were killed.
In 2023, another SF-260 crashed into a rice field in Bataan province, northwest of Manila, during a training flight, killing two crew members, according to the Philippine Air Force.
The latest incident adds to the military's challenges as it seeks to strengthen its aviation capabilities and improve the readiness of its forces.
The crash represents another setback for the Philippine military, which has long struggled to modernise its air force, navy and army because of financial constraints.
The country's armed forces have had to contend with decades-long communist insurgencies and Muslim insurgencies while attempting to upgrade equipment and improve defence preparedness.
At the same time, Manila faces increasingly tense territorial disputes with Beijing in the South China Sea, where competing claims have contributed to heightened regional security concerns.
The Philippines has been seeking to strengthen its military capabilities amid these challenges. However, limited funding has complicated efforts to replace ageing equipment and expand operational capacity.
The fatal collision highlights the difficulties facing the Philippine Air Force as it continues training operations while dealing with equipment constraints and broader modernisation requirements.
Authorities have grounded the remaining SF-260 aircraft pending the outcome of the investigation into Friday's crash. Further details about the cause of the collision and possible measures to prevent similar incidents were not immediately available.

Doctors are urging Americans aged 6 months and older to get vaccinated against the flu after an unusual early rise in cases on the West Coast that virologists are still working to understand.
It could be the strain itself. The predominant flu strain this year is H1N1, which caused the 2009 swine flu pandemic and is now a standard part of the flu shot. But this year’s version of the virus has a new mutation called G155E.
People who have been previously exposed to H1N1, either through infection or vaccination, would only have some residual protection from the older versions, scientists say.
"What people are a bit worried about is that the H1N1 strain this year hasn't been seen by a lot of younger folk, so it may be more severe in them," said Dr. Jennifer Duchon, a paediatric infectious disease expert at Mount Sinai Children's Hospital in New York, adding that her hospital has started to see some flu cases.
The 2026-2027 flu vaccines, approved by the FDA in August, target H1N1, H3N2 — the dominant strain last flu season — and one influenza B virus.
While most children recover, flu can be deadly, especially for the very youngest and those with underlying health conditions.
Promotion of flu shots has been reduced under U.S. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a longtime anti-vaccine activist who has engineered an overhaul of long-standing childhood vaccine schedules.
The American Medical Association recommends the shot for all people 6 months and older.
The vaccine's effectiveness fluctuates depending on how well it is matched months in advance to circulating flu strains. Over the past 10 years, it has been between 30% and 60% effective in reducing flu hospitalisations and deaths. Last year, an estimated 32 million Americans had the flu, 390,000 were hospitalised and 24,000 died.
Scott Hensley, a microbiologist at the University of Pennsylvania, said two of the three components of this year's vaccine appear to be very well matched to circulating flu strains.
However, the H1N1 mutation might affect antibodies in younger people, and with flu season picking up steam, "it is probably a good idea to get vaccinated early," Hensley said via email.
Geography changes
Typically, flu cases start in Southern states and move north. This year, it's coming from the west, said Caitlin Rivers, a Johns Hopkins epidemiologist who tracks pathogens in a weekly newsletter called Force of Infection.
“There's no clear reason to me why this would be the case,”Rivers said.
As last year was dominated by the H3N2, there could be an "immunological gap" because immunity to H1N1 virus is not as fresh. Or, it could be the new mutation, she said.
Jeanne Marrazzo, chief executive of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, said studies of antibodies from people exposed to the flu last year found they did not recognize this new mutation. That was especially true of antibodies from teens and young adults.
Marrazzo said the small studies were something to be aware of but not cause for alarm.
Falling shots, rising flu cases
Some 58 million American adults received a flu shot last season, according to data firm IQVIA, down more than 20% from the nearly 75 million in the 2019-20 season, the last season before the COVID-19 pandemic changed U.S. vaccination patterns.
Around half of U.S. children got flu shots last year, according to CDC data, compared with more than 60% in 2019-20.
Standard flu shots are made by GSK, Sanofi, and CSL's Seqirus unit. AstraZeneca makes a nasal spray inoculation called FluMist. A new mRNA vaccine from Moderna is also available.
Vaccine manufacturers say demand has been consistent with last year. Two pharmacists told Reuters vaccination rates have not picked up significantly.
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention dropped its recommendation for the shot for most children at the beginning of 2025, a move a court put on hold.
CDC also pulled its ad campaign to promote flu vaccination in 2025, according to press reports.
Paul Offit, a pediatric infectious disease expert at Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, said he believes immunisation rates have been hurt by HHS' decision to cut back on promoting flu shots, as well as by statements from Kennedy himself.
"He has done what he can to discourage flu vaccination," Offit said.
When asked about public health messaging on flu shots this season, HHS spokesperson Emily Hilliard pointed to the CDC's "Respiratory Illness Season Toolkit" on the agency's website. It says vaccination is the most effective tool to prevent serious illness.
Flu activity is low but has been on the rise since late August, CDC data show.
Positive tests reported to the CDC by clinical labs last week hit a 10-year high for this time of year at 5%. On the West Coast, that figure was 10.7%, compared with 0.5% a year earlier. At peak flu, the rates are around 30%.
Numbers are also elevated in eight Southern states including Florida and South Carolina, according to Hopkins' Rivers.

Severe thunderstorms and heavy rain will sweep across most Australian states this weekend, adding to the deluge in an already drenched Queensland.
Flash flooding in south-east Queensland this week prompted hundreds of SES callouts and the closure of multiple schools. On Saturday morning, the Bureau of Meteorology had nine flood warnings in place for south Queensland.
The BoM is now warning of severe thunderstorms, heavy rain and flash flooding across South Australia, Victoria, NSW, Tasmania.
Senior meteorologist at the Bureau of Meteorology, David Crock, said severe thunderstorms and heavy rain were forecast across multiple locations in central and eastern Queensland on Saturday, including Rockhampton, Gladstone, Bundaberg, the Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Roma.
Severe storms could also sweep through parts of Victoria, including Melbourne’s eastern suburbs and central and eastern South Australia. Heavy rain is expected to develop in Tasmania overnight into Sunday morning.
“There’s plenty of rain across the south-east, as well as plenty of showers and storms and rain across much of Queensland as well, after what’s already been a really wet week,” Crock said.
The cold front will move across NSW on Sunday, bringing severe thunderstorms to the west of the state as well as north-eastern Victoria, Sydney and Brisbane.
“Tomorrow is a threat for thunderstorms right across eastern Australia, with severe thunderstorms likely through a wide part of inland eastern Australia,” he said.
This week, multiple areas in Queensland were hit by more than twice their average October rainfall across a few days.
“It was an incredibly wet week in Queensland. Much more typical of summer or January or February than this time of year,” Crock said.
The Sunshine Coast hinterlands and Caboolture were hit by flash flooding and recorded a seven-day rainfall total of 300-400mm of rain, with some areas reaching 450mm.
“It’s been notable how persistent this weather pattern has been, how much moisture has pumped in … then how those rainfall totals have accumulated across seven to 10 days through Queensland and northern New South Wales,” Crock said.
On Thursday, torrential rain in south-east Queensland caused flash flooding, water rescues and hundreds of calls for help while several schools were forced to close on Friday.
Thursday’s heavy rain stretched from Caboolture down to the Border Ranges, with some places copping well over 200mm falls.
The Queensland fire department carried out more than 16 swift-water rescues, including using a raft to retrieve an elderly man clinging to the roof of his vehicle at Caboolture.

Karoline Leavitt appeared on HBO’s Real Time with Bill Maher on Friday and was questioned about the short stint of her successor as Donald Trump‘s White House press secretary, Katie Zacharia.
After doing just one briefing that lasted 14 minutes, Zacharia was ousted last Friday, after less than a week in the job.
Leavitt told Maher that “it’s a tough job” and one of the “hardest” in Washington.
“That pressure in that room is enormous,” Leavitt said. “The press are vicious, and you know I give her credit for standing up there. And as the president said, it wasn’t a good fit, and that’s okay. I wish her well, and we’re on to the next. And he has a lot of options.”
Maher, though, said that that “sometimes you give up a home run at the first inning. They don’t usually go to the bullpen that quick.”
Watch on Deadline
Leavitt responded, “Look, I mean, the president did have a hit show called The Apprentice, where he’s known for, you know, moving on from people. So hey, it’s in his nature to do that type of thing, I guess.”
Earlier, Maher quipped that Zacharia’s tenure was shorter than the dinner he had with Trump last week that lasted for four hours. At that sitdown at the White House, Maher was joined by Stephen A. Smith and Kid Rock. The HBO host credited Trump with listening to him as he challenged him on certain issues, like ICE, degrading Ukraine’s Starlink access, as well as telling the president that Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth “is dragging you down.”
“There are so many moments where he gets it,” Maher said. “Like I said to him, ‘You know, when you said the Supreme Court, they’re voting against me? You know that’s not how the Supreme Court is supposed to work, right? They’re not voting for or against you. You appoint them and they make decisions.’ And he went, ‘Yeah, I took that one too personally.'”
Maher added, “He gets it and then he doesn’t get it. Now I’m an optimist. I prefer to think of the president as half sane.”
In response, Leavitt tried for a bit of whataboutism, telling Maher that Trump is “very sane. He’s a lot more, I think we can agree, he is far more sane than the last one. We had a mental patient.”
“He’s far more energetic,” Maher said.
But Maher returned to what happened during the dinner with Trump. “We have a nice conversation and he goes, ‘You’re my enemy. Pass the peas.’ I mean, he will say that, ‘You’re my enemy,’ and then a minute later, we’re just talking normally, and we don’t act like enemies.”
Maher also told Leavitt that he was worried over what Trump will do if the midterms go bad for Trump and Republicans. “We know he likes vengeance,” he said. Leavitt, though, said that she doesn’t “worry about the president. Look, he loves our country very much, and he wants to make it right.” She even suggested that he would work with Democrats, noting that he has worked with D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser.
During her tenure, Leavitt was known for her steadfast defense of the president, even if that meant delivering regular lectures to the media on their coverage of the administration. Even though she was highly praised for her performance, it didn’t stop the fall in Trump’s approval rating, which has dropped to an average of 38.8% from 50.5% at the start of his term, per Real Clear Politics.
Maher pressed Leavitt on Trump’s recent moves to waive sanctions on Russia, calling it “unconscionable,” along with “basically putting a knife in the back of [Ukraine’s president] Zelensky.”
Maher asked, “Is there anything that could make you, because a lot of Republicans now say we’ve had enough, make you not be loyal to whatever he was doing?”
Leavitt, who is soon to become a commentator for Fox News, gave no indication that there was anything. “He was my boss, but to me, he’s also a friend, and he gave me the opportunity of a lifetime.”

Kartik Aaryan’s upcoming aviation drama Captain India, directed by Shimit Amin, is reportedly set against the backdrop of the conflict in Yemen. Inspired by a real-life humanitarian evacuation mission, the film will mark Kartik’s first time playing a pilot. He will portray a character tasked with leading a rescue operation in a war-affected region.
Kartik Aaryan’s Captain India to explore Yemen rescue mission against the backdrop of Houthi conflict
The Houthi conflict is expected to form an important part of the film’s narrative, bringing a geopolitical element to the rescue drama. While the makers have not disclosed the exact details of how the conflict will be portrayed, the film is expected to focus on the challenges involved in carrying out a large-scale evacuation mission amid rising tensions.
The backdrop of the story traces its roots to 2015, when Houthi forces took control of Sanaa, prompting Saudi Arabia to launch a military campaign in Yemen. During the same period, India carried out Operation Raahat, a major evacuation effort to bring Indian citizens and nationals of other countries to safety from the conflict-hit region.
A source familiar with the project shared details about the film’s inspiration, stating, “Captain India is inspired from India’s one of the toughest rescue missions in the war torn country Yemen in 2015’s, where the nation rescued not only our own citizens but people from across the globe. Kartik will be seen leading world’s one of the most impossible rescue missions in the actioner.”
The film will see Kartik take on a role centred on a high-risk humanitarian operation, marking a new addition to his filmography. With the story drawing from a real-life evacuation effort, Captain India will bring the challenges of rescuing people from a conflict zone to the big screen.
Produced by T-Series and Baweja Studios in association with Kartik Aaryan’s Dopamine Studios, Captain India is currently being shot in the UK. The film is scheduled for a theatrical release on August 13, 2027.

Student movement takes Serbia's Vučić to the wire in neck-and-neck election
- Published
If Sunday's parliamentary elections really are a battle for the heart of Serbia, then who better than a cardiologist to be one of the leading figures in the race.
Ilija Srdanović appears an unlikely opponent for Serbia's long-serving leader, Aleksandar Vučić, arriving for an interview by motorbike sporting a fluorescent yellow jacket emblazoned with pro-student slogans.
He has been selected as top candidate for an opposition movement posing the most serious challenge to Vučić since the Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) entered government in 2012.
The Student List has emerged from almost two years of anti-corruption protests led by young Serbians, outraged by the deaths of 16 people when a railway station's canopy collapsed in Serbia's second city Novi Sad.
- What you need to know about Serbia's pivotal election 
  - Published1 day ago
Instead of running for office themselves, student-led assemblies at the country's university faculties have chosen 250 candidates to stand in the parliamentary election, with Srdanović, professor at Novi Sad University, heading the list.
"It is absolutely normal to stand with my students to help them in their fair struggle," Srdanović told the BBC.
The Student List is up against a Serbian leader who has served successively as deputy prime minister, prime minister and president since 2012. When he called these snap elections last month, he stood down as president to run again for the role of prime minister.
Whatever Vučić's title, there has never been any doubt that he was the man in charge – an image enthusiastically promoted by Serbia's largely uncritical media.
He retains strong support among a significant section of Serbia's population. They view him as a strong leader who stands up for the country's interests. He can also point to significant economic growth over the past decade and numerous improvements in infrastructure.
Vučić has painted the student movement as foreign-backed and seeking to "bring down our state". "Let us always protect and defend it," he told supporters at a final campaign rally.
Just like the protest movement from which it developed, the Student List has no hierarchy or nominated leader. This makes it a proposition unlike any other in Serbia's relatively short democratic history.
Reliable polls are thin on the ground, but analysts are predicting an extremely tight vote.
Ilija Srdanović may head the list of candidates – but he is not the movement's leader and would not necessarily be first choice prime minister if they won.
Srdanović insists that the Student List has a clear vision: "We offer to our citizens the core values of civilised society, which this previous regime has taken away from our citizens for the last time."
The other candidates on the Student List range from academics to athletes – and economists to engineers. None of them has a political background. But the students who selected them believe that is a strength, rather than a weakness.
"We've gathered people who are actually the best in their fields, and we really think that they are competent enough to rule the country," says Aleksandra, a student at Novi Sad University who only wants to give her first name.
"All of them are gathered around the same vision of a country where the freedom of speech is ruling, where you can walk to your home in the middle of the night and you will not be beaten up by some hooligans," she adds.
The Student List and its supporters say that Aleksandar Vučić and the SNS dominate state institutions and media coverage.
At the last parliamentary election in 2023, the International Election Observation Mission noted "overwhelming ruling party advantage" due to "bias in the media" and "misuse of public office and resources".
The BBC approached leading figures in the SNS for an interview but was not offered a response.
For the past 18 months, there has also been a full-time, pro-SNS camp in the small park between the National Assembly and the Presidency building in the centre of Belgrade. Its residents have repeatedly attacked journalists and made the park a no-go zone for local people.
Vučić has called the camp "a symbol of resistance" against those who "cannot stand different opinions".
But his major challenge remains what happened outside Novi Sad railway station two years ago.
The station's renovation was a key part of his signature infrastructure project – the high-speed line linking Belgrade and Budapest. So it has been difficult for Vučić to distance himself from the disaster.
Protests followed, with participants accusing the authorities of corruption and having "blood on their hands".
"This is a problem for the government," says Magda Anastasijevic, the Eastern Europe analyst for the conflict monitor, ACLED.
"Vučić has survived this in the past, he was always able to find a scapegoat and blame whatever problems on them. This was not the case for the canopy."
On the diplomatic front, he has performed a delicate balancing act.
Membership talks with the EU continue, albeit fitfully, even as Serbia retains close ties with Russia and China – both countries that refuse to recognise Kosovo's unilateral declaration of independence from Serbia.
Vučić has warned those links could be severed if the Student List took power.
"When you ask them: will you impose sanctions on Russia? Silence, umming and ah-ing, but no answer," he told the audience at a pre-election rally.
"You know what the Chinese think, you've heard what Vladimir Putin said. So you decide. Think about who has our best interests at heart."
The final rallies of the campaign saw the SNS stage an event at Belgrade Arena, with Aleksandar Vučić as the only speaker. But on the other side of the Sava River, the Student List attracted a reported 150,000 people in Slavija Square to listen to a mixture of students and candidates.
The contrasting visions were clear to see: the strong, sole leader – or a collective approach. Now Serbia's electorate must decide which they prefer.

WHO, the United Nations Foundation and Illumination have partnered to launch a Public Service Announcement (PSA) that reinforces safe and healthy practices during these challenging times, featuring Illumination’s globally beloved Gru and the Minions. The PSA focuses on lifesaving behaviors to help mitigate the impacts of COVID-19, including physical distancing, being active at home and remaining kind to each other —all aimed at making sure people of all ages stay safe and healthy during this pandemic.
“At this challenging time, we must find all ways possible to provide hope to people while sharing advice that can protect our health,” said Dr. Tedros Adhanom, Director-General of the World Health Organization. “WHO is excited to be working with Illumination and Steve Carell and the joys of the Minions and Gru to promote the importance of physical distancing, keeping active and connected, and being kind and compassionate to overcome COVID-19.”
The PSA is voiced by Academy Award® and Emmy Award® nominee Steve Carrell, who voices the character Gru in the Despicable Me franchise. The PSA will be localized into multiple languages including Spanish, French, Portuguese and Arabic, among others.
“Storytelling is a powerful tool to accelerate positive social change in the world. It is an honor to partner with the WHO and UN Foundation to remind people around the globe to protect themselves, each other and our communities during this pandemic. I am also appreciative to Participant for helping to organize the collaboration and to my partners at Comcast/NBCU for helping to amplify this important message,” said Illumination Founder and CEO Chris Meledandri.
Illumination is the first Hollywood Studio to partner with WHO, the UN Foundation and the COVID-19 Solidarity Response Fund to create an entertaining and educational PSA for global audiences. Participant helped facilitate the collaboration between Illumination to the United Nations Foundation and the World Health Organization.
"As the world continues to grapple with the challenges of COVID-19, one of our most powerful weapons is kindness," said Elizabeth Cousens, President & CEO of the United Nations Foundation. "We are delighted that the Despicable Me characters are letting their love show and showing ways to keep themselves and their communities safe during this unprecedented time."

Zetwerk made its stock market debut at a 5.46% premium on the NSE at ₹159.25 against its issue price of ₹151
The listing gives investors a public-market entry into the B2B manufacturing startup, while the IPO proceeds will help it reduce debt and fund acquisitions
Zetwerk’s FY26 operating revenue rose 40.4% to ₹15,913.3 Cr, but its net loss widened to ₹1,606.2 Cr from ₹370.7 Cr in FY25
B2B manufacturing company Zetwerk made its stock market debut at a 5.46% premium on the NSE at ₹159.25 against its issue price of ₹151. On the BSE, the shares listed at ₹159, up 5.3% from the issue price.
The listing followed Zetwerk’s ₹5,012.3 Cr IPO, which opened for subscription on October 15 and closed on October 19. The company had set a price band of ₹143-₹151 per share.
Ahead of the public issue, Zetwerk raised ₹2,251.2 Cr from anchor investors by allotting 14.91 Cr equity shares at ₹151 apiece on October 14.
The IPO comprised a fresh issue of ₹2,830 Cr and an offer for sale (OFS) of 14.45 Cr shares worth ₹2,182.3 Cr. At the issue price, Zetwerk’s post-issue valuation stood at around ₹25,583 Cr.
Zetwerk increased the fresh issue from the ₹2,600 Cr proposed in its updated draft red herring prospectus (UDRHP). The OFS component also rose 49.2% from around 9.7 Cr shares.
Promoters and cofounders Amrit Pratik Acharya and Srinath Ramakkrushnan each offered to sell up to 1.42 Cr shares. Other selling shareholders included promoter group entity Creovate Innovation and funds associated with Peak XV Partners, Accel India, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Kae Capital. Kae Capital Fund II and Kalysta Capital Fund IIbagged 38.3X returns on shares sold through the OFS, pocketing ₹196.3 Cr and ₹63.3 Cr, respectively. Lightspeed’s funds collectively received around ₹440 Cr, while Peak XV’s funds realised ₹359.3 Cr from their share sales. (The story will be updated soon)

Two leaders of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement have been sent to jail for five days for violating a ban on protests at a site in central Delhi.
A court ordered that Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, leaders of the Cockroach Janata party (CJP) movement, spend five days in Delhi’s Tihar prison for jumping over police barricades, holding up slogans and waving the Indian flag at Delhi’s Jantar Mantar.
CJP leaders said the action was taken to demonstrate against the brutal crackdown on youth protesters in Delhi over the weekend and the decision by the Delhi police to shut-down Jantar Mantar – a stretch of road surrounding an observatory in central Delhi – as the capital’s designated protest site, a status it has held for more than 30 years.
“You cannot denotify the resistance,” said Abhijit Dipke, the founder of the CJP, in a social media post which showed three of his fellow leaders entering Jantar Mantar, before they were tackled and detained by police on Tuesday.
On Saturday, the CJP – a pressure group with a substantial following among India’s youth – called for a protest in Jantar Mantar to demand the resignation of the election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who is accused of overseeing the mass disenfranchisement of millions of Indian voters.
The CJP, alongside the opposition political parties and student groups, have accused Kumar of revising India’s electoral roll to advantage the ruling Narendra Modi government, a charge his Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) denies.
The election commission has denied favouring any party and said wrongly deleted voters can re-enrol.
Police denied permission for the protest on Saturday to take place and instead imposed a sweeping security crackdown. About 30,000 police and paramilitary were deployed to prevent the demonstration in Jantar Mantar, which was blocked with barricades. More than 7,000 people were detained, including the CJP leaders who were kept overnight.
In the aftermath, the police declared that protests would no longer be allowed at Jantar Mantar and instead proposed three alternative venues – all much further away from parliament – which provoked outrage among the CJP leaders. Prior to his arrest, Das posted: “Why is Narendra Modi scared of Jantar Mantar? Jantar Mantar belongs to the people of India.”
Ranka and Das were among about a dozen people who jumped the barricades on Tuesday to enter the grounds of the Jantar Mantar to wave flags and chant slogans.
In response to their sentencing, CJP founder Dipke accused the Modi government of resorting to “cowardly tactics” to “crush dissent”.
The jailed CJP leaders were also given the backing of opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who said the people of India would “reclaim Jantar Mantar”.
“Waving the tricolour at Jantar Mantar in a peaceful protest is not a crime. Jailing youth for it is an act of cowardice,” said Gandhi.
The response by the Modi government to the protests that have erupted nationwide – including the mass detentions – has drawn criticism from the UN human rights commissioner and human rights groups such as Amnesty.
The Indian government hit back at the UN statement on the protests, calling it “an unacceptable interference in the internal affairs of the country”.
The crackdown was also met with concern by a UK political delegation visiting Delhi, led by trade minister Jonny Reynolds who confirmed he had raised it with the Indian government.
Kiran Stacey contributed to this report

Black Friday is still over a month away, but if you’re hoping to upgrade your TV, you don’t need to wait until November. By the early 1880s, bacteriology was emerging as a rigorous science. Within the circle of German microbiologist Robert Koch in Berlin, investigators were attempting to isolate specific disease-causing organisms. The logic was to prove that a microbe caused disease, one had to grow it in pure culture, separate it from contaminants, and study its properties systematically. The available solidifying agent was gelatin. It provided a temporary structure to the nutrient broth, allowing colonies to form on the surface. But gelatin was fundamentally flawed: It liquefied at temperatures approaching 37 degrees Celsius, precisely the temperature required to culture many human pathogens. Even worse, several bacteria secreted enzymes that digested gelatin itself. The medium collapsed, colonies merged, and experimental clarity dissolved into formless fluid. For scientists attempting to establish causation of individual species in infectious disease, this was not a minor inconvenience: it was a structural limitation.
Who was Fanny Hesse?
Fanny Angelina Hesse was not formally appointed as a scientist. She assisted her husband, Walther Hesse, who worked in Koch’s laboratory. She prepared materials, maintained cultures, and drew meticulous illustrations of bacterial forms for publication. She was present, not as an investigator, but as a quiet labourer in daily experimental work. It was in that proximity that she repeatedly encountered the gelatin problem. Failed plates, melted surfaces, cultures lost at incubation temperatures. The frustration was practical and persistent. At home, however, she handled another substance entirely. Agar jellies prepared in her kitchen remained firm even in summer warmth. They did not soften as gelatin did. They did not seem to degrade. One evening, in what history records only briefly but imagination can render vividly, the domestic and the scientific converged. The problem of the laboratory and the memory of the kitchen overlapped. She suggested that if agar could withstand heat on the dining table, why would it not withstand incubation in the laboratory?
Before the laboratory
Agar is a complex polysaccharide extracted from the cell walls of certain red algae, mainly species of Gelidium and Gracilaria. Chemically, it consists primarily of two components: agarose and agaropectin. Agarose is a linear polymer made up of repeating units of galactose and 3,6-anhydro-L-galactopyranose, and it is this fraction that gives agar its remarkable gelling property. Agaropectin contains sulfate groups and contributes to viscosity and charge characteristics. The word “agar” is believed to derive from the Malay term agar-agar, meaning jelly.
Long before bacteriologists struggled with melting cultures in Berlin, agar had already lived a quiet life in kitchens. Extracted from red seaweed and known in parts of Asia for nearly two centuries, it was used to set desserts into firm, translucent gels. Unlike gelatin derived from animal tissue, agar did not collapse in warm weather. It held its structure. It was stable. It obeyed heat differently. In the nineteenth century, European cooks encountered agar as an exotic culinary thickener. But in scientific circles, its potential was invisible. The laboratory and the kitchen were separate worlds, divided by sex, habit and hierarchy. No one imagined that a domestic ingredient could resolve a foundational problem in bacteriology.
Thus, Fanny Angelina Hesse’s suggestion to replace gelatin with agar, was out of the box.
Moment of trial
When agar was introduced into nutrient media in Koch’s laboratory, the transformation was immediate and decisive. The medium remained solid at incubation temperatures. It did not liquefy. Most bacteria lacked the enzymatic machinery to degrade it. Colonies appeared as discrete, visible units, each derived from a single organism. For the first time, bacteriologists possessed a surface that was chemically inert, thermally stable, and optically clear. The ability to isolate pure cultures became reliable rather than tentative. Within months, the method was embedded in the experimental practices that led to the identification of the tuberculosis bacillus and other pathogens in the decades to come.
To understand why agar transformed medicine, one must first grasp the idea of culture. A culture medium is an artificial nutrient environment that allows bacteria to grow outside the human body under controlled conditions and at a controlled temperature. Individual bacteria are invisible, but when placed on a suitable medium, such as agar, they form individual visible colonies. This enables laboratories to isolate the exact organism from samples like blood, urine, or sputum. Once identified, the bacteria are tested against different antibiotics to determine which drugs are effective and to detect resistance. Imagine culture is like switching on a floodlight in a dark room. Agar becomes the illuminated stage where hidden microbes step forward, enabling precise diagnosis and rational treatment.
The breakthrough was not dramatic in spectacle. It was a shift merely in material. Yet that shift altered the trajectory of microbiology.
Aftermath and recognition
The scientific practice and literature of the period absorbed agar rapidly, but credit did not travel with equal speed. The technique became standard practice. Petri dishes were designed to accommodate solid media. Textbooks described agar plates as routine apparatus. The name of Koch became synonymous with bacteriological rigour. Fanny Hesse’s contribution receded into footnotes. For decades, the laboratory bench carried her insight without carrying her name. Only later did historians of science begin to recover her role and situate it within the broader narrative of microbiology.
Agar today
More than a century later, agar remains foundational. In every microbiology laboratory, from district hospitals to advanced research institutes, agar plates are prepared daily. Blood agar to detect haemolysis, MacConkey agar to differentiate lactose fermenters, chocolate agar for fastidious organisms. Selective and differential media, all structured upon the same seaweed-derived matrix. Antibiotic susceptibility testing depends on agar diffusion methods. Colony counting for public health surveillance relies on agar surfaces. Molecular biology workflows begin with bacterial colonies grown on agar plates before plasmid extraction or genetic analysis. Even in the era of automated diagnostics and genomic sequencing, agar persists as the primary tool for culturing living microbes.
Today, major production occurs in countries such as Japan, Spain, Chile, China, Indonesia, and Morocco, where seaweed is cultivated or harvested. Beyond microbiology, agar is widely used in the food industry as a vegetarian gelling agent, in confectionery and desserts, in pharmaceuticals as a stabilizer and laxative, and in biotechnology for gel electrophoresis to separate DNA and RNA fragments.
Its properties remain unmatched. It melts at high temperatures but solidifies at lower temperatures, allowing sterile preparation and convenient pouring. It is largely resistant to microbial digestion. It forms a clear, stable gel that supports nutrient supplementation without chemical interference.
Firming up microbiology
Without that transition from gelatin to agar, the systematic isolation of pathogens would have been delayed. The architecture of modern microbiology would have developed more slowly, along a more convoluted path.
Fanny Angelina Hesse recognised continuity between her kitchen and her laboratory. Today, when a microbiologist streaks a plate and waits for colonies to appear, the act is routine. Yet beneath that routine lies the insight of Fanny Hesse. Without her intervention, the discipline might have remained uncertain at its foundation, its cultures unstable, its conclusions tentative.
(Dr. C. Aravinda is an academic and public health physician. The views expressed are personal. aravindaaiimsjr10@hotmail.com)

Months of simmering public anger have given rise to a season of discontent in India. In its latest iteration, the demand is for the removal of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar and the scrapping of a controversial electoral rolls revision that has struck 130 million people off the register. Protests have erupted every day over the past week, prompting a violent crackdown on dissenters in the capital.
Over the weekend, Delhi was effectively under lockdown, transformed into a militarised landscape of barricades, road closures and paramilitary forces marching through the streets. Ahead of a protest led by the Cockroach Janta party on Saturday, authorities deployed a massive dragnet: 245 trains to Delhi were cancelled, 45 metro stations were shut, liquor shops were closed, internet services were cut off in the heart of the city and activists were put under house arrest.
The founders of the Cockroach party were removed from an Air India flight shortly after it landed at Delhi airport on Saturday. Opposition leaders were held for more than eight hours in various police stations. Video footage showed students and activists being manhandled, beaten and dragged off the streets while some journalists were also swept up in the detentions. A supreme court lawyer assisting those detained was carried away by police, his shirt torn in the process. The crackdown extended to Mumbai, where Tushar Gandhi, the great-grandson of Mahatma Gandhi, was whisked away by the police to prevent him from participating in a local demonstration. On Monday, the Delhi police denotified Jantar Mantar as a designated protest site, instead recommending three alternative locations.
“I have been in public life and have watched politics for four decades now, and I have never witnessed this kind of preparation for a demonstration. It was extraordinary by any stretch of the imagination,” political activist Yogendra Yadav, who was also detained, said of Saturday’s crackdown. Despite what he described as “terror unleashed by the state”, he said, small groups staged flash protests in several areas of Delhi defying the heavy security presence.
The crackdown was preceded by similarly aggressive police action against Congress party’s protests, led by Rahul Gandhi. Dramatic images of police personnel detaining Gandhi and his sister, Priyanka, amid scenes of chaos flashed across screens nationwide.
The ruling Bharatiya Janata party has defended its position, with spokesperson Ravi Shankar Prasad accusing the opposition of weaponising protests after electoral defeats. “One, Indian democracy has thwarted attempts to incite anarchy. Two, the country will be governed by parliament, not by the streets,” he said at a news briefing.
While suppression of protests is not new, what stands out this time is the scale of the crackdown in the capital. Government clampdowns in Indian-administered Kashmir have been far more severe, particularly in 2019, when sweeping restrictions were imposed after the revocation of Article 370.
The ferocity of the state response reflects the high political stakes for Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government, which faces mounting resistance over the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) and questions about the credibility of the electoral process.
The latest protests began with a demand for Kumar’s resignation after an Indian Express investigation reported that the ECI’s two other commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised concerns about changes to electoral rolls, registration procedures, and digital systems. While Kumar has not responded to the investigation, the ECI said in a statement that “differing views” were part of the “decision-making process”. But the anger runs deeper. The SIR exercise has faced criticism for putting citizens through a trial by fire and leaving the most marginalised in a Kafkaesque limbo. Critics and opposition leaders have gone further, charging that the exercise was designed to benefit the ruling regime.
Former election commissioner Ashok Lavasa told me that the SIR process is unprecedented and unfair, marking a departure from the Commission’s traditional emphasis on inclusion. “For more than seven decades the ECI took it upon itself, as a duty, to enrol everyone who was eligible to vote. And that was one of the basic differences between how Indian democracy works and how other democracies function, where you need to apply to get enrolled,” he said. Voters accustomed to a “friendly procedure” now face a hostile system, which he said “is not good for democracy” in the long run.
Yadav argued that the SIR controversy has exposed what he describes as a deeper process of democratic capture by the ruling party. “Elections are the only mechanism now left for the regime to stamp its legitimacy and election capture is critical to their survival. And therefore, Gyanesh Kumar is critical,” he said. He pointed to a 2023 law giving election commissioners legal immunity for actions performed in their official capacity, which he said is broader than even the protection afforded to judges.
As to what comes next, he envisions potential for three strands to find common ground: the opposition parties, organised civil society groups, and ordinary citizens. For a government that has shown no sign of budging yet, he said, the calculus will get harder. “The longer they delay, the higher the stakes.”
On Monday, the Keralam assembly passed a resolution seeking Kumar’s removal, as opposition parties marched toward the supreme court demanding action against him. And the Cockroach movement and leftist student groups have vowed to continue protesting. “People have refused to be fearful any longer. They will come again and again,” said left-wing student leader, Danish Ali. “We are living in a democratic country, and protest is a fundamental right that no one can snatch away from us.”
What else we’re reading about
Human rights | South African jurist and former international criminal court judge, Navi Pillay, who is of Indian Tamil heritage, has won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. In a first-person account published in 2023, she wrote about her grandparents, who came from India and worked on a sugarcane farm in South Africa for five years before being allowed to buy land.
Technology | The United States has suspended labour-certification processing for several major technology companies, including top Indian IT firms, as part of a crackdown on what it alleges is a misuse of its flagship green card program, fraud and the displacement of American workers. The impacted companies include Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL, Capgemini, Microsoft and Adobe. “We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” the US labour secretary Keith Sonderling announced last week.
Climate| Citing a significant rainfall deficit linked to the El Niño weather phenomenon, the Maharashtra government last week announced water cuts of at least 10% across urban areas starting 16 October. The state government had previously declared drought conditions in 74% of the sub-districts.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
With Delhi in the news for all the wrong reasons, I turned to Mayank Austen Soofi, who writes a daily Delhi column for Hindustan Times, to share a spot he returns to for a moment of reprieve. “Whenever I can, I spend a solitary afternoon at the tiny Sufi shrine of Hazrat Sarmad Shaheed, beside the Jama Masjid mosque. The bazaar outside the shrine is the Walled City’s noisiest quarter, yet inside one can sit in silence beneath the neem tree growing beside Sarmad’s grave. An Armenian Jew from Iran, Sarmad fell in love with a Hindu boy in Sindh, eventually became a naked fakir and settled in Mughal Delhi. Executed by Emperor Aurangzeb, his grave lies beneath a red cloth that recalls his blood-soaked beheading. These days, I linger a little longer at the resting place of a man who would just not submit to power.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
32
At least 32 children from the Indigenous community in Balaghat, Madhya Pradesh, have died since June, the Indian Express reported. An inquiry found evidence of measles and malaria. The children, aged between one and 13, experienced symptoms including high fever, skin rashes and abdominal pain.
Vibe check
For Mumbai-based cinematographer, Arbab Kamal Khan, the fleeting, unguarded moments of everyday life offer the most honest form of documentation. His Instagram account is an extension of this cinematic vision, capturing the languor of slow days, the beauty of the mundane and the quiet air of romance.
“When someone passes away, we don’t remember the curated moments,” he told me. “We always go back to the little things, the moments that are small or intricate.”
For me, the images and videos featuring his parents – their feet across each other besides teacups resting atop an Urdu newspaper, or his dad resting under his wife’s dupatta as she brushes her hair – are particularly striking because older people are rarely afforded such tenderness in visual culture. In his frames, his parents are not only elderly figures but also lovers who continue to find intimacy in each other’s presence.

I'm a firm believer that there are some people in this world you're simply destined to meet and have in your life forever. For me, one of those people is my sorority-Little-turned-soul-sister, Lisa.
After bonding over many things during recruitment sophomore year — including our shared love for Blink-182 and punk rock — we both unknowingly wrote down on the get-to-know-you quizzes for the committee that we hoped to be paired as Big and Little sisters.
We were, and the rest is history. Our college days were constantly filled with plans together, and by graduation, we couldn't imagine embarking on this next phase of adulthood with over 180 miles between us.
She's from the Boston area, while I'm from Connecticut and moved to New York City right after college. So, we agreed to prioritize our friendship and made a pact to spend time together in person every year.
Since graduating in 2015, we've planned a getaway together every summer.
Our trips haven't always looked the same, but they have some constants
Right out of college, Lisa and I looked forward to a few sun-drenched days spent catching up on Long Beach Island, New Jersey.
From the Victoria Guest House to the Engleside Inn, we'd book a charming yet affordable place steps away from the beach to spend long days working on our tans, cranking up the tunes, and sipping spiked seltzers.
At night, we'd head out for bar hopping and dancing to live music until the wee hours of the morning. The next day, we would rinse and repeat.
We initially chose the Jersey Shore because it's an easy ride to perfect summer weather and beautiful beaches. It became our go-to place, though we now switch up locations every now and then.
Fast-forward to more than a decade after graduating from college, and our summer tradition is still going strong — but it looks quite different.
For this year's getaway, we stayed in a charming room at Greydon House in downtown Nantucket, Massachusetts. (We've always taken the aesthetics of our accommodations seriously and became obsessed with B&Bs and boutique hotels early on.)
We brunched at Lemon Press, popped into all of the boutiques (and shopped for Lisa's little ones), enjoyed early afternoon cocktails at CRU (the restaurant's signature Crucomber cocktail was a must), pedaled our beach cruisers past the hydrangea-lined shingled homes, and relaxed at the beach while we gabbed and reminisced.
Although we're no longer partying like it's 2015, we've come to genuinely enjoy an early dinner reservation at an aesthetically pleasing restaurant, plus after-dinner cocktails. A perfect night usually includes slipping into our PJs and streaming a chick flick.
We're also more organized these days, sticking to a well-planned itinerary to ensure our experience is top-notch.
In fact, we both watched "Five Star Weekend" before heading to Nantucket and knew we absolutely had to grab morning buns from Wicked Island Bakery. (If you know, you know!)
Above all, we don't let life get in the way of our friendship or summer tradition
Our lives look very different now that we're in our 30s. Lisa married her high-school sweetheart and is a mom of two, while my husband and I recently purchased our first home and have been tackling countless renovation projects in between doing lots of travel.
It takes true commitment from Lisa and me to carve out time for our tradition amid this hectic stage of adulthood — and it's always well worth it.
We know the importance of prioritizing our time together and start planning our trip in the early spring so we can block off a time that works for both of us in the summer.
While, like fine wine, our getaways have improved in the best way, one thing has always remained the same: We still talk, let our hair down, and laugh until our sides hurt from start to finish.
There's rarely a moment of silence, and when there is, it feels completely natural.
We can go weeks or even months without gabbing and somehow always pick up where we left off. We listen, give advice, and discuss what we both have planned in the near and distant future. We celebrate each other's successes and offer endless support.
Our friendship has grown with us and is incredibly strong; it's exactly what a best friendship should be. Of course, our summer tradition is here to stay.

Meta is delaying its controversial new business terms amid scraping concerns
The new terms were supposed to take effect on October 30.
Meta's controversial new commercial terms of use won't be taking effect on October 30 after all. In an email sent to Reuters and Fast Company, a spokesperson said that the company was "extending the effective date of [its] updated Commercial Terms and Self-Serve Ad Terms to 20 November to allow more time... to explain to [its] partners and stakeholders what's changing and what's not."
If you'll recall, the company previously shared a planned update to its terms with language saying that Meta would have the right to use web scrapers and automated tools "to access, index, cache, analyze, collect, retrieve, or crawl the domains, web pages, or URLs (and any content available through them)" associated with business accounts on the platform. The updated terms would also state that Meta "may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features.
After publishers and other businesses raised concerns, the company changed its language to remove the reference to AI training. Since then, potentially affected entities have submitted complaints to antitrust authorities about the updated terms. The News Media Alliance, which represents thousands of news media organizations in the United States and in Canada, also sent the company an open letter, demanding that it withdraw its revised terms of use before October 30. "News publishers will be forced into providing their valuable journalism to support the development of products that may be used to compete with them for readers and advertisers, under duress and without compensation," the organization wrote.
Meta added in its statement that it will explain to its partners how it uses its web crawlers and make it clear that content owners and publishers will be able to use robots.txt. The plain text file will be able to signal the content owners' preferences to crawlers and AI bots and stop them from indexing their content. That said, Reuters previously reported that multiple AI companies' crawlers regularly ignore robots.txt instructions.

Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today.
Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory.
“Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity,” Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call.
Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said “irrational pricing” from fiber operators includes $30 to $40 monthly broadband offers “in specific markets in the third quarter.” He said $30 to $40 pricing is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, and is “getting more expensive with construction costs up as you get into more suburban and rural areas.”
“As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition,” Armstrong said. While he didn’t name any specific competitors, Verizon has been pitching FiOS fiber plans that start at $30 a month. Comcast’s network is a mix of fiber and cable, and it offers fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory.
Armstrong said more Comcast customers are leaving when they face “pricing transitions,” apparently referring to the price hikes customers get when promotional offers expire. “We’ve been refining our offers and retention strategies to better manage these transitions and strengthen customer retention,” he said.
Cavanagh said that “satellite is not yet a material factor” in the competition Comcast faces, but that Comcast is focused on “anticipating emerging forms of competition and positioning our business to respond as the market evolves.”
Fewer jobs, more AI agents
After the latest quarterly drop, Comcast has 28.3 million residential broadband customers in the US. Comcast said it has a plan to turn things around.
“We’ve embarked on the most significant operating and cost transformation in our company’s history, with an opportunity we believe will ultimately amount to billions of dollars over time,” Cavanagh said. The organizational changes will result in a “significant charge” of over $1 billion to be applied in the fourth quarter earnings report, Armstrong said.

France protests latest: 135 arrested and tear gas fired at demonstrators as unrest erupts
Some 70,000 police officers have deployed across France, while some of its tourist attractions and metro stations closed ahead of protests

Tear gas was fired at demonstrators and more than 100 people were arrested across France, as the authorities attempted to prevent a repeat of the riots and looting that rocked the country last weekend.
Interior minister Laurent Nunez said 135 people had been arrested nationwide by early afternoon, with around 70,000 police officers deployed.
Officers used tear gas to disperse demonstrators in Lyon and Nantes, while in Paris, luxury shops boarded up windows and added guards.
Some of the capital city’s top tourist attractions and metro stations closed before the protests.
Some shopkeepers have begun arming themselves with baseball bats, crowbars and shotguns to protect their businesses.
Clashes were reported between protesters and police in Marseille.
French president Emmanuel Macron met with high school unions yesterday in an 11th hour attempt to quell unrest anticipated over the weekend.
However, student leaders emerged from the talks dissatisfied, urging pupils to continue protesting until the government presented concrete proposals to address their demands.
The demonstrations, which began over deteriorating conditions in schools, have spread across France, fuelled by wider anger over rising living costs and strained public services.
Hundreds of thousands of protesters march in France
French media report varying estimates of the number of people marching across the country today.
CGT, one of the largest trade unions, said that nearly 800,000 people had mobilised in France, according to newspaper Le Monde. But the French Ministry of Interior put the number at 410,000 people.
In Paris, CGT counted 250,000 demonstrators on the streets, while the Ministry of Interior said there were 110,000.
In full: Louvre shuts down over fears of violence in Paris
The Louvre is closed on Saturday, along with several other major Paris museums, because of concerns about potential violence during planned protests, France's culture ministry says.
The Orsay and Picasso museums are also among those that are closed, the ministry said.
The ministry called on all institutions under its authority to adopt any necessary measures to ensure “visitor safety, staff protection and the preservation of artworks”.
France protests: Louvre shuts down over fears of violence in Paris
Clashes reported in Marseille
Clashes between protesters and police have been reported in Marseille near an arch where a planned demonstration was scheduled to conclude.
Young men, many with covered faces, had dragged large streets of metal into the street as barricades, according to The New York Times. Others threw rocks and bottles at riot police, and officers fired volleys of tear gas at protesters.
Mona Lisa off limits as Paris shuts museums over protest fears
Disappointed tourists poked their heads through the Louvre's locked gates on Saturday, shut off from the Mona Lisa as galleries and museums across Paris closed as a precaution ahead of fresh demonstrations.
"When we came, we thought there could be a problem but not that the museum would be closed," Italian social educator Selena Bertoni, 31, said in front of the Musée d'Orsay.
On a four-day trip to Paris she had paid €50 for two tickets to see its Impressionist paintings and other masterpieces.
"Bad timing," she said, with a shrug.
The closures came one week after nationwide demonstrations over the cost of living and deteriorating public services descended into some of the worst street violence that France has seen in years. The violence and damage prompted the government to impose localised curfews and close many public venues ahead of demonstrations planned on Saturday.
The shutdown extended across much of the capital's cultural sector, including the Orangerie, Jeu de Paume and Picasso museums, while the entire Tuileries Gardens complex that leads out of the Louvre was sealed off.
"This is the third museum we have come to that is closed. They should've warned us," French visitor Heidi Rosar, 21, said.
At the Louvre, the locked black iron gates blocked access to the entire site and the garden.
"We wanted to at least see the pyramid," 67-year-old Canadian Don Nowschuk said, referring to the museum's landmark glass entrance.
On a two-night stay in the City of Light, Nowschuk suggested the local authorities might be overreacting.
"There is so much security that you would think it would be enough to secure the museum," he said.
"It's a bit weird to see so many cops with guns around Paris. We are used to guns but not like this."
The disruption extended to the performing arts sector. The Paris Opera shuttered both the Palais Garnier and the Opéra Bastille, citing safety concerns for staff and audiences.
Organisers of `the prestigious Art Basel Paris fair also cancelled its weekend programme. The cultural centres posted warnings about the closures on Friday, but some people never thought to check.
"How could we have known? We didn't think a museum could be closed. We are a bit naive," 59-year-old French woman Catherine Sebbagh said.

Many demonstrators accused the government of over-reacting, with soldiers dispatched to patrol the Champs-Elysees.
"We shed tears for shops, not for the people who are being impoverished all year round," said Clara Lebbadi, a 22-year-old arts student.
"My friend and I almost didn't come because we were scared, but we came precisely because it's important not to let repression win," she added.
The first authorised march on Saturday passed off peacefully in Orléans, around 120 km (75 miles) south of Paris, where demonstrators rallied against Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally as it held a party congress in the city.

On Oct. 12, as federal agents searched the home of U.S. Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn, as part of an alleged criminal investigation, a rumor spread online that Omar had escaped to Morocco, which has no extradition treaty with the U.S.
One post (archived) on X read, "We're hearing from sources at the State Department that Ilhan Omar has fled the United States for Morocco, which does not have a billatral extradition treaty with the US."
There is no evidence Omar has escaped to Morocco. The source for this claim, Real Raw News, frequently spreads false and unverified rumors, many of which we have previously debunked. Additionally, Omar posted about the investigation on her social media accounts, describing her intention to fight back. As such, we rate this claim as false.
Snopes reached out to Omar's office for comment. We will update this post as we get more information.
The earliest example of this claim appeared on Real Raw News' X account. The same account posted an AI generated image claiming to show Omar appearing to hide in a tunnel claiming she "has gone underground":
We're haring more reports that Ilhan Omar fled her home 30 minutes before the raid and has gone underground, hiding, fearing arrest. Working on two orthe [sic] articles right now but will have this report out asap.
Real Raw News frequently posts false and unfounded information. It describes itself as a website for "for informational and educational and entertainment purposes" on its about page, which also says its content includes "humor, parody, and satire." Real Raw News' social media posts about the Omar claim did not contain a satire disclaimer.
Omar raid and investigation
On Oct. 12, Homeland Security Investigations agents carried out a pre-dawn raid of Omar's Washington, D.C., home. In a statement on her Congressional web page, Omar's office called the raid "an outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."
A few hours after the raid, Omar posted (archived) on X:
I'm ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement. For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.
I will not be silenced.
Omar also posted a series of older clips of herself making critical comments about Fox News and Trump and resisting questions from reporters repeating old and unfounded claims that she had been married to her brother — a rumor we have debunked before.
On Oct. 15, Omar posted another statement on X in response to the news that the Trump administration had also probed her immigration records in 2019 and found nothing. She wrote:
Thank you to everyone who stood with me over the years. It's been a scary journey but I have always been grounded in my work and ability to provide exemplary service to my constituents. Trump and his administration have been after me since I arrived in Congress. I have always stood up to him and that will never change. The pedophile protector will never silence me.
As of this writing, Omar has not been seen publicly since the raid. Federal agents also reportedly seized Omar's laptop, cell phone and passport during their raid, according to an anonymous source speaking to MS NOW. We are unable to confirm whether Omar got those items back.
A video shows Fox News asking Omar's husband, Tim Mynett, if the congresswoman had fled the country while he was walking outside their Washington, D.C., home. Mynett responded: "You guys are annoying the hell out of all the neighbors around here, man."
In an earlier interaction with Fox News on the same street, Mynett was asked about his reaction to the raid. He said: "My wife came here when she was 12 years old, a child war refugee. No concerns."
Omar is also running for reelection in her Minnesota district in the November midterms. In early October, her campaign posted a video of her appealing for donations "to help pay for security for her and her campaign" as she said she was "under attack" by Trump. Ahead of an important election, it is improbable that Omar would escape the country as the posts claim.
The scope of the investigation into Omar is unclear, but U.S. Vice President JD Vance previously accused Omar of committing immigration fraud. In September, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said his agency was investigating such claims. In October, The Washington Post reported the Trump administration had probed Omar's immigration records in 2019 for the same issues being investigated today, and found nothing.
Snopes has reported on numerous false and unverified rumors about Omar.

What if you gave yourself a day to cancel all the plans you dread?
This story is adapted from Life Kit's weekly newsletter. Sign up here to get expert advice on lifestyle topics like health, money, relationships and more.
How is your to-do list looking for the next few weeks? If it's already full of obligations and tasks you've been dreading, and ramping up toward the holidays, you might need a "say no" retreat.
Life Kit
Why you should take a 'say no' retreat
That's one of dozens of creative ideas in Caroline Sylge's book, How to Retreat: A Guide to Stepping Away from the Everyday to Find Space for Yourself, published this spring.
A "say no" retreat is a day to brainstorm all the things you want to say no to in your life in the coming weeks and months, she says. Then, you'll spend the last part of your day saying no to a few of those things.
Sylge, who has spent the last 30 years attending and organizing health and wellness retreats around the world, developed this exercise to help people reclaim their time.
"We often say yes for reasons that have nothing to do with what's good for us, because we feel like we should, don't want to seem difficult or fear missing out," Sylge says. "Saying 'no' is uncomfortable, but is a brave act of self-respect."
Devoting a whole day to saying "no" may seem like a wild idea, but with the holidays on the horizon, it may make room in your life for the things that matter. Here's how to do it.
Design your one-day, "say no" retreat: A suggested schedule
Before you start: Pick a day on your calendar to do your "say no" retreat. That might mean calling out of work or moving obligations. Then find a comfy place in your home to reflect.
Right when you wake up, make a list of things you want to say no to in your life. What immediately comes to mind? Name anything obvious you don't want to do. For example, coordinating a big potluck for your book club or making a complicated dish for that dinner party on Saturday.
Then eat some breakfast and get yourself into nature to give yourself some time to think about your list. Maybe take a bike ride or a walk.
After your break, come back to your designated retreat space and build on your list. Add to that initial "say no" list by thinking about your upcoming days, weeks and months. Look at your digital calendar if you need to, but make sure your notifications are turned off, Sylge writes in her book.
Review all your requests, appointments, volunteer work, scheduled phone calls, work and social commitments, and memberships.
Is there anything you've planned that you're dreading? Are there tasks you've given yourself that you don't actually have to do or even want to do?
That might be sitting at a time-consuming hair appointment, hosting a playdate at your house, traveling to spend Thanksgiving with your husband's family or moderating a panel discussion for a work event.
Jot down notes — and if you'd like, reasons why you are saying no to a task.
Take lunch, then spend the afternoon reviewing your list — and take action. It's time to start saying no. You probably won't be able to get to all the nos on your list today, but you can pick a small, easy win, Sylge says. Maybe you just cross the arduous task of planting tulip bulbs off your to-do list … forever. You can just enjoy your neighbor's tulips next spring.
Now, you'll also need to start thinking about the harder nos — the ones that involve saying no to someone you care about or work with.
Sylge says instead of saying no outright, you can try delaying your yes. For example, "I'd love to, but can we plan it for a few weeks later?" You could also suggest alternatives. Instead of cooking for your friends, could you order takeout?
Don't underestimate the power of "crafting a kind decline," Sylge says. It "takes effort, but it saves time in the long run."
