Govt to issue consultation paper on a new AI law in ‘coming weeks’: Ashwini Vaishnaw
Union minister Ashwini Vaishnav said the time has come when the risks of AI have crossed a threshold when we should come up with a law.
Union minister for railways, information and broadcasting, and electronics and information technology Ashwini Vaishnaw on Friday said the government will issue a consultation paper on a new Artificial Intelligence (AI) law “in coming weeks”, saying the risks from the technology have crossed a “threshold” that now demands legislation.
Speaking at the NDTV World Summit in Delhi, Vaishnaw said the proposed regulation will target the harms of AI while keeping humans in control of the technology.
Also read: Rahul Gandhi ignited enthusiasm among youth: Shashi Tharoor after PM Modi's ‘failed product’ remark
“Today the time has come when the risks of AI have crossed a threshold when we should come up with a law,” Vaishnaw said.
“We should come up with a new regulation where the harms from the new technology can be regulated. Having said that, we are already working on it.”
Why the shift on AI matters
The remarks mark a visible shift in the government’s public stance. The IT ministry’s India AI Governance Guidelines, released on November 5, 2025, called for focused amendments to existing laws instead of a standalone AI statute. The ministry’s secretary S Krishnan said in December 2025 that no dedicated AI law was being planned, and a 2023 parliamentary reply under Vaishnaw said the government was not considering a law to regulate AI’s growth.
Also read: TVK-led bloc, DMK walk out of ECI meeting in Tamil Nadu, seek CEC’s resignation
The shift matters because the government has so far argued that existing laws and voluntary norms are enough, a position that critics said left gaps on risks such as autonomous agents and accountability. A consultation paper will be the first formal step towards a statute. Vaishnaw, a BJP leader, did not say when a bill could reach Parliament, and he gave no details on its scope, the regulator or penalties.
Vaishnaw said that two schools of thought on AI exist globally. One argues that the technology should evolve sufficiently before it is regulated. The other, which he described as the European approach, is to “swat” every innovation early, a style he said stifles growth.
“Our bias has always been towards more towards innovation,” Vaishnaw said, adding that the state must “simultaneously” keep citizens safe. The line suggests the proposed law will be framed as a harm-based regulation and not a licensing regime, though the government has not spelt out the design.
The minister argued that no single country can write rules for a borderless technology. “In the digital world, the physical boundaries do not exist,” he said, adding that any initiative “has to be globally aligned”. He pointed to the nuclear industry, where countries sat together and agreed on principles that now govern the sector, as the template for AI.
Vaishnaw said India will sit at that table as one of the “top three or top four AI ecosystems in the world”, along with the other global giants. The race towards innovation, he said, “has to be moderated by safety of human beings”. Some principles, he added, are already established.
Those principles, in his words, are that AI “has to be human first” and “humancentric”. Control over the agents, the models, the outcomes and the processes “has to be in human hands”, he said, and there must be “some equivalent of stopping things if they go out of control”.
The remarks echo concerns about AI agents acting without oversight, though he did not say how such a stopping mechanism will be mandated or who will hold the switch. Those questions are likely to be central to the consultation.
On process, Vaishnaw said the paper will seek inputs from civil society, citizens, industry and other stakeholders. Banks, manufacturers, insurers and service firms are adopting AI rapidly, he said, so there is “a good understanding” of what the technology can deliver and what harm it can do.
“We have discussed a lot with the tech companies,” he said. “Now we need to discuss with the stakeholders who are users of AI.” The shift in focus from developers to users is significant, since sectors such as banking and insurance are where AI errors can hit citizens directly.

PHP, a programming language used to build websites, is at the centre of a major security concern after researchers uncovered two critical flaws that could let hackers take control of vulnerable servers. Called PHP2Shell, the vulnerabilities could let attackers run malicious code on affected systems without needing to log in. Since the vulnerabilities lie in PHP itself rather than individual websites built on it, businesses cannot rely on website-level security measures alone to stay protected. The vulnerabilities affect specific PHP versions, and fixes were released on October 21, 2026. Businesses must now check whether they are running affected versions, install the updates and investigate whether hackers exploited the flaws before the fixes were applied. The discovery story involves both independent research and AI-assisted security work. Security firm Calif credited pseudonymous researcher LCFR with first discovering PHP2Shell and developing a working exploit. Separately, AI company OpenAI said security research firm Calif identified a critical flaw using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, while cybersecurity firm Wiz independently discovered and reported both vulnerabilities. OpenAI's disclosure describes the collaboration that helped prepare fixes before public disclosure. The episode also highlights a growing cybersecurity concern: AI tools are helping researchers uncover complex security flaws, but organisations must be equally agile to fix them. Which Businesses Face The Risk? PHP powers around 70% of websites globally. This highlights the language's reach, but does not mean that 70% of websites are vulnerable. The actual risk depends on the PHP version, server configuration and exposure to attack. The vulnerabilities can allow attackers to run code remotely on affected servers without authentication. Amruta Moktali, chief product officer at Skyflow, a data privacy and security platform, said initial industry reports cited millions of potentially exposed instances because PHP is widely used across websites, content management systems, hosting environments and enterprise applications. For Indian businesses, Moktali said the immediate priority should be internet-facing PHP systems that handle sensitive information. These include systems connected to payment services, customer databases and identity and authentication tools. Small businesses and website operators may face additional challenges if they depend on third-party hosting providers or lack dedicated security teams. They may not know which PHP version their websites use or whether their provider has installed the relevant updates. Sooraj Sathyanarayanan, a cybersecurity researcher and program manager at privacy-focused web browser Brave, said successful exploitation could allow attackers to execute code without logging in or requiring user interaction. Depending on the server’s permissions, this could expose customer data and credentials, enable website changes or allow malware to be installed. However, the level of risk depends on the PHP build and server configuration, so not all installations are equally vulnerable. Legacy systems are another concern, as the flaw occurs within PHP's core engine before an application's own code runs. "One thing organisations must keep in mind with PHP2Shell is that because this flaw triggers inside the core PHP engine before any application code executes, traditional application-level safeguards won't stop it," said Niv Lanyado, security research team lead for PHP at JFrog, a software supply chain security company. He stressed that organisations need visibility into all their systems, particularly older PHP installations that may no longer receive security updates, so they can be patched or isolated. Fixing The Software Is Not Enough The PHP team released fixed versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 and 8.2.35 on October 21. Its official security advisory says there are no complete mitigations and urges users to update. Organisations should first identify where PHP is running across their servers, cloud environments and third-party hosting arrangements. They should then check which installations are affected and confirm that the updated software is active. According to Aditya Narayana K, the cofounder of cybersecurity company focused on AI security, Mirror Security, organisations need a repeatable process to identify vulnerabilities, fix them and verify that the fixes work. He pointed to the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 as a useful guide for managing this process. “Organisations must confirm that patches are active and the vulnerability is no longer reproducible, rather than assuming that applying a patch resolves the risk,” Narayana said. Where immediate patching is not possible, businesses should follow official guidance from PHP and their hosting or software providers. Temporary measures may reduce exposure, but they are not a substitute for a complete fix. Unsupported installations may need to be upgraded or isolated until they can be secured. The incident has also raised questions about whether businesses can keep pace with AI-assisted vulnerability discovery. Sriram Krishnan, a technology investor and former general partner at venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), wrote on X that the PHP disclosure will make the ecosystem safer by finding long-lurking issues. “However, the entire software supply chain will need the muscles to rapidly build and deploy fixes. We might need a lot more public + private partnerships to secure infrastructure across the country.” How Can Businesses Check For A Breach? Patching closes a known vulnerability, but it does not establish whether hackers exploited it before the update was installed. Businesses must investigate their past exposure alongside fixing their systems. According to Narayana of Mirror Security, investigators should identify which systems were exposed and review activity from before patching. This includes checking server logs, unusual system behaviour, unauthorised file changes and suspicious network connections. Organisations should also look for unexpected programs running on their servers or unexplained changes to files and configurations. Security teams can use monitoring tools to bring together information from different systems and identify patterns that may indicate an attack. Sathyanarayanan recommended reviewing activity from at least a week before the October 21 patch release, given that exploitation attempts were reported before public disclosure. Businesses should not assume that installing a fix eliminates the risk of an earlier compromise. If investigators find signs of an attack, they should preserve logs and other evidence, involve their hosting provider or an incident response specialist, and assess whether credentials need to be replaced. Patching alone may not remove malicious software or unauthorised access established before the fix. An attempted attack does not necessarily mean hackers gained access. Equally, the absence of security alerts does not guarantee that a system is safe. Timely patching must go hand in hand with continuous security monitoring, as attackers can move quickly once vulnerability details become public. The PHP2Shell disclosure demonstrates why cybersecurity cannot end with a software update. Businesses need to know what technology they run, fix vulnerabilities quickly and establish whether attackers gained access before the fix was applied. As AI tools make it easier to uncover complex flaws, the ability to investigate, patch and verify systems quickly will become just as important as discovering the vulnerabilities themselves.

Like "being shot out of a cannon" is the closest comparison that driver Susanne Callin can come up with for the extreme motorsport she competes in.
She is a two-time European champion in Top Fuel drag racing - often described as the fastest sport on the planet.
Races begin with a bone-shaking roar, as the world's fastest-accelerating cars leave the starting line, flames bursting out of their exhaust pipes.
The cars surge to more than 300mph (483km/h) in races that last just four seconds, with drivers experiencing more g-force than an astronaut launching into space.
It is the only elite class of motorsport where women frequently beat men to major titles.
Women have won seven out of the past nine European Championships, while, until recently, female US driver Brittany Force held the world speed record in the sport. In comparison, it is 50 years since a woman even competed in a Formula 1 Grand Prix race.
Women account for about 10% of participants across motorsport, and just 4% of elite drivers, according to campaign group More Than Equal. However, they made up 20% of the drivers competing in this year's US and European Top Fuel seasons.
So why is this high-velocity motorsport bucking the trend?
More Than Equal has described drag racing as "the most gender-equal motorsport in the world". Top Fuel is its most extreme form, named in reference to the powerful nitromethane fuel the cars run on.
Races take place on a straight track, just 1,000 feet (305 metres) long. Usually, two cars race each other. The intense g-force hits in the first second of the race, as the cars go from stationary to 100mph, with a second gut punch following as the clutch fully engages about half-way through.
It can look terrifying. The adrenalin rush is "extremely addictive", Swedish driver Callin, aged 43, tells BBC Global Women. Concern over the risks "is always there" she says, but "the safety really does work". Drivers are highly protected and safety precautions have been boosted further after fatal crashes in nitromethane-fuelled cars in 2004 and 2008, with races reduced in length.
Even just watching from the stands is a visceral experience, with vibrations shaking your body and the ground. Spectators are advised to wear ear defenders - the noise is comparable in decibels to standing next to a fighter jet taking off.
The highest official speed ever reached in a Top Fuel drag race is over 346mph, compared to 231mph in a Formula 1 Grand Prix. Brakes alone cannot slow the cars fast enough, so parachutes are deployed from the car's rear at the finish. The abrupt halt is "like someone kicking you in the chest", says Callin. "You lose your breath."
Top Fuel drivers need lightning-fast reactions and the physical endurance to withstand the intense forces. Precision driving skills are crucial as constant tiny adjustments are needed to keep the car on track.
"It has to be instant reactions with everything," says Callin. "By the time you've thought about it, it's too late… You really have to be one with the car."
And drivers need sheer guts. As Callin's rival and friend, 32-year-old Swiss driver Jndia Erbacher, jokingly tells the BBC - it takes "balls".
Callin clinched her second successive European Top Fuel title in September at the Santa Pod drag strip near Northampton. It is the fourth year in a row that a female driver has won the title. Meanwhile in the US, the record-setting Brittany Force won the US championship - run by the National Hot Rod Association (NHRA) - in both 2017 and 2022.
Drag racing is "highly unusual" among motorsports, says Fran Longstaff, chief innovation officer at More Than Equal, which supports and campaigns for women in motorsports.
Seeing women competing and winning in the sport has become "normalised rather than treated as exceptional", she says, including with "sustained success" in Top Fuel.
Research she co-led into why drag racing leads the way for equality in motorsport did not identify physical or biological factors, she says.
Instead, she points to a "continuous stream of visible female role models", as well as the sport's "accessible grassroots structure, junior programmes, open pits and family-oriented, collaborative culture".
In drag racing, points out Callin, women started winning major races "decades and decades ago".
The best known is Shirley Muldowney, dubbed the "first lady" of drag racing. The first woman to gain a Top Fuel licence, Muldowney won the NHRA championship in 1977 and went on to become the first driver to win three titles, with further wins in 1980 and 1982.
She had to battle to be allowed to compete at high levels, and faced hostility at times from other competitors and fans, but is now lauded for her perseverance.
When the BBC spent time with Callin in the pits between races at Santa Pod, surrounded by roaring engines and the smell of burning rubber, she signed autographs for fans - young and old, male and female - as her team prepared her car.
"I never feel I've been underestimated or treated badly for being a woman - never," Callin says.
This is in stark contrast to the experiences of women seeking to enter Formula 1. Young female drivers have spoken about being deliberately pushed off karting tracks by male competitors, and facing sexist comments in person or online.
More Than Equal's research also highlights a close-knit, family-oriented, collaborative culture in drag racing.
Like many top drag racers, Callin is from a racing family. She has been involved since childhood, following in the footsteps of her father and uncle, who both raced competitively.
Similarly, Erbacher's father Urs was a three-time European Top Fuel champion. And Brittany Force is the daughter of John Force, who holds 16 NHRA drag racing titles.
The 300mph motorsport where women keep winning
Watch the full documentary following Susanne Callin as she bids to retain her European Top Fuel title
Female drivers have also shown that success is possible in Top Fuel in the years after having children.
Callin took a break for more than a decade to raise her daughter and stepdaughters. It was when she returned, aged 35, that her career really began to flourish. Similarly, Finnish driver Anita Mäkelä has won the European championship four times – three of them after a six-year break focusing on her children and running her family's chicken farm.
For Callin, racing is ingrained in family life.
Her dad is still part of her team. Her husband, Keith Bartlett - sometimes referred to as the "godfather" of UK drag racing - runs Santa Pod Raceway. Two of their daughters were driving junior dragsters at 80mph before they were old enough to sit a standard driving test. The youngest, Jacqueline, is now 19 and racing in adult classes.
The culture is collaborative, despite fierce competition - evident at last year's championship, when Erbacher offered Callin spare parts after her car was damaged.
"We hate each other at the starting line, but we love each other at the finish line," Erbacher says.
Asked about safety, both Callin and Erbacher talk about having "respect" for the car and the risks.
Over the years, strict procedures and regulations in Top Fuel have evolved to improve safety.
Drivers wear fire-resistant suits and sit in highly protected cockpits. Even after dramatic accidents, drivers in many cases escape relatively unscathed. This includes Callin, who has had two major crashes, suffering a concussion and a bruised collar bone, but no lasting injuries.
She says serious accidents are a "very small percentage". Even so, she is still not sure she would be comfortable if her daughter wanted to race in Top Fuel, with its extreme speeds.
Erbacher says her father initially refused to let her race, but relented when she declared she would do it with or without his help. He now manages her team.
More Than Equal also points out that the financial barriers to participating in drag racing are lower than for some other motorsports.
It takes millions of pounds to reach Formula 1, requiring high levels of sponsorship. Elite drag racing is also expensive, but not on the same scale. At the lowest levels, accessible racing events called "track days" take place, where participants can turn up and drive their own ordinary cars.
In the biggest Top Fuel championships, drivers race for themselves and earn points based on how they perform against their competitors. The European championship consists of four events - two in the UK, and one each in Germany and Sweden - in which each driver takes part in six races. Prize funds are limited, mostly serving as a contribution towards costs.
The US championship is on a larger scale, with 20 events across the country. The NHRA has not published a breakdown of prize money, but according to drag racing website Competition Plus, there is $500,000 (£378,000) for the 2026 winner, and significant pots for winners of individual events throughout the season.
The US, Europe and Australia have all seen female drag racing champions, but in other parts of the world, the sport is less well established, Top Fuel is rare and the picture is more varied. Individual women are breaking barriers across a range of different motorsports, and in some countries female drivers are carving out space in drag racing.
Women have begun to make an impact in Brazil's popular drag racing scene, including Fabiola Dal Bo who has held a category record in recent years. A team in South Africa hosts all-female drag races, while the popular reality TV show The Fastest in Arabic has raised the profile of women racers in the Middle East.
In India, 35-year-old Uvashri Kannadasan Balajeyanthi has clinched victories over male rivals in India's major drag racing series, Valley Run, with wins across three different categories in events from 2022 to 2024.
Known as Octy Girl in reference to the modified Skoda Octavia she first raced in, she tells the BBC she has "mixed feelings" when her achievements are met with surprise: "Why do they have to get shocked? Anyone can drive, right?" But she adds "sometimes I feel proud… I'm breaking the barrier of being in a male-dominated sport".
Back in Europe, however, Callin says being a woman on the drag strip is "super-normal".
She describes winning the European championship two years running as a "massive achievement". And she is already looking towards her next goal: becoming the first person, male or female, to win the title three years in a row.

Severe flooding hits Four Corners region, more expected through the weekend
Looking out a window on Friday afternoon, Devin Neeley saw light, puffy clouds and a blue sky in San Juan County, N.M. The county's public information officer for emergency management called it "surreal."
Meanwhile, brown rainwaters were flooding homes in low-lying areas of the county and forcing sewage into the San Juan River.
"[The sky] belies really the danger that is coming down the river in historic levels," Neeley says. "We have not seen flooding like this in generations."
Neeley says, emergency responders rescued people on their roofs after floodwater inundated their homes. The county is under an emergency declaration and residents in susceptible areas were told to evacuate Thursday afternoon.
"These are communities that have beautiful riverfront places to live," Neeley says. "And unfortunately, that's a problem today."
Rare, heavy rainfall started to hit the Four Corners region — which includes New Mexico, Colorado, Utah and Arizona — on Wednesday.
Since then, severe, brown-colored floodwaters have led to road closures, mandatory evacuations and emergency declarations across the four states.
Thick, brown floodwaters
Areas of southern Utah, southwest Colorado, and the northern parts of Arizona and New Mexico were drenched with rain leading to rapidly rising floodwaters, Thursday and Friday.
In response to a post on X that showed brownish-red floodwaters in Hurricane, Utah, Gov. Spencer Cox, wrote on Thursday: "Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted."
We are closely monitoring the flash flooding in Hurricane. Our hearts are with the families whose homes and livelihoods have been impacted.
Please follow all evacuation orders and local emergency guidance. We’re grateful to the first responders working to keep Utahns safe. https://t.co/8hDQ85T0Xz
— Governor Cox (@GovCox) October 22, 2026
The southern Utah city issued an emergency declaration on Thursday after flooding damaged more than 100 homes and Rvs. People were seen leading horses to safety through ankle-deep water, in a video posted by the National Weather Service.
In Farmington, N.M., at the center of the devastation, Police Chief Steve Hebbe said at a press conference on Friday that "this is singular and this is real."
"So far, we have not had any deaths that is very fortunate, but this is not something that should be played with," Hebbe said.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis declared disaster emergencies for 11 counties. Polis also authorized the use of National Guard members to assist with rescue efforts in southwest Colorado.
The police department for the Navajo Nation, which spans across northeastern Arizona, northwestern New Mexico, and southeastern Utah, said on Thursday that authorities had rescued seven families, 30 people, from their flooded homes. The Hopi Tribe in northeastern Arizona declared a state of emergency on Thursday due to heavy rainfall damaging roads, bridges, homes and other infrastructure.
The Archuleta County Sheriff's office in Colorado warned residents to shelter in place Friday morning, and by the evening had issued an evacuation warning.
The flooding comes after extreme weather hit the Southwest throughout the week. Arizona saw baseball-sized hail and a possible tornado that injured at least one person Wednesday evening.
A record amount of rainfall
The region's mountainous terrain is conducive to flooding. In August, intense flash flooding in the Grand Canyon led to multiple deaths.
Severe thunderstorm warnings started earlier in the week, says Kris Sanders, a meteorologist at the National Weather Service in Grand Junction, Colo. The remnants of Hurricane Trudy, which was active from Oct. 15 to Oct. 18, in the Pacific Ocean formed into a slow-moving low-pressure system that worked its way southwest.
Sanders says a lot of the storms weakened as they came through the region, but the heavy rain did not. Portions of southwest Colorado and southeast Utah saw two to four inches, whereas areas with higher elevations, like the San Juan Mountains, got up to six inches. This caused small creeks and streams and rivers to flood.
"Those rainfall amounts are records in themselves," Sanders says.
While the amount of rainfall is rare, he says, these storms typically happen in the region at this time of year. An event last year caused major flooding in the same spots, "like a carbon copy" of this year, Sanders says.
The threat is not over, he says, and thunderstorm watches are active in many of the same areas through Sunday.
Daniel Swain, a climate scientist with the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, says the severe thunderstorms are fueled by the large amount of moisture in the air. He says that moisture comes from the record-warm waters off parts of the West Coast, which are driven by a strong El Niño event and a preexisting marine heat wave (which he attributes largely to human-caused climate change).
The flooding isn't a surprise, he says, pointing to a prediction he and others made in the spring — that if El Niño materialized according to forecasts, southwestern U.S. could see extreme precipitation events through October.
Now, "that is exactly what we've seen," he says, "because this isn't even the first event this fall."
Neeley, the public information officer in San Juan County, N.M., says his community will be on alert for more damage and safety risks throughout the weekend.
"People are concerned about their life and their welfare and their property," Neeley says. "This is going to be a long term impact to this community,"

A CCTV footage has emerged in the case involving the death of Lucknow businessman Shiva Sharma, showing him with the main accused, model Shraddha Dubey, before the incident. The footage, reportedly recorded at Awadh Green Apartment, also shows Shraddha’s sister, Rashmi, walking down a stairwell ahead of the duo.
The footage captures three people descending the stairs inside the building, with Rashmi walking first, followed closely by Sharma and Shraddha. The video has surfaced as investigators examine the movements of those present at the apartment and the positioning of CCTV cameras on the day of the incident.
Ajay Rai, the owner of a flat in Awadh Green Apartment, has raised questions about the circumstances surrounding Sharma’s death and alleged that Shraddha was aware of the cameras installed in the building.
According to Rai, Shraddha had an aggressive attitude and frequently used abusive language. He claimed that she had objected to his installation of CCTV cameras and allegedly abused him during a dispute before returning to her flat.
Rai also questioned the movements of people inside the apartment on the day of the incident. He claimed that nobody used the stairs that day and that everyone left through the lift. He further alleged that Shraddha knew the first-floor camera locations, including the camera installed towards the balcony.
According to Rai, the rear side of the camera faced the direction from which Sharma reportedly fell, leaving that area outside its view. He added that Shraddha’s flat and his own face the same direction. These claims have not been independently established.
Police To Recreate Fall With Forensic Team
Meanwhile, police will recreate the crime scene with the assistance of a forensic team to investigate whether Sharma died by suicide or was killed.
Before her arrest, Shraddha had posted videos on social media describing Sharma’s death as a suicide. However, Sharma’s mother lodged a police complaint alleging murder, prompting investigators to examine the circumstances of his fall from the fourth floor.
As part of the reconstruction, forensic experts will drop a dummy matching Sharma’s weight and physical build from the fourth floor. The exercise is intended to help determine how a person could have fallen from the building and landed at the spot where Sharma was found.
The team will examine different scenarios, including a person falling independently, being pushed or being forcibly thrown from the height. Experts will analyse the trajectory and distance of the fall, the angle at which the dummy lands and the effect of additional force on its movement.
Investigators will compare the dummy’s landing position with the available evidence to assess whether it is consistent with the possible scenarios. The team will also study the potential injury patterns associated with each scenario.
The findings will be compared with the injuries documented in Sharma’s post-mortem report. The analysis is expected to help investigators assess whether the physical evidence supports any of the possible explanations for his death.

Bavuma epic drags SA back into Test - have they time to beat Australia?
- Published
Second Test, Gqeberha (day three of five)
South Africa 425-9 dec: Bavuma 179, Jansen 85; Boland 5-81
Australia 3-1: Boland 2*; Rabada 1-0
Australia trail by 422 runs
Captain Temba Bavuma dragged South Africa back into their Test series against Australia with a masterful 179 on day three in Gqeberha.
Bavuma, who emerged in the gloom at 12-2 on day one, batted for 552 minutes across three days in making his highest Test score, allowing the Proteas to declare on 425-9 with half an hour to play having been 110-6 earlier on day three.
Kagiso Rabada nicked off Australia opener Nic Maddinson in the first over of Australia's reply to further boost the hosts' cause.
Bavuma's knock was every bit as impressive as Matthew Renshaw's 190 for Australia in their first Test win - arguably more so given the momentum that had built behind Australia since South Africa's batting struggles and the quality of the tourists' attack.
He remained composed in sharing partnerships of 132 with Marco Jansen and 183 with number nine Simon Harmer - the best eighth-wicket partnership in South Africa's Test history.
The century was Bavuma's fifth in Tests - 10 years after his first made him the first Black African to score a Test hundred for the Proteas.
He said it was "definitely" one of his best innings.
"That bowling attack, at least three are in the top 10 of the bowling rankings," he added. "There is a reason why."
More relevant for this series and England's tour to come over Christmas, it was Bavuma's fourth century in 14 Tests as South Africa captain.
He now averages 54.36 as Test skipper, compared with 34.53 across 93 innings before taking the reins. Few can match that improvement.
Should South Africa have declared earlier?
It was Bavuma's dismissal - caught behind off Mitchell Starc - which triggered South Africa's decision to declare with half an hour to go in the day.
They had resisted doing so earlier in the session and when Harmer was bowled by Marnus Labuschagne a ball before the Bavuma wicket.
With the floodlights on and skies dark, conditions were perfect for seam bowling when Australia's reply began. Maddinson was only able to resist four deliveries before nicking to third slip.
The umpires then deemed the light too poor for seam bowling to continue, however, and after three overs of spin with the new ball the players left the field.
Had South Africa declared earlier, Jansen could have bowled in tandem with Rabada in the gloom.
"There was thought of that," Bavuma said. "I was a little hesitant because of the weather.
"If we [had declared] a bit early we would have got one or two more overs. Saying that we got the one we wanted.
"Right now I hope things go our way and we set ourselves to be on the field for the majority of those two days."
After only 42 overs were possible across the first two days, South Africa now have an outside shot at victory over days four and five, ideally by dismissing Australia cheaply and enforcing the follow-on.
"We have given ourselves a chance," Bavuma said.
"There is the other side of the draw but going into [the third Test in] Cape Town whatever the confidence we can get here, being able to put their bowlers on their feet for a considerable amount of time, hopefully that can pay off in the long run."

With the new contribution, the Netherlands reaffirmed its position as a key supporter and strategic partner of WHO and a leading donor of flexible and predictable resources to WHO.
"Amid increasingly complex and connected threats, from pandemics and climate change to conflicts, the Netherlands remains an essential supporter of WHO and global public health," said WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus during the agreement signing.
"The Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport's new contribution reflects the Netherland's commitment to its long partnership with WHO, and its support of the sustainable financing for WHO that Member States have agreed. This will enable WHO to respond quickly to global health challenges, and strengthen public health worldwide, including in the Netherlands."
Dutch Minister of Health, Welfare and Sport Ernst Kuipers added that “the Netherlands values our strong and long-standing relationship with WHO. Given the global challenges we collectively face, and the added value the Netherlands can deliver, we believe this renewed arrangement with long-term flexible funds well represents our commitment to advancing health worldwide. These funds will be used to achieve our shared priorities in the WHO’s General Programme of Work, facilitate the secondment of Dutch experts, and to support the Dutch WHO collaborating centres.”
The Netherlands recently recommitted to its role as a leading voice for global health through its Dutch Global Health Strategy 2023-2030. The strategy aims to strengthen health systems at home and worldwide, better prepare for pandemics and address the impact of climate change on public health.
The Netherlands’ Ministry of Health, Welfare and Sport has provided for many years critical financial and technical support to WHO’s efforts to strengthen health security, improve the capacities of countries to address health emergencies, fight antimicrobial resistance, promote access to medicines, and support food safety, tobacco control and mental health.
The renewed partnership expands the joint work of the Netherlands and WHO into new global health challenges, such as those posed by climate change.
The interconnection between the health of the Earth and human health makes climate change a fundamental threat to decades of progress on health. The joint work of the Netherlands and WHO aims to make healthcare more climate resilient and sustainable while mainstreaming health into internal climate policies.
***
The Netherlands also funds crucial activities in sexual and reproductive health, water and sanitation, mental health in emergencies, emergency preparedness, tuberculosis, One Health, primary health care and antimicrobial resistance, while facilitating cooperation with top Dutch institutions.
Between 2022 and 2023, the Netherlands provided US$ 80 million to WHO, including over US$ 66 million in voluntary contributions.
The Netherlands also contributed over US$ 20 million in flexible and thematic funding to WHO, making it the third-largest flexible contributor to the Organization. Such support allows WHO to be agile and strategic in its efforts to help countries improve the health and well-being of their populations.
See more information on the partnership between the Netherlands and WHO.

Lindsay Powell, who releases records under the name Fielded, has spent most of her career subverting expectations and genre conventions. According to their Bandcamp page, Fielded started as an experimental noise project before growing into something closer to R&B. But from moment one, her take on the genre was restless, relentlessly playing with what R&B even means.
Fielded is obsessed with scammers and unhinged Japanese cyberpunk
Some Kind of Animal, the latest record from Fielded, jumps from slinky R&B, to neo-soul, to industrial funk.
Fielded is obsessed with scammers and unhinged Japanese cyberpunk
Some Kind of Animal, the latest record from Fielded, jumps from slinky R&B, to neo-soul, to industrial funk.
Her first album, Ninety-Thirty-Thirty, includes songs heavily indebted to ’80s synth-pop and features multiple saxophone solos. Boy Angel is a quirky electronic exploration with huge saw-wave synths, jittery percussion, and sky-high vocal stacks. While 2020’s Demisexual Lovelace is a slinkier affair, released on underground hip-hop imprint Backwoodz Studioz and features contributions from Billy Woods and Elucid (Armand Hammer).
Her latest record, Some Kind of Animal, pulls from all of these various versions of Fielded, placing organ-fueled slow jams like “That Bitch” next to a cover of Nine Inch Nails’ “Closer” that has strong 2000s neo-soul vibes, as well as the industrial funk of “Heaven,” which includes a guest verse from Pink Siifu.
We wanted to know what’s behind Fielded’s genre-defying madness.
What is your most indispensable tool?
My most indispensable tool in recording is my Universal Audio Apollo Twin audio interface. I love its ease of function and I love the Universal Audio digital studio plugins. I use them on all of my records during the recording process and beyond. I can mic up and get a professional sound in no time, plus my guitars and synths sound amazing and clear.
What sites do you have pinned to your tab bar?
Right now I have a pirated full-length version of the Japanese cyberpunk film 964 Pinocchio pinned to my tab bar for endless sonic and visual inspiration.
Which tech trend do you wish would go away?
I don’t know if it is a tech trend or a plague, but I deeply wish AI would disappear off of the face of the earth.
What creation are you most proud of?
I am most proud of my latest album Some Kind of Animal, specifically the single of the same title, and thank goddess for that; I’d be bummed if my favorite musical output was in the rearview.
What’s the best piece of advice you’ve ever received?
The best piece of advice I’ve ever received, throughout my whole life, is to be patient. Everything happens in perfect time; there is no reason to be jealous or envious because our journeys are completely our own and everything happens for a reason. What is meant for us will come for us, and what is not meant for us should be metabolized as a lesson that helps us grow and become exactly who we are meant to be.
What is your current obsession?
I am currently obsessed with stories about scammers. All stories about all scammers; big scams, small scams, scams that ended in minor jail time or a blow-out of incredible impact. I love scammers, and I am fascinated by their brains.
What’s the last piece of physical media you bought?
The last piece of physical media I bought was Alissa Bennett’s compilation of essays entitled Taxidermist’s Handbook, full of — you guessed it — stories about scammers (amongst other types of criminals).
What would the tagline for your biopic be?
Freak Today, Freak Tomorrow.

Some social media timelines, more recently, have been flooded with messages and reels promoting lymphatic drainage massage as a wellness and lifestyle option. Glowing tributes to the wonders of getting such a massage from healthy influencers ring a warning bell as non-medical specialists once again try to hijack a therapy as a purely casual lifestyle, aesthetics and weight loss hack. While doctors say facial lymphatic drainage may increase blood circulation and reduce puffiness in the face and give skin a glow, it certainly does not give the body a detox, flushing out toxins, or cause weight loss.
What is the lymphatic system?
The lymphatic system performs a drainage function. As per the National Cancer Institute’s definition, lymph is a “clear, watery fluid that comes from plasma (the liquid part of the blood) that has leaked through the blood capillary walls into the spaces around cells.” Lymph carries white blood cells, nutrients, and other substances throughout the body in lymph vessels. As lymph flows through the lymph vessels, it collects extra fluids, cellular debris, and harmful substances from the tissues and is filtered by lymph nodes. The filtered lymph returns to the bloodstream to help maintain fluid balance in the body and immune health. When this process is disrupted then, lymph fluid collects in your arms, legs, ankles or other parts of your body, making them swell.
According to the Cleveland Clinic, “lymphatic drainage massage is a gentle form of massage used to relieve inflammation related to lymphoedema,” which is a swelling of the lymph nodes that could occur as a common side effect of many health conditions. It is also said to be pretty common among people recovering from some cancer treatments, including breast cancer surgery, because several lymph nodes may have to be removed during the process. Other surgical interventions that warrant removal of lymph nodes might also cause inflammation, and there on, requiring lymphatic drainage.
Those suffering from such oedema are often referred to a therapeutic masseur who will use the lymphatic drainage technique to move lymph fluid from the tissues into the lymph nodes, thus easing the swelling.
When does one require the massage
Apart from post-therapeutic or surgical sessions, the following health conditions may also cause lymphoedema - chronic venous insufficiency, fibromyalgia, injury, lipoedema and rheumatoid arthritis. A congested lymph system may be gleaned from the following symptoms, according to the Cleveland clinic: bloating, brain fog, chronic sinus infections, fatigue, headaches, puffy, swollen ankles or hands, skin conditions such as acne, dryness or rashes, or a more tell-tale swollen lymph nodes in the neck.
A cosmetic facial massage is done primarily to restore glow to the skin.
How is a lymphatic drainage performed?
While recommending the services of a health care provider, the Cleveland clinic describes the massage as using light pressure and strategic massage techniques to prepare and clear the blocks in the lymphatic system. It begins with a massage to stimulate the areas of your body that house lymph nodes – armpits, neck, groin. Following this, the professional will attempt to coax the excess lymph fluid from your swollen tissues toward your lymph nodes, where the lymph can reabsorb it and send it back to the heart.
What are the benefits and risks?
A properly-done lymphatic massage could, over sessions, possibly reduce swelling and clear up clogs in the lymphatic drainage and reactivate absorption by the nodes. As such, it can provide relief and improve immune activity. While the risks from a lymph massage are few, therapists usually avoid doing it for people who have blood clots, or deep vein thrombosis, heart disease, and cellulitis. They also are advised to avoid massaging areas over cancerous tissues or skin that has been damaged during radiation. Some people might also suffer from fatigue, headaches and nausea, the Cleveland Clinic advisory points out, but a healthcare provider may be able to suggest measures to relieve that.
However, the Clinic also adds that while the benefits of a lymphatic drain massage could be valuable, “it’s not right for everyone” adding that it would be best to speak to a health care provider first.

This decade has been missing its big-impact midterm
Given all that's happened in American politics since 2019, it may be hard to believe there's been anything missing.
But the decade of the 2020s has yet to see a midterm that mattered much — or that ranked among the impact midterms of past decades.
That sets the 2020s apart, as every other decade over the past hundred years has produced at least one midterm that made a big difference in Congress and in national politics more broadly.
These big-impact midterms have also shifted power in the statehouses, often signaling changes in state and national political landscapes that have mattered and lasted.
Midterms do not attract the same level of voter participation or voter interest as presidential elections. When the White House is not at stake, "low propensity voters" tend to tune out. Overall vote totals slide by about one-third.
But those voters who show up for midterms elect just as many members of Congress and fill just as many state legislative seats as voters in presidential years. Moreover, midterm voters determine about two-thirds of the nation's governorships.
The big midterms have tended to come in presidents' second terms, when their popularity and political energy may be waning. And just because a president is not on the ballot does not mean he's irrelevant. Historically, each president's detractors have seen midterms as an opportunity, while his supporters have often been complacent — or at least less motivated.
All this contributes to the general expectation that the midterms arriving Nov. 3 will be important, and perhaps momentous.
Flexing midterm muscles
Because this is a decade with three presidential cycles (2020, 2024 and 2028), it is also a decade with just two midterms. One went by in 2022. Some expected at the time that a "big red wave" would sweep then-President Biden's majorities out of Congress.
It did not happen. Democrats held on in the Senate, and the House shifted from barely Democratic to barely Republican. That did bring an end to House Speaker Nancy Pelosi's second (and last) turn with the Big Gavel. But the GOP would spend much of the next two years struggling to unite behind a speaker of their own.
That's a far cry from the big midterms that have at times rivaled presidential elections for responding to the mood of the times and rearranging the landscape.
If we take the last hundred years as our sample, we can start with the midterms that followed the Wall Street "Crash of 1929." That financial panic set off a sequence of events that would be called the Great Depression, and the collateral damage included the closing of an era of Republican dominance in Washington.
That era ended with the midterms of 1930, which cost the GOP eight Senate seats and 52 seats in the House in November 1930. Although the GOP initially retained small majorities in both chambers, they lost it in the House with the results of a few special elections early in 1931.
The Senate remained nominally Republican but featured a working majority of Democrats and progressive Republicans. A page had been turned, and Democrats would take control outright in 1932 and hold that majority through World War II.
After that war had ended, the period of Democratic hegemony under President Franklin Roosevelt also ended, and abruptly, with the results of the midterm of 1946.
Pendulum swings both ways
Republican numbers in Congress had fallen so far in the FDR years (below 100 at one point in the 435-seat House) that it seemed impossible for them to return to power. But in 1946 they stormed back to majority control of both House and Senate in a single midterm cycle.
Midterms have continued to serve as political regulators in the generations since. Dwight Eisenhower won two landslide elections as president in the 1950s, but he lost the House in 1954 and needed the vice president to break ties in the Senate.
In his second term, the re-elected "Ike" did not control Capitol Hill, and in the 1958 midterms saw his party drop to just 35 seats in the Senate.
The Senate Democrats first elected in 1958 established a critical mass that would later drive the bipartisan super-majorities needed to break the filibuster and pass the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and the Voting Rights Act of 1965.
In the same era, Democrats in Congress enacted a raft of social programs that would become part of the language, such as Medicare and Medicaid. It was all part of President Lyndon Johnson's "Great Society" program.
What goes up …
But by the midterm year of 1966, much of the energy from LBJ's landslide election in 1964 had been expended — and much more had been siphoned off by his escalation of the war in Vietnam.
Right on time, the midterm arrived, and while the Democrats only took a haircut in the Senate elections they lost a painful 47 seats to the GOP in the House. It gave the party a new lease on life and encouraged its new emphasis on winning in the South. The redirection would guide the party's 1968 presidential candidate, Richard Nixon, and remain a focus for the onetime "Party of Lincoln" for decades to come.
Also in the midterm of 1966, out on the West Coast, a first-time candidate named Ronald Reagan won the governorship of California. People were starting to use the term "Sunbelt."
Yet another midterm correction
But what the midterms of 1966 gave the GOP, the midterms of 1974 would largely take away. Nixon had been elected president in 1968, pursuing what was called a Southern Strategy, and was reelected in a resounding 49-state landslide in 1972.
But by 1974 it had all gone the other way for Nixon. The "Watergate" scandals emerged from his 1972 campaign's use of burglary and electronic surveillance among other unsavory tactics. An attempt to cover it all up blew back on the White House and forced Nixon to resign on the brink of impeachment in August of 1974 – just three months before the midterm for his second term.
The result was a crushing defeat for the GOP, the loss of 48 seats in the House and several more in the Senate (where the Democrats already had more than 60 votes).
While it is tempting to attribute these losses to Nixon's downfall, the country had — to some extent — rallied behind his vice president and successor, Gerald R. Ford. The underlying vulnerability of the GOP was the state of the economy, which was suffering from inflation and the hangover from the oil embargo of 1973 by Arab members of OPEC, the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries.
That embargo, a side effect of the Arab-Israeli "Yom Kippur War" of 1973, temporarily raised the price of crude oil from $3 to $12 and introduced Americans to the phrases "oil shock" and "energy crisis."
Reagan rises and falls
Reagan became the dominant political personality of the 1980s, defeating incumbent President Jimmy Carter in 1980 and winning a 49-state landslide reelection in 1984. He was able to carry in a majority for Republicans in the Senate and establish a kind of working majority in the House with the aid of conservative Democrats in that chamber.
On the strength of those elections, restrained only marginally by the midterm elections of 1982, Reagan began his second term on top of the world. But he soon learned how hard that height can be to hold. As he neared his second midterm, Democrats were on the march nationally and restoring their strength in the more populous Southern states.
In 1986, Democrats defeated six GOP senators who had been elected with Reagan in 1980. The net gain of eight Senate seats gave them a 55-45 majority. In the session of Congress that followed, the Senate would override Reagan's veto of a highway bill and reject his nomination of Robert Bork to the Supreme Court. Reagan was a spent force.
Yet more dramatic reversals to come
Reagan was able to see his vice president, George H.W. Bush, take the White House in 1988, but the party's hopes for momentum into the 1990 midterms were largely unfulfilled. The presidency was also lost in 1992, when Democrat Bill Clinton won a three-way race with just 43% of the popular vote, defeating Bush and independent candidate H. Ross Perot.
Clinton's lack of a majority and list of frustrations in his first term set the stage for a bruising first midterm election in 1994. But what came was beyond bruising. Republicans stormed to their first majority in the House (54 seats net) in 40 years and recaptured the Senate with eight new seats there as well.
The new GOP speaker, Newt Gingrich of Georgia, was a hard-driving partisan who had portrayed the chamber as a House of Ill Repute, the title of a book he and other House Republicans had published.
The use of a "Contract with America" theme promised lower taxes, less corruption and a healthier economy in a compact agenda that had voter appeal as well.
Gingrich explicitly rejected the go-along-get-along attitude of previous GOP leaders in the House and advocated confrontation. The strategy proved less fruitful once he had the Big Gavel, however, and Gingrich spent much of his time as speaker making deals with Clinton. Internal dissatisfaction with him forced him out late in 1998.
Mood swings in the 2000s
In the new century that followed, parties have continued to prosper when their presidential candidates win and give ground in the midterms. George W. Bush was an exception as the president after the terror attacks of September 2001. In his first midterm the following year, theGOP made gains across the board.
But the larger dynamic caught up to him in 2006, when he and his party took what he called "a thumpin'" in elections at all levels. Bush had initially gained popularity with his "War on Terror" and won a second term. But thereafter, his invasion of Iraq had become an albatross. And in 2006 he paid the historic price, losing both his party majorities in the House and Senate. The new majority in the House made Pelosi the first woman speaker in history.
That created an atmosphere of optimism for Democrats, who elected Barack Obama president in 2008 and gave him majorities in the House and Senate (the latter briefly reaching 60 seats). But Obama felt the sting of the midterms early — much as Clinton had. Republicans in 2010 capitalized on an economy still experiencing the recession that had aided Obama's win in 2008. The GOP also capitalized on fears and confusion surrounding the enactment of the Affordable Care Act, or "Obamacare," in 2010.
Echoing his predecessor, Obama called this setback "a shellacking," and settled in to work with a much diminished Senate majority and a Republican-dominated House under Speaker John Boehner.
Obama managed to thread the needle well enough to win a second term for himself in 2012, but the House remained Republican and the Senate followed suit in Obama's second midterm election in 2014.
That second midterm revealed continuing GOP strength across the South and Midwest and to some degree augured the Electoral College majorities that would make Donald J. Trump president in 2016 and 2024.
If the 2020s are to have a midterm with the kind of impact others have had, roughly once a decade for a century, the last opportunity for that to happen is Nov. 3.
If the once-a-decade rhythm has any rationale, in fact, the pressure for a meaningful midterm ought to be building substantially. And in fact most pollsters, pundits and other prognosticators now predict Democrats could flip control of the House and even the Senate as well.
Just as in the previous 10 cycles, the current cycle combines economic concerns (including energy prices) and negative stories about incumbents in various offices. It is the party perceived as being in power that is exposed in a midterm, and it pays a price when voters perceive that party to have lost its mandate — or at least its momentum.

The United States and Israel are preparing for possible renewed attacks on Iran, with military operations potentially beginning before next week's Israeli elections, according to senior Iranian officials and a US official cited by Drop Site. However, the White House has denied plans to attack Iran before the US midterm elections.
The reported preparations come as Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a challenging political contest and US President Donald Trump grapples with historically low approval ratings ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Reports in the Israeli press have suggested that Netanyahu is seeking to use the standoff with Iran to his political advantage.
A senior Iranian official told Drop Site that Tehran's internal intelligence assessment indicated a high likelihood of large-scale bombing beginning before Tuesday's Israeli elections. The official, who was not authorised to speak publicly, said negotiations had stalled because Trump had not acted on Iran's proposed package to end the war.
"Trump has sat on Iran’s proposed package for ending the war, and negotiations have stalled," the official said. 
"Contrary to the show he is putting on, Trump has no clear or actionable plan for [ending] the war with Iran. This has been the cause of a diplomatic deadlock."
The official warned against underestimating Iran's military capabilities, claiming, "Should another war against Iran begin, given our knowledge of the patterns of American force deployment in the countries of the region, their casualty figures will be ten times higher."
The White House rejected the prospect of an imminent attack. "The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections," White House Principal Deputy Press Secretary Anna Kelly said in a statement to Drop Site.
US military assets move towards the region
A US official told Drop Site that military assets were being rapidly moved into position ahead of a possible order from Trump to resume operations. The official identified US Central Command chief Gen. Bradley Cooper as among those pushing for renewed attacks.
"CENTCOM is putting all the pieces into place to renew major combat operations," the official said. While expressing doubt that a new offensive would begin before the Israeli elections, the official added, "We did start Epic Fury without all our assets in place."
The USS Theodore Roosevelt aircraft carrier and the 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit are heading to the Middle East, bringing approximately 10,000 additional sailors and Marines to the region. The Roosevelt departed Japan on Monday and could arrive by the end of next week, ahead of its initially expected deployment in late November. It is expected to join the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington, both currently in the Arabian Sea.
Although the US official described the likelihood of renewed American and Israeli attacks as high, the official said Trump had repeatedly approached the threshold of military action before backing down.
"Trump has backed off major combat operations against Iran or the Houthis seven times since July," the official said, referring to Ansarallah, which launched a major offensive against Saudi-backed groups in Yemen. "At the last minute, he calls it off."
Trump signals possibility of another operation
Meanwhile, Trump said on Friday that the US could launch another military operation against Iran as the war approaches its eight-month mark. Rising fuel prices have added pressure ahead of the midterm elections.
"We may do another little Epic Fury," Trump told a rally in Florida, referring to the US military's codename for the war. He did not elaborate.
Earlier in the day, Trump said the US could end the war quickly but questioned whether Washington should pursue a swift conclusion or allow the conflict to wind down gradually. He has offered shifting goals and timelines for the war and said in recent campaign remarks that it would end soon, "one way or the other".
Trump had said earlier this month that the US would not attack Iran before the November 3 elections, which will determine control of Congress, where his Republican Party holds narrow majorities in both chambers.
Netanyahu threatens pre-emptive action
Netanyahu said on Wednesday that Iran was actively pursuing the development of a nuclear weapon, though he did not provide evidence for the claim. He also said he had directed the Israeli military to prepare for pre-emptive action.
"The Iranian regime still has not learned its lesson. Mojtaba Khamenei decided to follow in his father’s footsteps. He has taken off the safety, and Iran is once again trying to develop its weapons of death," Netanyahu said.
"There is only one way to remove this threat once and for all, to topple the regime in Iran, and that is my directive to the IDF, the Mossad and the security agencies," he added.
Iran warns of wider retaliation
Iran's top security official, Gen. Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the country's Supreme National Security Council and personal representative of Supreme Leader Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, said Tehran retained the capacity to launch missiles and drones against US assets across the region if hostilities resumed. He warned that Iran would also expand its range of targets.
"If the question is whether Iran still has the ability to continue missile and drone operations, the answer is yes," Rezaei told Drop Site in an exclusive written interview. "The United States has valuable assets in the region. In the event of war, cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could also come within range. If the conflict begins again, we will have a broader plan."
"Everyone must understand that action against Iran carries a cost," he added. "If diplomacy can bring about that understanding, we prefer diplomacy. But if the war continues, Iran has the tools it needs to keep responding."
The senior Iranian official said Tehran believes Israel would launch the initial strikes, targeting Iran's newly deployed air defence systems to clear the way for US bombers. The US would then likely target Iran's southern defence systems along the Strait of Hormuz and could attempt to seize an island off the Iranian mainland following heavy bombing.
The official also suggested that Trump might seek a limited strike on an underground Iranian nuclear facility, such as Pickaxe Mountain, and present it as a decisive victory.
"Trump is flat-out lying about Iran’s nuclear program," the official said.
The US and Israel launched attacks on Iran on February 28, prompting Tehran to retaliate with strikes on Israel and Gulf states hosting US military bases. The conflict has driven up global oil and gas prices, while US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions.

High health costs squeeze workers, even if you have good insurance through a job
Joseph Babbitt of Springfield, Mo. has a pretty good deal when it comes to health insurance. He works as a senior financial controller for West Plains Veterinary Supply, which employs about 50 people and distributes pet food, toys and vet supplies across the region.
Like about 157 million Americans, Babbitt gets insurance through his job. Unlike most Americans, his job has exceptionally generous benefits. "Our owners are very nice — they give all of our employees health care and they pay for it," he says. The company offers several different plan options and covers most or all of the monthly premium cost.
So why, even with free premiums, does it still feel like health costs are way too expensive? "Everybody talks about health care and how much it's costing them," says Babbitt. He explains that even without monthly premiums, a high deductible can be brutal — that's the amount the patient has to spend out-of-pocket before the insurance company starts paying for doctors visits and procedures, etc.
Now age 60, he remembers a time when it wasn't so bad. "Back in the '90s, our deductibles were $250 [or] $500 — now they're $5,000," he says. "That seems like a lot."
"We are the only country on our planet that forces people into bankruptcy because they get sick," he adds.
The cost of a new car, every year
Health care costs are rising fast in the U.S., and even workers with solid health care benefits through work are feeling it, according to an annual survey of nearly 2,000 employers about their health benefits. The report was published Thursday by KFF, a nonpartisan health research organization.
"The average health insurance premium for a family of four is now $28,000, which is just a ton of money," says Matthew Rae, associate director for the Health Care Marketplace Program at KFF. "It's basically the cost of a new car every year just to keep a family of four insured." Of that total for family premiums, workers pay about $7,000 per year on average and employers pay the rest.
A glimmer of positivity is that the costs for plans isn't growing as fast as it has in years past, he explains. "We're seeing a 5% increase in family health insurance premiums, which continues a period of modest growth," he says. That increase is roughly on par with worker wages and inflation.
However, "a 5% increase on a big number is still a lot of money," Rae points out. Plus, the growth for the portion of the premium costs that workers pay was 9%. "If this is the beginning of a shift of costs onto workers, that would be a big deal in terms of affordability," he says.
"We are asking people to chip in a lot of money," Rae adds. "Many people are committing a big chunk of their income to health insurance."
The uninsured rate is rising
Another report published Thursday demonstrates the way these high costs affect people's health. The survey, conducted every two years by the Commonwealth Fund, a nonprofit foundation that supports independent research, is entitled "The State of Health Insurance Coverage in 2026."
Even for workers fortunate enough to have health benefits, "about 43% of them said that they didn't get health care because of cost over the past year, and about 31% reported that they had medical debt," says Sara Collins, lead author of the report.
Another key finding was that the overall uninsured rate rose in the last two years. Collins says that's significant but not surprising, because of federal policy decisions like letting extra federal subsidies for people enrolled in Affordable Care Act plans expire, and people losing Medicaid after the pandemic emergency ended.
Federal data shows millions of people have lost health coverage already from either Medicaid or the ACA marketplaces. When work requirements take effect next year, millions more people are projected to lose Medicaid.
"There is a, I think, a strong feeling across the country that something probably does need to be done to the situation that people are facing in their health and health insurance — both on the cost side and then also on these coverage losses," Collins says.
"We asked people whether the federal government has a responsibility to ensure that all Americans have coverage and nearly three quarters said yes to that — that included about 45% of Republicans, 93% of Democrats and 76% of independents."

Quentin Tarantino surprised the crowd during a Q&A and screening of his 10-time Oscar-nominated Once Upon a Time in Hollywood on Friday night at AFI Fest in Los Angeles by screening the first 17 minutes of its sequel The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.
It marks the first public look at the film, a follow-up to Hollywood that Tarantino scripted and David Fincher directed. Brad Pitt revises his Oscar-winning role as Booth, a stuntman and sidekick to Leonardo DiCaprio’s Rick Dalton in the original 2019 film.
Netflix is gearing up for the Cliff Booth theatrical release November 25 in Imax before hitting the streamer beginning December 23.
Watch on Deadline
“Well, I could talk a little bit about The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, or I could show you the first 17 minutes,” Tarantino said at the end of his special-event Q&A session at the TCL Chinese Theatre in Hollywood. He had just been asked about the film and how it came about, and if he had anything else to say before the conversation wrapped.
He then stood up as the crowd began to figure out what was coming.
Here’s the moment:
Cliff Booth fast-forwards to 1977 from the original film’s 1969 timeline. The new logline: Los Angeles no longer needs a hippie-slaying stuntman the way it did. But Hollywood will always have problems, problems that can only be solved by someone with Cliff’s unique (occasionally extralegal) abilities. When he’s not earning his keep bartending or as a projectionist, Cliff Booth is a fixer — solving situations for Hollywood’s great and, sometimes, not so good.
The pic also stars Elizabeth Debicki, Scott Caan, Carla Gugino, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II, Peter Weller, Matt Groove, JB Tadena, Corey Fogelmanis and Karren Karagulian.
Buzz for the film has been building since it was announced in 2024 that Pitt and Fincher were teaming on the project that Tarantino originally wanted to direct. Seven missing after multi-storey building collapses in Kenya's capital
- Published
A search and rescue effort is under way to find seven people feared trapped under rubble after a building collapsed in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi.
Dramatic footage shows the bottom floor of the block, thought to have been 16 or 18 storeys, giving way before the rest of the building crumples, sending a plume of dust into the surrounding streets.
Dozens of builders had been working on the upper floors when it collapsed, but managed to emerge largely unscathed. Those missing were thought to have been in shops that had opened at the base of the building.
The incident has raised fresh concerns about construction standards and regulations in Kenya.
The block was under construction when it collapsed on Friday afternoon, with footage showing scaffolding still wrapped around the outside of the building. Officials said 11 shops had already opened on the bottom floors.
Interior ministry official Kipchumba Murkomen said 66 of the 67 construction workers in the building at the time had been able to get out unharmed, while the other had suffered injuries that were not life-threatening.
Images from the scene, in Nairobi's Eastleigh area, show the concrete floors of the building piled on top of one another, as rescue workers saw through metal to get to those believed to have been stuck underneath.
Rescue efforts have been complicated by concerns that excavation using diggers could limit the supply of air to those trapped, prompting emergency responders to cease using them, according to the Daily Nation newspaper.
Questions have emerged about why the building suddenly collapsed and whether it met planning regulations.
Kenya's National Construction Authority said in a statement that it had identified the company behind the development, as well as the architect and structural engineer, but did not say whether the site had been inspected before Friday.
Nairobi Governor Sakaja Johnson told local media that the owners of the building did not have the required paperwork for the building to be occupied.
He urged the national government to give local authorities greater powers to penalise "developers who disregard approved building plans and safety standards".
Building collapses are not uncommon in Nairobi, with poor construction or improper planning often cited as contributing factors.
